THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
JAZZ ORAL HISTORY PROJECT
BILL COLEMAN MANUSCRIPT

I was born in a place called CENTERVILLE, Kentucky, U.S.A., but my passport says that I was born in PARIS, KY, and the reason is that CENTERVILLE IS an BOURBON County and there was no court house, jail, police, or any one that represented the law. So the births were recorded in PARIS which was the ruling center of BOURBON County.

I was named WILLIAM JOHNSON COLEMAN, WILLIAM JOHNSON was the name of my grandfather on my mother's side. My father's name was ROBERT HENRY COLEMAN and most people called him HENRY. My Mother's name was ROBERTA JOHNSON. Dad had three brothers: JOHN, the eldest, HOWARD and ERNEST. Also one sister named AMANDA, but she was married to a Mr. SAM SPARKS when I was old enough to know her. My mother had three brothers. [ISIAH] ISIAH, WILLIS and PETER JOHNSON, and one sister named SARAH who was married to a Mr. CHENAULT. I never knew my father's father or my mother's mother.(grandparents).

I must have been 4 years old when I started to realise certain things. CENTERVILLE was a village with a population of 450 people, one Baptist Church, one Episcopalian Church, one barbor shop for men, a general store that sold clothing, farm ware and was also the post office, and had the only public telephone in the village.

The population was mostly negro, but the general store, the blacksmith shop, and the thrasher machine were owned by white people, and the village doctor for everybody was white. The village was beautiful because some part of it was on a hill and the houses were all built of wood except the Baptist Church, which was built with bricks. Uncle Coleman had built many of the houses as he was a Jack of all trades, and good at all of them. He built the school and his own house which was the largest in the village.

I also remember that my grand-mother Coleman lived in a 4-room log cabin. Any house built of logs was a cabin and this was the only one in Centerville. I never knew if it was Uncle John that built it.

All around Centerville were farms, and some of them belonging to one family which would run as far as the eye could see. The two largest farms were owned by the Fergusons and the Hagens. The Fergusons' land was on the Lexington and Georgetown Road and the Hagen's farm was on the Lexington Road which ran through Centerville. I loved ponies, and there were thousands of them on these two farms.

Uncle John was a paperhanger. He also put electricity in his house with some system that he bought from Sears and Roebucks mail order house in Chicago. He was the only person to have electricity in the village. He was also the professor of the school, which had studies from the 1st to the 8th grade, all in one room. He was a hard man on children and anyone else who crossed him.

He was also a kind man and would do anything in his power to help someone in trouble. If a kid did something wrong in school, he was sent out to get a switch to be whipped with, and if he didn't bring in a good strong one, Uncle John would send him back for another one. He had whipped his own children just as hard as anyone else and no one was a teacher's pet with him.

A few white people lived in Centerville, but most of the white men seen around the general store were farmers who lived outside the village. Most of the negro men worked on the surrounding farms and some worked on the railroad which ran from Paris to Georgetown, a distance of 19 miles. Centerville is 7 miles from Paris and 17 miles from Lexington, Ky., and like many towns and cities that I was to know about, and visit in later years, Centerville had its music. My father played the snare drum in the hometown band, my Uncle Ernest played the tuba and on rehearsal nights, he would pass our house blowing on his brass tuba as if he was already at the rehearsal. These "get-togethers" took place in the summer on the front lawn, of my Uncle Coleman's home, and besides being the professor of the school, Uncle John played a cornet. He and his friends played music for picnics mostly, because Centerville was only a country place of about two hundred families and there was nothing to make a parade for. They only played music for their own enjoyment. I remember that they were proud of the fact that they could read enough music to play marches by Sousa and so forth. There was a local hall for dances, but on these occasions, bands were brought in specially from Lexington or Paris, [Ky., Besides improvising on popular Rag Time and Blues, these dance bands also played Waltzes.

About two years later, my mother decided to come back to Cincinnati and live with an aunt whose name was Mary. Aunt Mary smoked a pipe as did sommany women from the South. Kentucky is not what is called the deep South but the problems of the Negro were the same as those that existed in any of the other Southern states. I mentioned this because I mentioned my Aunt Mary smoking a pipe, as I said before most women from the South smoked pipes,even the white ones. Aunt Mary was also a great beer drinker. There was a saloon very near the house, and she used to send me to get a bucket of beer for her. My mother drank some, but not half as much as my aunt. She would also eat Limburger cheese and cracker sandwiches, which I also enjoyed. She used to try and make me drink beer, but I did not like the taste of it. I did not mind going for the beer, and although I was too young to go into the saloon, I would stick the bucket under the swinging doors and the barman would see it and

and take it, fill it up for 5 cents, give it back to me under the swinging doors and also give me a handful of pretzels. I learned to do many useful things that have been very helpful to me in later years when we lived with my Aunt Mary. A child could not be lazy at the age of 8 years around her. So I had to sweep the floors, scrub the front and back steps every Saturday because we lived on the second floor. I also had to scrub and whiten the three front steps that led into the hall and I remember the product I used to whiten those steps, and was called Bom Ami.

Aunt Mary ruled me more so than my mother did and on Sunday afternoon, I was allowed to put on my special Sunday clothes and sit on the nice clean steps, if the weather was permissable, in the summer time.

One Sunday, there was a parade passing on 9th street, and the bands interested me to the point where I decided to follow one, and must have been miles away from home when I decided I had better return. I had never been so far away from those front steps alone and did not know where I was. But I remembered the streets that I had followed the band, and eventually arrived home, happy to discover that I had not been missed by my mother and Aunt Mary. That was a beautiful Sunday, because I heard some music, something on the style of what I used to hear on the lawn of Uncle John's in Centerville.

Looking back, I realize now that that kind of parade music was a basis for Jazz. That was how many Jazz players learned the harmonic connections. The rhythm came from the Churches. When I was about twelve years old, there used to be meetings of the "Holy Rollies", In the yard of a big house right on the corner near where we lived. They used to clap their hands, and the preacher was a wonderful tap dancer. He could really whip up the congregation with his rhythm. My mother was a Baptist, and we were all made to go to meetings every Sunday. And there was a certain sister who liked to "get happy" while the Preacher was preaching; once she started, then they would all get with it and throw their hands out, so that you would think that they were going to knock your head off if you were sitting next to them. It was like the Indians going on the war-path. It used to scare me at the time, but now I realize that what went on in those Churches helped the coloured musicians to 'let go' emotionally. There are many wonderful white musicians but if you take a good negro band like Count Basie, it has a natural emotion in the way it plays. I believe we learnt that emotion in the Churches.

I was going to school on 9th Street which was near where I lived and I had a playmate who was blond and Irish. In Kentucky the white and negro children never played together. But that was not the case in Cincinnati because the schools were mixed at that time. This boy lived near me on 9th Street and his mother worked in a laundry a few blocks up from the school and she used to give us pennies now and then to buy candy. We used to fight with two Jewish boys who were twins and whose names I remember being Ike and Mike Tennenbaum. When we ever caught one of the twins alone, my buddy and I would give him a beating because that's what they did to us whenever they were together and caught one of us alone.

Cincinnati was like New Orleans in many ways because the same boats that sailed up and down the Ohio river from New Orleans to Kansas City all stopped in Cincinnati which also had a levee. The ways and means of making a living in certain parts of Cincinnati from the levee up to certain streets was exactly like New Orleans, because there were saloons, gambling and prostitutes. The streets where the exciment took place were George Street from Mound to Central Avenue, 6th Street from Mound to John Street, Carlisle Avenue from Mound to Plum Street, John Street from the levee up to 5th Street, and on a few side streets running from the levee up.

When I was 12 years old my mother and father had arranged their differences and the family was back together again living on Barr Street. Often my brother Robert and I would go walking on George Street, Carlisle Avenue or John Street to look at what we called the pretty ladies. The prostitutes on some of the streets would sit in the windows of the house and call the men and they all had make-up which other women did not wear. Some stood in doorways and others on the streets. George Street was the district of the white prostitutes and Carlisle Avenue from Central Avenue to Plum Street and the other streets was where the negro prostitutes and their pimps held sway.

Another reason I would walk around those districts sometimes, one of the pretty ladies would want an errand done and they would always give a good tip, as they could not come out and needed something special from a store and I happened to be passing at the time, it was almost certain that I would get
a quarter for doing an errand and I could do many things with a quarter in those days when you could get a bag full of candy for two kids for 5 cents.

Every chance I had, which was quite often, I would go to a movie where I would stay to see the films 2 or 3 times. The movie houses were called Nickel-Odeons because five cents is also known as a nickel and it cost only 5 cents admission to see two or three comedy films and a feature film of 5 reels. There was an electric piano with a drum attachment in the Nickel-Odeons and most of the films were westerns better known as cowboy films.

Most of the Nickel Odeons were on 5th Street. In one theatre that was in the prominent negro district on 5th Street, they had a woman pianist named Amanda Randolph who played for the films, and there were also vaudeville shows [Theater Owners Booking Association] of a circuit called T.O.B.A.^ I learned that the show people said that T.O.B.A., which was an agency, was called "tough on black actors", and I supposed it must have been because of the conditions they had to suffer in going from place to place. Most of these shows had their own musicians and one I remember was quite famous. It was called Drake and Walker. Amanda Randolph was a very capable pianist and although I did not know music, I knew when it was well played and Amanda was the first woman I ever heard that played like a man.

Drake, of Drake and Walker Show, was a small man who had one leg shorter than the other and he played cornet and had one of those long coach horns which had three valves like the cornet and the bell of the horn was about two or three feet long. I did not know anything about jazz or styles but Drake and his band sounded good to me and it was different from the way the parade bands played. Of course he did not have as many musicians as a brass band which is the name for a parade band. He came often to this theatre which was called the Lincoln Theatre.

Then another cornet player came to Cincinnati from New Orleans and he used to advertise for the Lincoln Theatre by playing on a wagon which was pulled around town by a horse, and this fellow used to play alone. I would follow him for blocks whenever he came on the street where I lived.

Some other musical events used to happen on my street. Were were living on Kenyon Avenue and just across the street from my house, there were two brothers whose family name was Johnson. The oldest must have been about 22 and the other 18 years old and they both played piano. During the summer they had their front door open and would play for hours. I used to sit on their steps and listen to them and was very unhappy when my mother would call me to run an errand for her.

Other people used to stop and listen to these two young men play. The oldest one was better than the younger one and I suppose the reason was that he had more experience, but the younger one was no amateur although I found out that they did not read music. There were many pianists in those days that did not read music but had a natural talent for that instrument. They made their living playing for parties most of the time.

Another event that used to take place on Kenyon Avenue, was a jug band that used to come around often and play in the streets and pass around a hat for people to put money in. There was a harmonica player, a big glass jug that one fellow would blow in and make it sound like a bass, and a violin player named Luther who could make his violin sound like it was saying "Oh Luther"...They made good money because everyone enjoyed their music and gave freely whatever they could afford.

There was a family by the name of James that lived a few doors from me that had a piano player. The son, who was about my age, and I used to play together and I would go to his house very often and play the different piano rolls for hours. Many people who could not play music had these type of pianos..I loved music but never tried to play the piano at that time.

There was also in the neighbourhood a boy who's name was Willis Ivy and who's mother made him take violin lessons but I was not interested in playing music and for me a violin was more of an instrument for girls, although I liked the way Luther played it. I never told Willis what I thought of the violin because we were good friends and did not wish to hurt his feelings.
When I was 14 years old, we moved to Hathaway Street which was in the back of Kenyon Avenue. I never missed a show in the Lincoln Theatre and

eventually a trumpet player came to Cincinnati and was engaged to play at the Lincoln with Amanda Randolph. His name was John Nesbit and he made quite a name for himself as a trumpet player later, and as an arranger also. He stayed in Cincinnati for quite sometime and he was the best trumpet or cornet trumpet player of all those I heard before him. When Nesbit did leave town it was to join McKinny's Synco Septet.

One day while playing in front of my house with some of the other boys, we saw some young people going down the street and there were two women who had trumpet cases with them and later we heard music coming from a house further down the street. We stopped whatever we were playing and went in front of this house in order to hear the music better. Those sessions happened many times and I was always around to hear them from outside.

I knew a young fellow living on Kenyon Avenue, who had started to play saxophone and later he was engaged to play in the summer at an open air pavilion in Sinton Park. This park took up one block which was from Kenyon Avenue to Barr Street and from Cutter Street to Mound. There was a tennis court, baseball ground, swings, a small swimming pool for children of two or three years old and a sand pile for them to play in; there was also benches for people to sit on, to idle away the time. This pavilion was built in a way that people could stand around it on the outside and listen to the music and watch the dancers.

When the dances started, I always managed to have a ring side standing spot and a girl was playing trumpet. The saxophone player was the leader and the group was known as Clarence Page and His Syncopators. The girl playing the trumpet was Dolly Jones and it was her and her mother that I had seen going down Hathaway Street with trumpet cases and later heard them blowing. I was fascinated by Dolly's playing and she seemed at home with the rest of the musicians. A girl playing in an orchestra with men had never been seen in Cincinnati. I noticed that Dolly was very often putting something liquid on her lips but I didn't know why she did it.

Clarence Page played in the Sterling Hotel in the winter. The Sterling was on 6th and Mound Streets and had been a big time white hotel at one time. More and more negro people started to come to Cincinnati from the Southern states and this part of the city called Downtown was where they found homes and places of entertainment. There was a gambling house on 5th Street between John and Central Avenue which was run by a man named Ed Gaither. He later opened another one in Carlisle Avenue and Mount Street. My mother used to masquerade in a suit of my father's on Halloween, the 31st of October, which is known as the vigil of All Saints Day, and go into Gaither's gambling houses because women were not allowed in there. Everybody mostly put on some kind of mask on Halloween day and it was just as much fun for grown people as it was for young ones. It was also the one time when I could stay out until the wee hours of the morning and not get a whipping for doing so.

The Sterling Hotel had big dances in the winter and I could hear the music coming from the ballroom from outside, but it was not as interesting as in the summer when Clarence would play in Sinton Park.

I was 14 years old when a man by the name of Ernest Moore, who used to play in the band with my father, Uncle Ernest and Uncle John in Centerville and was now living in Cincinnati, started a band to teach young boys to play music; and I joined this band. I never knew how Mr. Ernest Moore managed to do what he was doing, because he was not a rich man and he did not charge for teaching the boys. I am certain that he could not afford to buy all the instruments he had and he allowed us to take them home. There must have been at least 25 boys in the band from my age to 17 and rehearsals were twice a week. After a few months, I was getting along quite well on my instrument which was the alto horn like the one that I had heard Sidney De Paris play in Crawfordsville, Indiana. We gave a concert once on the lawn of a house at 6th and Cutter Street.

I and some of the boys on Hatthaway Street started a shooting gallery down in the basement of a house where one of the boys lived. We had saved money doing errands for people and bought 3BB guns. Those were the kind of guns

that you put small ball bearings in. There were single shooters and repeaters, in which you put 10 ball bearings and pump them into the chamber of the rifle with a handle under the trigger. We used tin-cans as targets and we lit the basement by candle light.

My father left Cincinnati to work in another city and I started enjoying myself in the shooting gallery to the extent that I stopped going to band rehearsals. As my mother never worried about what I did when I was out of the house, I was my own little man. The result of my not going to the rehearsals was that Mr. Ernest Moore came to the house one day and took the horn. I was not interested in playing music.

Another movie and vaudeville house opened on Central Avenue between 4th and 5th Streets and it was there that I saw Mamie Smith, Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith, the most famous of all the women blues singers. I also worked for one week at this show place. There was a part in the show about a man, his wife and their many children coming from the South to visit some relatives in the North. There must have been about 10 of us and all living in Hathaway Street. We did two shows a day and were very proud that we were taking part in a stage show. We did not ask how much we would get and we took our job very seriously and was always ahead of time for the show. At the end of the week the producer gave us 50 cents apiece and we were very disappointed.

The Whitman Sisters show was another one that came very often to Cincinnati. I do not remember anything interesting concerning the musical background of the show but Alice Whitman was the first woman tap dancer that I had ever seen and she was a great one.

Negro people could go to the shows up_town but they had to sit in the second balcony which was known as the peanut gallery. There was no segregation in the peanut gallery because white people who didn't have enough to sit on the first floor or the first balcony, sat next to the negros and conversed with them. I used to go quite often to the Keith Theatre on Walnut Street which was in the shopping centre of the city. The orchestra in the pit was very good but I was attracted by the drummer for some reason that I can not explain. If a negro was outstanding in show business, he was booked on the Keith circuit

which had had theatres in most large cities in the United States. It was at this theatre that I saw Bill "Bojangles" Robinson who was a great tap dancer. "Bojangles" would stand almost perfectly still and his feet be tapping rhythms that many drummers could not imitate on their snare drums.

Another great musician I saw at Keith was a clarinettist by the name of Wilton Crawley. Crawley would put a glass of water on his forhead and do a slow summersault while playing his clarinet and never spill a drop of water from the glass. I also saw Rudy Weidoft who was known as the fastest executor on an alto saxophone in those times. There were also classical pianists that came to Keith's Theatre and one I remember had two very long grand pianos, one which was controlled by electricity and he played a composition in which he would play certain phrases, and the electric piano would respond with another or the same phrase which this artist had made on a piano roll.

There was a man living next door to me named Mr. Thompson who played trumpet and baritone horn in a band lead by Mr. Bert Ferguson who played trumpet. Mr. Ferguson came to Cincinnati around 1917 and formed a marching and concert band for the Knights of Pythians lodge. I used to clean and polish Mr. Thompson's horn for which he would pay me for doing it.

There were some buildings in Sinton Park that were used as a school for children and Bert Ferguson used to rehearse the band in one of these buildings. I went to many of these rehearsals with Mr. Thompson. If anyone played a wrong note in one of the numbers, Mr. Ferguson would tell just who had made the mistake and tell him what note it should be. It was very interesting to assist at these rehearsals because I loved to hear music.

I had quite a nice voice and I remember a girl that lived in the same building where I lived who was 17 years old. At times she would ask me to sing and if I refused, she would say, 'I'll give you 10 cents.' Then I would sing because I could go and see a movie for 5 cents and have 5 cents to buy some candy or peanuts to eat in the theatre.
I suppose that the reason I had no desire to play music when I was 14 and

and started to play in the kids band of Mr. Ernest Moore was because I was interested more in being a cowboy than anything else. Most of the movies I saw were of cowboys. Some of the stars of those films were William S. Hart, Tom Mix, Harry Carney and a man by the name of Noble Johnson whom I heard was a negro but he was as white as any of the other stars. Douglas Fairbanks, Senior was another star I enjoyed seeing although I don't remember him playing a cowboy role; he did play Zorro in the "Mark of Zorro" and he was very exciting because he was very athletic. His manner of running over roof tops, jumping over horses, executing movements that baffled his enemy were fantastic.

I had a very good friend who was my favourite playmate. He lived on Barr Street but spent most of his playing time on Hathaway Street. His name was Edward Partridge and we remained friends after we grew to be men. Eddie and I used to draw pictures of horses and cowboys. Our dream was to go west and get a job on some ranch. There was one thing that puzzled me about Eddie's family it seemed that every six months at least, there was a new baby born at his house. I never knew how many brothers or sisters he had.

My father and mother seperated again and my father took me and my youngest brother Ulysses to Kentucky for a while. My brother Robert died when I was 13 years old. My sister was left with my mother and my heart was broken when I had to leave Cincinnati because apart from drawing cowboy pictures with my pal, Eddie Partridge, we had started playing with electric trains. Eddie had an after-school job in a shop that sold miniature trains and now and then he would bring something to my house that we could use in the line of railroading. Whether he paid for those things or they were given to him, I didn't know or didn't care as long as it was something we didn't have.

Aunt Amanda, her husband and her children Mattie Parks, Agnes, Frankie Belle and Thomas were caretakers on a part of the Haggins farm and I stayed with them for months. There were cows, hogs, turkeys and plenty of chickens. Aunt Amanda was saving from every angle that she could to buy her own home and if any of her children or myself wanted an egg for breakfast, we had to pay her 2 cents for it. I became a real country boy in every respect except milking
cow. I just could not get the technique of how it was done.

Tom Sparks was younger than I and smaller in size because his mother and father were small people. But Tom was very smart and studious. He must have inherited something in that sense from John Coleman who was his uncle also. None of the children were going to school except Tom as children living in the country were not obliged to attend school in those days. Tom had to walk 7 miles to school and 7 back home. He and I slept together in a room on the second floor which was like walking into a refrigerator in the winter because it was not heated. We used to get undressed downstairs, run upstairs and jump in the bed which was also as cold as ice for a few minutes. The mattress was interlined with feathers and didn't take long to warm up, but we suffered for a little time from the coldness of it.

On a farm across from where we lived were two white boys and they had a pony and buggy. They drove to and from their school which was on the same road that Tom had to take, and when I first came there, Tom told me that these two boys would beat him up at times when they caught him coming home. I told him that I would meet him on the road one day and straighten the matter out. Eventually these two boys came along and when they saw Tom with someone larger than he was they must have figured something was going to happen because they started to whip the pony to make it run as fast as it could. But it couldn't run fast enough and when they came up to us I grabbed the bridle, stopped the pony and told them that Tom was my cousin and if they ever bothered him again I would beat their brains out. Tom never had any more trouble from them. I was not afraid of white boys because I had fought them on the streets and at school in Cincinnati. In fact I always had nerves.

Once when I was 12 years old, I had come to Centerville for the summer and as most of the boys worked helping with the harvest, I went to work also with a group thrashing wheat. I was what was known as a "jumper," which means the one on the wagon who stacks the wheat when it is thrown up from the ground. One day the thrasher machine broke down and everybody was lagging around waiting until it was repaired. There was a white fellow named Tom McVey who called all the negro boys "nigger" and he wanted to say something to me. Tom was a man

of 24 years old at least. I was sitting on a wagon and he was laying on the ground chewing on a straw. I heard him when he called me nigger but I pretended not to hear him. He pointed his finger at me and said "Hey! you nigger," and I pointed my finger right back at him and told him that my name was William Johnson Coleman and if he could not call me one of those names, not to say anything to me. His face turned cherry red but he didn't move and I never knew what he wanted to say to me.

Another time a pal and I were walking along the pike and we saw some farmers killing hogs, so we went over to see if we could do something and one of the wise guys said, 'yes, can you dance?' I said no I could not dance and he said, 'Well, I'll make you dance,' and he started to shoot at my feet with the rifle he was using to kill hogs. I didn't move and he was so angry that he said "get off this farm before I kill you". We left but he was the one who had lost face.

Some months later my father decided to go back to Cincinnati and that was very pleasing to me because the only boy around me on the farm with Aunt Amanda was her son Tom and I was happy at the thought of seeing Eddie Partridge, Eddie West, who lived on Hathaway Street and with whom I used to draw pictures of fine looking automobiles, and many of the other boys that were in my gang.

We lived on the 5th Street between Mound and Cutter Street over an undertaker parlor. The name of the undertaker was Mr. Copeland. When we lived on Barr Street, the Coplands lived across the street from me and I used to make candy-spending money from Mrs. Copland by watering her lawn in the summer and shoveling coal into her cellar in the winter.

Dolly Jones left Cincinnati along with her mother who's name was Dyer Jones. Some medicine shows came to town and they used to put on their show in any empty lot they could find and no one had to pay to see them. The supposed doctor sold bottles of syrup that was supposed to be good for the liver, rheumatism, heart trouble, and pills for blood circulation, aching bones or any kind of sickness that existed. Medicine to cure all ailments.

There were always some kind of musicians playing those shows and a couple of comedians. Some of the jokes were: How do you feel, Mr. Bones? and Mr. Bones would answer: Just like a stove! The other one would ask: How's that? and Mr. Bones would answer: Red hot and still a heating.

Another one was: How do you feel to-night, Mr. Sampson? Mr. Sampson would say: Just like that woman's mouth, and point to some woman in the crowd. The other one who was usually known as the straight man would ask: How's that? and Sampson would say: wide open.

A group of these medicine shows would travel from city to city and play in different parts of the town and I heard about one that was playing in a district which was quite some distance from where we lived and that had a family of musicians working with them. The trumpet player was called Gabriel and I was told that he was very good. We had moved again and were now living on lower Carlisle Avenue, two blocks from where the red light district was. Red light district was the name for any district where prostitution thrived.

One day I was playing in Sinton Park and I heard someone call another boy Gabriel and I was curious to know who this was because I have been told that I was a very fine trumpet player. He was playing baseball with some other boys and when I did get a good look at him, I saw that it was Sidney De Paris whom I had attended school with in Crawfordsville, Indiana and played the alto horn at church concerts.

The medicine shows were always on at an early hour of the evening and Sidney started playing with Clarence Page at the open air pavillion where Dolly Jones had played. I heard Gabriel blow many times that summer.

Wilbur De Paris played with some orchestra in the Sterling Hotel, so I never heard him. Sidney didn't remember me going to the same school as he, but I did remember my cousin Theophilus Chenault and I became better acquainted with Sidney De Paris after I told him that Theophilus was my cousin.

I never heard the De Paris family play together but I was told that the mother, father and a sister of Sidney all played music. I don't know if there were more than one sister but there was only the two boys, Wilbur and Sidney.
Those medicine shows usually stayed in a city one or two months and then moved on to another city. When they left Cincinnati, the De Paris family left also and I never saw Sidney in Cincy again.

I was 16 when I decided to leave home and my hangout was in Sinton Park with a group of other boys that had left home or had no parents and some of them had been in and out of reform school since the age of 12 years or younger.

When the weather was nice we slept anywhere we could find a place. I worked a few days at one time in a big Hotel as a bus boy and stayed in a room with another boy named Lewis who had lived on Hathaway Street at one time. We were about the same age. I didn't like the job at the Hotel so I quit. I still stayed with Lewis for a few days but one night I came to the room he wouldn't open the door for me, so I had to think of a place where I could sleep. Then I remembered that the door leading down in the cellar under Mr. Copeland's undertaking parlor was not locked because there was nothing down there that was worth anything. I believed in ghosts and would not go near a cemetary at night, so I was a little worried about sleeping in the cellar of an undertaker's parlor knowing that there must be some dead bodies just over my head. But I was so tired that I may have even slept in a coffin that night. So down in the cellar I went, with dead bodies over my head and my father in his bed up over the dead bodies. There was an old dusty arm chair there. I knocked some of the dust off and sat in and slept like a log.

Among these homeless individuals that hung around Sinton Park at night were three boys that sang barber shop songs. As I had a voice that was not too bad, I eventually started singing with them. One whose name I remember was Jessie Seltzer, who had lost one eye and was the oldest of all. Jessie had a voice [the] like a trained singer and he used to give me voice I was to sing in the numbers. I had the baritone voice. These three boys had been singing quite a while with another fellow who was a pimp and a down right hustler who carried a pistol. He was living with a prostitute and didn't hang out with the boys anymore. So, I had taken his place in the quartette and I wasn't doing too bad after some rehearsals.
One night we got an engagement to sing in a high school on Walnut Hill

where there was also a negro community, but it was a sad night for me because the other fellow that sang with the group showed up and Jessie asked me if it would be alright to let him take my place as he knew the song better than I did. I knew that he had a better voice than mine so there was nothing to do, except to agree. We had accepted to sing at this school for pleasure so I didn't loose any money, but I was disgusted as hell.

Jessie Seltzer had an uncle in Cincinnati and I stayed with them for a while. His uncle had more old papers and junk in his place than you could find on the city dump, but it was a roof over our heads and we had something to eat.

Jessie and I decided to make our way to Detroit one day and not having money enough to pay for a train ticket, the only way to get there was to hobo. I had never done that before but Jessie knew the ropes and advised me about the correct place to hop a freight train and how to do it. You go along the tracks on a side road near where the train has to pass and when you see a place where the train has to go up grade, you hide yourself somewhere near until the engine is well past and the train begins to slow down. Freight trains are always very long and when a freight car is empty, the doors are always open. You can also tell when a coal car is empty because you don't see it stacked up. So you choose a car and as the train is not moving at a great speed, it's very easy to hop on. The only worry after that is if the breakman comes along and makes you get off, which has happened to some hobos.

There is no way of knowing exactly where a train is going but we caught one going north of Cincinnati late one afternoon, found a nice box car and slept until morning. The train was not moving when we awakened and we looked out and found ourselves in a freight yard. That's a place never to be caught in because freight cars are robbed sometimes and if you get caught in a yard and have no business being there, you can be put in jail even if you haven't stolen anything.

We managed to get out of the freight yard without being seen and found out later that we were near Toledo, Ohio. We hit off on a road going back in the direction of Cincinnati. I don't know if Jessie was disgusted because we had not
made it to Detroit or had changed his mind about going there. He was older than I and the whole idea was his and I went along doing whatever Jessie suggested.

That same afternoon as we were walking along the road, we met a negro farmer and he invited us to come home with him to have something to eat and spend the night. It was wonderful because we had only apples and pears that we picked from some trees along the road and a good meal was something that we could really appreciate. We slept in a good bed that night and what happened after that is that we stayed on this farm for 3 days, helping this man do his farm work. I chopped him a big supply of wood for the stove because I was good at chopping wood as I had learned to do it when I stayed on the farm with Aunt Amanda.

We left this fellow and his wife on the 4th day and Jessie told me that the main reason we left was because he thought that the man was beginning to suspect that his wife was taking a liking to me. Whether that was true, I don't know; but I do know that at that time I did not think about women or girls. I had had some childhood sweethearts but that was nothing serious.

So we came back to Cincinnati and I stayed with Jessie and his uncle for a while. I was hanging aroung Sinton Park again and became aquainted with a boy whose only name I can remember was Harry. He may have been a couple of years older than myself and he had been in and out of reform school many times. Harry was born thief and I started going around stealing things with him and another boy.

Harry was the brain of the gang. He was a very nice looking boy, quite clear and had very nice hair. I never saw him smile or heard him laugh and he seemed to not have any interest in anything except stealing. We would steal silk shirts off the clothes line of people and sell them to pimps in the pool rooms. Cincinnati had plenty of alleys and women hung their washing in the back yards that had gates and were easy to get into.

We would also wait at a certain place on 8th Street near a viaduct for farmers' trucks that had come into the city to buy provisions and many of them had to pass over the viaduct going in the direction of Indiana, whose border
was not far from Cincy. We would hop on those trucks and take cartons of cigarettes and chewing tobacco which we would also sell in the pool rooms.

One day, I fell when I was jumping off a truck with a carton of cigarettes, chewing tobacco, and the carton broke scattering packages of tobacco over the street. There was not much traffic and no one saw this happen except Harry and the other boy that was in our gang of three thieves. We gathered the scattered packages and sold them the same as we had sold the others.

Another scheme of Harry's was that the 3 of us would go into a shop which sold stockings, handkerchiefs and many other things for women and children. We had to be certain that there was only one sales woman or man in the shop. One of us would ask the price of something in the back of the store and the other two would steal a couple of pairs of stockings which were usually on display on a line. Or we would take a box of handkerchiefs or anything that could be hidden in our pockets and was not nailed down. These things, we also sold to pimps who would give them to their girls.

My next hobo experiment was with Harry. He wanted to go to Lexington, Kentucky, to steal a pistol, so we made our way over one of the bridges spanning the Ohio river and we were in Covington, KY., but we had to go outside of town to catch a freight. There was a long trestle to cross before the train would come to an up grade and I could never walk across a trestle because I was afraid of missing my step and falling. This was a very high one but it did not span a river. I walked down one side of the hill into the valley and up the other side. It took me longer to get to the other side than it did Harry, but the trip would have been off for me if that trestle had crossed a river.

We caught a freight train coming up grade and had the nerve to sit in the door way of an open boxcar and wave to farmers plowing the fields or around the homes that were near the railroad line. We arrived in Lexington and slept in a wagon in someone's back yard a little on the outskirts of the town. But Harry could not find a pistol to steal and he could not think of any scheme to steal one, so we hoboed back to Cincinnati.

When the summer had passed and the weather started to get cool at night, that was the toughest part of being away from home and a nice warm place to sleep. But Harry's mind was always working like an 8-day clock and it was not long before he found us a place in a lumber yard under a shed that was heated to keep the lumber dry. There were no difficulties getting in because no one watched the place and it was just as easy to come out; so we had a nice warm place to sleep in after the poolroom where we hung out closed.

We had a special restaurant where we could eat a plate of home fried potatoes for 5 cents if we didn't have money enough to pay for some meat to eat with the potatoes. The poolroom where we hung around was on Mound and George Street just in front of Sinton Park and there was a bakery on 6th Street not far from the Sterling Hotel that made a cake with apples and raisins which was known as Washington pie. You could get a large piece of this pie for 5 cents and it was very filling. So when I wanted a change from potatoes, it was Washington pie.

Most of the time we could not afford but one meal a day. The bread was free in restaurants so we could get our 5 cents worth of potatoes and eat as much bread as we could and drink water. One waitress in the restaurant got to know our habits so well that when she saw us come in the door and especially if she was alone, she would yell to the cook: 'A nickel worth of spuds.' It was embarrassing but I was hungry and that was the only restaurant where I could get a good portion of hot potatoes for 5 cents.

One day we were in a part of the town quite far from the district we usually chose for stealing silk shirts out of back yards. The police must have learned that there was somebody or a gang that were stealing silk shirts from clothes lines, ladies stockings from shops, cigarettes, chewing tobacco and chewing gum from farmers trucks and someone must have eventually seen us doing those things and gave a description of us to the police.

So we were in this district and a policeman saw us and must have known or thought that we were up to no good and had no business being in that part of town. He stopped us and wanted to know what we were doing so we told him we were looking for a job. Then he said if it was the case we should come along with him because he

knew where we could get a job. But he walked us to a police station and we were locked up immediately. Later we were taken to court and brought to the Office of a juvenile court judge who knew Harry. I suppose that he had sent Harry to the reform school a few times. But as we had no stolen goods of any kind on us and there was no one to accuse us of having stolen anything from them, the judge gave us a lecture and the name of a place where we could get a job.

I alone went to this place which happened to be a factory that manufactured ropes. I was hired and worked half a day and never went back for my pay. The place was so dusty with the dropout of rope dust that it was difficult to breathe.

A few days later my father found out where I was and came to take me home. He was working in a cleaning and pressing shop, pressing mens' suits and certain kinds of women's dresses and coats and he lived in a two-roomed apartment in the back of the shop. This shop was owned by Mr. Thompson, the man whose horn I used to clean and polish, and Mr. Will Tarleton, who was a very good friend of my father. He had also played cornet in the Centerville band and he was a great collector of Bert Williams records. This shop was on Walnut Hills near the school where I was supposed to sing with the Jessie Seltzer quartet and it was in a part of the hill where the better class of negroes lived.

I had been with my father and brother Ulysses about 2 days when my father noticed a lot of little bugs in the bed. He knew what they were but I didn't, and he knew that I was the one who had brought them there. I had been away from home 4 or 5 months and had not had a bath during all that time, so I was full of lice. My father burned my underclothes and socks and bought me a new suit. Naturally I had to take a bath as hot as I could stand it.

I liked my surroundings because there was a Ford delivery truck driver, a boy named William Boyd, and I went with him on many of the pick-up and deliveries. I also learned to press clothes and enjoyed operating the pressing machine. I was now 17 years old and so was William Boyd but he acted much older than I did at the time.

Eventually the cleaning and pressing business went bad and the shop closed. We moved down town to a house on West 9th Street and I got a job as bus boy in the dining room of the restaurant in the zoo. This is not the first job I had in my days. At 8 years old, I used to light the gas on Saturdays for some Jewish families because it was against their religion to do that. I worked in Kentucky helping with the harvest of wheat. I planted tobacco and stripped tobacco also. I was the water boy in a rock quarry. I sold papers in Cincinnati and helped deliver ice. I was very good also at house cleaning.

As bus boy at this restaurant in the zoo I heard many concerts because the summer concerts took place on the stage of an open air theatre just in front of where the people would eat this was also open air. I remember particularly the anvil chorus and a man that played xylophones which impressed me so much that I started looking at the prices of some in a Sears and Roebuck catalogue.

There was a dance hall a few feet in the back of the restaurant and one night I heard a trumpet sound coming from there that I had not heard before at this dance hall. When I had the chance I walked over there to see who it could be and there was a little negro boy playing trumpet with his left hand. It was the first time I had ever seen a negro musician sitting in with a white orchestra at the zoo or any place else in Cincinnati and I knew this youngster was good because he sounded good and had to be, to be allowed to play with white musicians at a dance hall in Cincinnati. I found out the name of this trumpet player later because he had been going around town at the Sterling Hotel or wherever there was a dance and play just for the pleasure it gave him. His name was Freddie Jenkins and he was going to school at Wilberforce University. Freddie was upsetting everybody, but he did not stay in town more than two or three days.

I stopped working at the zoo restaurant after a few months. I never stayed on any job very long and always found an excuse to tell my father the reason I quit. My father had a little round savings bank that would hold only ten cent

pieces. The bank was round and just a little larger than a ten-cent piece and it had a bottom that was supposed to punch out only when the bank had 5 dollars in it. There was a screw at the top and when the bank was full, all you had to do was take a screw driver and turn the screw so that it would go down and that would push the bottom out. I was not working and needed a dime or two every day for spending money. When dad had some extra change and there were some dimes among the change, they went into the bank. I had found a way to pull the bottom of the bank out with a straight pin and eventually it got to the point where I could only have to shake the bank and the bottom would fall out.

Dad started to get suspicious when after a certain time his bank was not full. He found out what was happening and knew that it was me that was robbing him. My father never had to whip me, but this time he tied my hands with a rope and gave me the worse whipping I ever had. That was to teach me to never steal, especially from him.

That summer I went to Centerville for a vacation and stayed with Uncle John who had 3 daughters, Matty, Ida and Cora, A son named John Albert Coleman after his father. Matty and Ida were older than John and I. Ida played the Piano and was the organist at the Baptist church. For playing hymns, Ida was alright but when she played sheet music (popular songs) she would not give the measures their proper value. She could read very well but in some places, she just didn't have rhythm. Nevertheless, we used to have some swell times with Ida playing the piano and me singing. Uncle John had brought John, Jr. a C melody saxophone and he could play a few songs not bad. John Jr. could get anything he wanted from his father and I suppose it was mostly because he was the only boy in the family. He also had a Model T Ford, which was something that many boys in rich white families didn't have. Uncle John's wife was from a family named Bachelor and her name was Katherine, but everybody called her Kitty. She was a sweet and lovely woman and everybody loved Aunt Kitty.

Before coming back to Cincinnati, I stayed a couple of days in Paris and there was a dance one night with an orchestra called Edgar Hayes and his Collegians. I learned that the musicians were going to Wilberforce University and Edgar Hayes had

persuaded them to spend their summer vacation in Lexington, Ky., his home town, and play the summer dance season in Kentucky. The original leader of the band was Horace Henderson, a pianist, but he was not with the band then, because Edgar Hayes was also a pianist and a hell of a good one. Some of the musicians in the band at that time were Joe and Casper McCord and Henry Hicks. Joe and Cass played saxophones and Hicks played trombone; but the strong man of the band was Freddie Jenkins, the trumpet player I had heard at the dance hall in the Cincinnati Zoological Garden. One number I shall never forget that will always stay in my mind was 'May-time' and the way Freddie improvised the melody, I shall never forget either. The first few lines of the song were: 'I found you in May-time.' Freddie and the rest of the musicians in that orchestra were about my age and they were all students at Wilberforce. It was the first time I had heard a jazz orchestra of more than 6 or 7 musicians. This orchestra was composed of 10 musicians but my eyes and ears were closed to almost everyone of them except Freddie. He was the whole orchestra to me.

Dad, my brother and I moved from 9th Street to Hathaway Street and I went to work in a fruit sugar-coating factory. There was a family living on the first floor by the name of Haddins that were distant cousins of ours. One of the Haddins had married the daughter of my Aunt Mary. On the second floor was a family named Huston. We had two rooms and a kitchen on the third floor and there was a man that lived in a small room on the side of our front room.

The Huston's were from way down South and their son came to Cincinnati to live with them after we had been living on Hathaway Street a few months. This fellow was older than I and he loved to carry a pistol. He and I worked at this fruit sugar-coating factory which was at least 6 miles from where we lived. We rode the street car to work and walked home when the work day was finished. My sister stayed with us sometimes and with my mother at times.

My father was offered a job by a rich family near Lexington, Ky., as a cook and he accepted. He rented our apartment to a man named Wade and took my brother to Kentucky with him. My sister went back to stay with my mother and I was allowed to stay with the Wade family which consisted of Mr. Wade, his mother and his son. My father allowed me to stay because I was working, but he told me that if anything went wrong, I should come back to Kentucky.

After Mr. Wade was in our place a certain time, he started making bootleg whiskey. There were barrels of mash in the small room where the man had lived before he moved. He had a copper still that fitted on the gas stove. Mr. Wade started doing good business and I remember that a prohibition officer used to come there at times and drink with Mr. Wade. I used to taste the alcohol when it was hot and dripping from the still.

Then Mr. Wade made the acquaintance of a fellow by the name of Charlie who used to peddle his whiskey. This Charlie eventually got to know Mrs. Huston's son and one Sunday they were out drinking somewhere and Charlie persuaded the boy to sell him his pistol for 12 dollars. As Charlie was pretty tipsy, Mrs. Huston's son didn't trust him too much and took the bullets out of the pistol before he agreed to sell it to Charlie. Mrs. Huston's son was a real country fellow and Charlie eventually confidenced this guy into giving him the bullets. He gave them to him and took his 12 dollars.

Then Charlie went out on the street and two white men were coming along. They happened to be detectives and Charlie must have recognised them as such because he pulled out his pistol and started shooting at them. They kept coming towards him and pulled their guns also. Charlie turned and ran and the detectives took after him and finally cornered him in a lumber yard, disarmed him and took him to jail.

He must have given our address as the one where he lived because some detectives came there and questioned me. Wade must have gotten wind of something because the whole family had gone out and left me alone there. The detectives told me that Charlie had been burglarizing stores in the up-town shopping district. They had come with a search warrant to look for some/the stolen goods, but nothing was there. The door of the small room where Wade had his malt working, was locked. I had never seen what was in that room since Wade had taken over the apartment. They asked me for the key which I didn't have, so they broke the door in and for the first time I saw what was in the room. There were 4 or 5 barrels of yellow liquid substance known as mash, a substance that was to be left until it came to a certain degree and then it was put into the still and cooked. When it came to the boiling point, the liquid would drop into a hugh jug and you had moonshine

whiskey. The detectives took all the soap powder they could find, any old dirty rags and garbage and put them in those barrels of malt or mash to make certain that it could not be used anymore. I never saw or heard anything of the Wades again.

I stayed in the apartment alone for a few days and at with the Hustons. Then Mrs. Huston's son said he was going back to the South where he could carry a gun and I lived with Mrs. Huston, giving her a certain amount every week for my room and board.

One day I was out walking with one of my distant cousins that lived downstairs who's name was June, and two other boys in the neighbourhood named George Burr and Theodore Means. A nice little woman who must have been about 28 years old stopped us and asked if we could sing. Then she told us that she was a social worker and organist at a Presbyterian church and she would like to form a quartet of 4 boys. She offered to give us piano lessons and teach us some religious songs. We accepted her offer and a few nights later we went to the church and started to learn our first song and take our first piano lesson.

The only one of us that had a piano at home was June, so he and I could practice there, but we could get into the church any time we desired and George Burr, Theodore Means and myself did most of our practising there. The woman's name was Miss Hargrave and she lived in a very nice section of Walnut Hills. We used to go to her home some nights to play our lessons and learn songs. The main reason we liked to go to Miss Hargrave's house was because she had a young sister called Boggs who was very beautiful and we all had eyes for her. Sometimes we would go walking and take turns walking with Boggs and those were delightful moments. Boggs didn't show any special preference for any certain one of us and I don't know what I would have done if she and I had ever had the chance to really be alone, because girls didn't worry me at the time and I didn't have much conversation for them.
Now I think we all tried to get our piano lessons better than the next one just to show off in front of Boggs. We began to attend the church quite frequently and also sang at special church meetings.

After about 4 months of training, we sang well enough to be invited to sing in some white churches. These affairs were always for social purposes and our pay and reward was the piano lessons that Miss Hargrave gave us.

But eventually the novelty of singing, rehearsals and going to church, the attraction of Boggs also, began to fade away. It was not too agreable to practice the piano in June's house, because when I felt like doing it, he felt the same way, and as it was his family's piano, he had the right to practice whenever he felt the desire. To go to church to practice lost its charm and we put everything down. Maybe if there had been a piano in my family and my parents had not been seperated, I may have been able to play piano today.
Shortly after we broke our relations with Miss Hargrave, George Burr bought a clarinet and tried to get me to buy one. But I didn't have any interest in that or another instrument.
After some months in Kentucky, my father and brother came back to Cincinnati and we lived on lower Carlisle Avenue again. I was 18 years old and taller than my father.

One day I was looking in a pawn shop and a cornet-trumpet caught my eye. A cornet-trumpet is not as short as a cornet and not as long as a trumpet. Everytime I passed this pawn shop I would stop and look at this instrument.

I told my father about it and mentioned that I would like to have it. So he told me if I wanted it I would have to work to pay for it. I was not working at the time. My father was never a mean one to me but he was not like Uncle John who would buy his son almost anything he asked for.

I took a job in/a printing shop as errand boy and package wrapper. The price of the horn was 35 dollars and it was a used instrument. That was quite a large amount of money in those days. I earned about 8 dollars a week and paid 5 a week on the horn. But I could not even put my hands on it until I had paid for it. There was a box type of case that I got with it and the night I brought it home I suppose I was the proudest boy in town.

I did not sleep very well that night because I was over_anxious for the next day to come, so that I could blow my horn. I was still working and did not get the chance to try my instrument until I came home the day after I had bought it.

I must have taken an hour before I could get some sort of sound out of that horn and my lips were a little sore from trying so hard. Whatever I had learnt when I was 14 and played for a while in the kids band, I had forgotten. But each day when I came home from work, I would take my horn and in a weeks time I was able to play the C scale not too bad.

I was not the kind of genius like Max Kaminsky who was able to play and read a song two days after he got a trumpet and he had never played an instrument before. I began to try and play a number by ear. I didn't know the name of the notes so I would mark on a piece of paper. the fingering of the valves such as 1st and 3rd, 1st and 2nd, 2nd open, etc.

One day I decided to clean inside of the horn and that's when I found out that I had been cheated by the pawn shop where I bought it. I pulled out a slide and the outside of it came off leaving the inner part stuck in the stem. All of the 1/4 joints were the same. I had to take the horn to a music shop and have the parts repaired.

After a month of practising and seeming to get nowhere, I put the horn under my bed and forgot about it. My good friend Eddie Partridge was driving a small bus at a golf club where he had to go meet different club members that didn't have cars at the street car line and take them back when they had finished playing golf.

Eddie had bought a C melody saxophone quite some time before I bought my cornet-trumpet but I wasn't doing anything with it so I asked him to let me take it home and see if I could do something with it. I tried it a few times but never arrived to the point of playing as much on it as I did on my horn which was not much when I decided to leave it under my bed. The only successful thing I did with the sax was to take all the keys off one day and had a hell of a time getting them back in place again.

I had no idea of being a professional musician when I bought my horn. It was just a desire to play for my own amusement. My father didn't push me to continue trying when I had lost interest in my instrument because I had bought it with money that I had earned and he had not given me one penny to pay for it.

I started working at the Cincinnati abattoir, making a better salary then I had ever made. My first job was opening and cleaning the stomachs of cattle which gave me such a headache that after 4 days of working in what I called the stink hole, I told the boss of the department that it made me sick doing that kind of work, so he transferred me to the sheep department where my job was to chop out sheep brains. I had to be trained for this job and after a few days, I became an expert. It was pityful to hear the sheep bleating as they came around on a large wheel-shaped board with hooks on it, made to hang the sheep by one hind leg and when they came around to a certain place, there was a man with a long butcher knife which he would push through the throat of the sheep to kill them.

The heads were cut off and then skined, then they came to me. The technique of chopping out the brains was to hit the cell that contained the brains on two sides with a very sharp hatchet. If the cell bone was not hit a certain way, the brain would be split. In 3 seconds, I could chop out a brain and the heads came out to me every 5 seconds.
I worked about 3 months at the abattoir. I just could not stay on a job as some people could, 3 or 4 years or more.......

I was practising my horn again and playing a few numbers by ear not bad. Then I went to work in a factory that manufactured tin tubs and buckets. I was assistant to a worker that put rivets in tub handles. After a certain time I took over his place and had an assistant myself. All the machines in that factory were dangerous because sometimes the mechanism would get out of order and the hammers that were in the upper part of the machine would slip. Quite a few workers had the tip of their fingers cut or mashed off. My machine slipped at times but I was fortunate enough not to have my fingers in it when it happened.

I worked longer at this factory than any other place I had worked before, but eventually my lazy side caught up with me and I collected my pay one Saturday afternoon and that was the last time I saw the bucket and tub factory.
I didnt hear much music those days, except a parade band now and then.

The lodges were still burying their members the same way as it was done in New Orleans, but I didn't know anything about New Orleans then. When a lodge member died and his body was being taken to the grave, the band would march slowly, playing some hymns or sad songs. They would leave the funeral procession at a certain place and come marching back to their headquarters playing a lively march.
insert 8-10

Clarence Page was playing in the Sterling Hotel and there were no more dances in Sinton Park. I was not old enough to go in the hotel to listen to the music but I knew the trombone player in the band, his name was Parker Berry. Parker had started to play trombone in the kids band of Mr. Ernest Moore at the same time that I had started to play the u,-pa-pa horn. I stopped playing and Barker continued music and became a professional.

Another musician that was playing at the Sterling Hotel was a trumpet player named Harry Morten. Harry had been traveling with his mother in a circus. She was a snake charmer and had come to Cincinnati after quiting a circus. I think that she was born in Cincy but I never knew for certain. Harry was born in Ohio and had played with an orchestra from Columbus, Ohio who were known as the Whispering Serenaders. It was said that the style of this orchestra was to play so soft that the shuffle of the dancers feet served as a part of the rhythm section.

A very well known story in Ohio about the Whispering Serenaders is that they were engaged to work in big white exclusive hotels in different cities in Ohio, but they were also engaged to work in a white hotel somewhere down South. After being there for a while, they were asked to play for a party one night after work. This party was outside of the town at a private house, so some men were waiting for them in cars to take them and the instruments to this party. After having driven a few miles out of town, the cars pulled up at a certain place and there were a gang of other white men. This was the party but not like the Whispering Serenaders thought it was going to be. This was to be a head whipping part for no other mason than that the Serenaders were fine musicians but negroes. Being gentlemen didn't mean anything to the jealous Southern white man. The Whispering Serenaders were all beaten badly and their instruments destroyed, and they were told to get out of town as fast as they could. The only reason for an act of that kind to take place in the South where anything could happen to a man if his skin is black, is that these musicians were from the North, they played too well for somebody's taste and they had the nerve to accept an engagement in a white hotel down South.

A pianist by the name of Green came to Cincinnati and I met him along with a young fellow named William who played drums. Green was one of those pianists that played by ear and only in one key. There were at this time a couple of other young pianists around town who played by ear and were very popular. One was named Hershal Brown. He could play in any key although he could not read music. He played in an orchestra and he really could play fine.

But getting back to Green and William, I started going to different parties with them and playing a few numbers I had learned. I don't remember getting paid from these parties, but on Christmas night, Green, William and myself, I was known as Johnson, were going from place to place doing our numbers and drinking egg-nog. Many people gave open house parties on Christmas and New Year's and egg-nog was flowing that night like the water running over Niagara Falls.

I was not a drinker of alcohol and still could not stand the taste of beer. But the home-made egg-nog is so much like a milk shake with whiskey added that it was easy for me to drink it. When I was too young to know myself, my father and mother told me about a friend that had been to Paris and when he came back to Centerville he bought some whiskey and gave my parents a water glass full of toddy. They placed the glass of whiskey on the dining room table which was round and went in the kitchen to prepare supper. All of a sudden they heard me saying Ah! in a funny tone and they came running into the living room where I took a chair, pulled it up to the table and drank the whole glass of whiskey, down without stopping. They said that it didn't make me sick but I was so drunk that during the night I fell out of bed and they found me under it the next morning.

I had tasted whiskey a few times after that and once when I was 12 years old and we were living on Barr Street, Dad had bought a bottle of whiskey and hid it in the cupboard. My father was not a drinking man and I had never seen him drunk or on the verge of getting drunk. But he liked his toddy now and again and would give us one when we had a cold. I was always looking in the cupboard and closets to see what I could find and one day, Mom and Dad were out and I found this bottle of whiskey and took a big swallow. It was winter time and snow was about 15 inches high in the streets.
When Mom and Dad came home, I said something about being dizzy and right away

Dad jumped to the conclusion that I had found his bottle and I had... I don't think that he was really angry with me but he told me to get out of the house. I must have been high and didn't know what I was doing. We had a large closet under the steps that went upstairs to the second floor from the outside hall and there was a round top trunk that Mama used to throw dirty clothes behind until she was ready to wash them. Dad went in the kitchen and I got behind this trunk in the closet and went to sleep. Later when Dad didn't see me at the time he thought I should be home, he got worried and went out to look for me, when he came back, I had awaken and come out of the closet. Of course my mother also was worried that I may have laid down in the snow where I could have frozen to death.

But this time when I was going to different parties and drinking egg-nog was my first time to paint the town and when I left the last party about 3 o'clock in the morning, it was the first time I ever staggered home and I slept all day.

My father was not happy with me because I was not working and eventually told me that I would have to get a job. His buddy, Mr. Tarleton, who had been part-owner of the dry cleaning and pressing shop where we had stayed on Walnut Hills, was now the head porter at the main telegraph office up-town on the 4th Street and told my father that I could get a job there, so I started working and stopped hanging around with Green and William. I still practised my horn. Every other week, I had to go to work early and I would get off early and that was the time that I could practice without disturbing anyone.
I worked at the Western Union for quite a few months and used to see and hear William Smith, the pianist, very often because he was a professional musician and I was a beginner.

August came and every year, a certain majority of the population of Centerville went camping for one week. Those that could not stay the whole week could come for a day or two. These encampments were always on some rich white farmer's land near a creek that was deep enough to swim and to fish. There was a tent used as a dining room, where the women and girls slept, one for the men and boys. After supper which was usually about 6 o'clock, the middle of the dining tent was shared for dancing. Uncle John's piano or I should say, Ida's piano,

because she was the only one in the Coleman family who could play, was always brought to these get togethers and if no musicians were there every night who could play, Ida played alone and the people would dance to her music, even if she did skip a measure here and there.
Everyone would give a certain amount of money for the food that was consumed that week and if someone came just for one day and night, they could eat as much as anyone else and not pay a dime.

I was given a weeks vacation without pay from the Western Union and it was just at the time the encampment was taking place. I had spoke about the encampment to William Smith, called Smittie by everyone, and a young man named Edgar Courance, who was a beginner on clarinet. He also lived on Carlisle Avenue, and I used to carry notes to him from a girl named Annie Jones when I was 14, and lived on Hathaway Street. Edgar was only one year older than I, but he was the kind of teenager that started liking girls when he was very young. He would give me a nickel everytime I brought him a note from Annie and took one back to her. She would give me 5 cents when I brought an answer from the note she had sent Edgar.

Edgar, myself and an amateur alto player named Alex Baker, used to rehearse at Edgar's house or Alex's house twice every week. I dont remember how I met Alex but I remember that he lived on Court Street. We could get orchestrations from a couple of music publishing stores up town and one we received was "Three O'clock In The Morning", which was a waltz. There was one place in this number where the trumpet part went as high as A above the staff and that was a note I could not reach, so I made a turn on the note just before the A, which was D for the trumpet, as the number was in F, and played the A in the staff.

My reading started to get better when a piano player named Clarence Trotter joined out little rehearsals. He would play the number while we looked over the parts. Then we'd play them slowly until we had a good idea how the notes sounded. Then we'd give the tempo a little lift, and then a little more until we had the number up to speed. At that time, I never thought of taking lessons, although I could easily have done so because at that time there was a pianist called Arthur Matthews, who wrote "Worry Blues", who had a music school. I could have had lessons in harmony with him for 50 cents a lessons, which was not too much money, even for me. Instead, I learned by hanging out with older musicians. All they thought of doing during the day was getting together and buying together a bottle of Moonshine Whiskey. None of them would ever push me and say: "Well, why dont you study music?" So my musical skill was limited. I remember that sometimes when I tried to improvise, I would get lost, and be unable to get back into the key. I never lost the measure. I had a cousin that played piano and I always knew when she skipped the measure, but in those days I sometimes would lose the key.
34 (a) Hagen or Haggim?

But getting back to the encampment, Smittie, Edgar and I arrived in Centerville and was taken to the farm where this get together was taking place and which happened to be on millionaire Hagen's farm, where I had stayed with Aunty Amanda Sparks some years before.

We were joined by John Coleman, Jr., on C melody sax and a drummer from Georgetown whose name was James Coleman, but he was not related to my clan. It was the first time that Smittie and Edgar had been on an encampment and I think it was the first time Edgar had really been in the country as he was born in Cincinnati. Smittie had some relatives in Lexington which was not far from the site of the camp and quite a few people would come from Lexington and Paris to dance and return home when the dancing stopped.

I had a wonderful time and it was the first time that most of us making the music had played for an audience of dancers and listeners except Smittie, and I remember the first ad lib phrase that I played without rehearsing, was a thing that had been sung by someone which said, 'somebody gone tore their breeches', and this is how it would be written and I felt really proud of myself.

One night a fellow came to the camp from Paris and told me that he had an orchestra and asked me if I would come and work a few nights with him the following week after the encampment was finished. I accepted although I knew that I was supposed to go back to my porters job at the Western Union after one week vacation.

Smittie and Edgar went back to Cincinnati and I went to Paris for a week and played a job in that vicinity. I don't remember the name of this fellow that hired me or how much he paid me. The orchestra must have been amateurs the same as I, but it was the first time that I was paid to play music.

In those days a musician got work by word of mouth. Someone would speak about him, praising the way he played, so that if a band leader heard about it, he would hire you. Orchestras were getting bigger, because when I started to play, there were no more than six or seven pieces, but later on, they got to be nine or ten. I remember once in Cincinnati that the Alex Jackson band was visiting the city from New York. He wanted a trumpet player, and he asked me come and see him at his hotel. I was working with Wes Helvey at the time. Alex Jackson had the reputation for being a society orchestra, so I never went to see him, because I figured I could not read music fast enough for the band. A few years later I found out that one of his trumpet players could not read a note. He was one of those guys who would just take chorus like Wild Bill Davison.

I went home after the week was over but I had lost my job at Western Union, and my father was not happy about me staying away longer than I was supposed to and had no job when I came back. A trumpet player named Theodore Carpenter had left a carnival and was now playing with Clarence Page and I met him. Carpenter had only one arm having lost his left one in an accident somewhere on a machine that had pulled his arm off up to the shoulder. But that was no handicap for him when it came to playing his horn. He could put a mute in his horn as fast as anyone with two hands and he could wa-wa with a rubber plunger by putting it between his legs and working his body back and forth while sitting.

Carpenter was called "Wingy" by the musicians. Wings is slang for arms and there is not many instruments after a trumpet that a one-arm person can play. Because of the 3 valves, the trumpet can be held by the little finger and the thumb whereas a trumpet player with both hands can hold the trumpet with one hand and the other is free to manipulate the valves.
Freddie Jenkins fingered the trumpet with his left hand because he had lost the joints of the upper part of the digits on his right hand.

Carpenter started showing me different things concerning phrases on the trumpet and I've always considered him my first teacher although he was not teaching me to read music. Theodore had travelled with many carnival shows and told me many things about the places he had been. His mother lived in Cincy and at the time when I met him, he was living on Richmond Street which was not far from where I had lived with Aunt Mary. It was on the corner of Richmond Street and Mound Streets that I used to go get beer for my aunt.

It was at Carpenter's house that I heard my first Victor record. It was by a trumpet-player named Johnny Dunn and the side I remember was a blues called "I've Been Down So Long". The second line was: "Until down don't worry me".

I can not describe Johnny Dunn's style, but I had not heard anyone play the way he did.
