In fact I had not heard too many trumpet players except Dolly and Dyer Jones, Sydney de Paris, John Nesbit, Freddie Jenkins and the fellow from New Orleans that played around town on a wagon. There were mostly cornet players in the marching bands but they never played jazz and I listened to these bands and heard all the musicians as anyone else who loved music.

I did not care too much about the way Johnny Dunn played, but I did copy the way he played "I've Been Down So Long", because I was learning the trumpet and it was something to help me learn the horn better.

A month or so after I had come home, a drummer by the name of Lee Rainey asked me to play for a dance with him in a small town up state Ohio. Lee was an amateur drummer but he had played with Clarence Page at times. I accepted the engagement and had learnt the "Tin Roof Blues" well enough to make Lee compliment me on the way I played it, and we played it a few times that night.

A few nights later, there was a dance at the Sterling Hotel and the band was a pick up, one that was being lead by a trumpet player named Chet. He had played in Chicago for a long time and he was a good trumpet player. I never knew why he came back to Cincinnati. Actually he lived across the river in Covington but worked in Cincinnati most of the time.

Lee Rainey was the drummer that night and I came into the dance hall with my horn. When Lee saw me, he asked Chet if I could play "Tin Roof Blues" with the band. Chet looked at me and I suppose he could tell from experience that I was not good enough to play with him, so he told Lee; no, because the music was sounding bad enough already.

I was still rehearsing with Edgar Courance, Alex, a pianist named Trotter, a drummer named Bill Johnson. John Coleman eventually came to Cincinnati and rehearsed with us also. The group was now composed of trumpet, clarinet, alto sax, C melody sax, piano and drums. We had no job in sight but we were amateurs and enjoyed the music we were playing. Trotter, the pianist, was a professional musician who had been put down by most of the other professionals because he was an alcoholic. He played some fine piano as far as I was concerned. The rest of us did not drink, so we did not care about what Trotter did, and he was older than the rest of us anyway.

Sometime later, an amateur trombone player came to Cincinnati and he stayed rehearsing with us. His name was J.C. Higginbottom and it was at his sister's house that Dyer and Dolly Jones used to have their sessions when I lived on Hathaway Street. His siter was now living on Kenyon Avenue, very near the house of Clarence Page. We rehearsed at Higgy's sister's house at times, but
most of them were at Alex's house on Court Street.

Higginbottom's brother-in-law belonged to a lodge (the Elks I think it was) and through him we started playing for some of the dances the lodge would give at their meeting hall which was over a drug store at 6th and John Street. It was a famous market street, especially on Saturday. It was also part of the red light district. The street where one could hear the latest Bessie Smith records blasted over a loud speaker from early morning until late in the night.

Higginbottom was ahead of the rest of us as far as style was concerned. I had not heard many trombone players then. The few that I had heard never played the way Higgy did. I never knew who his inspiration could have been but he had been inspired by someone. All that I can say is that Higgy could blow better than anyone else in the orchestra.

We did quite a few dance jobs for the Elks at their hall and some dance jobs at the only negro hotel on Walnut Hills. Naturally we all felt very proud to be able to play for dancers. But we were not learning to read very well and John Coleman could not read at all. Nevertheless we had our repertoire and enjoyed playing our solos the best that we could.

William Smith the pianist was now playing with Clarence Page but I was at his house quite often. The Chocolate Dandies show came to one of the theatres up town and with them was a trumpet player featured in the show by the name of Joe Smith. William Smith met Joe Smith and invited him to come to his house for a session one night after the show. I was there with bells on because Smittie had told me what a great horn player Joe Smith was and I didn't want to miss hearing one note. I don't remember if Joe drank anything or not but I remember how sweet he played. And I remember Smittie asking him one time, which key he wanted to play a certain number, and Joe told him, any key.

One night during the stay of the Chocolate Dandies (shows of that type usually stayed for one month in Cincy) there was a dance at the Sterling Hotel and Clarence Page's orchestra was playing. I had been to a rehearsal and decided to stop in the Sterling Hotel and listen for a while. I put my horn on the band stand and stood there listening and watching the dancers. Suddenly Joe Smith was on the band stand blowing that sweet sound that I had never heard anyone play before. After a certain time, I wanted to leave, but I was ashamed

to pick up my horn and let Joe Smith see that I had an instrument. Why I felt that way I'll never know, but I didn't want him to know that the horn on the band stand, if he saw it, belonged to me. So I walked away and stood near a door and a friend of mine came along and I asked him if he would bring me the case that was on the band stand, giving him some sort of excuse for not going to get it myself.

Joe Smith was the greatest trumpet player to play straight melodies with a plunger and although I enjoyed hearing him in those days when I had not heard too many trumpet players, I did not try to play like him.
The next time I saw Joe Smith, he was with Fletcher Henderson, but that's another story and I shall speak about it later.

Shortly after the Chocolate Dandies show left Cincinnati, a fellow by the name of Hoskin came to town and contacted Trotter for some musicians to accompany a show that he was going to produce. This show was to play quite a few small towns in the state of Ohio and maybe a few in Indiana. It was natural that Trotter told Hoskin that he had some musicians. Hoskin had a young violinist with him. We rehearsed this show and opened in a town called Oxford, Ohio, which was not far from Cincy. I don't recall if the show was good, but I'm certain that it was nothing to write home about. The show played for three days in Oxford and then moved on to another small town. I don't remember the name of the place but we didn't get any money for the time we had played in Oxford. The theatre was never full, but there were a few people every night and we started to wonder where the little money that was taken in, had gone? Anyway, we moved on to the next town, played the show and Hoskin gave us some sort of sad story about the money and only had enough change to pay for our room and get something to eat. He promised that the next town would be better as it was larger than the last two. We had decided that the next town would be the last one for us to play because we did not want to be caught too far from home without money enough to get back, and we were beginning to suspect Hoskin of being a slicker.

There was a young man living in Oxford who became quite friendly with the musicians. His first name was Theodore and he was the first person I had ever known who was a negro but looked like a white person. He came with us when we left Oxford just to be with the show. We played a theatre in Middletown, Ohio and we told Hoskin that we wanted Theodore to sit in the ticket office with the other person that would be selling tickets for the show that night. We had our first full house that evening and after it was over Theodore came back stage with all the money that had been taken in, except the percentage that the theatre demanded. We divided the money in equal part and told Hoskin that we had done our last show for him. It was my first experience in show business as a musician. The violinist must have stayed with Hoskin because I never saw him again, but to my recollection he was very good and I regret that I don't remember his name.

A few days after we came home from the ill fated tour with the Hoskin show, Lee Rainey came to my house and asked me if I would like to work at a road house with him. He told me that the salary would be 35 dollars a week and that almost knocked me over, because my father was not making that much money in one week and neither were many musicians. 35 dollars a week and I was still an amateur! 35 dollars, more than my Dad was making in one week of working hard as a labourer on a construction gang. I didn't know anyone that was making 35 dollars a week and back in the early 1920's that was really good loot.

There were many places all over the United States that were called Road Houses because they were situated on a highway outside of a city or town and one would always get a meal, drinks, dance and listen to music. They all had some sort of music but mostly jazz. This was during prohibition and in Road Houses the sale of alcohol was forbidden, but the clientele could bring their alcoholic drinks and be served ginger ale and ice, or home brew which was a beer made by the bootleggers, the same as whisky was made. Some Road Houses sold bootleg whisky to their well known and regular customers but not to a stranger because they could be revenue officers and close the place if they could prove that whisky was being sold by the owners of the
Road House.

I was very elated to be asked to work in a place like a Road House every night and make the kind of money that Lee Rainey offered me. The place was about 10 miles outside of the Cincinnati city limits on the Highway going to Hamilton and Dayton, Ohio. The name of the Road House was Woodlawn Inn.

The other musicians that Lee engaged were Edgar Courance who was now playing sax-tenor. There was a banjo player who's only name I can remember was Clay. He lived in Wyoming, Ohio which is a suburb of Cincinnati. The Woodlawn Inn was in Wyoming also.

But the greatest thrill of the job after the nice salary I was making was the pianist whom Lee had engaged and he was it for all concerned. He was the great but unknown Edgar Hayes. The Edgar Hayes whom Freddie Jenkins and the musicians from Wilberforce College had played with. I had heard the Johnson brothers who lived across the street from me on Kenyon Avenue. Green who I had played house parties with before I knew my chromatic scales, and had heard two other young pianists Alonzo and Herschel Brown who was also a professional and played much piano as did Trotter.

Edgar Hayes was the greatest I had ever heard and I was working with him and hearing him every night. We did not rehearse new music during the day but we had at least one new tune to play every week. Lee Rainey would visit the music publishing houses for new songs and when we played them on the job, this is the way it was done.

Each one would take his part and place it on his band stand and Edgar Hayes would play the chorus about 7 or 8 times while we listened and watched the notes. Only Edgar Hayes and Lee Rainey would be playing until we thought we had heard the number enough and knew how to finger it on our instruments, and then, we came in. With Hayes, we didn't need to rehearse new numbers.
We worked from 9 pm until 2 am and had a big hot meal every night around
mid-night. None of us did any drinking, so we would have coffee, tea or milk with our meals.

One night, two young fellows and their girl companions came to the Inn after mid-night. Many couples came at that hoyr but these people looked as though they were coming from a wedding or a college dance because the men were dressed in tuxedos and the girls had on evening gowns and it was not often that people came to the Road House dressed in that fashion unless they were coming from a high society dance or wedding. But we found out later that that was not the case with these people because one of the young men came to the band stand and asked me if he could play my horn. He assured me that he knew what to do with a trumpet and he did!

I had not heard any white jazz musicians because negroes were not allowed to go to white dances, and they never went to those given by our people, although negro musicians were engaged to play white dances, private, public and in many of the white colleges.

This fellow really blew me out, which was not hard to do at that time, because I was still an amateur and he was a professional about my age. I found out later that he was 18 years old. I was 20. He blew a couple of numbers and then we talked together during the short rest. He told me that his name was Bill Davison and he was the solo man in the Chubb Steinberg orchestra that was playing at Castle Farm which was a big dance hall not far from Woodlawn Inn.

Bill Davison was born in a place called Defiance, Ohio, and was known as "Wild Bill" because he was able to drink a large quantity of alchohol at a very young age and I suppose he did some wild things as most young men do under the influence of alchohol.

At that time, even though he was two years younger than I was, he was blowing a whole lot more trumpet than me. I was able to read fairly well, but I was not too well educated in different keys. My range was not more than high 'C'. Probably I could have changed that by using different mouth pieces but I didn't get to know about things like that until I met Louis Armstrong later on. Even so, high notes never really bothered me, I had a good enough range for the time although I was not as gifted as players like Charlie Shavers or Dizzy Gillespie, who can stay up in the high register, for long passages. The bands I played with were not very ambitious in their choice of keys. We played in 'G' or 'B' flat, occasionally in 'D' flat, but hardly ever in 'C' or 'A'. This was not necessary since, at that time, in 1924, we only played dances, and were never called upon to play Theatre shows, which would have been more demanding in that way.

One week after the visit of "Wild Bill" and his friend, they came back to Woodlawn Inn and Bill wanted to play my horn again, but he was so drunk that he could hardly stand. I let him blow my horn but he really didn't play anything that night and I had my revenge because I blew him out. His friend came to get him and put him in a back room where he immediately went to sleep.

Then this friend of Bill's came back to talk with us and it was then that he noticed the playing of Edgar Hayes and it hit him like a man being hit on his head with a blackjack. He asked Edgar to play some numbers that we didn't know and after two or three numbers almost everyone at the Inn that night was standing around the bandstand listening to the pianist. We, in the orchestra were all ears as we were every night when Edgar played. This night we were very proud of him because we had never had a crowd of people around the bandstand before, and most of the time no one paid any attention to what we were doing. Actually it was only Edgar that was doing something because he was only accompanied by Lee Rainey on drums, but Lee was too busy listening to do much drumming.

A few nights later, this friend of "Wild Bill's" came back to the Inn alone and said that he came especially to talk to Edgar Hayes. When it came time for us to have our nightly meal, this fellow came into the dining room and sat at the table with us and he did the talking.

There was a big record and music shop up town in Cincinnati on 6th Street by the name of [Chubb] Cub & Steinberg who had sponsored the orchestra that was playing at Castle Farm. This fellow told us that his name was Saughtercamp and that he was considered the best dance pianist in Cincinnati and some other towns in Ohio, but he had never heard a pianist who could play as much as Edgar Hayes. He gave Edgar a rendez-vous to meet him a few days later because he wanted Edgar to get on the list of piano players that were making piano rolls for N.Q.S, the only company I knew of that made piano rolls in those days. They were the same label that I used to play on the player piano of the James family when I lived on
Kenyon Avenue as a boy.

Edgar started making piano rolls but I never heard any that he made. Another thing that Saughtercamp told Hayes the night that he sat at our dining room table was that Edgar had forgotten more piano than he (Saughtercamp) would ever be able to play. That was a great compliment for Edgar Hayes coming from a man who was considered the best white dance band pianist in our part of the country.

Lee Rainey had a model T Ford coupe 4 to go to work in. It was supposed to hold only 3 people, but 4 of us used to crowd into it. Edgar Hayes was living at Lee Rainey's house with a girl who was supposed to be his wife that he had brought from Kentucky. Her name was Ruby and she was a real fine frame. We finished work around 2 every morning and it would take us about an hour to get to the Sterling Hotel from the Woodlawn Inn. Edgar Hayes, Lee Rainey, Edgar Courance and myself were the 4 that crowded into the model T Ford Coupe 4.

Every morning as we were coming home Edgar Hayes had a song he would sing in the car. It was: 'I know where my baby is' and it never had any more words. He meant that he knew Ruby was home and waiting for him. Edgar Courance and I would get out of the car at the Sterling Hotel because we lived on Carlisle Avenue and it was not far for us to walk from the hotel. Lee and Edgar lived on West 9th Street between Cutter and Mound Street in front of the Y.M.C.A.

One morning, Hayes had sang his 'I know where my baby is' song, and after letting me and Courance out at the Sterling, Lee turned the corner of Mound Street and was going down 9th Street, and what should they see but Ruby and Lee Rainey's wife Alice, walking down the street with two men. When Lee and Edgar pulled up beside their wives and the two fellows saw them getting out of the car, they ran faster than Bill's brother when he went hunting and shot at something he thought was a bear and the doggone thing turned white. Edgar Hayes never sang the song about 'I know where my baby is' again.

I had copied the first 8 measures of "I Found You In Maytime" the way I heard Freddie Jenkins play it when I had heard him with Edgar Hayes in Kentucky. It was a phrase that stayed with me and I can still hear it today as Freddie played it. Freddie was still going to Wilberforce College and playing with the orchestra. One night they had been playing for a dance somewhere and they found out Hayes was playing at a Road House that was on the highway they had to take to go back to Wilberforce, so they stopped at the Inn to say hello to Hayes. We were on the bandstand at the time and Hayes asked me to play "I Found You In Maytime". I call it that because those were the first four measures. But the real title is just "Maytime".

So we played "Maytime" and I played the first few measures the way I heard Freddie play it and it pleased him so until he started calling me brother, and we called each other brother from then on, and the odd part about it, is that we did have similar resemblances in some certain degree.

The first time I ever shot dice was with Edgar Hayes and Lee Rainey. One morning after we had arrived in the city, someone suggested that we have a crap game and I joined the party although I did not know much about the game. We played tit for tat until Lee finally became broke or tired and went to bed. We were all playing in his flat. Edgar and I kept playing head and head until I finally broke him. I had snapped my fingers so much that morning until I had rubbed the skin off my thumb and middle fingers, and the side of the palm of my right hand looked like I had been playing in a pot of asphalt from the way I had scraped up the dice from the carpet whenever it was my turn to shoot them.

I had heard an orchestra by the name of Lois Dieppe once at Elmwood Town Hall which was another suburb of Cincinnati. In fact Dieppe was the first orchestra that I heard at Elmwood. Dieppe was from Columbus, Ohio, but I think his orchestra had played around Chicago and it was his first time to play in the vicinity of Cincinnati. There was no one in the orchestra that I gave special notice to except Lois who had such a powerful baritone voice that he stood behind the orchestra in back of the pianist and sang without a megaphone, which everyone used in those days to bring
out their voices, and the orchestra did not have to soften their tone when Deppe sang.

I found out later that the pianist in Deppe's orchestra was a young man by the name of Earl Hines. One night Lois Deppe stopped at the Woodlawn. This Road House did not cater for negroes, but the owner would allow them to come in and say hello to the musicians if they were musicians also. A few days after the visit of Lois Deppe, Edgar Hayes announced that he was leaving to go with Deppe's orchestra who was working somewhere in Cleveland Ohio.

We certainly hated to see Edgar Hayes leave the orchestra but Deppe had offered him more money than he was making at Woodlawn Inn and Hayes wanted to go places, so we said goodbye to him and he left Cincinnati still owing me 10 dollars.

William Smith was not doing much at that time so Lee hired him to replace Edgar. Although Smittie could play much piano, in fact to me, he was the best in town after Hayes, we had become accustomed to the way Hayes played and missed him very much. I think the owner of the Inn missed him also because the band was not the same and it was not very long after Hayes left that we lost the job.

The musicians would congregate every afternoon in front of a restaurant on Mound Street between Carlisle Avenue, and 6th Street. There was a small shoeshine shop next to the restaurant and the young man that owned the shop had not been in Cincinnati very long. But he was an ambitious fellow, and as the shoeshine shop did not bring him the amount of money he wanted to make, he started selling bootleg whisky.

I started hanging around every day with the musicians of whom most of them were older than I. In order to be in good terms with these musicians I used to give 25 cents every day and sometimes twice a day to help buy a pint of whisky. I was not a drinker so I was always offered to first taste out of the bottle. Usually there would be only 4 of us for one pint which cost a dollar which in turn was the reason each one only had to chip in 25 cents. The average one of those musicians could have a ball and only

spend a dollar by chipping in 25 cents with 4 different people. If you knew how to drink all 4 of you could get a nice taste out of a pint. The reason I was offered the bottle to take the first taste was because I didn't drink much and when the bottle came back to me, if it did get back to me, there would only be a very small taste left. They usually called it "taking the poison off" if you were the first to drink out of the bottle. We never drank on the street in front of the place we hung out because that would have been indecent and there was always the chance that a government revenue officer could be passing and arrest us for illegal possession of moonshine whisky. The name moonshine was what the mountaineers used to call bootleg whisky because it was supposed to be distilled in the night when the moon was shining and no revenue officers were around.

After a few weeks of hanging around these hard drinking musicians and putting in my 25 cents for a pint, I began to have the feeling that I was not getting my share of the deal. I would take the poison off and pass the bottle around and sometimes it never got back to me. So I started to open my eyes and look around to see what was the reason I was not getting my share, and it didn't take very long to find out what the trouble was.

I was taking a small taste and the others were taking a deep breath before they drank and therefore they could take a large taste in their mouths before they swallowed it. I soon caught on the trick so well that it was seldom that they asked me to take the poison off and I became one of the best alley drinking musicians in town. We would go in some alley or back yard to drink after we had bought the whisky.

I began to get some gigs with these musicians who were mostly free lancers and did not care too much to have a regular job. Most of them as I said before were 35 years old or more and I was the youngest in the bunch so they called me "the Kid." There was Edgar James, a fat drummer, Wilbur Coksey, an alto player from the West Indies, a pianist named Maycoks, and a few other musicians that came around now and then. But the regulars were Maycoks, Cocksey, Edgar James and myself.

The first job I did with these new found friends was a one-week gig in the lobby of the Pekin Theatre which was a movie house owned by a real American Indian. I knew the son of the owner of this theatre before I started playing music. There was a certain film that was showing for a week which was a rarity because the movie houses usually changed films every other day. We were engaged to play a few numbers, 2 or 3 at the end of each showing of this film and I really enjoyed the week.

The first out of town job came not long after we had finished at the Pekin Theatre. A fellow came from Richmond, Indiana and engaged the Maycock group to play a dance there. When the date came this fellow sent a car to bring us to Richmond. There we got as much food as we could eat, plenty of drinks and we made a big hit with the dancers.

Two weeks later we went back to Richmond and then the organizer told me that he would like me to be the leader of the orchestra the next time they had a dance. There was one about three weeks after that and I took Edgar Courance who was still playing C melody sax, William Smith on piano, Wilbur Cocksey, alto and Edgar James, drums.

When we arrived in Richmond and I saw the advertising bills and posters for the dance, I wasn't happy about the way they had been made. There was the name of the hall and the date of the dance and in big letters "Professor Johnson Coleman" and his band. I did not like the idea of me being called "Professor" because my idea of professor was an older person than I was and in the case of being a musician, a professor was one that knew all about music and was also a music teacher.

But I had been billed that way and although I played the best I could that night, every time someone called me "Professor" I would tell them that I was not a professor. We played Richmond a few more times and no matter how hard I begged the organizers not to put "Professor Johnson Coleman" on the posters, every time we went there, it was "Professor Johnson Coleman". I really never considered myself a leader to the extent of getting more money than the rest of the musicians, so we all had the same pay when the job was finished and that was another reason why I did not want to be
called professor. Fortunately the other musicians never called me Professor in a kidding way or otherwise.

William Smith, the pianist, rejoined Clarence Page, and I rehearsed with a pianist named Hershal Brown. Edgar Courance had moved from Carlisle Avenue [to ].... Alex Baker the alto player rejoined us and also Bill Johnson the drummer. Hershal Brown played piano by ear as did many of the pianists in Cincinnati. Some of those ear-playing pianists could only play in one or two different keys, but Hershal was one of the few that could play in any key. Myself and the others could not play in any key either but we could spell, which is said about a musician when he could not read music very fast. And that was the advantage that we had over Hershal.

But all that Hershal needed to hear was the melody of a number at least two times and he would play the right harmony, or it sounded like the right harmony. We could spell as I said before but our ears were not bad either and that is why we accepted the harmonies that Hershal would play on a song as being authentic.

And in my opinion, Hershal was the second best pianist after Edgar Hayes and he probably would have become considered one of the greats of that era if he had known how to read. He was about the age of Edgar Courance and myself.

We never had any job with Hershal which was a pity because I believe that we would have been more inspired playing for dancers than we were at the rehearsals which were quite inspiring with Hershal. Brown at the keyboard.

Sometime later a fellow came to Cincinnati from Kentucky who's name was Zack White. His name was really Zacharias White and he played banjo. There was also a pianist named Johnny Johnson that I had heard when I was living on Kenyon Avenue. Johnny Johnson also played piano by ear and he was well known in the higher society negro class.

One day Zack and Johnny came to my house and told me that there was a fellow in town from Michigan that wanted some musicians to play week-ends at a vacation camp not far from Kalamazoo, and they asked me if I would like to be a part of the group. I had never been more than a hundred miles from Cincinnati and this proposition sounded great to me. Zack and Johnny did not have to ask me twice if I wanted to go with them.

A few days later, we left Cincinnati with this fellow who was older than we were and he was the drummer. We were also joined by a young alto player from Wyoming, Ohio named Jimmie Smith. Jimmie was the second negro that looked like a white boy that I had come in contact with. I had gone south from Cincinnati but now I was going north. It was in the summer, maybe July or August, but the thing that excited me the most was that I was going further away from Cincinnati than I had ever been, leaving my father for the longest time in my life and getting out in the world by playing music.

We arrived in Grand Rapids, Michigan and that was our headquarters. Every Saturday afternoon we would go to Kalamazoo by bus, and there we had a rendez-vous with someone who had a car and would meet us at the Y.M.C.A. to take us to this camp where we played Saturday nights, Sunday afternoon and evenings. We came back to Grand Rapids every Monday morning and spent the rest of the week days there. We all lived in the same rooming house except for the drummer, who's name I don't remember. He lived in Grand Rapids, so I suppose that was the reason we made it our headquarters. Kalamazoo was nearer to the camp where we worked, but we were satisfied with the set up. We ate in the restaurants as the place where we were staying was a rooming house only. It was a thrilling experience for me to be away from home because it gave me the feeling that I was a man looking after myself instead of being home with Dad who went to bed at a certain time and was very unhappy when I came home late and blew the last puff of a cigarette in the room where he slept. I had no key, so my father was obliged to open the door for me at whatever time I came home.

There was a big white dance hall in Grand Rapids, and we used to go and listen to the orchestra that was playing there. We had to listen to them from the outside because there were no mixed dances in the U.S.A. at that time. It was a 12-piece orchestra and at certain places one could see into the dance hall if you stood on a box near one of the open windows.

This band sounded good to me as Chubb Steinberg and I remember that the get-off and hockum man was a stout fellow who had a brass trumpet that he never shined and that gave the horn the look of dark green copper. I didn't know anything about styles at that time, but this fellow could really play and I enjoyed listening to him. As we had nothing to do during the week, we went at least 3 nights every week to listen to this band.

I had got away from the hard drinking musicians in Cincinnati and I did not miss drinking. Johnny Johnson met some nice negro people and soon we were invited to some parties. I was very timid with girls and enjoyed mostly playing a few numbers because we were invited to bring our instruments along whenever we were invited to a party.

One day there was some sort of celebration which must have concerned only the city of Grand Rapids. There were parades with marching bands and floats with flowers and girls. But I was surprised and disgusted to hear a group on one of the floats playing the jazz songs of the time in unison. All the groups that I had played with also played their numbers in harmony and I thought that those guys must really be amateurs that didn't know anything. I was still an amateur as were the fellows I was working with, but we would have never thought of playing an ensemble in unison. It just was not done. And yet 'here were these fellows playing their numbers in unison! Not just one number but everyone that I heard them play, and I heard quite a few as I had time to listen to them. That was a disgrace to jazz to me.

But those guys were cats that were really ahead of their time. We all knew what's been going on for years in jazz since bop came on the scene. Now we play the melody in unison, written choruses and jive ones in unison and they sound good. But it just wasn't done in those days, except for this

group in Grand Rapids.
There was nothing outstanding about this group I was playing with. Zack played a not too bad banjo, Jimmie was alright on alto, Johnny Johnson played nice piano, the drummer was not too hot and I didn't raise too much hell on trumpet. Also I was not a critic. So we may not have been too bad as a group. I do know that we all enjoyed ourselves playing together and the public liked us, so maybe we were better than I could imagine we were.

At the end of the two months we came back to Cincinnati. I had decided before I left Grand Rapids that I was going to stay with my mother. My father and mother had separated for the last time ever since I was 14 years old. I and my brother had always been with my father and my sister had been with my mother all the time. I felt that I was old enough to do what I wanted to do, although I had a good father, I knew that I would always be like a young boy to him and not a young man.

The first thing I did after going to live with my mother was to buy myself a victrola. The one I bought was ther new style cabinet victrola which was another piece of furniture for my mother's house. The mechanical part of the victrola took up half of the cabinet and the other half was for records.

The first record I bought was recorded by a group called the Goofus Five and the title of the number(s) on the two sides: "Sadie Green, the Vamp of New Orleans" and "Crazy Quilt". It was an OKeh record which I still possess. I had another by the same group of which one title I remember very well was "In Your Green Hat". The Goofus Five were white musicians and there were not many race records, which was the name given to records that were recorded by negroes in those days. Bessie and Mamie Smith and Ma Rainey and some other well known blues singers of the early 20's were recording, but no orchestras or small groups of negro musicians. If they were, I did not know about it. Of course, the blues singers were accompanied by negro musicians whose names were never on the recordings in those days, neither were the names of the white musicians

for that matter.
My mother was living on Court Street between Mound and John Street. I liked the neighbourhood because it was not far from Central Avenue (2 blocks) where there were many shops and it did not take me as long to walk up town as it did from where I had been living with my father on Carlisle Avenue. I was happy living with my mother and sister who was going to high school. Mama let me do as I pleased and I had my own room which is something I did not have with dad as he had only two rooms, the bedroom and the kitchen living room combined.

I joined Clarence Page's orchestra shortly after my return to Cincy from Michigan. Clarence augmented his orchestra from the 7- or 8-piece group that he had before to a 10-piece orchestra including himself. The other trumpet player's name was Nassau. No one ever knew his other name or if that was his real name. He was from the West Indies Islands and probably had a name so different that it was hard to pronounce or he probably gave himself that name because he came from Nassau.

Nassau was not a very large fellow and he must have travelled a lot and had quite a bit of experience before he hit Cincinnati. He played a growl style of trumpet and I wondered many years after where could he have gotten that style, because it was the style of Bubber Miley and Bubber was not known in the middle West of the USA at that time and Duke Ellington was unknown and not recording.

Jessie Smith the alto sax player that had been with the group I was with in Michigan also joined Page's orchestra. The other members were: William Smith, piano, Wilbur Cocksey, alto sax, Page, C melody. Edgar James, drums, and two brothers, Clarence Logan, tuba, and Dan Logan, trombone.. The most outstanding musician in the group was a banjo player named Bob Robinson. Bob came to Cincinnati from West Virginia. I don't know if he was born in that state but that's where he came from when he joined the band. Banjos took quite a few solos in the orchestra at that time and Bob Robinson was considered one of the best in that part of the country.

We played regularly at a dance hall at George Street and Central Avenue, which was on the third floor which was called George and Central. It was at that time when a show came to Cincinnati that had a young trumpet player by the name of Cheatham. He came to one of the dances we were playing at George and Central and sat in with us. I could tell right away that he had quite a bit of experience after Bob Robinson. It was usually Nassau that had the biggest success because of his growling, which really did not impress me at all. But this night it was Cheatham that showed us all what trumpet playing really was. I talked with him later and he told me that everyone called him Doc.

I went to the theatre where Doc was playing and to my surprise he was playing alto sax and trumpet in the show. I never knew who the other musicians were in the group because "Doc" Cheatham was the only one that interested me. The show stayed for two weeks in town and I went to see it and mostly to listen to "Doc" Cheatham at least 8 times.

The first trip out of Cincinnati that I made with Page was a real catastrophe. He left one morning for Charleston, West Virginia, in a Pierce Arrow owned by a fellow named Richard Carpenter. A Pierce Arrow was and still is a wealthy man's car, and how "Rich", as everyone called him, came to own one, I never found out. It was a 7-passenger car but we could get 10 musicians in it with Rich driving and we were not uncomfortable. We were all on the slim side except Edgar James. Also we had our personal baggage, plus drums, tuba and the rest of the instruments. All cars had running boards on both sides in those days and with what was known as a luggage carrier, which was put on the left running board and it was surprising how much luggage could be packed on a car then. For one thing, the Pierce Arrow was a long car with the head lights on the fender. When seen coming down a road at night, it resembled two motorcycles, one of the right side of the road and the other on the left. That is if the road was not too wide. As the car was very long, the running board was also long, and that was the reason a very large amount of
luggage could be put on the side and on the fender between the hood over the left and right side of the front wheels.

So off we went in the direction of West Virginia. We arrived in Middletown, Ohio and were stopped by a motorcycle policeman who claimed that Rich had passed a car going in the same direction as we were at an intersection. I did not know anything about the rules of the road when driving a car because I could not drive. So I did not understand why we had been stopped.

The result was that Rich was fined a certain amount for which we all had to pay. Rich was not a wealthy man although he owned a Pierce Arrow car. The next trouble was with the tyres. (sic) Rich had used tyres on the car and as the weather was quite warm, one blew out in the rear. Rich patched that one up and a few miles further along the road, the other one blew out. The innertubes had been patched up so often and the tyres were wo worn that it was impossible to continue the trip without new tyres. Rich could not afford real new tyres so we all had to give from our pockets again in order to buy some used tyres that were like new considering the condition of the ones that Rich had on the car when we left Cincinnati.

We eventually reached Charleston, W.V. and did not have to play until the next night. The dance was a big success for us and Clarence Page counted the money in ten parts and then asked us to give a certain amount to Rich for the gas and the time he had put in to drive us, and we all went out and had a good time.

The next day we left Charleston for Bluefield W.V. To get to Bluefield from Charleston it was necessary to cross the Cotton Top mountains and the road was so narrow that two cars could not pass each other except at certain places where one had to pull in where the road had been widened a few feet especially for that purpose. There was one curve that was so sharp that the Pierce Arrow had to go forward, come backwards in a certain manoevre before the car could take the curve. (w) There was no protection to keep the car from going over the cliff and we were at least 6 thousand

feet above sea level. My heart was in my mouth because I thought that every curve we came to, we were going off the road. But Rich was a good chauffeur and when we finally arrived at the bottom of the side of the Cotton Top Mountains a few miles from Bluefield, it was one of the happiest moments of my young life.

That night at the dance the piano was so old, used and out of tune that Smittie was obliged to transpose every number we played. I thought that we would stay in Bluefield after the dance finished, but we packed up and left for Charleston and more trouble.

We had not gone more than one mile from the dance hall when a car with two policemen in plain clothes pulled up beside us and ordered Rich to pull over to the curb. Rich asked what he had done wrong and they told him he was speeding. When Rich and some of the others protested and said that he was not speeding, these officers said that he was speeding when he came in to town before the dance and that he would have to pay a fine of so many dollars or all of us would go to jail. We all had to give from our pockets again. But this was a racket that those police pulled on every coloured orchestra that played in Bluefield. They knew that if the dance was a success and they always were, because they didn't have many dances a year, so there was always a big turnout as there was for the dance we played. And those two crooks knew that we as well as other orchestras that they pulled this trick on, would have some money. They could put us in jail for breathing the same air if they wanted to. To make matters worse, we had to come back over the Cotton Top Mountains and at night, I was frightened enough when we came over them in the day and I could see what was happening. I was sitting in the back seat and as the lights of the Pierce Arrow were on the fenders as I said before, whenever we went round a curve, I could not see the road and I had the impression that the car was really going off the road. I felt like going out and walking but it would have taken me some days to get to Charleston. It was actually one of the worse nights I have ever known and I still get the shivers when I think of how dreadful it was having to cross that mountain at night.
We arrived in Charleston around 3 in the morning and although I had qu

quite a bit to drink before we left Bluefield, I was as sober as a teetotaler and so tired that the moment I entered my room in the hotel, and as soon as I got my clothes off and hit the hay, I was asleep before anyone could say Jack Rabbit and it was late afternoon when I awakened.

We only had those two dances in West Virginia and stayed in Charleston after coming from Bluefield to rest before hitting the road for Cincinnati. After having slept most of the day, a few of us met in a house where moonshine whisky was sold and we were having a grand time until suddenly there was a noise in the kitchen and in came some men (white) with revolvers flashing and told everyone in the room not to move. We all had glasses in front of us, but Edgar Haynes James was the only one that had a few drops in his glass and he was arrested because he had enough moonshine in his glass to prove that he was drinking. I never understood what kind of law they had in West Virginia concerning bootleg alcohol because these men were revenue men and although we had all been drinking, Edgar James was the only one arrested.

We went to the jail to see Edgar the next day before we left for Cincinnati and we were told that Edgar's trial would not be held for a week. So we had to go in our pockets to leave Edgar some money so that he would have enough to pay his fine and come back to Cincinnati when he was freed. The only profit that I received from my first trip out of Cincinnati with the Clarence Page orchestra was the ride in the car for my first visit to the state of West Virginia.

It was not always pleasant travelling through West Virginia because it was necessary to pass through many small towns and villages where mostly white miners and farmers lived and as the bass and drums and other baggage was carried on the running board of the car, we could be seen coming into a place from a great distance.

The white kids seemed to know that it would be a car with negro musicians and they would throw rocks at the car and call us niggers. It was a bitter pill to swallow and we could do nothing about it. This also happened going through places in Kentucky.
The first time I was ever in jail was when I went to Lexington

with Clarence Page. We decided to buy a gallon of moonshine whiskey in Covington, Ky., because it was cheaper than in Lexington someone said. We had some other jobs after Lexington and a gallon of juice would last for a time if we took it easy. We had a few swallows before we left to play the dance. We were all staying in a big rooming house owned by a woman named Kate and all the rooms were on the ground floor. Dan Logan and I were staying together, but Dan didn't drink.

I always had a good time when I went to Lexington and the dance was a jumping one. When it was finished, we had some food in a late morning restaurant and came back to Kate's place and brought out the jug. Dan went to bed and we all gathered in one room and started to drink.

After half an hour, I decided that I would have one more drink and hit the hay. I had the drink and just as I started for the door a voice hollered: 'Don't move anybody!' I looked around and there was a white hand with a gun in it poked through the window. It was summer and the window was open. In stepped a white policeman who told us that we were under arrest. Some more police came in after him and they put us in a black Maria, as patrol wagons were called, and took us to jail.

After we were booked for having bootleg whisky, which was against the law, they put us in a cell, I laid down on one of the benches and didn't remember anything until I was awakened at about 9 a.m. and was told that we were free on bond. I never heard anything about the case after that.

Page travelled quite a bit in Kentucky but we had more work just in Cincinnati, we played some dates for a river boat of the type that went from New Orleans to Kansas City. It would cruise down the Ohio River starting about 4 o'clock in the afternoon on a Sunday and return to the pier at 11 that night. Sometimes there would be a fight or I should say most of the time there were fights that would really get out of control for a few minutes and it would be dangerous for every one, because everyone that was trying to get away from the fight would run to the side farthest away and that would cause the boat to lean on that side, which could have caused the boat to turn over and many innocent people that had come to have a good time dancing could have been drowned.

As the fights never lasted a long time, most of the people would come back to the centre of the boat and start dancing. We never stopped playing when there was a fight, and we even played as loud as possible to detract the attention of every one possible from the fight.

There was a white dance hall up town on 6th Street between Race and Vine Streets that started renting to someone for negro dances held there. It was on the second floor and the band stand was about 4 feet high.

I did not pay much attention to girls at that time. Although I had had a few girl friends nothing serious ever came from the friendships. Girls didn't bother me the way it did some of the young men of my age and I was quite bashful also. One night Edgar James who noticed everything that happened around a dance hall, told me that a certain girl was watching me all the time we were on the band stand. When we went back after the intermission, I looked at the girl whom I had seen many times before at most of the dances we played.

Many people stood in front of the band stand and watched the musicians and listened to the music. Some never danced and I was one that never danced when I went to hear an orchestra. I knew that this girl liked to dance but all that she did that night was to stand in front of the band and look at me. I knew that Edgar James expected me to act as a young man should after he had told me this girl was watching me.

At the next intermission, I asked the girl to have a drink with me and she accepted. Alcohol wasn't sold in dance halls so we had some kind of soft drink and talked until I went back on the band stand. I did not ask her for a date until I had talked to her at a few other dances. It then started to get serious and we were together quite often. Her name was Madelyn Grant and as time went on, I learned that she had been among the young girls that went to the house on Hathaway Street when Dolly and Dyer Jones went there to rehearse, which was also the home of J.C. Higginbottom's sister.

Madelyn was a tall brown-skinned girl, not fat but strongly built with large eyes. She and I were about the same height, me being perhaps 2 inches taller than she. She was one year older than myself and had come to Cincinnati from Birmingham, Alabama, with an aunt, as both of her parents were dead when I met her. I don't believe I was seriously in love with her,
but being 21, it was more of a fancy to have a girl friend or a lover.

Not long after this romance started, a band leader by the name of Broadus from Lexington, Ky, asked me if I would join him for a month and I told Page that I would like to leave for a change of places. So I accepted the offer of Broadus. Broadus had been quite a big name in jazz and had played many Fraternity dances at Yale, Harvard and the college of Lexington among others. Love did not have such a hold on me that I did not want to travel even if it was not far.

The first night I played with Broadus was for a dance in Dayton, Ohio. Broadus and his musicians had come to Cincinnati early that morning and as I was not ready to leave with them, he told me that I could come to Dayton later by train. Dayton is about 50 miles from Cincinnati. Broadus travelled by car as did most of the orchestra then and today.

Broadus played C-melody sax and the alto player was Henry Jamerson who was known as "Speechless" because he was not a great talker. I had seen Jamerson in the orchestra of Lloyd Scott when they had played at Elmwood Town Hall. Steve Dunn was a trumpet player with a very nice style and Slaughter Campbell was a banjo player as good as Bob Robinson. I can't remember who the pianist was but the drummer was and the tuba player was a big fellow who weighed 240 pounds. He could just get a double B tuba around his body and you could not get a toothpick between him and the tuba.

Broadus had a big second-hand Packard and the tuba player sat in the back on the left side which made the car sag in a manner that seeing the car from the back it looked as though it was going to turn over. We left Dayton after the dance and headed for Lexington and my place in the car was in the middle in the back seat next to the tuba playen and slept almost as comfortable as if I was in bed.

The first morning of my stay with Broadus almost became catastrophic because Broadus had stopped somewhere on the road in Kentucky early in the morning and we were all asleep in the back seat. Suddenly I awakened to find that the car was in a position as if we were going up a steep hill at

about a 45-degree angle. I straightened up from the sleeping position that I had, laying on the tuba player, and I noticed that we were not on a road, Broadus and the two musicians that sat in front with him were not there and I could hear water running.

What had happened was that Broadus had stopped in a small town to have some sort of cold drink because he was tired of driving and wanted to rest for a while also. He had not put the brakes on tight enough and the car had rolled backwards down a hill. Fortunately, the musicians that sat in front had not gone with Broadus but were standing on the side of the road and saw the car when it started to roll down this hill and they managed to get two big rocks under both back wheels and stop the car about 5 feet from a stream that was at least 5 feet deep in that particular place.

In Lexington I stayed with Henry Jamerson and his mother. Jamerson had been with an organisation known as Musical Spiller when he was very young. He told me that Spiller had a musical act made of members of his family and other talented young musicians that he discovered, and arranged with the families of these young musicians to let them travel with him. Therefore Musical Spiller had a musical act. Jamerson travelled quite extensively with Spiller and then joined the orchestra of Lloyd Scott who was from Springfield, Ohio, and when I had heard
Jamerson had left the Scott orchestra because his mother's health was not very good and she was alone. He was the only child and he decided to stay at home with his mother until she passed away.

Steve Dunn, the other trumpet player and I got along well together and worked out some nice duos on certain numbers. Broadus did very few dances in Lexington and when we were not on the road we practised quite a bit because there was not many other distractions except movies.

After one month I got homesick for Cincinnati so I left Broadus, came home and rejoined Clarence Page. Madelyn and I were seeing each other every night and I was happy to be home with my mother and sister. My brother was still staying with my father and I went to see them often.

Page was not getting much work when I was offered a job to work in a Road House by a fellow named Wesley Helvey and as it was an every night affair I accepted to join him. I may have been lazy about doing other work but once I had gotten to the point where I could play something on my trumpet, I wanted to play as often as possible. I may have been late going to school at times or late getting to another kind of job, but I was never late when it came time to blow my horn.

Helvey also engaged Edgar Courance, who was now playing tenor sax, and a trombone player that had not been in Cincy very long. I don't remember his name except that he was called Pluto. There was a special water sold in drug stores at that time called Pluto water. Maybe this young fellow drank it and got the nickname in that manner. Pluto is also the name of the god of the underworld, but this fellow certainly was not the gangster type. One thing that he really could do was read music. Once at a rehearsal, we were reading a number and came to a difficult part for everyone except the pianist who only had chords to play and the drummer who did not read anything, and the only one that kept going was Pluto, the pianist and drummer. It took the rest of us two more rehearsals before we could play the number.

The pianist's name was Vincent Thomas and he was one of the few band pianists around town that could read music. The drummer was Leslie Towles and later a banjo player who's/only name I can remember was Jimmie, was added to the group.

One day the word got round that a famous New Orleans pianist was in town and as it happened to be a night that we were not working, most of the musicians in town turned up at the place where this pianist was staying and he took charge of every pianist that was in the place. His name was "Jelly Roll" Morton and he was a real talker. He had a diamond in one tooth and when he wasn't playing piano, he was talking about what he had done, where he had been and what he was going to do. He didn't drink any of the bootleg whisky that the rest of us were drinking. He didn't play the same style of piano as Edgar Hayes but I never heard anyone play the way he did and there he was not bluffing.

At that time, there was no books on jazz and the musicians that played it, so I didn't know if this Mr. "Jelly Roll" as he called himself, had done all the things he said he had. He was a pimp, gambler, hobo and pianist, but he was not looking like a hobo then and he could play piano.

Some months after, "Jelly Roll" came back to Cincinnati with the orchestra of Fate Marable. Fate played piano also but he directed the band most of the time. I never knew who the musicians were in this orchestra, but me and everyone that heard them knew that we had heard one of the best jazz orchestras that had come to town in those days, and I always found a way to hear the bands that came along.
Others that I heard in Cincy that had big names where "Speed" Webb and Alfonso Trent and Bellson, an orchestra from West Virginia and [that] Bobby Robinson and John Nesbit had played with.

Helvey took a job across the river in Newport, Ky., at a Road House and a new drummer joined the orchestra. Towles left with a T.O.B.A. show called the Whitman? Westman Sisters. I had seen this show in Cincinnati and I remember that one of the sisters named Alice was a wonderful tap dancer. The new drummer was John Hargrave and he was a better drummer than Towles.
And it was at that time that Madelyn and I got married. I had said when I was younger that I would not get married until I was 35 years old and here I was, getting married at 21.

A funny story happened to me three months after I was married. I was sent a message to ge see a certain woman whose daughter I had been seeing at times before Madelyn and I became real close. The girl's name was Leah and when I arrived at her house, the mother took me in a room and told me very nicely that her daughter was pregnant. I asked her what did that have to me with me and she said that I was the one her daughter said that did it. So I told this woman that it was just three months that I was married and there was nothing I could do about it.
I also denied to others that knew about the affair that I was not responsible. The mother of the girl was not angry with me or upset and only
[wanted]
me to know that I was going to be the father of her daughter's baby.
I told Madelyn about it but denied the facts to her also. I really did not believe that I was responsible for the pregnancy.

About one month before the baby was born, I began to get sick with my stomach. I didn't know at the time that this could have some relation to the pregnancy. My teeth started hurting and I had a good one pulled out because it seemed to be the one that was giving me hell. As times went on, nothing I ate would stay in my stomach. I was only comfortable when I slept in a chair. Naturally, I couldn't play my horn and eventually my weight came down from 145 pounds to 128 and I was looking like a walking skeleton.

Madelyn and I were living with my mother and sister. My mother thought that perhaps if I changed the climate and went to Crawfordsville, Indiana, it may be good for me. I had seen a couple of doctors and couldn't find out what was wrong with me. So Madelyn and I went to Crawfordsville and stayed with my Aunt Sarah. After being there for one week, one night my pains stopped suddenly. The next day a message came from my father, saying that Leah had given birth to a girl at a certain time and that time coincided with the time that the pains in my stomach stopped bothering me. I came back home the next day and started getting better every day and was happy that I could start blowing my horn again.
They named the girl Louise but my brother and the rest of the family called her Sis. We were very fond of her but unfortunatly Louise died from a brain haemorrhage when she was 5 years old.

We worked quite a long time at the Road House in Newport and when we left that job, Helvey decided to enlarge the orchestra because we started doing dance work in West Virginia, Kentucky and other cities in Ohio.

Word got around that the Synco Septette were going to play a dance in Dayton. Synco is the short name for Syncopation and the Synco Septette was later to become known as the famous McKinney's Cotton Pickers. McKinney's first name was William.
This orchestra had a very big name but it had never come to Cincinnati so Helvey and a few other members of the orchestra including myself decided to go to Dayton to hear the McKinney orchestra.

We made the trip in Helvey's 5-passenger model T Ford. Dayton was 50 miles from Cincy and it was a trip well worth taking because I had never heard an orchestra like the Synco Septette. John Nesbitt had joined this group when he left Cincinnati. McKinney, who was a drummer, had stopped playing drums and was the business manager for the orchestra. I knew Nesbit and the other members we met that night. Cuba Austin was the drummer, Todd Rhodes, piano, Dave Wilborn, banjo, Claude Jones, trombone, Milton Senior, George "Fathead" Thomas, alto sax, June Cole, tuba.

The Synco Septette were a show band and dance orchestra combined and they were the first and only negro orchestra that I've ever seen with the high quality of musicianship and showmanship that they possessed. I remember seeing a white show band on stage at a theatre in Louisville, Kentucky, the first time I went to that city with Helvey, and I remember them doing a tune called "Sunday" which is a standard tune today. I had also seen other white show bands in some theatres in Cincy and they were always good. But the Synco Septette did their show numbers that the public could dance to and at the same time be entertained by songs in which the musicians would be putting on funny hats, mustaches, women's dresses, false faces and even the rhythm section were participating in those numbers, and the beat was going on at a tempo that none of the dancers would lose a step and they would be looking and listening to what the band was doing.

None of the bunch that had come to hear the Synco Septette moved from our places which was a little on the left side of the band stand until there was an intermission, and we were back before the band got on the stand again because we didn't want to miss a single sound or gesture. It was really an unforgettable night and we talked about it for days.

The dance finished around 2 or 2.30 a.m. and we were a real happy bunch of fellows that piled into Helvey's model T Ford and headed for home. But the morning was not as pleasant coming home as it had been when we were going to Dayton because half way back, the motor started knocking. The only thing that Helvey knew about the car was how to drive it and the rest of us didn't know that much. Eventually there was no power in the motor and we managed to go to Woodlawn Inn where Helvey called a taxi and we arrived in Cincy near 8 a.m. and no one was disgusted because of the mishap with the car because we had had a great thrill hearing the Synco Septette.

When "Jelly Roll" Morton came to Cincinnati with Fate Marable, he was telling everyone whose ear he could catch, that he was going to bring an orchestra to town that would wash Fate Marable's band away. So a few months later, Jelly came with his orchestra and to make a long story short, it was the worst sounding band I had ever heard. Where Jelly got those musicians, only the Lord and Jelly know. I remember that one of the trumpet players was the funniest looking red head, yellow complexioned person I had ever seen. And in a certain way, I felt sorry for Jelly because none of the musicians were doing anything outstanding and poor Jelly was working so hard to try and make the piano cover the band that he was wringing wet from perspiration and looking so downhearted that he would probably had given his diamond tooth not to have been in the predicament he was in that night.

Eventually some record of a band known as Fletcher Henderson of New York reached Cincy and the first one I heard was at Edgar James's house. On one side of the record was a number called "Money Blues" with a great trumpet solo. Later I found out that the name of the soloist was a man called Louis Armstrong. This was without doubt the greatest trumpet solo I had ever heard, and I bought the record as soon as I could find a copy.

From then on, Louis Armstrong was my dominant influence, and no-one in any orchestra that I ever heard enthused me as much. I thought it was the most wonderful sound I had ever heard on any instrument, because he sounded so different from everybody else in the whole band. He was like a star shinning on a stormy night. I started to buy Armstrong records - this was after he had left Fletcher Henderson and had returned to Chicago to record on his own. I remember I bought "Wild Man Blues" and learnt to play the solo note for note. If there was a slight mistake, I copied that also, because Louis could get over his horn so fast until the few things that I considered mistakes were not heard by someone if he was not a musician with a good ear. His mistakes were so beautiful that they sounded as though they were made purposely. Before this, the only trumpet player I ever heard of was Johnny Dunn, whose style I did not care for.

In those days, we did not have musical papers, and only a few of the guys bought records. The recording of "Money Blues" with Armstrong's solo on it, was the first Fletcher Henderson recording I had heard. Perhaps that is why there were quite a lot of players who were not influenced by Louis Armstrong; For instance, the trumpet player Frankie Newton, who joined Lloyd Scott's orchestra the same time as I, was more influenced by Bix Beidebeck, as was another trumpet player, whose name was Hicks, who was in the band before Frankie. Perhaps this was because it was easier to buy records by Bix in 1927 than Louis Armstrong. On the whole though, it was nearly as unusual for black musicians to be influenced by white as the other way round.

I enjoyed Fletcher's band and eventually found out the names of the musicians and especially the soloists such as Charlie "Big" Green, trombone. Joe Smith and Armstrong, Buster Bailey, and Coleman Hawkins-who was the tenor sax and bass saxophone player that could swing a band into bad health. You could hear his sax cutting through when the whole band was giving everything they had ensemble.

Then there were Henderson records with Armstrong and Joe Smith and these were somthing to write home about, except that I was at home! But they were great, Armstrong and Joe Smith as a team. Suddenly there were records of Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five and I learned that Louis had left Fletcher and gone back to Chicago where he had been before joining Fletcher.

The first Armstrong I bought was "Heebie Jeebies" and after that, any record that Armstrong made I was one of the first to have it in Cincinnati, because the people at the record shop began to know me as an Armstrong fan and would always put one of his records aside for me when they came in because they knew I would buy it.

The next thrill of my life was when Fletcher Henderson came to town. Zack White and a partner he had were the bookers of the well known orchestras that came to Cincinnati and bringing Fletcher Henderson was one of the high lights of their booking career and for us musicians, it was like having heaven sent to us.

The band came a day before they were to play and I remember the first one I saw but I didn't know, was Russell Smith. My instinct told me that he was from New York because he was dressed so well, and no-one around town had the class he had. So I asked him if he was the band and he told me yes. I told him that I would be at the dance because it was on a Sunday and they were playing that afternoon and night at the Crystal Ballroom which was at 5th and Plum Street.

I was there that afternoon before the band played their first number and I never moved from the place I had in front of the band until they played the last number of the afternoon. Joe Smith was the only one that had been in Cincinnati before and it was the first time to see Coleman Hawkins, Buster Bailey, Don Redman, "Big" Green, Charlie Dixon, banjo, Kaiser Marshall, drums, Bobby Escudero, tuba, Fletcher himself and the three Smith brothers, Luc, Joe and Russell - known as "Rops".

Fletcher played most of the songs I had heard him play on records and many I had never heard, but the thing that amazed me mostly was that "Big" Green usually took his solos after Joe Smith who was the only trumpet soloist for the jumping numbers in the band, and Green played note for note everything that Joe played. Joe's solos were played sweet in the Joe Smith style, and there were no solos on trumpet the way Armstrong had played "Money Blues".

Hawk was amazing and Buster Bailey was great. I had not heard too much of him on records. The arrangements were the greatest I had ever heard and I wondered if the day would ever come when I could be good enough to play in a band like that. We had to work that Sunday night and we were all pretty much inspired by the lesson we had received from the Fletcher Henderson orchestra. The only thing missing was that Louis Armstrong was not there.

The next time that Fletcher came to Cincy was the day before Helvey was to go to Lexington to play the fair. There was a dance at the Crystal Ballroom this Sunday afternoon with the Horace Henderson orchestra from Wilberforce College and Fletcher was such a big drawing attraction that Zack White was having him at the Armory, which was the biggest place in town to give a dance.

I was at the Crystal and Horace's boys with Freddie Jenkins, Joe and Casper McCord and Red Hicks on trombone were sounding real great. Fletcher gave Horace quite a few of his arrangemnts and Horace came close to playing them almost like Fletcher. There was a little fat brown-skin guy that was standing against the wall near the band stand who looked like he was mad at the world and only smiled occasionally when one of the musicians in the band looked his way.

I didn't know any of Horace's musicians well, but I talked with some of them the same as I had done with other musicians that I didn't know very well. So I asked one of the musicians at the intermission who the little fat salty looking guy was, and he told me that he was Rex Steward, a trumpet player that had taken Joe Smith's place in Fletcher's band.

Sunday night I was at the Armory to hear Fletcher Henderson's orchestra for the second time. Naturally my place was right in front of the orchestra which was placed on the floor in the middle of the Armory. There was not a band stand because it was not a place where dances were given and the only one that I know of, that did take place there, was this dance that Fletcher was playing this night.

The sax section had not changed since the first time the band had played in Cincy. Another trombone had beed added and he was a young fellow named Benny Morton and Rex Stewart had replaced Joe Smith. My interest was mostly in the trumpet section and I noticed that Rex was extra fast in his execution and although I didn't know much about styles, I knew that his was different from Joe Smith and what I had heard Armstrong do on records. Rex was amusing to watch but I did not understand or care for the way he played.

But the band was just as great as it had been the first time I heard it and the Armory was crowded. We of the Helvey orchestra left Cincy for Lexington full of praise for Fletcher Henderson and his orchestra and we felt as though we had gotten religion and were on our way to heaven instead of Lexington.

An orchestra came to Cincinnati in 1926 from New York under the direction of a man named Alex Jackson. It was mostly a society orchestra of 10 musicians: 2 trumpets, trombone, 3 saxes and 4 in the rhythm section. With the leader Alex who sometimes played soprano sax, they were 11. This orchestra had nothing in common with Fletcher Henderson or some of the other orchestras such as Lloyd Scott, Alfonso Trent, Horace Henderson and Speed Webb because they did not play the kind of jazz music that I had heard from other bands.

They made a big hit with the women, and wherever the women went, the men were sure to be there. So Alex stayed in the vicinity of Cincinnati for months and even worked at a white open air dancing place on Vine Street in Walnut Hills where no other negro orchestra had ever worked. Walnut Hills is a suburb of Cincinnati.

There were some nice musicians in Alex's orchestra and I became acquainted with Leonard Fields who had a technique like Rudy Wedolf on alto sax, Clarence Wheeler, who was the first trumpet man and Joldie whose last name I don't remember, who played a growl style of trumpet like Nassau whom I had worked with in the Clarence Paige orchestra.
Page 7

One day someone brought me a message from Alex Jackson saying that he wanted to see me. I never went to see him because I had an idea that he wanted to ask me to join his orchestra and it was not because I did not care for the style of the orchestra that kept me from going to see him. It was because I was afraid that I could not read music fast enough to be in the band. I found out later that Joldie could not read a note as big as he was and he was a good 195-pound man.

Early in 1927 I received an offer to join Lloyd Scott orchestra which I accepted because I had admired the band the first time I heard it and I also thought that I could read music better than I could when Alex asked to come and see him. I had refused another offer to join Speed Webb's orchestra who had been campaigning up state in New York and was getting ready to go to California.

When I told Helvey that I was going to join the Lloyd Scott orchestra he didn't want me to leave and threatened to make trouble for me even if he had to come to New York to do it. I had no idea if or when Scott would be going to New York, but I wanted to join the orchestra and told Helvey that I was leaving regardless of what he intended doing.

There was a tall trumpet player who had come to town from Virginia named Frank Newton and he had been playing with Clarence Paige for quite some time. Frank had been asked to join Scott also and we both joined the band in Lexington, Ky. and played a dance without any rehearsal. When Steve Dunn, the trumpet player that I had worked with in the Broadus band, saw me with Scott, he was so happy for me, that he hugged me like a long lost brother.

Scott played dances on percentage the same as most travelling orchestras did. The percentage was 60 % for the orchestra and 40% for the promoter of the dance. Lloyd paid me and the rest of the musicians $17.00 for our part and he must have had twice that much for himself and

his brother Cecil who stood in front of the orchestra with a top hat on his head like Ted Lewis. That was the most money I had ever made in one night and I never thought that Lloyd had cheated me out of anything if he took a bigger cut from the percentage because he had the responsibility of transportation and other things. I never expected to find another leader like Clarence Paige who counted the money out in packages of ten and gave everyone the same amount from a percentage dance and then asked everyone for only a certain amount to pay gas for the car when we were playing away from Cincinnati. I said I never expected to find another leader as honest with his men as Clarence Paige and I never did....

But I was so happy about the money I received from Lloyd Scott after the first job I did with the group that I saw myself having a bankroll large enough to choke an elephant in a few days. The next job we did, I received $ 7.00 but that was not at all bad for those days. My bankroll did not grow as I thought it would after the first night's pay, but I was happy because I was with a bunch of musicians that had been some places and had musical ideas that I had not experienced before. The musicians other than Frank Newton that I did not know were Dickie Wells, trombone, Lloyd Scott, drums, the leader Cecil Scott, tenor, clarinet and director, Don Frie, piano and Harold McFerran, alto sax.

The Scott brothers and Don Frie were born in Springfield, Ohio, Dickie Wells, Harold McFerran and Mack Walker came from Louisville, Ky., Frank Newton was from Virginia and Hubert Mann from West Virginia. (Harold McFerran and Mack Walker were half-brothers).

The band had no engagements to return to New York when I joined them, so I went to live in Springfield which was the home town and headquarters for Lloyd and Cecil. My wife joined me there after I had been in the town a few weeks.

Springfield was a very small town and there was not much in the line of excitement to interest anyone. That did not worry me but my wife began to miss her friends and relations and we began to quarrel and she decided to go back to Cincinnati, which was the last place I wanted to go back to, to live.

We separated and I moved [in] with a family named Jackson, where Frank Newton and Dickie Wells were staying. Don Frye lived across the street and the Scotts lived two doors from the Jacksons. There was Grandma Jackson, Joldie, one of the grandma's two daughters and Wilhelmina, the daughter of Joldie.

Frank Newton and I roomed together and he became the sweetheart of Wilhelmina and ate with the family. Dickie Wells, Mack Walker, Harold McFerran, John William and myself ate in restaurants. Hubert Mann was married to a Springfield girl and lived with her family.

The band was not getting much work so Grandma Jackson let us stay with her and when we did get a job or some jobs, we would pay her the back rent. There was a restaurant and poolroom near where we lived which was owned by a man named Rick and we ate there on credit and paid him the same as we did grandma when things were going alright. Neither Rick nor Grandma worried about their money if we were three weeks or more behind in our rent or eating bills.

We had plenty of time to rehearse and we did so everyday. We would play a popular number taking the first chorus as it was written on the orchestration, sometimes leaving the introduction as it was, or giving it another intro. Then we would all think of an idea to put in certain places. If the idea was good, it stayed. If not, we would pull some other ideas until we had the number sounding the way we wanted it.
