The piano player would probably give out the harmonies to the saxophones and the brass, then we'd decide to make a riff which would correspond with something that the saxophones were playing. Afterwards the saxophones would do the same thing for us. We worked on one number at each rehearsal and after a few months we had a fine repertoire, although nothing was written down on paper. The only problem was that, although these numbers were all worked out together, Cecil used to take the credit when they were recorded, because at that time, we knew nothing about ASCAP or Royalties.

Eventually the band got an offer to go to Canada for one month to play in a dancing place in Hamilton, Ontario. The engagement was during one of the spring months but we did not know anything about Canada except that it was supposed to be a cold country, so we took our over-coats and other winter clothes with us. When we arrived in Hamilton, the weather was as nice and warm as it was when we left Springfield. This was the first job that the band had for one month's stay at the same place since I joined it, and we really enjoyed playing every night for a wonderful audience.

There was not many negroes living in Hamilton and none ever came to the place where we were playing. There was no prejudice in Canada. Some of us stayed with a negro family and the man that owned the house had a very large cleaning business with at least 25 employees and they were all white.

A person was allowed two 2 quarts of whiskey or other alchohol drinks a month and could only buy it at government stores. One could also have a case of 12 bottles of beer and there was one label called White Horse Ale that I could get a fine feeling from after I drank two bottles. There were 4 of us staying at the same place, so we had no worries about drinks as we had 8 quarts of whiskey and 48 bottles of beer between us for the month and none of us were really heavy drinkers although I had learned to drink and get my share in Cincinnati.

John Williams got homesick for New York and eventually left the band and another sax-player from Louisville named Lester Carr took his place. The next one to leave the band was Hubert Mann. He received an offer to join Speed Webb's orchestra in California, so Rudolph "Bull" Williams, [who] lived in a town not far from Springfield was hired as banjoist.

Rudolph was a very stocky young fellow who had played football at Wilberforce College and because of his big face, big hands and broad shoulders, he was given the name of "Bull". His father was a preacher but "Bull" was everything except religious. I had met "Bull" a few years before when Edgar Courance and I had made friends with a couple of amateur musicians from Hamilton, Ohio, and we would go there for a couple of days every week and play in a small cabaret. It was the first time that I played for a radio in Ohio and "Bull" knew someone at the radio station who had invited him to join us for the season.
After our return from Hamilton, Ontario, I was able to pay Grandma Jackson back the rent I owed her and also pay Rick for the food I had eaten on the cuff before we left for Canada.
We rehearsed and had a few jobs that did not pay as much as one I remember well, was in the town where Ted Lewis was born.

Alex Jackson and his orchestra were playing in a town not far away and people from miles around had gone to hear him. It was another percentage deal and when Lloyd paid us, we received 35 cents each. That was a big drop from the first night I had played with the orchestra in Lexington, Ky., and received $17 for the night.

But I never complained because I was working with the best jazz musicians as a group that I had ever worked with. The Scott Brothers, Don Frye and Dickie Wells had New York experience and I was learning more and more about music and improving my style which was different from Frank Newton. It was a good thing to have two trumpet players in the same orchestra with different styles who worked well together in the ensemble.

We were like brothers that loved each other and the band was sounding better and better/with each rehearsal when the next offer came for a one week engagement. We never realized the actual quality of our playing until we were engaged to replace an orchestra called Warmack at the Arcadia Ballroom in Buffalo, New York and alternated with the house band who were known as the Buffalodians. The only thing I knew about Warmack was that he was from Louisville, Ky.

But the "Buffalodians" was an orchestra well known in the eastern states and were in the same category as the CASALOMA orchestra which was one of the best white orchestras ever organized. It was the first time that we had played in a dance hall that engaged two orchestras at the same time.

The ballroom was very long with tables on the side. The Buffalodians were on a high band stand at one end of the ballroom and we were on a stand at the other end. Our stand was not quite as high as the other one, and I suppose the reason was that the Buffalodians did more show numbers than we did. They also had 12 musicians and we were 10.

I enjoyed listening to the Buffalodians and one number they featured, I have never forgotten. The Title was "She's The Last Word," "She can't dance, but for real romance, she's the last word," etc. I still remember most of the words and when I think of the number now and then, it takes me back to my first week in Buffalo.

Jazz battles did not exist in the terms of battles that were to become known a few years later when we played opposite the Buffalodians, but it was a jazz contest every night and we were not as well known in Buffalo as the Buffalodians who had been playing the ballroom for years, but we blew enough and sang enough to have a big majority of the public applauding for us after each number.

The Buffalodians were throwing their best numbers at us, which is normal, and were throwing our best ones back at them. They, the public, and ourselves enjoyed every night of the week that we were in the Arcadia Ballroom.
Buffalo was the first city that I had been during the prohibition era,

that was wide open. It was the same as Cincinnati had been when I was a kid and used to walk up the streets where the "pretty ladies" (as I called the prostitutes) lived and worked. The saloons were open 24 hours a day and there were plenty of whore houses, especially in the district where we were staying, which was not far from the centre of the city.

This was something new to me as a young man and it was perhaps a good thing that we only had a one week engagement because I did not sleep more than 15 hours during the week we were in the city. I was getting my first real taste of night life, and I didn't want to miss anything.

There was one particular saloon where all the coloured musicians came after their nights had finished in the different ballrooms and clubs. There was a back room that had a piano and jam sessions or "cutting contests" as the sessions were called, was the order of the day from 3 in the morning, until 11 or 12 o' clock the next day.

I got my first kicks being able to stand at a bar drinking and talking until the cutting contests were getting hot. Then I would go in the back room, take out my horn and join in with the rest of the musicians. Each one would take turns in buying a round of drinks and no-one paid any attention to how much money he was spending, especially me;

I learned quite a lot from those contests because sometimes there were 3 or 4 trumpet players in the room and no-one played the piano. So we would see who knew how to do some difficult exercises that the others could not do. I learned how to jump from 'C' below the staff to the one above in the back room of the saloon, from a young trumpetplayer who had a style like Joe Smith. They used to have sessions of the [at] Rhythm Club in New York. One week, it would be for trumpet players, and different trumpet players would come round and play that night, and there would be three or four piano players to replace each other. We learnt a lot from those sessions.

It was also in Buffalo that I heard the greatest jazz violinist that ever lived. His name was Robert "Juice" Wilson. Juice played in a ballroom not far from the saloon where the musicians congregated and I went to listen to him almost every night before going to the saloon after I had finished work at the Arcadia. Juice worked until about 4 a.m, and we finished at 2 a.m.

I had not heard many jazz violinists because voilins were not played as a jazz instrument, although there were some orchestras that used violins in a very commercial way in some arrangements. I've heard the best jazz violinist since the first time I've heard Juice and to my estimation, there never was one greater than Robert "Juice" Wilson

Juice was playing clarinet also and I used to sit in for a couple of numbers with his group. But the violin was the instrument that he would cut everybody on, so he only brought his clarinet along to the saloon after he had finished his job. I suppose he was called "Juice" because of his drinking habit, but I never saw him drinking more than anyone else.

Cecil Scott stayed in the same place where I stayed which was not far from the jam session saloon and one morning he was so [loaded] leaded that I had to bring him home. That was not an easy job because I weighed 145 pounds and Cecil was on the short fattish side and weighed around 175 pounds. But I managed to get him home and in the bed and then I went back to the saloon. When I came home a few hours later, I looked in Cecil's room to see if he was alright, he had rolled out of bed and was snoring on the floor and that's where I left him because I was in no condition to try and lift 175 pounds of dead weight which can feel like 200 at certain times.

We ended the week in Buffalo and came back to Springfield. I had enough money left after all the spending I did in Buffalo, to pay Grandma Jackson and Rick the back debts I owed before we left for Buffalo.
Finally we were engaged to play a dance in Cincinnati which made me very happy because I would be able to show some of my friends and musicians

that I had known what a big step I had made when I joined Scott's orchestra. My father came to the dance this night, but he listened mostly to Lloyd because drums were still his love in any band or orchestra. I had never missed Cincinnati or been homesick since the day I left to join Scott, but it was nice to be home playing in a fine group for all my friends and old buddies to hear me.

I had bought a large handbag in which I carried the few clothes that I need for two or three days and there was enough room in it for me to put my trumpet which was in a bag that I usually carried under my arm. The day after we had played in Cincinnati we had a date in Springfield. We were fortunate enough to be travelling in two cars at the time and had a rendez-vous to meet at a certain time in front of the Sterling Hotel.

Some of the baggage we carried on the running board of the car, so I put my bag in the usual place where I always put it, which was on the fender near the motor and left front wheel. The bag was supposed to be tied on before we left. I was supposed to ride in this car also but as I had promised my estranged wife that I would come and see her before we left town, I told the chauffeur of the car where I was going and that I would not be gone long.

When I returned, the car with my bag on the fender had left and the chauffeur of the second car said that the other one had left because he wanted to get some gas and he would wait for me at a certain gas station in Elmwood. I was a little upset because I did not know if my bag had been tied on the fender as it should have been. When we arrived at the rendez-vous the first thing I heard was that my bag had fallen off the fender, two cars coming in the opposite direction had hit the bag and a third one had ran over it. I thought the fellows were kidding me, but when I saw my bag I found that it was not a joke.

The bag was split half open and when I took my horn out and looked at it, it was as flat as a pancake. I was broken-hearted to the point of almost crying and I asked the driver of the car why he had left without tying the bag on to the fender, he said that he thought it was not necessary.

I had no idea how I was going to play the job in Springfield that night. As it was the first time we were to play in the same town where we were living, I really wanted to be in the deal. I was rescued by a fellow who had a business of delivering ice. When I had nothing to do at times, I used to help him just to be doing something.

This fellow was an amateur trumpet player, so I got in touch with him soon after we arrived in town and he was pleased to let me use his horn which was not as easy to blow as mine had been, but I made the night which could have been a let down for the band if I had not been able to play.

The next day I took a train back to Cincinnati with my smashed up horn and went ot Wurlitzer's music shop where I had bought my other horn and I picked myself a new gold-plated Martin trumpet with a beautiful design on the bell. It was a 150 horn which was expensive in those days. My credit was good at Wurlitzers because I had bought and paid for my other trumpet on credit. They allowed me 25 dollars as trade in on my flatenend horn and I was able to pay 25 on my account and promised to pay 10 dollars a week until the horn was paid for. That never happened, but I'll tell about that leter.

I came back to Springfield the same afternoon and I was as happy as a mouse in a cheese factory because I had such a new beautiful and easy blowing instrument. A few days later, we played a dance in Dayton, Ohio, and I had the feeling that I had never played as well as I did that night. I had a case for this horn and I never put it on the fender or running board of any car.

There was a family named Paterson in Springfield that were in the undertaki ng business and sometimes Lloyd would engage one or two of their cars to take us on some jobs around Ohio. They had some beautiful black limousines, but most of the time, if the jobs were not too far away from Springfield, they had a big old high limousine that 10 of us, instruments and the driver, who was the one of the Patersons, could get into without being crowded. Every time we went somewhere in this car, which had been transformed from a hearse into a sort of bus, one of the back tyres would blow out. A car made like that one today would be historic phenomenon because the wheels
with tyres included were 3 feet high which made the car at least high from the ground level to the top.

The car had inside and outside rims and when one blew out, the outside rim would jump off, it would go rolling ten yards away from the car. The inside rim would hit against the body of the car with such force that it sounded as though a bomb had exploded. So much dust would come out up from the force of the rim hitting against the car that it looked like a foggy day in London town. But it didn't smell like that. There must have been dust in that wagon that was there from the coffin of the first person that died to ride in it.

We started going to Pittsburg, Pennsylvania and playing dances there and in Duquesne and mining towns not too far from Pittsburg. In most large cities or I should say in every large city in the country, there was wide open vice. Bootleg whisky, home brew, gambling and prostitution. Pittsburgh was jumping and Wiley Avenue was the main drag for the pimps, musicians and hustlers. We stayed at a hotel in Wiley Avenue and ate in a big restaurant near by, which was owned by a fellow named Gus Greenly.

Gus had known the Scott orchestra before I joined it and he was very fond of Lloyd, Cecil and the other members that had been and those that were now with the orchestra. Gus also had a gambling place next door to the restaurant and there was always a thousand dollars in silver dollar pieces stacked on the crap shooting table. Lloyd Scott was the only one in the orchestra that liked to gamble. He very seldom won anything.

With Gus in our corner we had nothing to worry about if we did not make much money working around Pittsburgh, because our credit was good in his restaurant. He would lend the orchestra his personal car if we needed transportation and he would bail us out if we could not pay our rent in the hotel who's owner was a friend of his.

One night in Pittsburgh I went to a club and was jamming with the musicians when a young boy 17 years old came in and took out an old trumpet that had no caps on the top of the valves. He did not have any experience and had not been playing long. But what he played there had plenty of fire in it

and I could tell that he was trying to play Rex Stewart's style of playing which was very fast. We started talking and he told me that his name was Roy Eldridge. He also told me that he was married and he was only 17. I don't know if it was true, but after I got to know Roy better, I believe that he could have been married because he was wild enough to do many things that most boys his age would not think of doing.

Shortly after we came back to Springfield from Pittsburgh, Bull William lost his father and inherited a model T Ford coupe. When we went on trips to different places Walker and I rode with Bull. The T Ford would run alright on a level road but when we came to a hill, if it was very long the radiator would heat up and steam would be coming from it like a puffing locomotive and we would have to stop and let it cool off. If we were near someone's house when this happened, we would ask for a pail of water and when the radiator had cooled down, Bull would put fresh water in it and we were off again. Everything would be alright until we came to another hill.

We drove to Pittsburg in this Ford one time and as Pittsburgh was a very hilly town, and when we were going down hill the car would coast down and Bull would give it the gas ans we would make the maximum speed possible to get up the next hill.

Some of them we made and the others we would automatically stop and have to push the car to the top of the hill. We always left for a job long before the others just in case the car really had trouble before we arrived at our destination. The others could pick us up along the way.

Eventually that happened. The car was quite old when Bull's father died, so one day we were rolling along not very fast and both the rear axles came out of place and down went the rear of the car. We managed to push it over to the side of the road, waited for the others to come by and pick us up and Bull never bothered to see if he could sell the thing for 5 dollars!
Life was the same routine with very few dull moments. Sometimes we made good money and sometimes we were broke.
But whenever we played a dance, our enthusiasm was always high and even if we had only a few pennies in our pockets, we played as though we had pockets filled with gold.

Just before Thanksgiving day in 1927 we were in the Buffalo New York area, and although Buffalo was till jumping, our luck had not been very good and I remember for Thanksgiving Day, I could only afford one meal in the Italian restaurant and that meal consisted of two hot-dogs and two tablespoons of Boston baked beans. Bread and water were free. The weather was one of the coldest that I ever experienced.

We played one good dance after Thanksgiving and when we came back to our hotel, Lloyd called a meeting in his room. He had not paid us yet and the idea of the meeting was to say that we had enough money to either take us to New York City or back to Springfield. We could go to New York, if it was satisfactory to everyone and try to get a job. The idea appealed to those that had been to New York before: Dickie Wells, Lloyd, Cecil and Don Frye.

I was the first one to speak about not wanting to take the chance. I had plenty of nerve and would go most any place without being asked twice, but I was afraid of going to New York City without a fixed job and knowing no one. Frank Newton, Bull Williams, Mack Walker, Harold "Hoggy" McFerran and Lester Carr felt the same as I had and the result was that we came back to Springfield.

Three weeks later Lloyd received an offer for a tryout at the Savoy Ballroom in New York City which I had been told, was the largest and best negro dance hall in the country. A well known orchestra leader named Fess Williams had been the house band leader since the place had opened. The tryout was to take place the Saturday before Christmas day which came on Sunday and the following Monday, the Saturday before New Year's Eve, New Year's Day and again the following Monday.
There was a woman in Springfield by the name of Miss Americus who seemed
quite wealthy. She was a friend of the Scott brothers family and she sponsored our trip to New York.

Many stories have been told about musicians arriving at certain places with holes in their shoes and this also was my case. I was happy about the idea of going to New York because we would have work for a few days, but Cecil had told me that sometimes in New York the snow was so high that you could not see at the other side of the street which was true after the sweepers had passed when there had been a real heavy snow fall. I was lucky that no snow had yet fallen in Springfield before we left. I had cardboard in my right shoe, which had a hole in it the size of a half dollar, and I was really upset about what the weather would be like when we arrived.

Cecil had also told me about the subway trains that ran underground which was certainly something I had not seen. He said that the doors closed automatically and that if one got caught between them, they would risk getting killed.

We left Springfield one afternoon by train and arrived the next day before noon. I recognised the city when the train hit the outskirts and saw the tall buildings with clothes hanging on the back windows. It was really a sight to see. And I was happy otherwise because the sun was shining and there was no sign of snow on the ground, so I knew my feet would not get wet. It was two days before Christmas and still no snow.
We had taken the New York Central lines which ran from Louisville, Ky., through Cincinnati, Springfield, Buffalo to New York City and arrived at the Grand Central Station.

Then I had my first ride on a subway. We could not afford a taxi because the little extra money we had left from what Miss Americus had advanced us for the trip, we had to be careful and not spend too freely. So I rushed into the subway train as fast as I could because I did not want to be killed or hurt in any manner when I had just arrived in the city of cities.
We all had our baggage with us in the subway and we must have looked
like a bunch of farmers to the regular New Yorkers because none of us were very well dressed except Dickie Wells.

But I was quite surprised when we came out of the subway and saw how dirty the streets were. The musicians that I had seen that came from New York were all so well dressed and from other things that I had heard about the city, gave me a certain impression like it was like Paradise on earth to see. The tall buildings were something that I had seen in magazines and photographs, but the streets littered with dirt and paper were something I did not expect to see. But here I was, in New York, the "Apple" as it was called by those who were born in the city or had been there for a long time.
Rooms had been reserved for us on 135th Street between 7th and 8th Avenue just in front of a police station. I also remember that it was a very sunny day.

That night the Scotts took us to the famous Savoy Ballroom on Lenox Avenue. The ballroom stretched from 140th to 141th Street and was on the second floor. There were different kinds of shops on the ground floor and a restaurant on the corner of 141st and Lenox Avenue.

I had never seen such a beautiful dance hall before, although I had seen some that were as large. The Savoy was long but not too wide, and 2000 people or more could get in the place. I had been told that there were hostesses for men who came alone to dance with. You had to buy a ticket at the end of the week. There was a bar for soft drinks, sandwiches, tables with water service and a cigar, cigarettes, chewing gum and candy stand.

There were two band stands and one of the bands that were playing when I came in was the Fess Williams Orchestra which I had heard about. Fess was dressed in a tuxedo with rhinestones in the lapels and a top hat with the same kind of stones around the band of the hat. The other musicians were dressed in regular tuxedos. I recognised having seen one of the trumpet players when I was younger and had to put/long pants to get into the

Theatres up town in Cincy. I did not know his name but the face I remembered so I asked Cecil who he was and he told me that it was George Temple. George and his brother had been in Cooper's Black and White Show which was a mixed show that I had seen in Cincinnati when I was about 16 years old.

The rest of Fess Williams Orchestra was another trumpet, trombone, 3 saxes and a full rhythm section, piano, banjo, tuba and drums. But I did not hear anything from this orchestra that was sensational or excited my emotional feelings and in fact it was a corny band as far as I was concerned, which did not merit the praise that I had heard.

Fess was a sad clarinet player and a corny singer who was also known as the black Ted Davis. George Temple had most of the trumpet solos and all that he did was growl them. But regardless of what I thought Fess and his musicians were the pride of the Savoy.

I was standing by a railing just in front of the two band stands where I could see and hear everything that happened and when Fess had finished his set, the other orchestra came on. Both orchestras had their names above their stands and this orchestra was under the leadership of Arthur Gibbs. I had never seen or heard about these musicians but when they started their first number, I knew that it was an orchestra that had something to say, and during their set they said plenty. There was one trumpet player who played more and better than the two in Fess's orchestra, one trombone, 3 saxes and full rhythm section. The tuba player took ad lib choruses that I had never heard a tuba player do before. I had heard bass saxophone choruses and Mac Walker could riff on the tuba. But this fellow was tops.

When Arthur finished his set, they came off and I left my place to go and find the trumpet player. I told him my name, and that I was a trumpet player and it was my first night to New York. Also, that I liked his playing very much. He told me that his name was Leonard Davis. Later I got to know the other musicians who were Edgar Sampson, alto sax, Happy Cauldwell, a little fellow with a big voice and big tone on tenor sax; George Washington, trombone, Paul Barnet, banjo, and Billy Taylor, the tuba man
The drummer was Ralph..... I don't remember his last name, nor the name of the other alto.
I did not bother to listen to Fess Williams anymore but every time Arthur Gibbs played a set of 4 numbers, I found a place across from them where I could hear everything they did.

Once while I was listening to the orchestra a girl was dancing with a fellow but she started smiling at me, so I decided that I would ask her for a dance. I was not a lover of dancing and very seldom did it. But I had a desire to dance because the music of Arthur Gibbs was so inspiring.

I went to the booth where the tickets were sold to dance with the hostesses and bought a ticket because I was under the impression that I had to have a ticket to dance even if the girl was not a hostess.

When the girl had finished dancing with the other fellow, I invited her to dance and when we got on the floor, I offered her the ticket, she was surprised and must have thought that I was really a dumb one. She told me that tickets were only necessary when a man danced with a girl that was hired for that purpose. I felt ashamed that after one dance I made an excuse to leave the floor and never saw the girl again.

Then came the great day of our tryout for the job. The matinee started at 4 in the afternoon on the 24th December 1927 and we were replacing the orchestra of Arthur Gibbs at 7 o'clock for one hour while they had dinner. That was alternating with Fess for one hour and then with Gibbs for another hour.

Before coming to New York we had uniforms made by a mail order place and when we received them in Springfield, none of us had a perfect fit. But it was a uniform made of Oxford grey cloth with a black band around the collar and lapel of the coat and the same band around the side of the pants. We bought green checkered ties to go with the costume.
When it came to our time to replace Arthur Gibbs, there was no announcment but the name of Lloyd Scott had been printed on a sign which was
placed over the name of the band we replaced. No one knew us and we knew no one.

We got on the stand which had music stands that high that they almost covered our faces when we were sitting down. We had no music because all of our arrangements had been memorised and we didn't need any music.

Everybody was anxious to hear what we were going to do. The manager the hostesses, waiters and some of the Gibb musicians delayed going to dinner to hear what we were going to do. The "Lindy Hop" was the rave dance at the Savoy where it was started by a group of the wildest dancers I ever saw. When we hit our first introduction to one of our many arrangements these dancers of the "Lindy Hop" almost had a stampede trying to get to the dance floor and that was enough to show everybody that we could play. We were not nervous about playing in the famous Savoy Ballroom in the great city of New York for the first time.

We became very popular with the "Lindy Hop" dancers and after we had finished our two hours of alternating with the two other orchestras, I hung around to listen mostly to the Gibbs band and talked with Leonard Davis who told me that we looked like a bunch of country boys when we were waiting to play our first set, but that we really had a jumping band.

We brought something new to the Savoy that was later copied by the Fess William's bunch and became a fad that every orchestra that played in the Savoy copied also. Cecil stood in front of the orchestra as did Fess Williams and he also wore a top hat and could do the Charleston while playing the tenor. But the rest of the musicians played sitting down. As the music stands were so high at the Savoy, Dickie Wells, Frank Newton and I decided that we would stand up when we had a solo. That made a hit with the public and also gave whatever number we were playing more salesmanship and attracted the attention of the people who were not dancing. I believe we were the first musicians in the country to start the style of a soloist standing for his solo.

I became acquainted with some of the musicians of Fess Williams' orchestra. Bobby Robinson played alto, Jelly James, trombone; a little fellow called Stony played tenor. Kenneth Roane was the first trumpettist. The rest, I do not remember their names except George Temple whom I talked with and told him that I had seen him before. His brother was known as Red Temple. They were both light coloured and the brother had red hair.

After having played three days we were paid and the first thing I did was to go to 125th Street to a big shoe shop called Adler and buy myself a pair of shoes. Before that, I almost was ashamed to walk because I thought that people would see the hole in my shoe and I didn't dare to crook my leg for the same reason.

Mack Walker and I were room mates and always have been when travelling. In Springfield Frankie Newton and I were room mates. Mack and I started getting acquainted with Harlem from 125th Street up to the Savoy, Lenox Avenue over to 8th Avenue which had an elevated line, the first I had ever seen. The streets were dirty but the city itself and the pleasure I was having taking in the sights was very exciting.

I had been told about a cabaret called Small's Paradise, so Cecil took Mack and I there during the week that we were waiting to play the New Years holidays at the Savoy. He had told me as I said before about the place but nothing about the band that was playing there. The leader was a pianist named Charlie Johnson and we had gone to Smalls quite early as Cecil said the first show was always the best to see.

The band started and Charlie Johnson left the piano and I never saw him anymore that night. But what a band! it had been quite some time back when I heard Fletcher Henderson and here I was listening to an orchestra that was in the same class as Fletcher and I had never heard of the band before. There was an outstanding trumpet player who played fast, clean as a whistle and also used a derby which he waved over the bell of the horn to get an open horn wa-wa effect. I had not heard Armstrong in person and I couldn't see how Armstrong could be better than this man whom I had not heard a word about before.
I asked Cecil who he was and was told that his name was Jabbo Smith

I was overwhelmed with joy at hearing and seeing this man who to my estimation played more trumpet than all the trumpet players I had heard put together, and the band was swinging like no band I had ever heard could do.

Cecil pointed out an alto sax player whom he told me was Benny Carter. I knew nothing about him but Cecil said that he was one of the best in the business and a fine arranger. But Benny didn't kill himself blowing that night. He wore a shade on his forehead to keep the bright light from shining in his eyes and sometimes held the sax to his mouth but not a finger was moving.

The banjo player was very good as were the rest of the rhythm section and it was surprising how the band swung along without the pianist. The drummer was another outstanding personality, especially during the floor show when there were fast numbers that the girls danced to and the finale which was very fast.

It was my first time to see a floor show which was not much different from shows in theatres. The girls were beautiful and the comedians were funny. The show was good and exciting but the finale was really something to see because when the last girl had gone off the floor, the band kept playing the fast number and the waiters came on twirling their trays, spinning them on their fingers, on pencils and tossing them back and forwards to each other. And these were the regular size trays that were used in big hotels and weighed as much as two or three pounds, perhaps more.

Charlie Johnson came back to the piano only when the band played the last number of the night. I did not know if he was a good pianist or not because he didn't take a solo on the number, but he had the second best orchestra that I had heard in person.

Saturday the 31st of December 1927 finally came around and we were back at the Savoy to alternate with the two regular bands. And we would also know at the end of the 3 days if we had been good enough to be engaged at the Savoy as a regular house band.

What surprised us this Saturday was to see the trumpets and trombone player in Fess Williams's orchestra stand up when they took their solos. We had been first to do that and of course it was something that we could not copyright or have a musician arrested for doing it. In fact, it gave us a good feeling to know that we had been watched as well as listened to by the musicians as well as the public.

Two of the many tunes that we had in our repretoire that made a big hit with the dancers were "Willie the Weeper," which the two trumpets and trombone played in three-part harmony, the way Louis Armstrong had recorded it, and "Springfield Stomp" which was a collective head arrangement of a number composed by Cecil Scott and Don Frye.

When we finished our last hour on New Year's Monday 1928, we hung around talking with different people until Lloyd called us all together in a corner and told us that we had been accepted to play at the Savoy as a regular orchestra for 6 months, starting in February. I had been taking it easy on the drinks because my loot was not too long and I did not know before how our six days' audition would turn out. But when Lloyd gave us the good news, Mack Walker and I went out and got juiced.

New York City was like Buffalo concerning the bars which never closed and there was always plenty of people on the streets at any hour of the night and morning. I really felt like I was in heaven because I had a new pair of shoes, I was in the apple and would have a regular job in the following month. What happened in between now and the time we started at the Savoy did not matter just then.

The next few days were real rough because my money was very short and so was that of Mack Walker. We were real buddies and shared what ever money we had between us. We could manage only one hot meal a day, so we ate sweet rolls which we could get 10 for 15 cents in a bakery. That was our breakfast which we had around one or two o'clock in the afternoon, and we ate a hot meal for 25 cents with coffee, tea or milk in a big cafeteria on 8th Avenue not far from where we lived.

After one week of eating in this manner, Lloyd came around and told us that he had a job for us in a cabaret for the rest of the month in January. The name of the place was the Capitol at 140th Street and Lenox Avenue under a big Chinese restaurant. Lloyd had played in the Capitol with a famous orchestra. The owner manager was a Mr. Johhny Powell and the cabaret had been one of the most popular clubs in Harlem.

We started working there on a percentage basis because Johnny Powell could not afford to pay a regular salary. The Capitol had lost its popalaty and business was not good, but Johnny was trying to keep the place going in hope that it would become popular again. We had to play behind a couple of women singers who's names I don't remember. They went from table to table when ever there were enough people for them to sing to. I had not worked in a cabaret before and this was something new to me. If the singer recived a tip for singing at the table, she was to divide half of it with the band. She sang the same song at each table and it automatically an obligation for someone at the table to give her a tip.

Depending on how many people were in the place, a song could go on for as long as 45 minutes in which time we could each solo behind the singer 4 or 5 times. There was also the kitty which helped us also. The kitty was the box with a slot in the top and/whenever a person demanded the band to play a certain number and if we knew the number, they were obliged to put some money in the kitty which we did not have to divide with the singers.
We never made much on this job but it gave us a chance to become well acquainted with the new numbers we rehearsed during the day and I did not have to depend on eating sweet rolls for breakfast.

We were at the club every night to start at 9 o'clock but if there was no one in the place we just sat around and talked. There was a doorman upstairs at the entrance and he would always warn us when someone was coming in by shouting 'PARTY' down the stairs. We would jump on the band stand and
strike up a number that made whoever was coming in, think that the joint was jumping. We would be playing until 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning.
We were also playing the two-hour dinner break for the musicians at the Savoy on Sundays. The Savoy only had matinees on Sundays and holidays.

I met a fellow about my age named Bob Sawyer who became a good friend of mine. The first new friend I had made in New York. The dancers that were regular customers and top "Lindy Hoppers" became our friends also. There were such names as Shorty, Twisted-Mouth George, the Sheik, Slim Willy and Fats Rolland. They and the girls they danced with were our real supporters but Bob became a real friend of mine. He showed me how to tie a bow tie. I bought them already tied before that. He showed me around Harlem and took me to parties. Bob became like a brother to me and I never forgot him because he really showed me what New York was made off.

Now and then, musicians would drop by the Capitol to listen to the band and some would sit in for some jam sessions. One that I had not heard about was a trumpeter named Cuban Bennett. This man was a musician's musician because he had a style in the order of Joe Smith but he did more changes, as harmony was called, and he did not use a plunger like Joe Smith did. I mean that his tone was like Joe's because it was mellow and round. He played a few numbers with us and then he asked Don Frye if he knew "Fascinating Rhythm". I had never heard the number but Don Frye knew it. It was difficult number to play straight and that's what Cuban did on the first chorus. But after that he ad libbed and I never heard so many changes played on a trumpet. "Fascinating Rhythm" was fantastic when played by Cuban Bennett.
Cuban was a cousin of Benny Carter but I was told that he was an alcoholic and no one could rely on him. He could have been in some of the best

orchestras in the city I was told, but if he was hired by anyone they knew the chance they were taking. He was a swell person to know and more than a wonderful musician. The only harm he ever did to anyone was to himself. Of course he was not the only musician that alcohol would not let go anywhere, but it was a pity that this happened to such a talented man as Cuban Bennett.

We composed a number and called "Lawd Lawd" and decided to really break it one Sunday at the Savoy. Frank Newton sang the words and we answered him repeating the same words. Frank scatted the middle part and there were not other words except "Lawd Lawd". We played it on the second set alternating with Fess Williams and it went over so big with the crowd that it was the only number we played on that set. The people kept shouting Lawd Lawd ever time we finished it. And when we came back on the stand again, it was the same shouting for the same number.

The manager of the Savoy, a Mr. Charles Buchanan, the owner of the place, a Mr. Moe Gale and his father, came out of their office to see what all the shouting was about and everyone was so enthusiastic about "Lawd Lawd" that it was the only number we played for the rest of the two hours that we were there. And that really tied up the contract for our coming engagement at the Savoy.

Playing the numbers was one of the biggest and best paying rackets in New York City. Gangsters had complete control of the racket and they also controlled the bootleg alcohol racket and controlled most of the bars. Almost everybody played the numbers from one penny to dollars. For one cent it paid 5 dollars so that even the poorest of the poor had a chance. The last three numbers of the total amount of the result of the days receipt of the stock market were the winning numbers. Bob Sawyer taught me how to play the numbers which could be played straight or in combination form.
I still had the bag that had fallen out of the car with my horn it it and one day, I hit the numbers for 5 cents which brought me 25 dollars and I bought a new bag.

The band decided to buy tuxedos to open at the Savoy so we went to a store at 125th Street that sold clothing on credit and bought new tuxedos which made us look better than with the mail order uniforms that were so badly cut.

Then came the great day of our opening at the Savoy. We had rehearsed hard during our stay at the Capitol and even had some written arrangements so that we would have some music to put on the high music stands.

There was a big surprise waiting for us on opening night. Fess Williams band had left and so had Arthur Gibbs. The second band was Horace Henderson. Fletcher had to aid his younger brother by hiring Benny Carter who had left Charlie Johnson and Rex Stewart especially for Horace's debut at the Savoy.

We were on the stand that had been occupied by Fess Williams. I sat on the end on the right side of the stand, Frank Newton on my left and Dickie Wells left of Frank. Cecil stood in the middle, Lester Carr left of Cecil, Harold McFerran in the back, Mack Walker and Lloyd were on the same level as Don.

Rex Stewart was on the left side of the other bandstand and that put him and I next to each other. From the very first night until Horace finished at the end of February it was a battle of jazz which ended in a draw. Benny and Rex did a lot for Horace's orchestra. Benny played much more than I had heard him play with Charlie Johnson orchestra and Rex was the fastest man I had ever heard on trumpet. He was better than he was when I first saw him with Fletcher in Cincinnati and I especially liked his fast execution on Tiger Rag which was faster than many clarinets could play.

Each band would have what we called a killer- diller number to finish every set and as the dancers and listeners roared their approval, it was difficult for one band to start after the other had played their killer- diller. Both bands had their fans and there were always discussions amongst the dancers and the connoisseurs of jazz. Both sides were connoisseurs. The dancers heard everything that was happening on the band stand while they were still flying through the air, Lindy-Hopping.

The Savoy was jumping so much every night that Mr. Buchanan was afraid that the floor would give in and it was true that without dancing, one could stand on the floor and feel it bouncing up and down. The music stands on Horace's bandstand would be bouncing like mad when we were playing, and the same thing would be happening on our bandstand when Horace was playing.

So Buchanan told both bands to cool down a little on each set by playing a medium number, then a slow number, a waltz after that and make the last one jump. What happened was that the dance floor would be half empty during the first 3 numbers. Each band leader was given a placard that he would hold up for the public to see which announced what kind of dance number would be played next.

When the sign for the last number would be held up and the band that would be playing the last number of the set hit the introduction of the number, the hoppers would come out jumping from every corner of the Savoy as if there was a stampede to see who could get to the middle of the dance floor first. I really got my kicks when it was time to play the last number of the set watching those cats come out jumping like broncos.

Rex and I became very good friends and we started going to bars and jam sessions together. A fellow from Chicago came to New York and opened a hangout for musicians called the Rhythm Club on 131st Street near 7th Avenue. There were pool tables and card games and like the bars, the club was open 24 hours a day. Bert Hall was the name of the owner. Musicians who were married and had sweethearts that wanted to get in touch with them could have their chicks call them on the phone or receive letters at the club. When musicians were wanted for a gig, there was a board on which a notice could be posted.

The big attraction however would be jam sessions at least twice a week. A sign would be put up on the board announcing a supper for a certain date in order to let the word get around. Jam sessions were called suppers. Saxophone supper, trumpet supper etc. The musicians and occasionally a drummer banjo and bass. But the majority of the time there would only be some pianists.
who would relieve one another when one became tired.

Jam sessions were also known as cutting sessions, meaning that the musicians that played the best had cut the other or in other words, had won the battle. As many as 10 or 15 instrumentalists could be counted on to be at the club whenever their particular instruments was announced for a supper.

Rex and I used to attend these sessions together and I would sit in when the feeling hit me. And when it got too hot for me, Rex would come in and then the joint would really start jumping. No one could quit just because Rex came in but he was a master and everybody would play their hearts out to make him play more. The tunes would always be something that was popular and well known.

Another popular place for jam sessions was the back room of a bar known as Greasy's at 129th Street and 7th Avenue. The place was owned by an Italian as most of the bars in Harlem were and Greasy was a barman well liked by everyone. Cuban Bennett used to make this place his second home and that's where I really became acquainted with his style of trumpet. Most of the time the sessions were strictly trumpet suppers with a saxophone or trombone sitting in at times. The accompanists would be a guitar which was becoming popular in orchestras. There was no piano in the back room so the accompanist had to be a banjo or guitar and many were the mornings that it would be 10 or 11 o'clock when I would leave Greasy's looking dirty and greasy after all the juice I had downed besides blowing my horn for hours. I learned many things in those sessions and many of them would be a record collectors dream idiom today if they had been recorded.

Mack Walker and I had moved into a room in the apartment of Billy Taylor, the tuba player that had been with Arthur Gibbs at the Savoy. We were living now on Manhattan Avenue and 116th Street and I would take the elevator train at 135th Street after the sessions and get off at 115th Street and 8th Avenue. People used to look at me in the train at 10 or 11 o'clock in the morning dressed in a tuxedo at that time of the day and they must have thought that musicians were crazy people.
I would sleep all afternoon and get up in time to go and get something to eat and then get to the Savoy for another night which was always a pleasure.

There was a girl that worked at the candy and cigarette counter in the Savoy named Margie who was very beautiful and I used to talk to her sometimes when I was not on the bandstand. I never flirted with her or tried to make her my girl friend and she had no eyes for me in that sense. Rex saw me talking to her quite often, and as he was bashful, he asked me to introduce her to him which I did one Sunday when another orchestra was playing the supper hours.. A few months after Horace had left the Savoy, Rex and Margie got married and later had 2 or 3 children.

I hated to see the Horace Henderson group leave the place at the end of February because I had enjoyed the competition between the two orchestras and so had they. It had been a new experience for me and it was different from the way we had competed with the Buffalodians because they were at one end of the hall and we were at the other end. But at the Savoy the two bands were next to each other and we were real friendly enemies which made the competition greater and the desire to blow stronger. Rex and I were running together and jamming also and we had become buddies but the best of friends must part and they were as sorry to leave us we were to see them go.

Fess William Royal Flush Orchestra came back under the direction of a musician from Louisville, Kentucky named Lockwood Lewis, because Fess had been engaged to direct the pit band of the Regal Theatre in Chicago. We changed to the bandstand where Horace had been because Fess had always used the one we had been on. Lockwood played alto sax and clarinet and was a very good showman and a loveable person. Dickie Wells and quite a number of other Louisville musicians had come up under the guidance of Lockwood.

The Royal Flush Orchestra didn't jump like Horace so the sign announcing the different dances was not used anymore. But we continued to play the hard driving swing that we did against the Henderson boys because it was our style and we made the Hoppers really take off when we were on the stand. But Lockwood and the members of the Fess Band who had been working there for
a long time, were well liked by the Savoy clientele and employees.

Bob Sawyer always knew where a party was taking place and sometimes I would take out my trumpet and blow with the pianist who would be engaged to put life into the shindig. Chicks were jumping, I was working and New York was like Heaven on earth for me.

Harlem was booming and I had been there 3 months before I had gone further down town than 125th Street. I had had all the enjoyment that I sought from there up to the Savoy. But one day I got the feeling to go down town and see what the centre of Manhattan was like. I asked Bob to be my guide and we took the subway from 135th Street and Lenox Avenue and came out at 42nd Street and Broadway. Broadway was the busiest Street that I had ever seen and suddenly it seemed to me that all the people in the world must be in New York. We walked up Broadway and past the famous Roseland Ballroom where the Fletcher Henderson and Jean Goldkette orchestras were playing. Goldkette had the best white big dance band in the country and I had heard much talk about the band.

The tall buildings in down town Manhattan were amazing. Cincinnati had a tall building called the Skyscraper, but to me most of the buildings in down town New York were skyscrapers and the Woolworth building was almost twice as tall as the skyscraper in Cincinnati. There seemed to be thousands of movie houses and theatres. This was an Alice in Wonderland land that the Indians had sold for 25 dollars. They really were not booted.

To get back to Harlem with the subway, it was necessary to change at 92nd Street. The same procedure was necessary going down town to Broadway and 42nd Street. Bob showed me how to change but the first and second time that I went down town alone I made the wrong changes. After that it was no sweat.

The Savoy had something every Sunday afternoon called Opportunity Day which was for amateur performers to compete for 3 prizes. the first 10 dollars, the second 5 dollars, and the third, seven admission tickets which the winner could use at his own discretion. There were amateur Lindy Hoppers and the regulars that we knew. We had composed a number called

"Hop Off" which the regular hoppers who would compete in the Opportunity contest would ask us to play for them. They would rehearse in a corner of the Savoy during the week nights and cooked up tricky steps which they would present on Opportunity day with 2 couples dancing together, then 3 couples that would change partners and they would all execute the same step just like a section of instruments playingthe same riff in unison.

In a weekly local paper that covered the activities of entertainers and musicians, a reporter wrote: Every Sunday afternoon at the Savoy is Opportunity day and no wise person will pass up a honest to goodness opportunity. Let us see you next Sunday, hopping on it as Lloyd Scott's orchestra hops on "Hop Off".

Another edition read: And Lloyd Scott's "Too bad" band every Sunday oh boy! If you have not heard them, don't miss next Sunday. They hop in "Hop Off" and you 'll hop up and hop around while they jazz. No way to make your feet behave, you'll have to let them have their way.
The things those amateurs did was worth more than the admission fee to get into the Savoy to see. But there were other amateur acts, acrobats, contortionists and musicians.

One amateur who became famous especially in New York at Connie's Inn was a young fellow named Earl Tucker. He had come from Baltimore and wore sailor pants and shoes with tap dancers taps on them. He was a double-jointed fellow and could twist his body like a snake dancer and tap dance at the same time. He could stand back on his leg in a way that one would think they were going to break and he won the first prize the first time he came to Opportunity night. People started calling him "Snake Hips" and it was not long after that that he became one of the start at Connie's Inn.

The most fantastic personality to take part in these amateur contests was a violinist called Brother Brodie. Some people had asked me if I had ever seen or heard him. I hadn't so I asked for some information about him and all that they would tell me was wait.......

So one Opportunity night I saw a fellow with a long back frock coat like the Jack-Legged Preachers wore and a violin case. He was a queer looking bird of a certain age and I knew this must have been Brother Brodie and it was.

After all the other contestants had done their numbers, Buchanan came on the stage which rolled in and out under the bandstand. He made a big announcement to present Brother Brodie: and now ladies and gentlemen, it gives me great pleasure to have in our presence tonight the greatest of great violinists, none other than the one and only Brother Brodie!
I couldn't believe it because the truth is that he could not play at all. It was so comical that I and those that had known about him almost died of laughing.

And he made his living by playing for people just to make them laugh. He visited the clubs and theatres and never asked the public to give him anything because the owners or the managers enjoyed having him make their clients laugh. They would give him a few dollars. Brother Brodie was a nut but he was a wise one because he never came to the same place too often and in that way he was always an attraction whenever he came around.

Connie's Inn and the Cotton Club were in the heart of Harlem but the only negroes that went there were the ones that worked there. These two cabarets catered for the wealthy clientele that called going to Harlem, slumming. Both clubs had extravagant floor shows and the artists were the best in the business as were the orchestras.

I don't remember what orchestra was playing at Connie's at the time but I think it was a semi-classical one. At the Cotton Club which was 2 blocks from the Savoy going in the direction of 145th Street an orchestra called Duke Ellington was playing and I heard that Freddie Jenkins was in the band. I had heard some records of Duke with a growl trumpeter named Bubber Miley and a growl trombone player named Tricky Sam.

Next door to the Cotton Club was the Lenox Club which was for negro but white people were also admitted. The leader of the band was Banjo Bernie and there was a breakfast dance every Monday. It started at 5 o'clock in the morning and most of the club musicians and entertainers would meet there to enjoy being together after a week of going to work in the places they were engaged. I started going there when I first heard about the breakfast dance when we were at the Capitol. The thing lasted until the last party left which was ad mid-day sometimes.
Now and then a musician would sit in with the band but it was never a jam session. The guy would sit in because he felt like playing which I never did because I has having a good time otherwise.
At one of those breakfast dances I saw Freddie Jenkins, who was known as "Posie" for which reason I was to comprehend later. We were happy to meet again and told each other our experiences.

I met another musician whom I had known since childhood at the Savoy. He was Sidney de Paris whom I had known in Crawfordsville, Indiana when I was 6 years old. Sidney really knew that I knew him when I called Gabriel because it was a name that he had been given only when he had come to Cincinnati. Sidney started to call me Crawfordsville. He had been living in Philadelphia but was now playing with Charlie Johnson and had come to the Savoy during a break that the band had at a certain time between shows. His brother Wilbur was still in Philly.

Sidney told me that he was surprised to see me playing trumpet and with the Scott brothers whom he had known when they had been in New York before. He also told me that here had been changes in the musicians that had been with Charlie Johnson. Jabbo Smith had left. He and Leonard Davis had been hired and Edgar Sampson had taken Benny Carter's place.

When I spoke of hearing Charlie Johnson's orchestra for the first time, I forgot to mention that Jimmy Harrison, the great trombonist, was in the band. But the night I heard it, I don't remember him having any solos. Jimmie was

not in good health and the one thing I noticed was that he held a hand on his stomach when he was not playing. Jimmy was replaced by George Washington which made 3 musicians of the Arthur Gibbs orchestra that joined Charlie Johnson after the Scott band went into the Savoy, Jimmy Harrison died in July, 1931.

Lloyd informed us one night that John Williams would be coming back with the orchestra and gave Lester Carr two weeks notice which a few of us did not quite agree was correct although we had nothing against John. Lloyd was the leader and it was his privilege to fire and hire whom he pleased. No-one ever signed contracts in those days. Instead of legal security, there was always an agreement; if you wanted to leave, you would give the leader two weeks notice, and he gave you the same if he wanted to fire you. If, on the other hand, he fired you straight away, the union obliged him to pay you two weeks salary.

Mr. Buchanan had given us the name of Lloyd Scott and his Bright Boys, because we were always doing something new in the line of entertaining while playing without making a number real showy. In "Lawd Lawd", we all had little washboards on which we scratched the rhythm behind the scat singing of Frank Newton and the baritone sax of Cecil. Sometimes, there would be a sharp whistle at the end of some chorus before a soloist would come in for the next chorus. Once we cooked up a gimmick on "Tiger Rag": When it came to the part of where the words are "Hold that Tiger", we had cap pistols and everyone except the rhythm section would jump off the bandstand and run around the floor shooting these pistols and shouting "Hold that Tiger; Where's the Tiger? Hold that Tiger"...it made many of the clients wonder if there was a fight and some one had started shooting and some would head for the nearest exit. Buchanan asked us not to do the number in that manner because it frightened some people.

During these months at the "Track" which was the nickname for the Savoy, (because it was as exciting for some people to come there as it was to go to the race track), we were paying back the money that Mrs. Americus had advanced us to come to New York and other debts we owed in Springfield. Our salary was 40 dollars a week which I thought was good at the time, and it was coming in regularly. I had never worked such a long time at such a salary and if I had not been a great spender, I could have had a quite nice bankroll put away in a short while.

I had written to Wurlitzer in Cincinnati where I had bought the new trumpet on credit when my other one had gotten smashed, to let them know where I was. I thought that they would send someone from their company in New York to give me information on how I could continue paying for my horn but I never heard from the, and no-one ever came to see me about the payment which really did not worry me in the least.
The Royal Flush Orchestra left for 2 nights during the summer season and Alex Jackson who had worked his way back to New York was engaged to play

the two nights. And this was when we got our revenge against his band because they had played a town not far from where we were playing in the town where Ted Lewis was born and they had drawn all the people to their dance and we made 35 cents each for our nights work.

It was revenge in a satisfactory way because we had always been a better swing band then Alex Jackson's and we proved it these two nights. We threw everything except the kitchen stove at them and after every set we went off of our stand with the dancers still applauding and after every set it would be 10 minutes before Alex could start his set. In a certain way I felt sorry for them. They had been big shots in Ohio and perhaps other places, but they received a lesson in how jazz should be played for two nights and they were a sad looking and downhearted bunch of fellows during those hights.

I had been told about a trumpet player named Ward Pinkett who was said to be one of the best in New York. I eventually met Ward and saw him quite often but never heard him play which I regretted very much. Ward was not in very good health and had been told by a doctor that he had only a few months to live. I think he was born in Virginia and he went home with the thought that maybe some rest would prolong his life, but he soon became lonesome for the gay life in New York and came back. He said that if he didn't have long to live, he was going to enjoy himself and that's what he did until he died a few months after he came back to the Apple.

The Lafayette Theatre located next door to Connie's Inn was the most popular gathering place for Harlem entertainers in New York and the Rhythm Club was just around the corner from the Lafayette. So there was always plenty of activities in that block between 131st and 132 street with all the musicians going/in and out of the club and the show people all along the block in front of the Lafayette and Connie's.

The Tree of Hope was just in front of the entrance to Connie's Inn. It was said that when you touched the tree and made a wish, you would have your hopes come true. That was a superstition mostly among theatrical people but there was seldom a time if a musician passed the tree that he would not touch it to bring him luck whether he w as superstitious or not. How long this legendary tree had been there I do not know, but I became one of those who touched it every time I passed it and most of the time I had no particular wish to make.

When I came to New York and long before that, I was known as Johnson Coleman and sometimes people call others by their last names only. So some called me Johnson, and others called me Coleman which made some people think that my name was Coleman Johnson. And some of the hoppers at the "Track" knew the names of most of our group but they were not certain as who was who and I've had many of them calling me Dickie and they would call Dickie Wells, Coleman, when they saw us on the streets and we were not together.

August 1928 came and we went on a tour. We had been in the Savoy for six months, the longest run the band had ever had in the same place. Our first stop was Pittsburgh and we left New York on a Greyhound bus in the early afternoon and stopped in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania where I got the surprise of my life. This was a regular Greyhound stop at a restaurant where the buses were timed from their starting point to stop during the lunch or supper hour.

We went into the restaurant as did the other passengers and after going to the men's room we came out and sat down at the counter where food was served. A girl gave us plates, knives and forks and water which are the usual things that are done in a restaurant. After that, the girl never came to take our order. For sometime we did not think that it was unusual but eventually after seeing everyone else being served, we wondered what was the reason we were not being served.

After about 10 minutes of waiting, a man behind the counter came to us and said that he was sorry but they did not serve colored people and that there was a Greek restaurant around the corner where we could be served.

Here we are in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, which I had studied the history of when I was in school, the history of Abraham Lincoln and his issue of the proclamation of Emancipation. And we were refused to be served in a restaurant that was a regular Greyhound bus stop for Greyhound bus passengers.

We didn't raise any hell because we tried at all times to be as gentlemanly as possible, and anyway it was no use but it was something that I never dreamed could happen in Gettysburg. I never paid much attention to prejudice at that time because I was born in to it and I knew where and where not to go if I did not want trouble.

It was embarrassing to us and I think that the chauffeur of the bus should have told us because he must have known about the situation as we certainly could not have been the first Negroes to pass through Gettysburg on a Greyhound bus. The girl that had given us the seat must have been new in the restaurant and she was probably also embarrassed.

I had eaten in white restaurants in Michigan and New York and I just could not believe that something like that could have happened in Gettysburg which is in a Northern State and especially where Lincoln had made his famous speech about the freedom of mankind.
Of course the situation did not upset us and after we had eaten in the Greek restaurant, we came back to the bus to continue the journey as if nothing had happened.

I was with some of the group from the band that was sitting in the back of the bus. There was not prejudice pressure put on us to sit at the back of the bus and those that did go to the back went of their own free will.

A young white fellow came in the bus in Gettysburg and sat in the back with us. He became friendly and a few miles outside of Gettysburg he asked us if we had ever smoked reefers. I had heard about them but had no idea about what they really were. I told him that I had never smoked one and asked him what their effects were to a person that smoked it? His answer was that it makes you laugh. He really enjoyed himself until we all finally went to
sleep because it was night when we left Gettysburg.

We played one week in Pittsburgh for a marathon dance which was the rage all over the country. How long it had been going on and how long it lasted after we left, I do not know. It was amazing to see some of the couples so tired that they would take turns to sleep on each others shoulders. We played slow number, fast ones and waltzes but the dancers never changed their pace which was the slowest of the slow drags.

From Pittsburgh we went to Cincinnati where we stayed for one week playing the Greystone Ballroom on a Sunday, Wednesday and Saturday for white dancers only. Then we played one night at Ed Gauthier's country club which was one of the very few country clubs for Negroes in the States and owned by a Negro. Gauthier had become a millionaire from the two gambling places that he owned in Cincinnati and the club which had golf links and a country swimming hole, was about six miles outside of Avondale a suburb of Cincinnati.

We stayed in Cincy two weeks and although I did not stay with my parents, I went to see them every day. Dickie Wells would always manage to get to my father's place before me because my ole man had learned to make home brew and always had a few bottles on ice. But when I arrived there, Dad would tell me that I was too late as Dickie had been there and drank all the cold beer.

From Cincy we went to Lexington where we played one week for the fair and it really jumped. Came back to Cincy and played at the Crystal Ballroom and then went to Louisville, Ky., I had been there a few times with Helvey but this was the first time with Lloyd.

We had two cars driven by a couple of wild Lexington fellows and we went through a certain part of Indiana before crossing this river to the Kentucky side. As we were going along a very wide dirt road these two drivers started racing. The car I was in passed the other one and then the other one would

pass us. This went on for a few miles until finally as we were about to pass the other car again, the other driver made a manoeuver as if he was coming over to the left side of the road to cut us off and our driver pulled over to the left at the same time and our car went over on the side in a ditch.

We were saved by a miracle. The ditch we went into was about 5 inches deep at this particular place. Our car went over on the left side and bounced back onto the road. We were shaking like falling leaves when the driver stopped the car. The miracle was that just a few feet from where we went over, there was a ditch about 3 feet deep. The only damage/that was was done was the rack that was on the left running board in which there were some bags was torn off and John William's bag was busted. The car had only a small scratch on the front fender.

In Lousiville we played a big dance and stayed there a few days. All of Dickie's friends came to the dance and there was no question of us paying for all the juice that was passed to us. I and most of those in the band that drank could carry the load so we were never drunk while working. Bull Williams, the ex-football player, didn't drink and Harold "Hoggie" McFerran drank very little.

There was a bar in Louisville that I had known from the first time I had gone there with Helvey, which was very popular with musicians and entertainers because one could get the best home cooked beans that were ever cooked in this place. For 5 cents you had a big bowl of beans, 5 cents was also the price of a pair of hot dogs and the same price for a big mug of beer. The bread was free and I ate in this place many times even when I had enough money to afford a meal in a good restaurant. I always loved beans and this place cooked them like the real country people did.

One day Dickie's parents invited the gang to have supper at their home They made home brew the same as my father and so many other people did during Prohibition. We were all at the table in the dinning room, eating a fine meal that his mother had prepared when suddenly we heard a noise

as if someone was shooting a pistol in the closet. Then there was the same sound a few seconds later and after that it sounded as if a war had begun. What happened was that Dickie's parents had made a new batch of home made brew and there was a little too much yeast in it. So when the stuff started to formulate, the proportion of yeast made the bottle tops blow off and when someone opened the closed door it was covered with foam. Bottle after bottle blew it's top and there was nothing to do but to let them blow.

A few days later we left Louisville and went to Springfield and played in a park near Xenia, Ohio, not far from Springfield. People came with their lunches and picnicked on the grounds of the park and we played the late afternoon dance. Then we came back to Springfield and Lloyd stayed to collect the money.

For two days we did not see Lloyd but news got around that he had been seen with two girls in a rented car drived by a chauffeur and money was all over the floor of the car. The next day, we received notice that there would be a meeting at a certain time.

When the meeting started it was not difficult to see that Lloyd was drunk. He announced to us that he had lost all the money gambling which was something that we knew Lloyd loved to do. But he had never taken the money that we had worked for to gamble with. He said he was sorry and started to cry. Then he became indignant and started saying that some of us ha done certain things against him and told me that I had been afraid at one time of losing my job with the band and being replaced by Rex Stewart, which was something I had not heard about until he spoke about it at that moment. He was drunk, had lost our money and could not think of any good excuses. But we had always been such a brotherly bunch that none of us was really angry with him although we were to leave for New York in a few days and I for one, did not know how I was going to get there. We had made nice money during the tour but we had some days that we did not work and I was a

nice spender also. A few days later, I was almost knocked off my feet when I received the news that Lloydhad gone back to the gambling place, had won a few hundred dollars, bought himself a new top coat and had taken a train to New York which left the rest of us to get back to New York the best way we could.

I knew a girl in Lexington that was quite friendly with me and she had loot, so I wrote and told her my situation and asked her to send me enough money to get back to the Apple. She sent me enough money to get back to the Apple and a little more so that I would not arrive broke.

We started working at the Savoy in September. In November we recorded four numbers for Victor which was the first record date for me and most of the others in the Scott band. The titles were "Bright Boy Blues" "Lawd, Lawd", "Springfield Stomp", and "In a Corner". These were the numbers that had brought us fame at the Savoy. The only one that had vocals was "Lawd, Lawd". Frank Newton sang and we answered him. He scatted the middle and then went back to "Lawd, Lawd" with the rest of the ensemble answering as in the first 16 measures. Cecil Scott took credit as the composer of "Lawd, Lawd" and "In a Corner" and included Don Frye as co-composer of "Bright Boy Blues" and "Springfield Stomp". But the fact was that we had all contributed to composing the numbers and there was no written arrangement of any of them.

Wednesday the 12th of December, there was a big battle of jazz with 6 orchestras from 8.30 in the evening until 3 a.m. the next morning. Duke Ellington, Ike Dixon a band from Baltimore, Maryland. Charlie Johnson, Arthur Gibbs, Lockwood Lewis and the Royal Flush Orchestra and Lloyd Scott. the Savoy had special publicity printed and this was the way it read!

When Christmas of 1928 came, the Savoy management gave all its employees a gift of gold pieces. It was our first year as regular employees, so each received a five-dollar gold coin. The other employees, depending on the length of time they had worked there, received ten and twenty dollars in gold.

In January, Lloyd and Cecil wanted to bring Hubert Mann back into the orchestra, and we all chipped in to send Hubert his fare. The reason for bringing Hubert was that Bull Willimas had a dispute with Buchanan and took a poke at him, but missed, and some of the bouncers grabbed Bull to keep him from taking another kick at Buchanan, and he had Lloyd to fire Bull.

We took a banjo player named Teddy Bunn, until Hubert arrived from California, where it was said that he had been a member of a Holy Roly Church. Hubert arrived at the time that we were having rehearsal, with a straw hat, a light-weight suit, summer shoes, and no overcoat. Lloyd managed to get his tuxedo for the night, and when he came to work that night, he was so drunk that he went to sleep on the top of the piano, which was up, and he sat next to it, in a manner that made it easy for him to lay his head on and forget everything.

When Buchanan saw Hubert sleeping on the piano top and bouncing with the rhythm that was coming from the dancers, that made the floor bounce, which in turn made the bandstand and piano bounce, he was so angry that he could have bitten a nail in two. He told Lloyd to get rid of him right away, and there went the money we had chipped in to Hubert's train fare to New York! Teddy Bunn came back the next night and stayed with us until we finished the last of January to go on the road again.

Lloyd asked Bull Williams to come back and he accepted. Our first stop was in Baltimore, which was our first time to play in Maryland. Baltimore was a paradise for travelling musicians, because there were more women than men during those days, and five or six girls would be after one musician at the dance. Too bad we were there for only one night.

The only gigs that we ever played on tour were dances. Once we played a fair in Kentucky in Lexington, which went on for a week, so we played for a whole week for dancing. The hours were long but I never paid much attention to them. Usually, we would start at 9 in the evening, and work until 2 in the morning.
