Sometimes at the Savoy, when we played there on a holiday, we'd play from 3 in the afternoon, and work until 2 the next day, with an hour off in the middle. Buchanan would hire a relief band to play for that hour. In fact our first audition at the Savoy, was when we played for two hours as a substitute band. Usually, we alternated with another band. We would play a set of four numbers, followed by the other orchestra, which also played four numbers. Like that, an hour goes very fast, particularly, as most musicians in those days seemed to enjoy playing. We didn't find the touring too hard. We were young and did not pay too much attention to the difficulties of things. Many times, I had gone to work having only had just enough time to eat a sandwich. Also with Scott, our tours were arranged so that we would have two days in a place. Mostly we played black dances and the atmosphere was quite gay. There were quite a few knife fights and sometimes I saw people badly hurt, but the trouble was usually over another woman, or a bottle of whiskey. It wasn't like playing dances for white folks in the South, where the trouble was racial. That could be very dangerous for black bands.

We were travelling by bus the same as we had done to Pittsburg when we had stopped in Gettysburg. We did not have enough steady one-nighters to hire a private bus and no agent as most bands booked themselves at the time. Our next stop was a dance in Frostburg, Maryland and it was really a frosty place because it was in February and below zero. There were not more than 10 people that had the nerve to come to the dance because we had been engaged to do so.

There were two big coal stoves on each side of the hall that were red hot but they did not heat up the place, which was like being in one of the large frigidaires at the Chicago stockyards. Our instruments were like blocks of ice and we had our gloves and overcoats on. It seemed as thought we were playing in the open air at the north pole. And we almost had a tragical night because there was no hotel and only one Negro family in the town. Whenever there was a dance in Frostburg for colored people, they came from the farms where they worked in surrounding towns.

So here we were without transportation as the bus we were going to take the next day would not arrive until 8 a.m. and it would not have been possible to sleep in the dance hall. What saved us was this one Negro family who offered to let us sit in their living room by a hot fire until it was time to take the bus. I never found out what Frostburg could be like in the spring or the summer but I know what it was like the night we were there.

We played Philadelphia for the first time and there I met Wilbur de Paris and told him that I had known him as a kid in Crawfordsville. He remembered a cousin of mine that was about the same age as he and we had a good time talking about those days.

Then on to Pittsburgh where we were very well liked. Roy Eldridge had left to join Speed Webb. We did towns in Ohio such as Youngstown where I stayed in a hotel that had so many chinches in the bed that it
was impossible to sleep. I killed one or two and there must have been at least five hundred that came to their funeral.

We played Gron ton, Middletown, most of the mining towns, Columbus, Dayton and then went to Detroit where we played in Jean Goldkette's famous Greystone Ballroom. Lloyd must have really cleaned up that night because he gave us fifty dollars each, the most money I had ever made on a percentage job in one night. I had learned by now that Lloyd would really look after himself first on percentage jobs, so if he gave us fifty each, it was certain that he a Cecil had three times that much or more.

But I did not worry about that as long as he treated me fairly. He never paid us for the date we did at the park, after he had lost all the money and then winning it back took off for New York leaving us to get back the best way they could. We forgave him and forgot it in a manner.

We played a battle of jazz with Zack White's Orchestra in Cincinnati which had as its Director a young alto player named Tremb but better known as Inky because he was so black. I had met Inky some years before in Richmond, Ky., where he was born. I had gone there with Clarence Page and Helvey. Inky had seen Cecil Scott work and had copied the style of wearing a top hat which Cecil and Fess Williams had copied from Ted Lewis. Zack had a very nice orchestra but we were too much for them because we had been together longer and were ahead of them because of our being from New York, which was aleays ahead of everything in the line of good bands as far as those around that part of the country were concerned.
We also washed away the orchestra of Speed Webb in a battle of jazz in Cincinnati. Roy Eldridge and Teddy Wilson were in the band but I did not know Teddy then.

Once in Pittsburg we alternated with the Cotton Pickers when they were under the leadership of Don Redman and Joe Smith was in the band. I had been ashamed to take my trumpet case from the bandstand in

Cincinnati when Joe Smith was on the stand sitting in with the local band, but now I was not afraid to play at the same dance as he and someone told me that Don Redman asked who I was because he liked the way I played.

The first time I played with three trumpets was when Gus Mo Clung, whom I had first heard with Scott, came back in the orchestra. Gus had a dispute with Don Redman when Scott had been in New York long before I joined them. Gus played with Clarence Page in Cincinnati in preparation to joining the Cotton Pickers after he left Scott and when Don was engaged to lead the Cotton Pickers, the first thing he did was to fire Gus.

So Gus joined our band in Cincinnati and Lloyd let Frank Newton go when we returned to the Savoy. We were in the Savoy when Marion Hardy's Alabamians came with Cab Calloway who sang through a megaphone three feet long. Eddie Mallory, one of the trumpet players became one of the ex-husbands and Charlie 'Fat Man' Turner eventually opened a bar called 'Fat Man's' on 155th Street and St. Nicholas Avenue that became very popular. Cab took over the leadership of a band called the Missourians which eventually became his band. Sammy Stewart was another orchestra from Chicago that came to the Savoy when I was there and he had some men of whom two became famous and some very well known. George Dickson and Walter Fuller were on trumpets. Sammy played piano and Chu Berry whom I had met in Wheeling, West Virginia, was the tenor man. On drums was Big Sid Catlett.

Fletcher Henderson was engaged for one night and we had played some numbers which I don't remember what it was, but the dancers did not want us to stop and we played for a half hour longer before we finally left the stand and when the public saw that we were not coming back,
they left Fletcher play. That was one night that I thought the public was very unfair because I knew and we all knew that although we had a good band, we were really not in the class of Fletcher.

And when Fletcher did start to play, I came back on our bandstand to listen to them and after that it was hard for us to play for two reasons. One was that Fletcher had scored with the public which wanted more from him when they had finished their set and the second reason was because we had lost the battle and really did not want to play any more although we still tried, but there was not much fight left in us. Without a doubt Fletcher Henderson had the greatest dance orchestra in the world, before, then and long after that. Its worse than a shame that a guy like Paul Whiteman who could hardly hold a violin was known as the King of Jazz at the time when Fletcher could have made him wish that he had never heard the word jazz.

Another thing that was a thrill for me at the Savoy was the masked ball once every year. The first one we played was called 'Arabian Nights' and the second 'South Sea Island'. There was also a big ball once a year called 'Female Impersonators Ball'. We called it the 'fag ball' as these sort of individuals were called faggots or sissies, which would make it a sissies ball.

I never cared much for dancing myself and seldom did it, but on 'Faggot night' if I did dance it would be with a girl that I knew was a girl. This was the biggest mixed ball of the season and some of them actually were beautiful and looked like women. There were black, brown, yellow and white ones who came from uptown, downtown and all around the town. Some looked like sweet young girls and others looked like prizefighters with their

big muscular arms sticking out of short-sleeved evening gowns. Prizes were given for the best dressed, the best hairdo and the most feminine. This really was the biggest ball of the season and the most funny also.

For the Arabian Night and the South Sea balls, all the employees which included the hostess and musicians, wore special costumes. We were dressed like Arabs and the hostess' like harem girls for Arabian night. For the South Sea Island ball we were in pirate costumes and the hostess' in Hawaiian straw dresses. For the Sissie's ball we were in our regular costumes to show at least there were a few men there.

Another well known dance hall at 7th Avenue and 138th Street was called the Renaissance. It was not as large as the Savoy but was very nice with a large balcony around three sides of the walls and one big bandstand. Usually private balls were held there and the leader of the regular orchestra or house band was named Vernon Andrade. Most every musician in New York worked for Vernon at one time or another because Vernon did not have a regular bunch of musicians that worked with him. As the Renaissance was not open every night, whenever there was a ball, Vernon would hire whoever was available. But the bands usually sounded not bad.

Another place smaller than the Renaissance was the Bamboo which had a band under the leadership of Joe Steel, a fine pianist. And Chick Webb whom I had not met but had heard much talk about, was leading a band at a white dancing school on 125th Street and 7th Avenue which included a trumpeter named Bobby Starke whom I had met at the Rhythm Club. I had heard about Bobby only after I had been in New York a certain time and was told that he
was a terrific trumpet man.

The Lafayette Theater changed shows each week and bands also. We were engaged for a week which was the first time we ever played a theater and accompanied the entertainers, dancers and chorus girls. The bands always played in the pit and if there were not more than ten musicians they would supplement the band with two or three more musicians.

But we preferred to remain as we were and after the first two shows, we found out that our experience in that kind of work was not very strong. We had to play a curtain call number which is a number that is played before the show begins and we could not get ourselves together sitting in a pit below the stage. We thought that if we played on the stage it would be better. The manager of the theater let us try it and we went over big. The public could see Cecil with his high hat dancing in front of the orchestra and we stood up for our solos as we had done at the Savoy. We also played the rest of the show from the stage and it was something new that the manager of the theater decided should be done by the other bands coming in also.

After Christmas of 1928 and New Years 1929 we went on another tour and came back to the 'Track' on Easter Monday of 1929. Three orchestras played that Monday for 12 hours of dancing. Fess Williams, Lou Russell and Lloyd Scott.

Things went fine for us at the Savoy until Lloyd got drunk one night, had an argument with Buchanan and took a swing at him. But like Bull Williams, Lloyd missed because Buchanan knew that it was going to happen as it was not the first time someone had tried to knock his head off. He knew when to duck. One of the bouncers who was always near when Buchanan had words with someone,
grabbed Lloyd and held him and Buchanan fired the band then and there. This happened in June 1929.
I knew New York well by that time and I was not afraid to face the facts. I started to go to the Rhythm Club every day and started getting some gigs.

One night I had nothing to do and as I had been invited by Bobby Starke to come and listen to Chick Webb's bank whenever I had the chance, I decided to do that. The dancing school was for whites only but coloured musicians could go in and sit near the bandstand to listen to Chick and talk with the fellows when they had a smoking break.

Chick was a little humpbacked fellow about 4 feet tall but that was no handicap for him when it came to playing drums and he was doing things with those drums that I had not heard another drummer do. He was taking breaks and playing the cymbals with a different beat behind each soloist. He had a real swinging group with a bunch of musicians that quite a few of them became famous. Those that I had not know except Bobby Starke were Russell Procope, Elmer Williams(alto and tenor), Jonny Hodges, alto, Cuffee Davidson, trombone, John Trueheart, banjo, Howard Scott whom I had seen in the Alex Jackson band when they played the Savoy for two nights, was the older trumpet man and Don Fitzpatrick on piano. I think the bass was Elmer James.

When Chick found out who I was he told me that he had heard about me and some day he was going to have me in his band. I was to hear this statement from Chick many times and would have been very happy if it had ever come true. Chick had then and after a band that any jazz musician would have been happy to be a member of.

After Chick had finished the night, Bobby Starke asked me if I would like to go downtown with him to see an uncle who lived in a district called 'Hell's Kitchen'. So we took the El at 125th Street and 8th Avenue and got off somewhere downtown in the 50s on the west side. Bobby's uncle made his own moonshine and he rolled out a 5 gallon jug and invited us to help ourselves. He was very proud of Bobby and especially because he was a good musician. Bobby could put away a lot of juice and so could I, but we didn't make a dent in the jug of his uncle and we were flying high when we left.

When we decided to come back uptown Bobby suggested that we take a taxi and I agreed. When we arrived at 131st Street and Lenox Avenue, Bobby told the taxi driver to turn left and go in the direction of 7th Avenue. He told me to get out when the taxi stopped and to wait for him in a hallway down the street in back of the taxi and he would take care of the fare.

I thought there was something fishy about this but did as he told me. As I was going into a hallway I saw Bobby say something to the driver and walk away. I was watching what was happening but the driver could not see me. Bobby had disappeared and after a few minutes, I saw the driver get out of his taxi, look up and down the street and then get back in and drive away.

I came out of the hallway and walked in the direction of 7th Avenue and then I saw something that put me wise to what Bobby had done. On the corner of 7th Avenue and 131st Street was the building where Connie's Inn was situated and the Lafayette Theater was next to it on 7th Avenue. There was a space between the two buildings going from the back of the one on the corner around to 7th Avenue. The stage door of the theater and the back entrance

to Connie's was in this alley. What Bobby had done was to tell the driver of the taxi to wait a minute for him and he had gone in the alley and come out on 7th Avenue. I did the same thing out of curiosity, came out on 7th Avenue and walked around to the Rhythm Club. There was Bobby as unconcerned as if nothing had happened. He told me that he had not intended to pay the taxi and that was a trick he had pulled before. I didn't like it but couldn't do anything about it.

There was a well-known restaurant next door to the Club called Tabbs that never closed and it was very practical for entertainers and musicians who worked late and wanted to have some food before they went to sleep. There was also a great hamburger stand on the other side of the Club owned by a fellow named Jesse Wynn. Jesse made hamburgers so tasty that they almost melted in your mouth.

Tabbs had the best hominy grits, sausages and eggs with hot biscuits and butter oozing from them, that you ever stuck a tooth in. And thats what I decided to have after I left Bobby to feed some of the juice that I had drunk at his uncle's place. Bobby Starke and I became very good friends.

I dont remember who was in Lou Russell's band when they played at the Savoy on Easter Monday 1929 with us and the Royal Flush orchestra of Fess Williams but he was advertised to play two nights with Louis Armstrong. Russell's first name was Luis but the Savoy had him billed as Lou. Armstrong was being called Satchelmouth now and this was the first time he was coming to New York since he had left Fletcher Henderson. I was still in Cincinnati when that happened and as Armstrong was not with Fletcher when he came to Cincy, I was filled with joy at the prospect

of being able to see and hear my idol for the first time. That night, I went quite early to the Savoy because I did not want to miss a note coming from the horn of Satchel. There was a trumpet player with him whom I had met named Louis Metcalf. Metcalf sat on a high stool, wore a cardboard gold crown and called himself 'King Louis'! He had on his crown when Armstrong came on the stand after a big announcement by Buchanan. From the moment that he started the first number until the end of it, Russell's band sounded like a 12-piece band and there were only 8 which was the smallest group that had ever played at the Savoy.

When Satchelmouth came on the stand I was pleasantly surprised because he was a much better looking man than the few bad photos I had seen and collected of him. He was not as fat as I thought he would be but he was stocky and not as dark as the photos had me believing. His trumpet looked like the most beautiful golden horn that I had ever seen. The more he played, the better he sounded and he was not playing the things he had recorded in the same manner that I had heard them. They were sounding better and much different which means that he was not copying himself but playing the way he felt. And he must have been feeling mighty good. His fingers seemed to be flying over the valves and the things that were coming out of his horn were things that I had never heard from any trumpet player before and that's when I realized that Armstrong was the king of all kings of jazz.

And Metcalf realized it also because when the next set came he did not put on his crown. The following set he did not come back on the stand. I would have loved to have gone back the next night but I had a gig. I was told that Metcalf did not come to work the next night.

But Metcalf could play and he had a fine style with plenty of technique. He never wore his crown after Louis Armstrong left. It was one of the greatest thrills of my life to have heard this man who was destined to do so much for jazz.

One week before the end of June, Dickie Wells came to my house and said that he had a job for us with a drummer he knew by the name of Dewey Beasley. We met Beasley and he told us that the job was up-state in a place called Poughkeepsie, New York. This was Dewey's home town and the job was at a place called Woodcliff Park, which was an amusement park. The job didn't pay much but we could live and have a little group of our own.

So Dickie, myself, Mack Walker, Harold McFerran, and Don Frye got together again with 'Bull' Williams, an alto player from Dayton, Ohio named Melvin Scott and a tenor named Bobby Sands. So Beasley had a 9-piece orchestra to take to Poughkeepsie. We worked 4 days a week, Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays and Sundays and played matinees on special occasions and holidays which were not many in the summer.

I had started writing to my estranged wife and we decided to get together again, so she came from Cincinnati after I had been to Poughkeepsie about 3 weeks. The job went fine and Dewey was very happy because he had been able to bring a group to his home town. We got plenty of rest because there was not much activity in Poughkeepsie except for the park which had a dock on the Hudson river and excursion boats stopped there with tourists.

One day near the end of the season which was in September, I received a letter from my old buddy Higginbotham. He was playing with Luis Russell who was now at the Roseland Ballroom where Fletcher had worked and Higgy told me that he could get me in Russell's orchestra. So when we finished in Poughkeepsie, I lost no time getting to New York. I took a room with a
woman that Mack Walker and I had stayed with before for my wife and myself. We could cook there and that was much better than having to eat in restaurants and cheaper for two people.

I joined Russell's orchestra which was composed of mostly musicians from New Orleans. And those that were not were strangers to me. There was Henry 'Red' Allen, trumpet, Albert Nicholas, alto and clarinet but he played clarinet most of the time, George 'Pops' Foster whom I had seen carrying a bass violin once but had never met him. Paul Barbarin was the drummer. They were all from New Orleans. The others were Charlie Holmes, alto, Teddy Hill, tenor sax, and Higgy who was the only one I knew.
Metcalf had left the band, I was told, because Russell had sent for Red Allen when he went into the Roseland and Red played too much horn to suit Metcalf, so he quit.

I never knew how long Higgy had been with Russell or when he came to New York but we were both happy to see each other after the year we had been with Helvey and before that when we were amateurs. I told him that I was married and that my wife had known his sister in Cincy.

Red Allen played first trumpet on everything and took all the solos. Of course Higgy had plenty of solos and so did most everybody except me. Finally I got a one chorus solo on a number called 'Feeling the Spirit', which was recorded the 9th September along with 'The new call of the Freaks' and 'Jersey Lightning'. This was my second recording date and for the third one also with Russell, I had an 8 bar solo in the middle of the second chorus of a number called 'Broadway Rhythm' recorded on a label called Banner and Russell used the name of Lou and his ginger-snaps.
Eventually I got a solo on a head arrangement of Sweet Sue. But I never played a first part or had any other solos.
I had been working on a transfer Union card which was not acceptable to 802 any longer, so Russell advanced me the money to get an 802 card from the Union.

Metcalf took Russell to the Union claiming back pay. The Union scales were different for white dance halls and negro ones. The difference was that the white ones were supposed to pay more than the Negro's. The scale at the Roseland was supposed to be 65 dollars a week. The whole band had to go before the Union trial board which was the same as any court with a judge and jury. The only thing we did not have was a lawyer.

They called us into the trial room one at a time and we all swore that we were getting the correct scale. They tried in every way to break one of us and if that had happened we would have all been fired. But each one of us stuck to our story and when they called Russell in and could not break him, they dismissed the case and told Russell that his men were really with him. The truth is that we were not getting the Roseland scales but I think it was not very kosher of Metcalf to have enjoyed himself playing with Russell which I think he did, accepting to go into the Roseland with him when he knew he would be paid less than the scale of the place, quitting the band because he was displeased about something and then try to make a disagreeable situation for Russell and the rest of the musicians.

At the Roseland the coloured musicians had a dressing room down in the basement of the building that housed the ballroom. The boilers for heating the building and hot water were in the basement and it was necessary to walk up three flights of stairs which were in the back of the building and come out of a side door to get to the bandstand that we occupied.
After we had played each set, if one did not want to walk down three flights of stairs and sit in a room that

had nothing in it but lockers in which to put overcoats or other clothing, you could stand in the back stairway near the electrician's booth and play cards until time to go back and do another set. There was no such thing as socializing with the dancers or having a special booth inside the dance hall with a table where we could sit and play cards or drink as the white orchestra could do.
White people could come to the Savoy and the men danced with the hostess or any Negro girl if she felt like dancing with the man or a white girl accepted to dance with a Negro.

So after each set at the Roseland, we stood on the back stairway and played cards. I never played and did not know many card games before that, but I got interested in playing Black Jack or twenty-one as the game is also called. We only played for 10 or 20 cents but it was possible to win from three to five dollars a night if one was lucky. And one of the luckiest of lucky guys was Teddy Hill. Teddy never lost and he would also win in card games at the Rhythm Club which was one place I never played cards at. I only played at the Roseland to pass the time.

After about six weeks with Russell, I began to feel the effects of not having a first part to play and only two solo spots, because we did not play 'Broadway Rhythm' where I had an eight-bar solo. Cecil Scott had reformed the Bright Boys under his name with a new drummer in place of Lloyd and had started working in the Savoy. I got lonesome for the 'Track' where I could socialize with the people and plus the fact that I was not satisfied with the role I was playing in Russell's band, so I went to see Cecil one night and asked him how were the chances of my coming back to the group. He was very happy about it so I gave my two weeks notice to Russell and when it terminated, I joined Cecil.

The band was now almost the same as the Original Lloyd Scott Bright Boys except for the drummer whose name was Arnold 'Scrip' Boling (L) and a banjoist named Casper Tow ...... who was later replaced by James Smith. I felt the results of not having enough to play in Russell's band and it was almost two weeks before my chops began to get set and strong the way they had been before joining Russell. I was not disgusted with Red Allen because he blew more horn than I did. In fact I enjoyed hearing him play because he had so much of Armstrong in his playing and was the first trumpet player after Louis that I had heard who had the real New Orleans style. He had technique, a pleasant tone and really knew his instrument.

But I think that Russell could at least have let me play some first parts. I suppose he thought that I should be happy because I was playing in the Roseland, but that kind of prestige and under the conditions that I was playing, didn't mean a bag of beans to me and I love beans.

After a few months at the Savoy, Cecil wanted to bring Lloyd back in the band and one night in the dressing room he told us of his intentions. But it did not go as Cecil expected it because 'Hoggy,' who seldom disagreed with anything, spoke up and said that if Lloyd came back he, Hoggy, was giving his two weeks notice then and there. Then one after the other gave their notice. I was the third one to give mine and Cecil accepted them all with an air of arrogance.

I knew that blood is thicker than water and Lloyd was Cecil's blood but we had had enough of Lloyd taking our money, getting drunk and doing crazy things. I suppose Cecil must have conned Buchanan into forgiving Lloyd for taking a poke at him, but we really didn't want any part of him.
Cecil thought the matter over and when we came to work
the next night, he announced that Lloyd would not be coming back and everything was fine again.

One night when I came off the bandstand there were three fellows sitting at a table near where I came off the dance floor and as I passed they stopped me and asked me if I wanted some reefer. They told me they were Mexicans. I asked them the same question I had asked the fellows on the bus going to Pittsburgh about the effects of the reefer. They told me again that it makes you feel good and laugh. But I had no desire to try it and two sets later when I came off and passed them again, they were all three laying on the table fast asleep. I didn't know if they had laughed themselves to sleep or not, but they were not having a good time as far as I was concerned.

But my first experience with reefers came eventually. We were playing a matinee on a Sunday and I started drinking gin early in the afternoon and felt fine. This continued until the Savoy closed and I was feeling real groovy but not drunk. There was a bar on the corner of 132nd and 7th Avenue called Pete's, and naturally it catered to the theatrical people and musicians as it was near the Lafayette theater, the different clubs in the neighbourhood and the Rhythm club.

So I went to Pete's, ordered half a pint of gin and had drunk about half of it when I saw Cecil and a banjo player called Ikie come out of the back room and go in the toilet. For some reason I had an idea that something was up so I went in the toilet also. I saw Ikie taking out a cigarette and he said it was a reefer. He asked me if I wanted to try and I did. I took one big puff and held it in my lungs for a few seconds and another which I also held as long as I could, passed it to Cecil and went back to the bar.
Two minutes later I thought the world was caving in on

me. My legs got weak, I grabbed the railing on the bar and my mind started to turn as if I had been spun around like a top. A few seconds later I was able to ask the bartender in a very weak voice how much did I owe him. I felt as though I was going to faint and knew I had to get out of there very quickly. So I paid for my drink, left half of it and went outside.

It was a good thing that I had left my horn at the Savoy, which I did when I had no intention of going jamming somewhere. I was living on 140th Street between 7th and Lenox so I decided that I had better walk home as the air would do me good and I was afraid of blacking out in a taxi. I was staggering all the way up 7th Avenue and when I arrived at 135th Street I decided that I had better hide my money so that if I did fall out in the street, I would not be robbed.

I had seven dollars and wanted to put it in my shoe. I was so weak in the legs that I was obliged to lean against a house to put my money in my shoe without falling on my face. I eventually reached home and when I got into my room I fell across the bed and asked my wife almost breathlessly to take my clothes off for me. That was the only time anyone ever had to undress me since I had been big enough to dress myself and it was the first and last time that I was ever cut from drinking and smoking.
We moved to a house on 139th Street between 7th and 8th Avenues which was supposed to be an exclusive block called Strivers Row. We were two houses from where Fletcher Henderson lived.
The Bright Boys came from the Savoy for a few weeks and played at a country club for negroes called 'Shady Rest' in New Jersey. Then we came back to the Savoy.
One afternoon we had a rehearsal and I left too early and arrived at the Savoy 45 minutes in advance. I was
tempted to go back home because I lived about 5 minutes walking distance from the 'Track'. Then I decided to stay put and sat in a window watching the happenings on Lenox until rehearsal started.

When it was finished and I was on my way home, I met a woman who was from Cincinnati and a friend of my wife and I. She told me to hurry home because something had happened but she would not tell me what.

I arrived and found my wife crying and then she told me we had been robbed. What had happened was that our room was on the 3rd floor of this private house and the kitchen was downstairs on the ground floor. Two fellows had moved into the room next to ours the week before but I had never seen them. So while my wife was washing the dishes downstairs in the kitchen, these fellows heard me when I left the room and as there was no special lock on any of the doors, they opened my door and took all my clothes, a nice Big Ben alarm clock that my mother had sent me for the past Christmas and ten dollars that I had given my wife from a five-cent hit on the numbers a few days before that. She was going to buy a new dress for Easter which was the coming Sunday. I lost seven suits and the one I had on had been one of the band costumes that I had taken from the cleaning shop the day before.

The landlady offered us two weeks free rent as compensation but before the end of the first week, she told us that she was going to move. We found another room on 135th Street facing the police station. I had lived in this block between 7th and 8th Avenue when I first came to New York, but in a house two doors from where I was now living. Higginbotham had lived in the same room that I was now occupying.

June, 1930 came and we went on our first tour under the leadership of Cecil Scott. Pittsburgh, our old stomping ground and a few mining towns near by. On every job we went, when the night was finished, Cecil would give us a certain amount and tell us that the place owed us 25 dollars which he said they had promised to send us.

We began to think that it was strange that after every job there was 25 dollars coming to us, so one of the fellows asked the manager of the place why he could not pay us the complete salary he was supposed to. The man said that he did not owe us anything because Cecil had asked him to send 25 dollars in advance as guarantee on the price he was supposed to pay us as we were not working on percentage.

So we decided to put a stop to that as we were not happy about what had passed. We were like brothers and thought that Cecil felt the same about us as we felt about him. We had a valet for the band named Louis so we put him at the door of every place we played after that to control the admission tickets. When the night was over, we divided the money in equal parts, took a certain amount for the valet and gave Cecil the same amount as we had.

When we came back to New York, we were supposed to go back to the Savoy. We had been getting 45 dollars a week since the beginning and as we were very popular there, we felt as though we deserved a raise and told Cecil that we wanted 50 dollars to go back there again.
Cecil said that he would ask Buchanan but he didn't think that he would give it to us. We told him that if we didn't get the raise, we were not going to work there anymore.

The next day, we had another rehearsal, and Cecil arrived with the news that Buchanan would not give us the raise, so we refused to work at the Savoy any more for 45 dollars. That was the end of Cecil Scott and his Bright Boys.

The irony of what happened, and I suppose some of the other members of the band found out a few years later from Buchanan, was that, we had been getting 50 dollars a week ever since we had come to the Savoy under the leadership of Cecil.

He was getting a leader's fee of 65 dollars a week and taking 9 times 5 dollars a week from us, which made him have a 115 dollars a week. That really broke my heart, to think that we had such a promising future, and because of Cecil's greediness, it all went down the drain.

Sy Oliver, whom I had met not long after I had joined the Scott band and who was still quite young when we played his home town of Zanesville, Ohio, heard us at the Savoy one time (that was before he came to New York with Jimmie Lunceford) and told me that we did not have the best brass section in the business, but that we had the best YOUNG brass section he had ever heard.

Dickie, Frank, and I knew each other's feeling so well that if anyone of us wanted to play a riff behind a sax solo, which we often did, one would start a riff and the other would pick it up and get the feeling of it before one measure had passed, and we played them in harmony and not unison. And a riff was never exactly the same every time although the number was played often.

So Cecil lost the chance of being nationally known because he wanted to make big money but sacrificed the opportunity because he had stolen 45 dollars a week from us for Lord knows how many weeks and he did not want to stop the operation. Both Scott brothers were finished as orchestra leaders.

Even when I was gigging around with Cecil Scott, I was managing to get in quite a lot of practice. Mostly I was concerned to develop a stronger lip, to be able to play a long phrase, or sometimes to see how long I could hold one note. Range was important, but I never tried to be an altissimo trumpeter. Today I can make 'A' or even 'B' flat, above high 'C', though I cannot stay there. Even then, I could easily make 'F'. Trumpet players started to be able to do that after Louis recorded "I Can't Give You Anything But Love." Then Jimmy Lunceford came to town. His first trumpet player was named [Tommy] Stevenson, and he was the really first high note man I ever heard. He could make double high 'C' and things like that.

In addition to playing scales or a phrase that I had never played before, I'd listen a lot to other people. I not only copied Louis Armstrong records, I also copied from pianists in order to try to see what they were doing. Even if you never use the same phrase, it's good to know it. People say that I play a lot of phrases with a lot of notes in them. I don't think the influence for that came from saxophone players. I was impressed by players like Jabbo Smith and Rex Stewart. But my idea was not to be a fast executioner, to play more notes than other trumpet players; it was just the way my style came out of the horn. Red Allen, for instance, had a faster execution then I did.

Most of us at that time were not experimenting with harmony for its own sake. We were more concerned with good melodic ideas - how to put a certain idea into a song. Therefore, when you practiced the song, you'd start playing the melody, and then see what you could do with it. Harmonic ideas were only used to get further inside the melody, and so develop it better. I don't remember practicing harmonic substitutions. I never sat down and tried to put an 'E' flat chord on top of a 'A' minor 7th, or something like that. Instead, we were satisfied with the basic harmonies.

Sometimes in a song, there is a passing tone, and I would practice finding a chord which fitted that passing note, but on the whole, horn players had not got very far in the understanding of flatted fifths substitutions. Perhaps some of the piano players were, but it wasn't the style to find the most complicated harmonies for a song. Musicians often improvised without knowing what they were doing. It didn't become a science until Dizzy Gillespie came along.

Even though I play melodically - the tune never leaves my mind - it helps to know the chords when you are improvising. The only thing that bothers me is when I know what the harmony is and I hear somone playing something else. In"St. James' Infirmary", there is a passage which different people play differently. I have my special way of playing that, and when I hear it played another way, it makes me flinch, and I think that they don't know the harmony I play. So therefore, I always have my chord book with me, in order to make sure that everyone plays the same chord.

Whenever I am improvising on a tune which I have played before, it's very important for me not to remember what I did the last time I played it. I never think of what I did beforehand. It comes to me instantly. This is a question of knowing your instrument and what key you're playing in. It takes a long time to acquire, but once you know it, it's not difficult. It's like writing a letter. You write to your sister, and then you write to your brother, but you dont say the same thing, that's the way it is with taking a number and learning to improvise on it.

I went into a dancing school for the first time with a pianist named Johnny Monnegue with Paul Barnes, alto sax, Jimmy Wright, tenor sax, Paul Burnett who had played banjo in Arthur Gibbs orchestra when I first heard him at the Savoy, was now playing guitar with Monnegue. The other trumpet man was Theodore 'Ted' Colin whom I had seen at the Rhythm Club many times. Ted was the loudest blowing trumpet player I have ever known and he did not blow out of tune which is blasting when a guy plays loud and not in tune. Ted was a fellow with a big head and big face and talked almost as loud as he blew.

Working in a dancing school was not as interesting as working at the Savoy, Roseland or any other ballroom and the work was harder and especially with Monnegue. For one thing, the band was smaller. I don't remember who the drummer was and there was no bass. We were working in a dancing school on Broadway which was situated on the second floor of the building, just next door to the Roseland. The job started at 8 p.m. and finished at 2 a.m.

All dancing schools had the same regulations which was ten cents a dance. The orchestras played the introduction and first chorus of a number which were most of the time Tin Pan Alley orchestrations with the sax section playing the melody of the first chorus and the brass section playing the counter melody. At the end of the first chorus, the band stops and that was one dance. The band leader counts one, two, three or stomps his foot three times and the brass section plays the second chorus with the sax playing counter melody. Stop at the end of that chorus which is counted as another dance.

Then to the second ending which goes to a special chorus with figures for brass and sax. Stop, stomp and back to the first chorus and ending. Stop, stomp off on another number which is played in the same manner. Each time we stopped was the end of the dance and the man who was dancing with a hostess had to give her a ticket before the next dance started. Couples never came to a dancing school as it was a place where men were supposed to learn to dance, although I saw many who seemed to know how to dance for many years.

We played 55 minutes continually and had a five minutes smoking break. Dancing schools were the joy of music writers because there were so many of them in New York and the way they functioned it was not necessary for a leader or band to have special arrangements as in a ballroom. Someone who had composed a number (or stolen one as was the case sometimes) and had it published would distribute his song to the leader of a dancing school band and he could be 100% certain that the number would be played regardless of whether it was good or bad.

Johnny Monnegue had been a leader of dancing school bands for years and had a book of two-hundred numbers or more. When our night would begin, it started with number one and on through the book until we came to the last number and then we went from there back down the book until closing time which meant that we were reading music from the time we started until we finished the night.

The only time we relaxed and played a few popular jam session numbers that we didn't have to read was when Johnny would go on a binge (drunk) and not come to work which happened about every two weeks. We played what we wanted and had fun then because we knew that when he came back to work the next night it would be back to the mines again.

There was no flirting with the girls because the bouncers were always watching them and us also, so Ted and I used to have our drinks to make the time pass. Ted could drink like a fish and was never drunk. He would bring a bottle one night and I brought one the next night. Although the job was hard we were never too tired to go to some bar when we arrived in Harlem after our job was finished and drink until the wee hours of the morning.

A few weeks after I started with Johnny, he hired a trombone player named Herb Gregory. Herb had come up in the music game with Rex Stewart and was a great admirer of Jimmy Harrison and I got a good idea of how Jimmy had played from listening to Herb. He had the worst looking teeth of any horn blower that I ever saw. They were snagged and looked as though they were going to fall out at any moment, but when he put his horn to his mouth and started to play, the sounds that came from his horn were unbelievable.

Herb had not been working much before he joined Monnegue, so the first week with us Ted and I shared our bottle with him and he promised to bring in a bottle after he had received a week's pay. There were no nights off in ballrooms or dancing schools and at this place we were paid every Sunday night. Neither Ted nor I brought in a bottle on Monday night because Herb was supposed to bring one. After we played a few numbers Herb brought out his bottle and passed it to me. I took a taste and almost brought up my supper. This was the worst alcohol, if it could be called that, that I had ever tasted. There was moonshine whisky known as bathtub gin and white lightening but this stuff was like cigarette smoke blown into a bottle filled with water straight from
the gutter and it tasted as if it could be embalming fluid, if embalming fluid has a taste.

I passed the bottle to Ted who could drink anything. But he couldn't drink this stuff and when he did get his breath after a few seconds he hollered 'Goddamn' so loud that the couples on the dance floor stopped and looked up at the bandstand to see what was happening. Herb was surprised that we did not like his stuff and I supposed he finished the bottle eventually. I know that neither Ted nor I tried anymore of whatever it was and the night was really long before the job was finished and we could get to the bar and have a decent drink.

Sometimes at the dancing school if there were not many men in the place, the manager would open the front windows on Broadway and give Monnegue a sign to tell Ted to blow out for a while. Then Johnny would be kind-hearted enough to call a number that we did not have to read and Ted would blow so loud that he could be heard for five blocks in any direction.

After a few months with Johnny Monnegue I left and went to another dancing school and worked with a leader named Bobby Neal. Bobby was a little fellow about 4 feet tall who played a double-B tuba which was the biggest tuba made. It was much easier playing a dancing school job with Bobby than it was with Monnegue because we played many numbers that we did not have to read. And Bobby would do a little show by walking through his tuba and twirling it around the floor. In the band was Arthur Bowie, a pianist, John Collins and Stanley Payne, alto sax, Joe Garland, tenor. On drums Burt ......... Joe Garland later became well known as the composer of 'In the Mood' which Glen Miller made popular in the 40s.

Bobby was working in a small dancing school on the east side of town, but a big school opened on Broadway over the Strand Theater and was called the Strand Ballroom. Bobby was engaged to play the Strand, so he hired Frank Newton and a trombone player named Jonas Walker. That augmented the band to 9 pieces and this job became the easiest dancing school job in New York because another band was also engaged.

It was a high place with plenty of space on the stage for two orchestras and they employed 50 hostesses whereas most places had no more than 15. With 3 brass and 3 saxes we were able to play some special arrangements which were numbered from C-one up to C 15, and one was an arrangement by Benny Carter on Rhapsody in Blue which had been one of the special arrangements played by the Scott band when we started playing other than head arrangements.

Most of the negro bands of ten pieces or more in Harlem were playing the arrangement of Rhapsody in Blue by Benny Carter and this arrangement was number C7 in Neal's book. Arthur Bowie called the number and there was a system at the Strand where a long dance was announced at the discretion of the orchestra. C7 was the special of specials for Bowie. Some musicians had the habit of visiting the different dancing schools for the pleasure of listening or to see if they could get a job. Whenever one came to the Strand and if Bowie knew that he was a musician, as soon as we had finished whatever we were playing, Bowie would call for C7. We played that number so often that we started calling Bowie C7.
Very often, a young fellow used to come to the Strand but he never danced and spent most of his time in the dressing room that we had next to the bandstand. Sometimes

he would be high and go to sleep in a chair until he became a little sober. We found out that his name was Charlie Barnet and that he was from a rich family. But it was some years later when Charlie took a band in to one of the big white hotels that I found out that he was a musician. He talked with us at the Strand but I don't remember him ever mentioning that he played sax. He really must have liked Neal's band because he came so often and spent his time in our dressing room.

Horace Henderson had a band playing in the Dunbar Palace which had been called Bamboo Inn when I first came to New York. It was a small dance hall on 7th Avenue between 139th and 140th Streets. He was using two trumpets, Gus McClung and Jack Butler, when he decided to add another trumpet. Gus left the band after Horace hired the other trumpet and I joined the band. The new guy was from Boston and was named Wendell Culy. Wendell was a first chair man with a beautiful tone and so much technique that Horace gave him many solos on ballad numbers.

The only musician in the band who had been with Horace in Wilburforce and at the Savoy was Talcot Reeves, the guitarist, and John Williams, ex-Scott altoist. The other men were new to me but I learned who they were in a short time. Cully, Jack Butler and myself on trumpets, Bob Carroll tenor, Rupert Cole and John Williams, altos, Sandy Williams, trombone, Talcot, guitar and Manzie Johnson, drums.

Sandy Williams was the second trombonist I played with who had a style like Jimmy Harrison and they both loved him. The other one was Herb Gregory. Sandy came from Washington, D.C. and had not been in the Apple very long when I joined the band.
We did not stay very long at the Dunbar after I joined the band because Don Redman had left the Cotton Pickers to form his own orchestra and wanted Horace and some others of
the band also. I was one of those whom Don wanted. He must have remembered me from the time when Scott's band had played a dance in Pittsburg with the Cotton Pickers and had asked who I was.

Don recorded 4 numbers with a band that included Leonard 'Ham' Davis, Red Allen and myself on trumpet, Claude Jones, Fred Robinson and Benny Morton, trombones, Edward Inge, clarinet and alto, Rupert Cole, alto, Bob Carroll, tenor, Horace Henderson, piano, Talcot Reeves, guitar, Manzie Johnson, drums, Bob Ysaguire, bass, Lois Deppe and Don, vocals. The titles were 'Chant of the Weed ', 'Shaking the African ', 'I Heard' and

The only trumpet solos were done by Red Allen and when these records came out with the names of the musicians, Langston Curl's name was on the cover instead of Bill Coleman. It probably happened because I never joined Don's band before.

After the recordings were made I did not hear anything from Don. Bobby Neal was working in a small dancing school and asked me to join him which I did. A couple of weeks later Bobby Ysaguire came to see me and said that Don was rehearsing at Connie's Inn and wanted me to join the band. I didn't think it was correct on my part to leave Neal so soon after I had joined him and explained this to Bobby.
Don opened in Connie's with all the musicians that had recorded with him except Red Allen, Leonard Davis and myself. His three trumpets were Sidney de Paris, Shirley Clay and Langston Curl.

Dickie Wells was playing with Charlie Johnson who left Small's Paradise in 1931. Charlie asked Frank Newton and myself to join his band. I accepted because Charlie was better known than Neal and the salary would be better also. The members of Charlie's band were Ben Witted,
Harvey Boone, alto sax, Benny Waters, tenor, Bobby Johnson, guitar, Dell Thomas, bass, Leonard 'Ham' Davis, Frank and myself on trumpets, Dickie on trombone and George Stafford, drums.

The band went on tour and Sidney de Paris was added which made four trumpets and gave the brass section an even bigger sound and more punch than it had before. For my money, Charlie Johnson had a band that was second to Fletcher Henderson and he used to give Fletcher some tough battles before I joined the band.

We played a few days in Buffalo and it was at a club called 'Ann Montgomery' that I met a trumpet player called 'Peanuts' Holland who was a blowing cat with a lot of technique and a big sound. Another young musician I met at this same club was a fellow named Willie Smith. I didn't know anything about Jimmie Lunceford, but Charlie Johnson wanted to hire Willie the first night he heard him. I jammed with Willie and Peanuts almost every night.

A boy that I had played with at one time in Helvey's band named John L. Henderson was working in a band at the biggest Negro hotel in Buffalo, so I went to listen to him the night before we were to leave. I had a ball and got so drunk that John L. told me that I could go to sleep in his room as he was also living in the hotel.

I told him that I would have to get up at 10 o'clock the next morning because the band was leaving at 11 a.m. He said that he would have the desk clerk call me at 10 which he did. I was still under the influence of the kickapoo joy juice that I had drunk the night before when I answered the 'phone and instead of getting up then, I lay in the bed to get myself together but went back to slumberland. When I woke up it was mid-day. I jumped sky high because the bus was supposed to leave at 11 and
I was an hour late.

Would Charlie wait for me was the question I kept asking myself as I put on my clothes as fast as I could. The bus was leaving from 'Ann Montgomery's' place as we had rooms upstairs over the club. The hotel where John L. lived was two blocks from 'Ann's' place and when I came out of the hotel and looked up the street, I got the answer; the bus was not there. Had the bus driver gone to gas up and come back to the hotel?

That question was answered when I arrived at 'Ann's' place and was told that Charlie had waited for me until 15 minuted before I arrived. I had spent most of the money I had the night before, so I went back to the hotel and told John L. what had happened. I had left New York being owed a week's salary by Bobby Neal which he had not paid me when I left his orchestra and I had not bothered to collect it because I could trust Bobby and knew that I would get the loot whenever I asked him for it.

I told John L. that I was going to send a telegram to Joe Garland who took care of Neal's business and have him send me the money and John L. told me that I could sleep in his room with him until the money came. When the employees of 'Ann's' club heard about what had happened to me, someone offered to take up a collection among them and give me train fare back to New York, but I refused the offer because I knew that I would have my money from Neal in a few days and I did.

I waited three days but had a ball every night at Ann's place jamming with Peanuts and Willy Smith, with both of whom I became well acquainted. Luckily, Sidney de Paris was with the band because there were still three trumpets for the job they played the day I missed the bus and it was the last job of the tour.
When I arrived back in the Apple, Charlie didn't have much work for a few weeks and Sidney went to Philadelphia where he had been living before he joined Charlie Johnson.

It was summer in 1931 when Charlie landed a job playing at a big swimming pool called the Lido, which was at 146th Street and 7th Avenue. It was a pleasant job because it was not too hot during the night and as it was near the pool that we played which had no roof, we could not play after midnight. So I went to the Savoy at times because I did not have to pay to get in and was usually at some bar where musicians hung out before most of them finished their jobs.

Charlie Johnson had not changed his habit of playing the first number with the band and then disappearing until it was time to play the last number. But he got hooked when the band played a week at the Lafayette theater. The name of the show for that week was called Chocolate Drops and we were in a big stage built like a box of candy.

We had to enter this set-up from the basement by climbing up some steps. When the band was seated before the show started, the top of the box was closed and slowly opened when we started to play the opening number. The piano was in the right-hand side of the box and Charlie had to go in first. There was no way for him to get out and it was the joke of the week because it was the first time that he had ever been in a position where he was obliged to stay at the piano until the end of the show or dance.

One of the attraction numbers that we played that week was an arrangement of 'Ding Dong Daddy' from Dumas which I sang and the trumpets played in three parts harmony, exactly as Louis Armstrong played it and it made a hit with the audience, stage hands and chorus girls.
A theater on 125th Street between 7th and 8th Avenue called the Harlem Opera House had been a burlesque showplace but it turned into a theater that showed movies and had

stage shows. Charlie Johnson and orchestra were engaged to play a week there. On the bill was a magician who had a trick stool and he would invite someone from the audience to come on stage and sit on it after he had performed some other magic tricks with them.

When someone sat on this stool, the legs would flop down leaving the person sitting flat on his fanny. The musicians had a crap game after every show and Charlie lost most of the time, and when 15 minutes was called before the next show went on (there were 4 shows a day) the band would be back stage and Charlie would be explaining why he lost or what he should have done to win and the guys would manoeuvre him to the collapsible stool of the magician which was always at a certain place and Charlie would sit down on it every time because he would be so busy trying to get over a point that he forgot that the stool would collapse when it was sat on. This was our backstage attraction.

But the kicks of the show that week for me were that we were accompanying the one and only queen of the blues: Bessie Smith. Bessie was not as popular as she had been, but to me she was singing better than she had ever sung and I found out that she could sing other types of songs as well as she sang the blues. One of the songs in her repertoire was 'Someone Stole Gabriel's Horn' which she swung out of this world and the whole band enjoyed hearing her sing this more than any of the blues numbers.

Charlie didn't get much work after the Harlem Opera House date and the band finally broke up. He never had a band after that and went into a dancing school job which surprised everybody because he had been the laziest piano player in New York and was known never to stay at the piano longer than 10 minutes when he had a big band except for the week in the Lafayette Theater when he was boxed in.

I joined Luis Russell again in 1931, replacing Otis Johnson. Russell had been working at the Saratoga Club which was the old Capitol, but the band was in the Arcadia ballroom on Broadway and 53rd Street when I rejoined him. The Arcadia was the second best white ballroom after the Roseland, but for Negro bands it was better than the Roseland because there was a decent band room up over the bandstand and it was not necessary to stand on the back stairway between sets. We could sit down and play cards or write letters the same as the white orchestra did in their band room.

As for socializing with the clientele was concerned, no band, white or coloured, was allowed to do that. And everyone, clients, musicians, bartenders and hostesses came in and went out the front door. We came and left by a back door at the Roseland.

Russel was now employing three trumpets and Higginbotham was not there. The line-up was Jimmy Archey, trombone, Henry 'Moon' Jones had replaced Charlie Holmes on alto sax, Greely Walton had replaced Teddy Hill on tenor-sax, Albert Nicholas, alto-sax and clarinet, Bill Johnson, guitar, Paul Barbarin, drums, Pops Foster, bass, Bill Dillard, Red Allen and myself, trumpets. And this time I had more solos and played some of the first parts also.

One night the orchestra of Noble Sissle who was working in a big white hotel was engaged at the Arcadia to play a battle of jazz between Russell and the other white orchestra whose name I don't remember. I had seen Sissle on stage when I was in Cincinnati and in my estimation he was pretty much a ham actor. So it was a night that we were looking forward to, and the Uncle Tom in him was really shown when his band came in dressed in red frocktail coats which made them look like a circus monkey band. There were some good musicians in the band, one of them being Wilbur de Paris,

trombonist and Sidney Bechet who was supposed to be the jazz man of the band, but I was never a lover of the soprano sax so Bechet didn't tell me anything. The band as a whole was the most jazzless negro orchestra I had ever heard. The white band made Sissle's sound like a fifth-grade school band and Russel's orchestra made Sissles sound like it was the first time they had ever played musical instruments. It has been said that a band is no better than its leader and I felt sorry for the musicians because they had no leader that knew beans about jazz.

We went to Philadelphia to play one week at the Earl Theater and that was the hardest week I ever worked in a theater. Paul Barbarin left Russel then and went back to New Orleans. He was replaced by James Smith who became a good buddy of mine.

The Mills Brothers were the stars of the show. They had been very popular radio stars for a long time and the biggest attraction that ever worked in Connie's Inn. As a rule, the Earl Theater worked on the same basis as the Lafayette which was four shows on Friday, five on Saturdays and Sundays and a midnight show on Saturday also.

But the Mills Brothers were such a big drawing card that we did seven shows a day. When we finished one show, the half-hour for the next one would be called as we were coming off the stage. One short film and the newsreel were shown and we were on stage again. I and everyone else ate the fastest meals I ever ate and no-one was ever late for a show.

Two young boys of 12 and 13 years old were engaged to dance during the week, but after two days they had to stop because the law did not allow kids that young to work in a theater. They were the Nicholas Brothers.

The band played an opening number, then the chorus girls did a number. After that a comedy sketch. Then one more time, band number, chorus girl's number, comedy sketch and it would be the Mills Brothers show for a half-hour.

There was a line a quarter of a mile long after every show, every day, waiting to get into the theater. The Mills Brothers were great to work with and one could easily tell that success never went to their heads. But brother, Oh, what a week...

A few weeks later we played the Howard Theater in Washington, D.C. and the Royal in Baltimore, but not with the Mills Brothers. Then we did a few days in Bridgeton, New Jersey before coming back to New York. Russell had no regular work after that; just a few gigs now and then.

When I was not playing in a regular orchestra which was very seldom, I would work in a dancing school or I was lucky enough to get gigs now and then. Some musicians around the Rhythm Club only worked gigs and would not accept a regular job. I could stay on a dancing school job for only a certain length of time because it was too much for me to have to read one number after another for five hours with only five minutes in every hour to smoke a cigarette.

The dancing schools were run by gangsters and the musicians were not supposed to look at the girls in a friendly manner. But the girls who really wanted to be with a musician would always find a way but it was the work and not the girls that I did not like in those places. Bobby Neal was the only dancing school leader that could work those places and make it more like working at the Savoy than any other leader of that type. I really had pleasure working with him. The musicians could relax by playing head numbers or standards that they knew and did not have to read.

The Renaissance Ballroom at the corner of 138th Street and 7th Avenue was a place where most of the Negro clubs held their dances and the leader of the orchestra was a fellow named Fernand Andrade, a banjo and guitar player. Fernand never had a band of regular musicians although there were certain ones that usually gigged with him and I did a

few with him. There are many name musicians in the 20s and 30s that gigged at one time with Fernand; Benny Carter, Rex Stewart, Bobby Starke, etc. When I gigged with Fernand, I met one of the greatest alto sax men in the business. His name was Hilton Jefferson. Jeff was a very quiet man but he made his horn talk for him and all the musicians loved him.

Another musician that always had the highest paid gigs was a drummer named Peek-a-Boo Jimmy. Peek-a-Boo had played with James P. Johnson, Willie 'The Lion' Smith and 'Lucky' Roberts in the days before I even dreamed of going to New York. I gigged with Peek-a-Boo twice and both times it was really enjoyable. The music we played was not very jazzy because Jimmy was a drummer who had lost sight of what the other drummers were doing. And most of the musicians he hired were a certain age and not up to date on jazz either.

But Jimmy was in with the rich folks downtown and he played many high society functions. The first one I did with him was a stag party for some business men who had rented a Hudson River cruising boat and invited about 400 men to cruise up the Hudson. We played but there was no dancing as there were no women to dance with. Finally we docked somewhere and everybody went ashore where a big picnic with all kinds of seafood and kegs of beer were waiting for everyone including the band. The committee of this outing had engaged Primo Carnera, the giant heavyweight boxer, to give an exhibition.

I received 25 dollars for that gig and the same for another I did with Peek-a-Boo in the city, which was not a stag party but a dance and we had all the steaks and beer we could eat and drink. That was something that Peek-a-Boo always asked for his musicians and himself when he was having a gig.
Ralph Cooper, who was a dancer turned orchestra leader,

was playing at the Lafayette one week and he had a very good show band. Ralph really knew show business. I saw the band during the early part of the week and really enjoyed its presentation. The shows at the Lafayette always started on Fridays and naturally finished on Thursdays.

I had been out drinking most of the Tuesday night that week when Ralph was at the Lafayette and could sleep late on Wednesday. Russell had a dance to play Wednesday night in a hall up over the Alhambra Theater at 7th Avenue and 126th Street.

I was deep in slumberland when someone knocked on my door about 12.30 in the afternoon. It was the landlady of the rooming house where I was staying on 135th Street. My wife was working as a housemaid down town so I could sleep the whole day, so I had thought when I came home. The landlady told me that three men were at the hall door and wanted to see me. I told her to let them in. They were Gus McClung, Henry Goodwin and Residus 'Mac' Horton, three members of Cooper's orchestra. I had known Gus since the first time I had seen Lloyd Scott's orchestra. Goodwin was a trumpet player and Horton played trombone.

They told me that the other trumpet player whose name was Louis Hunt was having lip trouble and felt so embarrassed because he had a feature number to do and had been missing the ending for a few days. So he did not show up for the first show and they had come to ask me if I would come to the theater and be on hand to do the next show if Hunt did not appear. I was so beat and knowing that I had to work with Russel that night, I told them I could not make it.

Two and a half hours later, Gus and Henry Goodwin came back this time with Paul Burnett, the ex-Arthur Gibbs guitarist. They told me that Hunt had not shown up for the second show and would I please come to do the last two ones. As it was the second time they had come for me, I told them 'yes' because my rest had been broken after the first visit
and I was feeling better than I had in the early part of the afternoon.

Ralph asked me if I knew 'I can't give you anything but love' the way Armstrong played it. Of course I knew it after the many times I had played it for myself along with the record. He asked me if I knew the ending and could I go out and play it in front of the band. That was the number Hunt had been featured on and had missed the last note a few times because of bad chops.

When the time came to do the number, I walked to within three feet of the footlights and played it the way Satchmo did, and it was the first time I ever received so much applause in my career for playing a solo. When I played it for the last show, all the chorus girls and most of the stage hands were standing in the wings of the stage. I suppose they had heard it the show before and had gathered in the wings to see if I would do it the same as I did the show before and I did, thank the Lord.

Between the third and last show I had gone to the job that Russell was playing. I told Luis that I had a show to do at a certain time and told him the reason. So he gave me time off to do the last show and I came back later to finish the night with him.

As I said already, I had known Gus McClung for many years but I never saw him as happy as he was after I had done '......anything but love' for those two shows. The rest of the band, the chorus girls and stage hands were all smiles for me. Ralph asked me if I would do the show the next day and I accepted. I went straight home after the dance because the first show was at 11 o'clock the next morning and I wanted to get as much rest as possible.

The four shows on Thursday went down great and Ralph had some theater dates to do the following week in New Jersey and I did them with him. After those dates he was going on a theater tour and asked me if I would stay with the band. As Russel was not working regularly, I accepted and told Russel who agreed that I should do it and wished me luck.

Ralph had signed a contract with R.K.O. which was the biggest theatrical circuit in the country. There were three tap dancers; Blain, Rice and Berry known as the Three Sams; Bessie Dudley, who was a snake hip dancer and the band. Ralph danced and also did a parody on 'Penthouse Serenade'. Ralph was a very handsome light-coloured man and sort of stocky for a tap dancer. He had teamed with a dancer named Eddie Rector who was one of the best that ever wore a pair of dancing shoes. He looked good leading a band and that was a big factor in the success of his orchestra.

The first hop was Chicago and following is a critic that ran in one of the local papers: 'Ralph Cooper and Band hit. Ralph Cooper brought his famous band into Chicago last week for an engagement at the Palace Theater and scored an instant hit. The opening of the show found the theater packed and they drew well throughout the engagement. Ralph had assembled some of New York's best musicians and whipped them into a selling outfit. Cooper directs the band, sings a number or two and does a dance number that equals Robinson (Bojangles) or Eddie Rector in their best days'.
I remember that the film that was showing at the Palace during the week was 'What price Hollywood' starring Constance Bennett.
The musicians other than McClung, Goodwin, Horton, Burnett and myself were Arnold 'Scrip' Boling, ex- Cecil Scott,
drummer, Eugene Anderson, piano, Booker T. Pittman, Leroy Hardy, alto sax, Alfred Pratt, tenor sax.

Duke Ellington was playing some exclusive place in a suburb of Chicago and I saw Freddie Jenkins and Rex Stewart many times. The fattest musician I ever saw was also in Chicago. His name was Tiny Parham and he played piano. He had an orchestra but I never heard it. I did, however, see his car in which he had had the steering wheel put almost in the middle of the front seat in order for him to drive it. I thought that the tuba player with Broadus was the biggest, fattest mucisian I had ever seen until I saw Tiny Parham who must have weighed 400 pounds. I also saw and talked with a man I had known about and admired when I was very young. He was the ex-heavyweight boxing champion of the world, Jack Johnson.

From Chicago we went to Cleveland at the R.K.O. Theater for one week and from there to Denver, Colorado which was the farthest west I had ever been. We played the R.K.O. vaudeville theater and visited the Rocky Mountains.

Salem Tutt Whitney who played Noah in the show of Noah's Ark said this about Denver: 'Denver is a beautiful City. A mile above sea level. The altitude would make me lightheaded if I had not been like that all my life. It is hot as blazes here. One has to look at the snowcaps on the distant mountains to convince oneself that there is any cool weather anywhere. I am certain that the coloured people here have more beautiful homes than anywhere we have been'.
And that was true, and to protect those homes they had their own fire department which was something I never saw anywhere else in the U.S.A.
As the theater was in the center of the downtown

district, once we were at the theater we did not come back to the coloured district where we stayed until after the last show. There was a white restaurant in the street behind the theater. An alley ran between the two streets. We ordered our meals from this restaurant and ate them in our dressing rooms. The dressing rooms in the R.K.O. theaters were more comfortable than many hotels I have been in. Thick carpets on the floors, showers, and some had kitchens where the actors could cook.

One day the owner of the restaurant came to the theater and said that he would like to invite us for supper, but there was one hitch. He had a banquet room on the second floor of the restaurant, and as his clientele was white only, we would have to come in through the kitchen from the alley. We accepted his invitation and what happened was that we went in through the kitchen, came out into the main dining-room and went upstairs.

It seemed such a simple thing because we went through the dining-room which was the only way to get upstairs. A negro could not come through the front door. Of course, that was a southern custom, and Denver was as southern as Kentucky, Alabama or Mississippi in many ways.

We had a wonderful supper and the owner even entertained us by playing songs on a mandolin. He told us that he was from Detroit and he thought the idea of us having to come through the kitchen to get upstairs was silly, but he had been in Denver quite some time and had a wonderful business and he could not change the ways of narrow-minded people. We had a wonderful time and before we left he gave each of us a box of Chinese matches made of gum.

There was a photo-developing shop around the corner from the theater, and as I took many photographs, I gave my films to this place to be developed. Negroes did not have to go in the back doors of shops, thank the Lord. I had gone to pick up some photos that had been developed

and crossed the street to go to a drugstore on the corner. I was walking on the outside of the sidewalk. I thought it was one of the fellows from the band playing a joke on me because these things happen. But when I turned to see who it was, a little old white man with grey hair turned around and said 'Get off the sidewalk, nigger' and kept on walking.

I was the only negro on the street, and when I saw who it was, I was mad enough to bite a ten-penny nail in two, but there was nothing I could do because I was in a southern town and the only negro on the street.

From Denver we went to the R.K.O. Orpheum Theater in Omaha, Nebraska. During the week, there was a dance which we went to after the last show. The name of the orchestra playing was called the Blue Devils, and one of the trumpet players I had met in Buffalo, New York, when I was there with the Scott band. His name was George Hutchinson.

He informed me that some of the orchestra were staying at the same place we were which was a very big rooming-house called the White House, because it was painted white. There was a room with a piano and one could buy bootleg whisky there. So we went to the White House after the dance which finished at 2 a.m. and started a jam session. The tenor sax in the Blue Devils band was a light-skinned, red-headed fellow and he told me his name was Lester Young.

Booker Pitman, Alfred Pratt and Leroy Hardy used to practice in between most of the shows and so did I. When the jam session was announced we were the only ones in the Cooper orchestra who sat in. I didn't remember any of the other musicians in the Blue Devils except George Hutchinson (whom I already knew) and Lester Young. I remember Lester because I had had so much enjoyment
drinking and jamming with him. I suppose his playing had made an impression on me without my really realizing it at the time.

After Omaha we played the R.K.O. Theaters in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and Minneapolis, Minnesota. In Minneapolis we shared the bill with Hobart Bosworth, a movie actor whom I had seen many times in films. I also met my good friend and teacher, Theodore Carpenter, who was playing in a club there. We were really happy to meet again and he was elated with me because I had come a long way since he had shown me some riffs back in Cincinnati.

Everywhere we played Ralph Cooper and his band headlined the show. Every theater had big pit bands to play for the acts that were not musical, and the musicians in the pits gave us very high praise for our musical ability. We came back to Chicago for a repeat performance of one week and from there we jumped to Boston,Massachusetts for one week at the R.K.O. Keith-Boston theater.

As we had been the main attraction everywhere, someone thought that we deserved to have a little more money and everyone agreed. We told Ralph and he had the same idea. He said that he would look into the matter, and at the end of the week we received a raise. We came back to New York and never worked another R.K.O. theater after that. Here is the reason.......

Ralph loved his musicians to the point of doing almost anything to please them and it was one of the most brotherly orchestras with which I had ever worked. There was never a dispute or no fungus among us. When we asked for a raise, Ralph telephoned the office in New York and explained our case. This I found out later. The office did not agree to giving us more money, so Ralph had kept the percentage he was supposed to send them and gave us the
