raise. I can't remember what was his reason exactly, but perhaps he thought he could arrange things when we returned to New York, and he would have a face to face talk with the directors of the circuit. But nothing happened.

The band did not break up, however, and we continued to do theaters that were not run by R.K.O. We played the Lafayette, the Mount Morris, a theater on 125th Street and 5th Avenue, went on a tour of upstate New York playing Glen Falls at the Empire, the Playhouse in Johnstown, and a theater in Syracuse. Mattie Hite was added, and there were 12 chorus girls, with the comedy being handled by George Williams and Galli de Gaston, two favourites of Harlem.

The tour ended in November and so did the Ralph Cooper orchestra because no more bookings were coming in. Living with Madeline had also become so unbearable that we separated for the third and last time. Grandma Jackson and her family had left Springfield and moved to New York three years before I separated from my wife. Dickie Wells was staying with Grandma and I took a room with her also.

I had met a girl in the subway on New Year's day, 1932, when I was playing Lowe's theater with Luis Russell. I thought that this girl had known Dickie Wells, but she hadn't. She told me that she lived in Leonia, New Jersey, and gave me her address. Her name was Beatrice Twiggs, and she told me that everyone called her Beezie.

I wrote to Beezie during my tour with Ralph Cooper, and when we came back to New York I went over to New Jersey to see her. And that was the start of a romance that eventually led us to start living together after I separated from Madeline. I went back into Russell's orchestra after Ralph Cooper and we played Baltimore at the Royal theater and some small towns in New York State before

being engaged to replace Don Redman in Connie's Inn. Ed Kirkenby wrote in his book about 'Fats' Waller, (Ain't Misbehavin), that Don Redman was the last orchestra to play Connie's Inn, but Russell was the last band to play there. Connie still owes me and the rest of Russel's men $200.00 in back pay.

The show was great in Connie's with Louise Cook who was a beautiful shake (1) skane-dancer, Paul Meers, one of the greatest classical dancers that New York ever knew and his second wife, 'Jazz Lips' Richardson, a comic acrobat dancer, the one and only 'Snake Hips' Tucker, The Lucky Seven Trio, three fellows who danced on big blocks made to represent dice, three girls who had a singing act, and 12 beautiful chorus girls.

But Connie's was beginning to lose the white clients from downtown because Harlem was turning bad and so many white people were getting robbed when they came uptown. And negros, the few that ever went to the place, were treated so bad they got the tables where it was almost impossible to see the floor show, so they did not come there when the place started losing the white customers. This happened in 1933. I had rejoined Russell in 1932.

We doubled in some theaters including the Lafayette and that was hard work because we would be in the theaters all day from 11 a.m. until 11 at night and then have to come to the Inn and do two shows. We were paid on time for doing the shows but not at the Inn and each week Connie was getting deeper in debt to the band and the other folks in the show.

Russell's band had changed musicians considerably. Paul Barbarin had come back from New Orleans, Pops Foster was still in the band and I had rejoined it. The other two trumpets were Bobby Cheeks and John Brown. The sax
section consisted of Glyn Pague and Henry 'Moon' Jones on altos, Bingie Madison tenor. Jimmy Arckey was still there on trombone and Lee Blaire played guitar.

'Snake-Hips' Tucker was a tough guy and loved to fight. When he did his number the customers would throw dollar bills on the floor just to see him do a summersault and go into a split to pick them up. One night a table of college guys were with some girls and one of these fellows heated a half-dollar and threw it on the floor. 'Snake' didn't know that the piece was hot but he found out when he picked it up. 'Snake' finished his dance near the table where the smart alec had thrown the hot half-dollar and hit the guy so hard that he was knocked out of his seat. All the waiters and Connie had seen what had happened and they knew that 'Snake Hips' was not going to let the guy get away with it.

Connie was a reasonable fellow but did not stand for his show people to be abused. And the waiters were tough also so no client could get away with whatever they thought they could with the entertainers or the orchestra when their drinks got too heavy for them to carry.

When Snake Hips hit the one who had thrown the hot piece, the others - three men - jumped up to defend their friend. But some of the waiters were already standing at their table, so they dug and froze. Connie came up and ordered them to pay their bill and get the hell out of there before he took a poke at one of them.

I never cared for gangsters the same as many other people, but one night one of America's biggest gangsters came to Connie's and I talked with him. He was Dutch Shultz. Dutch was a big man with a pleasant voice when we talked together. I don't remember what the conversation was but I know that I did not ask him how many guns he
carried or how many men were in his gang.

Eventually Connie closed the Inn and Russell went back to Roseland. I had been the featured soloist in the trumpet section and had some fine solos. Beezie and I had not yet started living together but we were sweethearts.

Russell had engaged a drummer singer to direct the band when we went in to the Roseland. His name was Tiny Bradshaw and he had been the drummer in the Blue Ribbon band. Tiny was a light-skinned, red-headed fellow who sang in the type of growl voice that was associated with Holy Roller preachers. Today its the way that most rock and roll singers sing. Tiny made a big hit at the Roseland, and the band was jumping.

Lucky Millender, who had been one of the directors of the Blue Ribbon orchestra, had an orchestra at the Harlem Opera House and was the regular house band. In June, Lucky sent one of his musicians to ask me if I would like to join his outfit for a job in France because Gus Akins suffered from some kind of sickness that did not permit him to travel overseas. I refused the offer because I was in love and did not want to leave New York, and at the same time I wanted to accept the offer. Everything was rosy for me because I was the star trumpeter in the Russel band, and I was in love.

Red Allen came back to the orchestra, but I had my solos and everything was fine. But Beezie had the feeling that I wanted to take the trip to Europe and one night she told me that I should go and see Lucky and accept the offer if it was not too late. It was not too late, and on the 29th June 1933 the Lucky Millender orchestra left New York aboard the Conte Grande, an Italian ship. Destination - Monte Carlo.

It was generally known among musicians that France was less prejudiced than America, and that life was generally easier for black musicians. However, I never gave that a thought at the time. The prejudice in the United States was not something that worried me. I don't think musicians paid as much attention to those things as a teacher or a lawyer, or someone with a different sort of education. Musicians travelled around and they knew what was happening - they knew that there was prejudice, not only in the South, but in the North as well. Most of us took it for granted that you couldn't go into certain restaurants and theatres. If you went to a theatre up-town, you had to go into the gallery. Even when the Fletcher Henderson band were playing at the Roseland Ballroom, they were not allowed to stay in the dancing area when they were not on the bandstand. They had to go out the back, and that was in New York, which was not supposed to have any prejudice at all.

As far as prejudice from other white musicians was concerned, this was mainly confined to the bad musicians who could not get a good job. You never heard that sort of thing from people like Gene Krupa. Even though blacks and whites belonged to the same union, they could not earn the same salaries, and even if a black orchestra got a job in a downtown district, they got paid less. It was a rotten system, but one which left the black musicians freer, to play their own music.
When we set sail for France, Carol Dickerson of Chicago came to see us off, as he was a friend of Eugene Anderson, the ex-Cooper pianist. Most of the musicians in Lucky's band had been with Cooper.

Booker Pittman, Leroy Hardy, Alfred Pratt, R.H.'Mac' Horton, Henry Goodwin, Arnold Boling and myself. I had not played with the other members but knew them and they were Bill Dillard, trumpet, Arnold Adams, guitar and Wilson Myers, bass.

The Conte Grande was a 25,600 ton ship, and I was very excited about being on a big ship sailing for Europe and trying to picture what Monte Carlo and France would be like. We stopped in Boston and left there on 30th June and hit the high sea or the deep blue sea. In the dining room we were placed four at a table where there was a bottle of white wine and a little of red for each person.

Like most Americans I had never drunk wine with my meals. The passengers could have as many bottles as they desired and I drank one white and two red ones with my first meal. After that I started drinking two white and two red bottles with every meal. I only ate twice a day although there was breakfast, dinner, afternoon tea and supper. I was never awake in time to have breakfast and tea did not interest me. I was drinking eight quarts of wine a day and was never drunk. But I was quite gay for the whole trip which lasted 11 days.

With our group there were two chorus girls, Ethel Moses and Mary Hart, Freddy 'Snake Hips' Taylor, Lucky's wife Clara Townsend, Booker's wife Joyce, and Jimmie Daniels, a singer. The band rehearsed every day, we swam in the pool on deck and played cards at night. The trip was fine and the weather beautiful.

We arrived at Gibraltar and small boats came out to the ship with souvenirs to sell and kids dived in the water to retrieve pieces of money that the passengers threw to them. Gibraltar was very interesting to see
from the ship but we could not visit because there was no port for large ships to enter.

Then we sailed into the Mediterranean Sea and the next day I saw schools of dolphin and flying fish which I watched for hours. The dolphins would follow a boat for miles. We stopped at Naples, Italy, the 9th July, and it was possible to visit some of the city. On July 10th we disembarked at Ville- and went by special bus to Monte Carlo. The houses looked different and so many other things made me know that I really was in a foreign country, 4053 miles from New York.

Rehearsals for the show to be put on at the Sporting d'Ete began the day after our arrival and included the orchestra of Henri Madriguara who featured Latin American music, and Bela de Racz, a Hungarian orchestra. There were also 16 dancing and show girls, most of whom had been in the Ziegfeld Follies, plus the stars who were Gloria Grafton, a singer, Carl Randall, a dancer, Tito Coral, a singer, the Arnaut Brothers who did a violin act imitating birds, Reva Rayes, a Mexican girl singer, Moha_med Ben Jamai, an acrobatic dancer, Vilma and Buddy Ebsen, a sister and brother comedy act, Dave and Dorothy Fitzgibbons, a dance team. Freddy Taylor, Mary Hart, Ethel Moses and Jimmy Daniels were also included in the show which Lucky and Madriguara's orchestras accompanied. Bela de Racz played dinner music before the shows.

This was an amazing orchestra because they played Hungarian gypsy music which I had never heard before, using a which looked like a small piano but was played with mallets. There were 3 violinists, 2 viols and bass violin. I really enjoyed listening to this orchestra whose musicians got a big kick out of listening to us when we played jazzy dance numbers.
After the show was well on its way, we had the chance

to do some visiting which included Nice at least once a week, the palace of the Prince of Monte Carlo and Ventimiglia in Italy which was not far from Monte Carlo. There were many cafes open all night which I visited after we finished the night at the Sporting and I didn't feel like going home.

One day an orchestra that was playing in some resort in the vicinity of Monte Carlo came over to see us. I knew one of the musicians vaguely. He was June Cole who had played bass with the Cotton Pickers and Fletcher Henderson. I was introduced to Willy Lewis who was the leader, Ted Field and his wife Evelyn, Bobby Martin and a couple of fellows whose names I don't remember. Willie played alto and clarinet, Ted - drums, and Bobby, trumpet. Willie and Bobby had played with Sam Wooding who had brought an orchestra to Europe in the 1920s.

Alfred Pratt met a girl in Monte Carlo and married her before we left for Paris on 6th September. We left Monte Carlo on an early evening train. I had a bottle of cognac and one of the other musicians also had a bottle. I was so excited about going to Paris that I could not sleep, so I drank cognac and walked the corridors all night. The coaches with compartments were new to me and I did not disturb anyone who wanted to sleep while I walked the corridors.

I drank my bottle of cognac and the other one before we arrived in Paris in the morning of the 7th. The cognac had burned my throat to the point of my being so hoarse that I could hardly talk. I was taken to a hotel on Rue Henri Monnier which was in the heart of the Pigalle district. I had never heard of Pigalle but the day was beautiful and I was in Paris - not the one in Kentucky but the P A R I S. I was not sleepy although in a way I had walked from Monte
Carlo to Paris.

There was a bar downstairs in the hotel owned by Madame Liseux who was a beautiful amazon perhaps in her late 30s. I started to drink with some people in the bar and my voice was getting hoarser and hoarser. Finally someone persuaded me to go up to my room and get some rest, but it was 11 o'clock that night before I got to bed. I slept until 6 p.m. the next day and when I awakened, I had my voice back again.

The day after, we started rehearsing the show we had done in Monte Carlo with a French orchestra at the Rex theater. This was the largest theater I had ever seen or played in. There was plenty of space for the show at the Sporting d'Ete and it was the same at the Rex because the two bands were on the stage opposite each other and we still seemed to be a mile apart. In a few days, I learned how to walk from my hotel to the Rex. I met a journalist named Edgar Higgins who wrote for the Chicago Defender under the name of the Street Wolf of Paris. The Defender was the largest negro weekly paper in the U.S.A.

There were quite a few American negros in Paris and many of them made the Hotel Liseux their meeting place. There was an American negro girl singer named Neeka Shaw who had a cabaret where a fine pianist by the name of Freddie Johnson was playing. I had heard some musicians in New York speak about Freddie Johnson and he was everything I had heard about him concerning his piano playing. Neeka's place was called the Hot Feet and was on Rue Pigalle 53.

I went to Neeka's and jammed with Freddie. One morning I met a trumpeter named Arthur Briggs in the Hot Feet but we had met before in New York when Briggs was there in 1931 with Noble Sissle at the Lafayette. Sissle also had a fine young first trumpet named Joe Keys with him.
For a young man Joe could drink more juice than any two drinking men I knew and still play his horn.

Briggs and I jammed at the Hot Feet until the wee hours of the morning and Freddie played more piano than I had ever heard. Briggs was a first chair man but he could play things at a jam session that made everybody know that he could also take hot choruses which very few first trumpet players in a trumpet section could do.
Later, during my sojourn in Paris, I met a handsome young quiet sax player from St. Louis, Missouri named Cle Sadler. We used to drink together in Lisieux's but I never heard him play.

Another famous personality that hung around the Lisieux was Spencer Williams, the composer of 'Basin Street Blues.' Kid Chocolate, the famous Cuban boxer was in Paris, so was Jimmie Monroe, the husband of Nina Ma McKinney who was one of the movie stars who played in the first all negro movie called 'Halleluiah'. Freddie 'Snake Hips' Taylor and I lived in the same hotel and Freddie was hip to gage as marijuana or reefers were called.

I went to Freddie's room a few times and it would be like walking into a London fog. The windows were closed and reefer smoke would be so thick that you could cut it with a knife. Freddie and Jimmie would be smoking and to my surprise Kid Chocolate was in the room also. I didn't see the Kid smoking but I thought that being in a closed room full of marijuana smoke was not good for a prize fighter but that was his business. I didn't smoke the stuff either after what it had done to me the night I saw Cecil Scott and Banjo Ikie go into the gents room in a bar in New York where I had followed them and taken a couple of puffs that knocked me out after I had been drinking gin all day at the Savoy.
Freddie had some Armstrong records and a record player.

As Satchmo was my man with a horn, I would go to Freddie's room to listen to them. It was said that a person could get high from being in a room full of reefer smoke but I never noticed feeling any different when I came out of the room than when I went in. Maybe it didn't bother the Kid either and he was also a lover of Armstrong's playing, so perhaps he was there for the same reason as I.

Another club I jammed in was the Cabin Cuban, which was on the Rue Fontaine, not far from the Hotel Ligieux. I had not been acquainted with Cuban music and to my surprise it was swinging like mad with rhythms that were different from what we played in jazz. But the musicians had an idea about jazz also and when a jazz musician came to sit in with them, they played jazz tunes and not bad at all. Jazz was really not their music and Cuban and South American music was not my type, but we got together well enough to have some fun jamming and the clientele liked it.

When the show closed at the Rex, we had a few days to stay before we returned to New York. There had been some talk about taking the show to England but it didn't work out. We received a last minute notice that we were to leave the morning of October 4th. There was a rush to pack and do some last minute shopping for souvenirs.

And because of the last minute notice to leave, Leroy Hardy and I arrived at the railroad station two minutes after the train had left. There was a Frenchman named Georges who was taking care of the departure of the band as none of us could speak French, so he told us when another train would be leaving for Nice and we didn't miss that one.

The conductor came for our tickets later and when he saw them, he started telling us something in French which we did not understand. The train made a few stops and at one station I got off and was standing on the platform when a Frenchman came up and asked me if I was Kid Chocolate. He had probably seen a picture of the Kid in the papers and knew that he was in France. I told him I was not the Kid.

When we arrived in Nice, I saw all the heavy baggage we were carrying still at the station. I thought something was funny because the baggage had come on the train which the others had taken. From Nice we had to go to Villefranche to board the Italian steamer REX which was the largest ship plying the Atlantic and was the holder of the Blue Riband for being the fastest ocean liner in the world.

The Rex was supposed to sail from Villefranche at the same time our train arrived in Nice but Monsieur Georges had telephoned the steamship officials in Villefranche and arranged the difficult task of postponing the sailing time of the crack Italian liner one hour in order for us to get aboard.

A launch was waiting to take us out to the Rex. There was no landing port in Villefranche for large steamers, so the passengers were put ashore or taken out to the ships in launches. Most of the passengers on board knew that the ship was delayed from sailing because two passengers were arriving late so the decks were lined with passengers, curious to see who these two persons could be. And they really did wave and cheer us when we were climbing up the steps to the boarding deck.
But our baggage, trunks and Arnold Boling's drum case

and Wilson Meyer's bass which was in a specially made trunk were not put on the launch. In fact they were still at the station in Nice when we boarded the bus to go to Villefranche. We found out the reason from the baggage commissary; the baggage had been sent from Paris in a collective group ticket and as Leroy and I did not arrive with the group, all the tickets were not available so the baggage could not be collected by those that had arrived before us and there was not enough time for it to be put aboard ship when we arrived. However, everyone did have a few changes in their hand bags and it cost us a certain amount to have the baggage sent by another boat which would be sailing in a few days.
Two musicians were also missing. Booker Pittman and Alfred Pratt had decided to stay in France with their wives. Freddy Taylor also stayed.

I had not drunk too much wine with my meals during my stay in France, but I started again on the Rex. I did not drink as much of it as I had on the trip coming to Europe. The flying fish and dolphins in the Mediterranean Sea were as interesting to watch as they had been the first time I saw them. The weather was fine until after we passed Gibraltar and got into the Gulf Stream which was a little rough for a couple of days. We arrived in New York on Columbus Day which is the 12th October. (1933)
Back to the U.S.A.

A few days after my return to New York, I was contacted by Benny Carter who was forming an orchestra. Benny had formed some orchestras before this, one of which had played the Savoy and another the Arcadia. I was very happy about the opportunity of working for Benny because he was my favourite arranger and alto player.

Benny said that he would let me know when the band would begin rehearsing so I went to Leonia, New Jersey, to spend a couple of days with Beezie whom I had not seen for four months. She was working and could not meet me when I returned to New York. When I came from Leonia I learned from Dickie Wells who was also engaged to play with Benny that the band had made some records for an English arranger named Spike Hughes. No one knew where to contact me in New Jersey so I missed my first chance to record with Benny Carter.

But I made the other rehearsals. Benny had discovered three musicians who were in New York. The pianist, Teddy Wilson, Frederic 'Keg' Johnson, a trombonist and George Johnson (no relation to Keg) an alto sax player. The rest of the musicians were Charlie 'Big' Green, ex-Henderson Trombonist, Dickie Wells, trombone, Bill Dillard, Lindon (Lincoln) Mills and myself on trumpets, Glyn Paque, alto sax and Johnny Russel, tenor. There was Lawrence Lucie, guitar, Ernest 'Bass' Hill, bass and Cosy Coles, drums, as the rhythm section.

I had seen Big Green with Fletcher Henderson. Dickie Wells and Bill Dillard I had worked with, but I did not know the others although Russell, Paque, Mills and Lucie were New York musicians. I had seen Cozy with the Blanche Calloway orchestra. Benny had brought Wilson and Keg from
Chicago but I never knew where he had found George Johnson.

I had heard any number of Earl Hines records and there was no greater jazz piano player for me at that time, but when I heard Teddy Wilson, I knew that a new star was going to make his footprints in the sands of jazz. Earl was great and Teddy was destined to become great. He had certain Hines ideas but his style was not a strict copy. He had a very personal way of using his left hand in a modern stride manner.

Benny was well known for organising musicians who had never worked together as a group and have them sounding as if they had been together for years. The arrangements he made were more difficult for the sax section than they were for the brass, but he had good men because he knew the ones he wanted and the brass section's work was very effective with the passages he wrote for the reeds.

Benny was admired by a very successful negro bootlegger named George Ricks whom most of us knew very well, and one of the reasons for Benny forming this orchestra was because George wanted to open a club and Benny to have the band there. The salary was not great but the other musicians, like myself, admired and loved Benny to the point where they would have worked with him for the pleasure of playing his arrangements, if a job actually could not pay.

George Ricks opened the ex-Connie's Inn and named it the Harlem Club. There was a floor show the same as Connie had but the entertainers were not big names although they were known in Harlem. The band was sounding greater every day and I was the main soloist in the trumpet section. Benny was beginning to play trumpet also but he had not brought it out until he had it under control. There was
no singer in the band but things were sounding so good that Benny was inspired to sing and made an arrangement of a number called 'Ole Papy' and sang it.

Another theater on 125th Street called the Apollo started having stage shows and it was Benny Carter's band that inaugurated the grand opening and also played the first two weeks there. But there existed a system that was called kick-back to the 802 Union delegate.
Mr. Menton, who later opened the famous Menton's Inn, was the Harlem delegate and if the kick-back system benefited anyone, it must have been him.
It was the days of gangsterism and a leader and his men had to go along with the system if they wanted to work.

We still came back to the Club every night after the last show and worked until 3 a.m. Big Green was beginning to suffer from ulcers of the stomach but he had been, and still was, a heavy drinker. He came to the theater and did the first show every day and then he would be feeling so bad that he would lie on an army cot for the other three shows and eat nothing but clam chowder. When we got to the Club he would be feeling better and when the Club closed he was feeling good enough to go to a cellar joint across from the Rhythm Club and drink until it was time to make the first show. He did that for two weeks and Benny never said anything because he liked Big Green and so did the rest of the guys.

I suppose that when Connie's Inn was in its heydays and most of the time refused negro patronage, this had something to do with negro's not coming to the Club even after it re-opened under a different name and leadership. True, there were some nights when the crown was very good but a successful spot must have a good crown every night.

The band was wonderful without a doubt and quite a few white musicians from down town came to hear us at different times. Benny Goodman before he became famous was one whom Benny knew and introduced to the band. The show was good and had some beautiful girls. Charlie Barnet was another down town bandleader who came to the Club quite often. It was after I knew him at the Strand Ballroom that he formed a band which played in a big hotel down town.
Insert p. 71
a while. It was also competition for the Roseland as they were opposite each other.

A white band was on the second band-stand but I don't remember the name of the leader or any of the musicians. The conditions were better for us at the Empire than they were for the negro bands that played at the Roseland because we had a band room and a big one right on the same floor as the ballroom. There was no mixing with the public and a bouncer always stood by our bandstand when we were playing to see if some girl was going to flirt with us.....

I sat on the end of the stand and some girls would put their purses under my chair when they wanted to dance. The bouncer did not like that because he had the idea that it was a possible way for them to flirt with me or vice versa. When they asked me if they could leave their handbags under my chair, I told them it was not allowed but if they wanted to do it anyway, I was not going to be responsible. When the bouncer would get salty with me for letting them do it, I always told him that I warned the girls but could not force them not to leave their things there if they wanted to.

There was one way that the girls could talk to us if they wanted to and the bouncer could not do anything about it even if they knew the trick. There were five telephone booths next to the band room. The door was never closed so we could always hear the 'phone when it rang. If a chick wanted to get in touch with one of us, she would use a booth. One of us would always answer and the girl would say who she wanted to talk to. 'Are you one of the musicians?' would probably be one of the first questions, when whoever answered the 'phone would say hello. Then she would say she wanted to apeak to a certain one that sat at a certain place on the bandstand and that was it. And the moral of that story is that 'Love will find a way'.

One night we were quite surprised to see a tall blonde fellow standing to one side of the bandstand dressed in full dress clothes, because no one ever came to the Empire ballroom dressed like that. I thought that perhaps the guy was a high society cat who had probably been to a society wedding and had decided to go slumming in Harlem, but this fellow seemed to be slumming down town.

When we came off the bandstand, he introduced himself to Benny Carter and we all went to the band room to play our usual ten cent tonk which we did to pass the time between sets, as I had done on the back stairs of the Roseland ballroom with Russell's band.

Benny brought the fellow into the room and introduced him to us. His name was Baron Timothy Rosenkranktz and he was from Denmark. We later found out that he was a jazz fan and knew a lot about some of the big swing bands and the musicians. But Benny's was the first negro band he had heard in New York because he had only been in the city a couple of days when he learned that Benny had a band at the Empire ballroom. Timmie (as he was later to become known) had come to the ballroom in full dress because that was the way a person of his class went out in Europe at that time.

The next night he was back again but dressed like an ordinary human being! When we finished the night Timmie wanted to go up to Harlem, so Linden Mills the trumpeter we called Link, took Timmie up town. Link smoked reefers and he was the one who introduced the stuff to Timmie who became so fascinated with Harlem that he finally moved there.

For some unknown reason, Benny began to lose interest in the band and Bill Dillard left to join Teddy Hill who had been the tenor man with Luis Russell at one time and now had his own band at the Savoy. Two weeks before the time for us to finish at the Empire, Benny told us that he would be disbanding.

The word got around very quickly and Teddy Hill asked me and Dickie Wells to join his band. Willie Bryant was an M.C. and showman who had an act with another showman named Leonard Reed, who was forming an orchestra, and he engaged Teddy Wilson, Johnny Russell, Glyn Pacque and Cozy Cole. We all hated to see this band of Benny's break up and I considered and still do consider it the best band I ever played with.

So in January of 1934, Dickie Wells and I joined Teddy at the Savoy and I was back home again. The other members of the band were Bernard Flood, who along with Dillard and myself were the trumpet section. Hoe Britton was the other trombonist. Howard Johnson and Harold Blanchard on alto saxs and Leon 'Chu' Berry on tenor sax, Sam Allen, piano, John Smith, guitar, Richard 'Dick' Fullbright, bass and Bill Geeson on drums.

The Savoy was jumping as it always did and I was happy to be back in a place where it was not necessary to stand on the back stairway or go to a band room when I finished playing a set. The girls didn't have to call me from a telephone booth and I lived five minutes walking distance from the Savoy if I decided to go straight home after the night was finished. But that happened very seldom.

Dickie Wells and I were living with Grandma Jackson who had moved to New York a few years after I came there. Grandma's two daughters and granddaughters were also living there. Sometimes when I decided to go directly home after a night at the Savoy and would be peacefully sleeping, Dickie would come home high as a kite and knock on my door at 5 or 6 o'clock in the morning. There were no locks on the doors of the rooms because we were all like a family. But I had a latch on my door and so did Dickie.
When he came in at that time of the morning and knocked on my door, I knew he was high and did not answer. After a

few minutes he would push against the door real hard and pop went the latch and in came Dickie with a half pint of juice. I would not be in a drinking mood but he wanted me to drink with him. If I said I didn't want to drink he would threaten to throw some on me. I suppose I hated to see good liquor thrown away so I would take a drink and then we would talk until the bottle was empty and only then would Dickie go to bed.
I never got angry with him because we were almost like brothers who really loved each other and sometimes I would come home juiced and do the same to him as he did to me.

During the months that Teddy was at the Savoy, an orchestra by the name of the Alabama State College was engaged for a few days. The leader was named Erskine Hawkins and he was the second trumpet player I ever heard that could play altissimo C or C above the high one in the treble clef. The first one was with Jimmie Lunceford whom I heard at the Lafayette shortly after I came back from Europe.

After a few months at the Savoy, Teddy Hill and orchestra were engaged to play at the Ubangi Club which had been Connie's Inn and Harlem Club before. In place of having girls in the line up, there were six female impersonators and the main attraction was a lesbian named Gladys Lentley. Gladys was quite plump and wore a man's full dress suit for her act and dressed like a man except for a skirt when she had on street clothes. Gladys played piano, sang and tap danced a little.

Allen Drew was a cigar-smoking manager of ceremonies and comedian. A girl pianist and singer by the name of Una Mae Carlisle was also engaged at the club and she was a protege of Fats Waller when he was playing for the WLLW. radio station in Cincinnati.

The six female impersonators were not bad as chorus girls and some looked almost like girls. But later the manager added six more sissies and some of them had muscles like a prizefighter and they really looked funny in those chorus girls costumes and the big muscles showing in their arms and legs.
They all XXXXXX had chosen female names and one called itself

Clara Bow, another was Theda Barra and one quite famous was known as Mother Smothers. One night a few of us were talking very seriously with Clara Bow and we asked him or her! if he had ever had any sexual relations with a female, and he said, never. He had always felt that he was a female. The band got along with these female impersonaters very well and none of them ever tried to have an affair with any of us, that I know about. And I know that I was not bothered by any of them. I always was and always will be a guy that digs chicks and the real ones at that.

A few weeks after we were in the Ubangui, Roy Eldridge joined the orchestra. He had been barnstorming with the McKinney Cotton Pickers and wanted to stay put in one place for a while. Roy had already acquired the name of "Little Jazz" and it was an exciting pleasure to work with him and be in a position to hear him night after night. Teddy had let Bernard Flood go in order to make a place for "Little Jazz".

Grandma Jackson died before the end of 1934 and her daughters decided to move to Jamaica, Long Island, so I found a room with kitchenette on 142nd Street near Lenox Avenue and not far from the Savoy. Beezie, the girl I had met on a subway in 1932 had become my sweetheart. Her mother died shortly after I met her and she was living with her stepfather in Leonia, New-Jersey. Beezie had a son and daughters born out of wedlock. Her son was living with the parents of his father and the daughter was with her father's parents who was not the father of her son.
Things started going badly with her step-father and eventually she came to live with some friends in New York and when I moved into my one room appartment, Beezie and I started living together.

Everything was fine until my wife whom I had been separated from, almost two years, found out that I was living with a girl and one night when she knew I was at work, she came to see what Beezie was like and that really must have upset her, because Beezie was a very pretty girl who had blue eyes, wavy dark red hair and looked like a white girl. Madelyn told her that she was the real Mrs.Coleman because I was not divorced from her. Beezie knew that but she had never seen her and Madelyn had never bothered me until she heard that I was living with a girl who was calling herself Mrs. Coleman.

And not long after Madelyn's visit, I received a notice to appear in the domestic court on a certain day. I was ordered to pay five dollars a week alimony to Madelyn. I had no cut because I was the one that had left her. She didn't really need the money because she was working and making a nice salary for a woman. But she was getting revenge because I was with someone else.

One day I was contacted by Billy Taylor to do a recording date with Fats Waller. The Victor recording company had their studios in Camden, New Jersey, so the trip was made by train from New York to Philadelphia and Philly to Camden. Fats had two bottles of Whisky which we drank between New York and Philadelphia and he bought two more before we taken the train to Camden. Fats was really the most happy of lucky person I ever knew and he did not ask any of us for a cent to help him buy the whisky and when he taken a drink, he would then pass the bottle around and we all had a fine trip to Camden.

The musicians were Billy Taylor Sr. (bass), Harry Dial (drums), Gene Cedric (clarinet & tenor) and myself. The recordings got off to a good start and Fats ad-libed on all the singing numbers as though he had been playing and swinging them all his life and he had not seen any of them before they were given to him in the studio. The numbers were chosen by the recording company and not by himself.

Before each number was recorded, Fats would run it down on the piano and then we would go over it a couple of times to set the solos and get the idea about what riff Cedric and I were going to play in certain spots.

Of course drinks were passed around between each number that was recorded and everybody was groovie. We recorded 6 numbers, but when Fats was doing "Night Wind" on the organ, a reed broke on one of the pipes and it took an hour before someone found out which one it was that needed to be repaired. During that time we had a big meal which was paid by the recording company and more drinks.

Finally we finished the session and entrained for New York. In Philadelphia, Fats bought two more bottles of Whisky which we drank before arriving at the Penn Station in New York. I didn't feel drunk but when I arrived home Beezie had prepared a nice dinner for me and I didn't have any appetite and accused Beezie of cooking some mess that nobody could eat. So I left for the Ubangui Club.

I took my horn out and started warming up and take my place on the bandstand. We always played a few sets before the show came on, so Teddy called three numbers and when he gave the starting beat on the first number which was one that I had to read because I had not memorised my part, I couldn't even see the part. The notes started running together and I could not play 8 bars of the tune. I didn't feel drink when I got on the bandstand, but my mind just wouldn't function. My fingers wouldn't move and I couldn't see the music.

Teddy asked me what was wrong and I told him about the recording session with Fats and how much I had drunk. We called Teddy 'Fess' as so many other orchestra leaders were called. So after hearing my story, Fess told me to go out and get some air for a while and come back later. I went out for half an. hour and came back, but I was not feeling any better as far as being able to play was concerned. So Fess told me to take the night off. I had seen a trumpet player named Ovie Alston going into the bar of Big John's when I was out getting some air. Ovie had lived with Billy Taylor whom everybody called Hoss at the same time as Mack Walker and I had lived in the same appartment, so I knew Ovie well.

I went into Big John's, saw Ovie and told him my troubles and asked him to finish the night for me. In that manner, Teddy's band was not without a third trumpet. I made it home without staggering and went to sleep as soon as I got undressed and into bed. And I had learned a lesson that I never forget, and that was never try and drink as much as Thomas "Fats" Waller. The next session I did with him, I drank, but not every time the bottle was passed to me.

After our run at the Ubangui Club, the band played a week at the Howard Theatre in Washington and an engagement in the Roseland ballroom and then came back to the Savoy. During that time I had gotten behind in my allimony payments and shortly after I had made the second record session with Fats, I received a notice to appear in the Domestic Relations court again and was ordered by the judge to pay 10 dollars a week until
the back payments were in order.

But I decided that I was not going to pay any more alimony and sent a telegram to my father in Cincinnati, telling him to send me one saying come home at once. This I showed to Fess Hill because I did not want to give a two-weeks notice and have the word get out that I was leaving the band, which may have gotten back to my wife.

I figured that I would stay in Cincinnati long enough to get a divorce which was much easier to do there than it was in New York. So Beezie and I packed our few belongings and left the Apple by bus one afternoon and arrived in Cincinnati the next day. We lived with my father who had two rooms on Outter Street near Court Street. My mother was living on Court Street not far from my father, so I saw her every day. My brother was living with my father also.

I was not in town very long before all the musicians knew I was there. The two best known orchestras amongst the Negro musicians were Jack Jackson's orchestra who had come on the scene after I had left Cincinnati, and Clarence Page who was the best known and most popular orchestra. Clarence contacted me a few days after I arrived and I started working with him doing one-night stands in Kentucky, West Virginia and Ohio.

Harl "Inky" Tremble whom I had known for many years played alto sax and was director of the band because Clarence prefered to sit and play tenor. Inky was a nice front man on the style of Cecil Scott, and he was always inventing names for people and things that already had a name. He was the one that started calling Melvin Oliver, "Sy" which was a short name of psychology. When Sy joined Zack White's band, Inky was also in the band. He told me that whenever Sy came to rehearsals with a new arrangement, he had such a psychological way of explaining how a certain phrase should be played that Inky started calling him "Psychology" which he later changed to Sy.

There was a trumpet player named Thomas "Sleepy" Grider whom I had met years before in West Virginia, playing in the band and Sleepy was the only musician that I can think of back in those times that could probably drink as much as Thomas "Fats" Waller and not get drunk enough for anyone to know it. Sleepy played a nice strong first trumpet and could have become well known in that category if he had been more serious about music.

The drummer I had met some years before in Columbus, Ohio. His name was Tommy Smith and he was a nice trombone player and I don't remember the name of the rest of the musicians except the pianist who's last name was Grant.

Edgar James and William Smith, drummer and pianist respectively, were the only two musicians other than Page still around Cincinnati that I had played with at the beginning of my career. Wes Helvey who had been the second band leader I had worked with in Cincinnati had quite the game, moved to Detroit, and was in the insurance business. I was considered a star trumpet man with Page because I had lived in New York and made a name among the musicians. Nobody knew the real reason for my coming back home except Beezie and my parents.

I went to see one of the best Negro lawyers in town, a fellow by the name of Bailey and he told me that I could get a divorce for 35 dollars but I would have to stay in Cincinnati for three months before I could apply for it. It was the month of June 1935, that I had come home. I gigged with Clarence Page and we played the Lexington, Kentucky fair in July. My father decided to move into a larger apartment because he liked Beezie very much and thought that she and I would stay in Cincinnati if we had more rooms.

We moved to 9th street near the Shermann school which was the first school I had gone to when my mother was living with Aunt Mary, which was between Mound and John Streets. There was three rooms, kitchen and bath on the second floor of a three-story house. Tommy Smith the drummer
with Clarence Page lived a few doors from us. Everybody was happy and I really did not miss being away from New York very much.

But in August I received a letter from Freddy Taylor whom I had given a beat-up trumpet when I left Paris, France. Freddy had stayed in France but was now back in New York looking for some musicians to take back to France. He had asked for me especially and had gotten my address in Cincinnati from someone in New York and sent me a letter saying that he had made good in Paris as an orchestra leader and wanted me to join him. I had bigger eyes for going back to Europe than I did for getting a divorce and I figured that I could get a divorce there also.

So I jumped at the idea and sent Freddy a telegram saying that I would accept his offer and later sent him a letter in which I explained why I was in Cincinnati and told him not to say anything to anyone, even the other musicians he had engaged whom I did not know who they would be. I knew that if the word got around that I was going to Europe, it would get to Madelyn and that would have been the end of that. New York is a very big city with millions of people, but if you are known in a certain circle, the grape vine is the same as in any small town. Everybody in the circle knows why you were born, where and when.

But sometimes there is a possibility of a secret being kept, and there is a certain honour among thieves considering what circumstances may be. So the word did not get on that I was going to France. Beezie and I arrived in New York around 10th of September 1935 and went straight to Leonia, New Jersey and stayed with her step-father.

I had to come to the big city for my passport and before going downtown, I was sitting in Freddy's car on 138th street between Lenox and 5th Avenue when I saw a musician that I knew coming down the street. I ducked down in the car like a criminal that was being hunted by the law because I could not afford to have my plans go wrong at that stage of the game.

I was to leave on the French Line's Normandy, the 25th of September and it was decided between Beezie and I that I would send for her after I had been in Paris one month. The night before, there was a boxing match between Joe Louis and Max Baer and I took the risk to come over to New York that night and celebrate Joe's victory in a bar on 7th Avenue and 143rd Street after hearing the fight on the radio. Harlem was jumping but I didn't run into anyone that I knew, and it would not have mattered much that night anyway because if I had been seen by anyone that may have told Madelyn whenever they saw her , that they had seen me in the city, I knew that I would be out of the U.S.A. before she could have done anything to stop me.

I think the sailing time for the "Normandie" was 10 a.m. and I had to see my buddy Dick Wells before I left. I have not even written him from Cincinnati to let him know that I was going to Europe although I was certain that he would have kept it a secret if I had asked him. But I just wasn't taking any chances. So we came from Leonia early in the morning of the 25th and I woke Dickie up about 8 and told him what was happening. He was real happy to see me. I told him why I had left New York which he did not know the real reason before.

Freddie had told me in New York who were the other two musicians that were coming with us. George Johnson who had played in Benny Carter's 1933 band and my long time friend Edgar Courance who had acquired the name of Spider because he was working in a club by that name when Freddy had approached him about going to Europe.

Spider told me later that he was not too enthused about going to France when Freddie asked him. He asked Freddie who else was going and Freddie broke the promise he had made to me and told Edgar that I would be the trumpet man. He asked Edgar not to say anything about me going to anyone else and Spider accepted to go after he knew that I was going.

The Normandie was the second greatest Ocean liner that I had the privilege of sailing on. The first was the Rex and the Conte Grande was far from being a row boat. But the Normandie was a floating hotel and a few days after leaving New York, we were taken on a tour of the ship.

The second night before we were to arrive in Le Havre, George Johnson and I arrived in the dining room dressed as we always were every night, but to our surprise, the men were dressed in tuxedos. It was gala night which was something that we knew nothing about. So the next night, George and I decided that we would not be caught with out pants down and we came to dinner the last night on board with out tuxedos and to our surprise, no one was wearing tuxedos, except us. That had not happened on the Conte Grande nor the Rex, so it must have been only on the French lines that they had gala nights. George Johnson and myself were two embarrassed fellows the next day when we debarked on the shores of France the 30th of September 1935.

It was a beautiful day when we arrived in Paris and Freddie had rooms for us at a hotel called Eden on rue Pigalle. Later, after we had arranged things in our room, Freddie took us to the cafe Lizieur, a place that I had known when I came to Paris in 1933 and lived in the hotel above. We met the drummer that was engaged to play with Freddie's group. His name was William Diemar. I think that Diemar came to Europe in 1927 with a group from Buffalo.

After rehearsing for one week, we opened at the Villa d'Este on rue Areene-Housaaye near the Arc de Triomphe and the great Avenue des Champs Elysees. The pianist was French by the name of Jean Ferrier, the bass was Eugene D'Hellemes. The guitarist was from America and his name was Oscar Aleman.

Back in the U.S.A. I never played a matinee at the Savoy except on Sundays, National holidays and very special events. At the Roseland and Arcadia, I played them every Thursday, Saturday, Sunday and holidays.

But at the Villa d'Este, we played matinees which were called teen-dances every day from 5 until 7 in the afternoons and 9.30 until 2 the next morning and had no nights off. My first visit in Paris had been so short that the city was still new and exciting at this time and the routine of playing two hours every day and four hours and a half every night was like a happy game.

One of the first young French jazz musicians that I made acquaintance with was a tenor player named Alex Combelle. Exactly how we met, I cannot recall, but I remember that Alex Combelle used to come to my room in the Hotel Eden and ask me about many musicians in the States and especially about ones around New York. Alex spoke English quite well. All that I knew to say in French was : 'bonjour, monsoir' and 'oui' (wee).

I had a photograph album with some photos of different musicians I had worked with and showed them to Alex. He knew about quite a few of them and besides Armstrong, he had heard about Henri "Red" Allen but never seen a photo of him. He pointed to Red's photo and asked me who he was. I told him it was Red Allen. His comment was: Hum, funny face!

I also had a nice collection of records mostly Armstrongs and a portable phonograph and Alex enjoyed listening to the records he had not heard before. I also remember that I caught a cold once and told Alex that I would like to have something to cure it but I didn't know what to ask in French. So he brought me some pills and when I saw them, they were white and about the size of a beer bottle cap and I knew I could not swallow something the size of that. But Alex told me to take one, put it in my mouth, then take a mouth full of water and let the pill disolve for a couple of seconds and it would get soft and then I could swallow it. And to my surprise it worked, but I will never forget how big those pills looked to me, but it knocked my cold out in almost nothing flat.

I was astonished because I had never heard a guitarist play the way he played, and I was even more surprised that a foreigner could play such wonderful jazz. Grapelli was also very good. I had heard Joe Venuti when I was an amateur musician. Later, when I became a professional, I had heard Robert "Juice" Wilson playing in Buffalo. We used to go to the place where he worked every night after we had finished our job at the Ballroom. But Grapelli was really a surprise, because no-one had ever mentioned him to me. In fact, I had not heard anything about French or other European musicians apart from Nat Gonella, and I can't remember how I had heard of him.

Django had an approach to the guitar unlike any other guitarist playing in the States. He had a phenomenal execution, and he was taking a lot of solos at a time when solos were not known about on the guitar as a rule. Teddy Bunn, for instance, didn't have Django's speed or technical mastery. In fact the quintet as a whole, liked to play numbers fast. However, Djano was also an excellent accompanist. He seemed to have ideas which would stray a little from the original harmonies, so there was always something which was pleasing and logical to inspire the soloist. His chords were very unusual, because at that time, most accompanists did not extend the harmonies beyond the 7th, whereas Django was using 9ths and 13ths.

About two weeks after we had been in the Villa d'Este, I was asked if I would accept a job to sing in a club called "l'Heure Bleue" on rue Fromentin, after I had finished my night at the Villa d'Este. I had never done much singing except for a few group vocals with Lloyds Scott, but I knew the words to many songs and my voice was not the worst that could be hears so I thought it would be kicks to do a little singing and I accepted the proposition.

The musicians playing at l'Heure Bleue were known at the Quintet of the Hot Club de France. I had not met any of them before and had not heard them in action either until the first night I went to sing with them. I had to sing 4 numbers and then I was finished. That wasn't what anyone could call a hard job. I don't remember how much I was paid but I do remember that these musicians knew every song I wanted to sing.

It was a strange formation to me because it consisted of three guitars, a violin and bass violin. I had never heard any groups like them for the simple reason that none like them had ever existed. The violin player was the best I had ever heard playing jazz after Robert "Juice" Wilson on one, the guitarist was the greatest I had ever heard because guitars in those days, most guitar players played rhythm style. But this fellow took solos and had ideas and techniques that were out of this world.

The violinist spoke English and told me that his name was Stephane Grappelli. The solo guitarist was Django Reinhardt and the other guitarist was Django's brother Joseph. The bass was Louis Vola and Pierre Ferret who played rhythm guitar with Joseph.

Grappelli told me that Django and Joseph were gypsies. Django had had an accident with his left hand when he was younger and could only use three fingers. But he used those three fingers as if they were ten.

There was a woman from the USA who had been in France quite a long time, who was also singing at l'Heure Bleue. Her name was Ida Smith, but she was known as Bricktop, because she had red hair and she was a light skin negro woman. She was quite popular in the night club circle of Paris. But she was jealous of me because I had ideas about singing jazz and she didn't. The result was that after singing in the club for 4 nights, I was told that I was not needed after that. I didn't bother to ask the reason because I knew it and I wasn't hurt because of it, for I had enjoyed my new experience for a few days and I had met the greatest quintet of its type and was destined to remain a very good friend to Django, Grappelli, and the rest of the musicians. Bricktop was a very clever woman. She knew how to handle everybody, and all the snobs of Paris used to go to her place. But to me, she was just a plain ole' bullshitter. The French thought a lot of her, but I didn't.

Paris in 1935 was much more lively than it is today. There seemed to be a certain sort of happiness among the people which you do not see today. No one seemed to concentrate on money. Everybody could go to a bar, and if they couldn't pay, they had their credit. The economy didn't interfere with anybody's way of life. Life was cheaper and it was much gayer. On the big Boulevards, they had a lot of large cafes, and they'd have Hungarian orchestras playing in those days, sometimes with as many as twenty pieces as well as singers. This would last from 12 o'clock in the day, until midnight. Gay Paree! That's just the way it was! There was a lot of work for musicians, and many Americans were over here in various aspects of show business and music.

The war changed everything. In the 30's, the bars were open all night, /after the war, they limited the hours and life got much more expensive. Before the war, they had the brothels here, but after the war, some woman, who worked for the administration, put up a vote to have those places closed. In my opinion, that was the wrong thing to do. Because it was revenue for the Government, and there were less crimes of violence than today.

Some of those brothels were pretty remarkable places. Some of them were very exclusive. They had different rooms. Each one representing a different culture. If you thought you wanted to be out in the desert, they had a room with a tent in it. This was an amazing thing in those days, and I think had a certain value as far as crime was concerned. It was certainly attractive to anyone from the States, and particularly for the Blacks who were unable to mix at home. They had a chance to experience the opposite side of the fence, just as the American white men used to take advantage of the slave women.

I renewed my acquaintance with Willy Lewis whom I had met in 1933, in Monte-Carlo with June Cole and Ted Fields. Willy was leading an orchestra in a high society club called "Chez Florence", on rue Blanche and not far from the bar and hotel de Lizieux where many of the American negro musicians would congregate when they had finished their nights work.

But the surprise of surprises was meeting Benny Carter one night at the Lizieux's bar a few nights after I had arrived in Paris. As I had been in Cincinnati a few months before coming to France and the way I was obliged to pass through the Apple, I had not picked up on the latest events, so I had no idea that Benny was in Paris until I saw him this night. He was working with Willy Lewis who had an all-Negro band which was the only one in Europe. Benny had come to Paris with a young pianist named Garnet Clark. I think that Garnet was from Washington D.C., and I had seen him once in some club in New York with another young pianist named Ram Ramirez.

Between Boudon's and Lizieux's, that corner was a little Harlem in the early morning when all the night spots were closed and the American musicians and entertainers gathered in those bars and the "tabac".

Another musician that had gone to Wilberforce College and was now in Paris was a trumpet player named Jimmy Bell. Jimmy was married to an American white girl whose name was Grace Edwards and who was a singer.

Other American entertainers in Paris at this time were Opal Cooper who sang at the melody bar just in front of the tabac and Boudons; Snow Fisher, a dancer and drummer; Alberta Hunter, a blues singer; Glover Compton, a singer that accompanied himself on piano; Al Brown the ex-boxing champ; Irene Bullard who had a gymnasium on rue Mansart; Marino and Norris, singers; and Edgar A. Wiggins a journalist for the Chicago Defender, a negro weekly paper. Also Cle Sadler, an alto-sax player; Ray Stokes, pianist; Harry Cooper, a trumpetist who had played with Duke Ellington at one time.

Another musician and song writer that I had seen in New York who was now living in Paris was Spencer Williams who composed the famous "Basin Street Blues". I met the members of Willy Lewis's band that were not with him when I met him in the south of France. Joe Hayman played alto-sax and Frank "Big-Boy" Goodie, tenor and clarinet, who was really a big boy about 7 feet tall and must have weighed 280 pounds. He had also played cornet but eventually gave it up. Johnny Mitchell was the guitarist.

I think that Garnet had worked a short while with Willy and it did not go so well because Garnet was quite wild and flighty. So Willy had engaged Herman Chittison whom I had met some years before in Boston accompanying the comedian Stepan Fetchet.

One week after I had started playing at the Villa d'Este I was able to go from Place Pigalle to the Etoile or Arc de Triomphe with the bus and I had the feeling that I was learning more about the great city of Paris. When I first came to New York, that was the first real big city I ever saw. And it was also a thrilling and wide open town. Buffalo was wide open also and when I saw the red light district there, it
reminded me of the days when I was in my early teens and used to walk up George Street or John or Upper Carlisle and look at the prostitutes whom I called pretty ladies.
If New York City had a red light district when I arrived in town, I never knew about it. But it had so much of everything else which was thrilling to a country boy like me.

And Paris had everything that New York had and then some. The cafes or bars stayed open 24 hours a day, living was not expensive. The people were friendly and a jazz musician was considered as a human. There were interesting brothels, the likes of which the ones in Buffalo never dreamed could be possible. Some were so unique that tourist agencies had night tour visits to them. One very famous and well known to tourists was called "Aux Belles Poules" at 32 rue Blondel. The calling card mentioned that English was spoken. Another was known as the House of all Nations because it had rooms furnished in the style of every well known country in the world. A certain American musician had his mother in Paris for a vacation had taken her on a tour of some brothels. Most of the girls in these places walked around nude and a few would have on a short dress of a little apron and that was all.

After being in the Villa d'Este for one month, I asked Freddy Taylor to avance me enough money, as he had promised me he would do, to send for Beezie. I was surprised and very unhappy when Freddy told me that he could not advance me the money. But I had a trick up my sleeve, because I knew that Freddy could not play more than three or four numbers that he featured in his snake hip act.

So the following afternoon I came to work high as a kite and that night I was so juiced that I could hardly hold my horn and that really broke the ice. Freddy only directed the band and sang a few numbers when we played for dancers, and with me in no condition to play the arrangements, the band did not sound at all the way it had been.

When the night was finished, Freddy said that he would bring me the money the next day and he did! He must have had the feeling that I would repeat the same performance as the day before and it was possible that I may have. Two days after the incident, a ticket was on the way to Beezie and everything was going well again at the Villa d'Este.

There was a young couple that came quite often to the Villa d'Este and they eventually became good friends of the band and especially Spider and myself. Their names were Maurice and Venette Cullaz. The father of Venette was Siamese and she was a very beautiful girl with long dark hair. They invited us to dinner in their home; Venette was doing wonderful oriental dishes. I was surprised at the collection of records they had. Maurice had also the records I had made with Fats Waller. They had a little son about two years old who's name was Pierre.

Another fellow who became quite friendly with the band was an Egyptian musician who played drum. His name was Pierre Fouad. He had recorded with Django and had quite a solid beat with brushes. He also invited us to dinner at his home and he had a fine collection of records also.

It was there that I heard for the first time Billie Holiday's recording of 'Miss Brown To You' with Teddy Wilson at the box. Fouad also had a photo of Bunny Berigan whom I had heard but never seen. Bunny's recording of 'I Can't Get Started with you' was the greatest he ever did to my estimation. And it is the only record other than some of Louis's that I copied note for note and I still play it the way Bunny did at times just for my own pleasure.

I went to Fouad's home many times for dinner and recording sessions because he was from a rich family and could afford to buy the latest records as soon as they were issued. The Cullaz couple were quite wealthy I presumed because they had a very nice appartment in the

Saint-Cloud section of Paris were many wealthy families lived. Venette cooked Asiatic food with the right amount of curry that made the food almost melt in one's mouth. I had never eaten curried food before and after the first visit to the Cullaz's, I never refused an invitation from them.

Garnet Clark was living in a house that rented furnished appartments and I decided to take an appartment in the same building which was on the Rue de la Tour d'Auvergne, about 15 minutes walking distance from Boudon's cafe and restaurant and the bar next door that sold tobacco and cigarettes, situated rue Fontaine and rue Mansart. Boudon and the tabac next door were the American musicians headquarters.

The appartment I rented was to be a surprise for Beezie because we had lived in rooming houses except for the few months we had lived with my father in Cincinnati. The appartment consisted of a bedroom, living room, kitchen, bath room and toilet.

Beezie arrived the third week in November 1935, the train that brought the passengers on the boat to Paris from Le Havre arrived between the time that we did the tea dance at the Villa d'Este and the time we started at night. Freddy Taylor and his girl friend Alice came to the Gare St. Lazare with me to meet Beezie and the four of us had dinner together at a restaurant at Place Clichy.

I had learned to eat raw oysters which I had never eaten back home and that was a surprise to Beezie. I had moved into the appartment two weeks before Beezie arrived and after the dinner I took her home and she was surprised again when she saw the appartment.

The 21st of November I did a concert at the Ecole Normale de Musique with George Johnson, Jerry Mengo a drummer who was half French, half American, Django Reinhardt and a French pianist named Leo Detemple.

It was the first time I ever did a jazz concert and I must say the French were way ahead of Americans in the line of giving jazz concerts because I had never heard of any being done in the States. Armstrong had
given concerts in Europe long before the Americans ever thought of using the term concert for jazz session.

I don't remember what the style of the pianist was like but Jerry played nice swinging drums and Django was great. I thought he was great because I could not speak French and he did not understand English. And I had never before played for such an enthusiastic crowd of people as those French jazz fans. The hall could hold about 300 people and it was almost if not full and our success was overwhelming.

On the 25th of November, I made my first recording in France with Garnet Clarke, George Johnson, Django Reinhardt, and June Cole the bass player of Willie Lewis's orchestra. June had played with the Cinco Septett that had later become the McKinney's Cotton Pickers and with Fletcher Henderson before joining Willie Lewis in Europe. And it was the first time that I sang a song solo on a record. The title was 'The Object of my Affection'. We had a fast tempo and I almost choked trying to sing the last four measures of the middle part. But I made it and Garnet played great piano on this recording.

Garnet seemed to be a little deranged. When I recorded with him, I didn't know too much about him. Apparently, what had happened was that he had been down in the South of France, and all of a sudden he decided he wanted to come back to Paris. When he arrived there, he was going to stay at a certain hotel but he wanted first to see a lady friend of his. Unfortunately when they arrived, this lady was out, so he asked his taxi driver to drive around for a bit, but when they returned the lady was still not back. So they drove around a bit more, and the taxi driver began to get upset because he wanted his money. So the next time when they came back and the lady was still not around, he drove Garnet down to the police station, where he was arrested for not being able to pay his bill. While he was there, the police beat him up terribly badly, as a result of which he never fully recovered. In fact, there was another case where the same thing happened. An American dancer called Herb got into trouble in a clip joint in Pigalle. They had been over-charged for their drinks, and when they refused to pay the bill, the management called the police. He and his friend, and their two white girlfriends were taken down to the police station and badly beaten up. Fortunately they all recovered. So I think there was prejudice in France also, in particular, the French never really liked the Algerians and the Tunisians, especially the poorer classes. Those people had almost as bad a time in France as the black man in the Southern part of the United States. Even if there were no lynching they were often beaten up by the police.

Not long after I made my recording with Garnet Clarke, I met a fellow named Hugues Panassie and his friend Madeleine Gautier. I found out that Hugues was a jazz critic and president of the Hot Club de France. He knew

more about many of the American jazz musicians than I did and it was because of him that I was as well known as I was in France for my recording with Fats Waller. He had reviewed and written critics about the records before I knew that I was coming to France again.

It was amazing to black musicians from America to find how much specialist interest some Europeans were taking in our music. At that time, the average American didn't know Count Basie from Duke Ellington. Even when Duke Ellington came over here in the 30's, people knew all about him. They wanted to know who was the trumpet player and who was the saxophone player - their interest and enthusiasm was so high they wanted to know the whole history of the band! In America, nobody could care less. You'd see it on the Marquees, or on the theatres: "Duke Ellington and His Orchestra", but there were never any programmes saying who was who. When I realized that I was appreciated in a country not only for my playing, but that people knew where I had been born and who I had played with, I thought it was a really great event.

I was invited to visit the club which was on rue Mansart not far from Boudons. There I met the secretary of the club who was a fellow named Charles Delaunay and the treasurer whose name was Pierre Nourry. The club was on the ground floor and when I walked into the reception room, I saw the names of Coleman Hawkins, Louis Armstrong, and all the known jazz men of the time, written on the wall. The club was also a meeting place for jazz lovers, who were members of the club and French jazz musicians who would come there and listen to records, discuss about jazz and get information about concerts and ndws about what was happening in the jazz world.

It was about this time that I began to get interested in studying harmony. My first attempts were not too successful. When I was in New York, just before leaving France, I'd been taking harmony lessons

who was alcoholic. He'd come to my house and I'd show him the lessons I had done, and he'd say:"Yes, that's alright, but you could also do this." Then he'd rub out all my lessons and write in something new, which kept me confused. Finally, I'd offer him a drink, and he would accept one, and then several more, and that would be the end of the lesson. In the end, I decided it was not worthwhile. I didn't study harmony again until I came to France this last time. Instead, I continued to play by ear.

Christmas came and on New Year's Eve going into 1936, William Diemar got high and around 2 a.m. New Year's morning, he felt that someone had insulted him. If it was someone in the orchestra or one of the clients, I don't remember, but the Villa d'Este was packed like sardines in a can and Diemar picked up his bass drum and carried it through the crowd, came back for the rest of his material, ordered a taxi outside and went home. [out] We finished around 5 that morning with drums. The next afternoon, he was back at the club and didn't remember why he had left the night before.

At one time before I started working at the Villa d'Este, Freddy had a guitarist working with him whose nationality I don't remember. This guitarist left the country suddenly, and left four guitars in one of the bins in the basement of the Villa d'Este. Freddy showed them to me one day and I asked him to let me take one home with me. I really had the desire to learn guitar at the time.

But Freddy refused me because he was afraid the guitarist may come back someday for his instruments [and] although I promised that I would give the guitar back if the fellow came back and wanted it. But Freddy would not consent to my taking one, and there were four guitars in the basement going to waste! I may have been able to play guitar today if Freddy had allowed me to take one then.

January 24th 1936, I recorded for the first time under my own name. The date was supervised by Hughes Penassie and I had Herman Chittison on piano and Eugene d'Hellemes on bass. I believe it was the first jazz trip in the history of recording to be composed of trumpet, piano and bass. We recorded "What's The Reason" and "Georgia on my Mind". I had only heard Chittison play one time and that was when I first met him in 1932

in Boston. "Chit" was fast as [and] lightning and he must have heard Art Tatum many times and studied his style. He was the next thing to Art as far as technique was concerned. But he never wanted to bass to accompany him on his solos. He had a good left hand and I suppose he had the idea that the bass did not play the same pattern as he did with his left hand and it disturbed his ideas.

D'Hellemes was a good solid bass player who preferred to play trombone. He was also a very agreable fellow and we began to be good friends although I did not speak French and he didn't speak English. The first date with Chit and Eugene was recorded for Ultraphone. We recorded again the 31st of January '36 for His Master's Voice and did "I'm in the Mood for Love" and "After You've Gone". Those two records added more to my European success than the Fats Waller ones in the sense that I had more solo space and I was not under the influence of kick-a-poo joy juice as I had been when I recorded with Fats which some critics could not know that was the cause of me missing some phrases and they wrote about my mistakes and at the same time they praised my ideas.

A little earlier than the January 31st date with Chittison and d'Hellemes, I recorded "Coquette" and the first number I ever composed called "Joe Louis Stomp" with Edgar Courance (tenor), John Ferrier (piano), Oscar Aleman (guitar), Eugene d'Hellemes (bass), and William Diemar (drums). This date is registered in the French discography as being done on the 31st of January also but I don't remember having two recording dates the same day.

A few months after New Year's day 1936, it must have been in February, Freddy didn't come to work one night. Spider, George Johnson, were paid the equivalent of fifty dollars a week which was very good salary for a musician working in France as living expenses were about half of what they were in the U.S.A. The custom in France was and still is that musicians and other artists working in night clubs are paid every night.

So when we had finished this night when Freddy didn't show up the cashier said that she would pay us and asked each one how much he earned for a night. The three of us that had come over from the States and were considered the stars of the band were getting 150 franks a night (the equivalent of 50 dollars for 7 days work).

The cashier seemed quite surprised that we were not getting more but not as much as we were when we learned that the pianist was getting 165 franks a night. The bass player, guitarist and drummer were getting a little less than Spider, George and myself. We never learned how much Freddy was getting but it must have been a big taste.

The next night when Freddy came to work the owner of the club told him that he was finished but the band could continue. Freddy started pleading with us not to accept the deal and stick to him which meant that we should refuse to work. But we thought that Freddy had not been fair with us by giving the pianist (who was very good in those days but not considered as an outstanding artist) more than we were getting although we had accepted to come over here for fifty dollars a week.

So we turned a deaf ear to Freddy's plea and continued to work and it was a good thing we did because I realise not that if we had walked out we would not have been able to work any place else in Paris and may have been expelled from the country, because the owner of the Villa d'Este had the permission for us to work in France but only at the Villa d'Este until the 6-month contract that Freddy had signed was terminated.
