Spider, George and myself got a raise that equaled the pianists and I was considered as leader of the group although the three of us combined to call the numbers we played. There were no other problems because each one of us received our nightly salary from the cashier.

George Carpentier, the ex-heavy weight boxing champion, had a bar next door to the Villa d'Este and he came in the club every night. He always danced at least one a night when we played and he always spoke to each one of us as he danced by. Oscar Aleman the guitarist was a

small built fellow who was from Argentina and was very full of life. When George Carpentier spoke to Oscar, he always called him "little Monkey". George spoke English as well as I did whereas Oscar didn't know one word of English. But George had called him a little monkey so often that Oscar began to know the word and became suspicious about it being something unusual to call someone.

The pianist Jean Ferrier spoke and understood English not too bad, so one day Oscar asked Jean in French naturally what did the word monkey mean. Jean told him "un singe" which meant monkey in French. The next time that George Carpentier came in he was standing at the bar and Oscar was so impatient to let George know that he finally knew what a monkey was that he yelled out while we were playing a number: "Hellow George Carpentier, you big white monkey!"

We were all surprised because we didn't know that Oscar had found out what a monkey was and added big white to the word. George started to dance and when he was in front of the bandstand he asked us what Oscar had said. Maybe he had not caught all the words because we were playing at the time when Oscar yelled to him or maybe he couldn't believe his ears! Before any of us could say a word Oscar said again and loud "Hello George Carpentier, you big white monkey!" George laughed about it but he never referred to Oscar as a monkey again.

As we never had a night off and working under those conditions for months, one day I decided that I was going to take a free day and I did. But I was very sorry after when I heard of the great event that had happened that night. Coleman Hawkins had come to Paris a few days before from Holland and he came to the Villa d'Este that night and sat with the band.

The people never applauded when we played except when Freddy and Oscar did attraction numbers. Freddy danced his snake hip routine and played a number on the trumpet and Oscar who could not read a note as big as the piano, could play classical numbers on the guitar and also

did some numbers on a ukelele. Edgar told me that when Hawk first started playing no one paid attention to him. When they played a second number, some people at the bar turned away from their drinks and started to give an ear to what was happening. And by the time they finished a third number, the whole place was digging Hawk and nobody ever was applauded at the Villad'Este the way Coleman Hawkins was. I always regretted taking that night off. But after that, the public paid more attention to what we had to offer, thanks to Hawk.Hawkins and Benny Carter had a jam session one night which I also missed. Benny got Hawker roused by telling him he'd heard about the rise and fall of Coleman Hawkins - They were good friends and used to talk to each other like that. Finally, he got him to play and apparently, that was some night too, but again, I was not around.

And here I would like to mention that there was a second orchestra at the club which played tangos. We each played half-hour sets and therefore the job was not hard. We finished at 2.a.m. every morning, and it was seldom that I went straight home after work. Some mornings, it would be between 9 and 11 o'clock before I got to bed, but I always was on time for the job at 5 p.m. matinee time, and I always felt in good condition.

There was a club on rue Fontaine not far from Boudon's called "la Cabane Cubaine" (Cuban cabin) that had a fairly nice orchestra who were mostly Cubans. The owner played alto-sax and his name was ___. I had not heard much Cuban music in the States and the rhythm they played at the Cabana Cubaine was sensational and so lively. The musicians loved it when a jazz man would sit in for a jam session because they wanted to know more about jazz and the best way to learn it was to hear it played in person. They knew many of the jazz standards, so I went there quite often and jammed. The place never closed until about 6 a.m.

Willie Lewis started broadcasting to England from a station on the Champs Elysee called Post Parisien and asked me to join him for the broadcasts. It was good publicity for me because I started getting letters from jazz fans in England, some who told me that they had the recording or some of them that I had made with Fats Waller and they were happy to hear me broadcasting to England.

The 15th of May 1936, I recorded with Willie Lewis and George Johnson was also engaged for this date which augmented Willie's orchestra to 11 pieces, band plus two singers, one of which was Adelaide Hall who had been famous in many of the New York Cotton Club revues and Alice Mam, whom I never heard of before.

Billy Burns was the trombonist and I had met him only a short time before Willie started broadcasting to England. Billy was a fellow whose complexion was so clear that he could pass for an Italian. He had played in Europe with Sam Wooding who was known to have brought the first Negro Jazz orchestra to Europe after the war of 1914-1918. Burns had also played with Noble Sissle in Europe and Freddy Johnson the pianist whom I had met when I came to Paris in 1933. Burns told me that he had been offered a trombone chair in Paul Whiteman's orchestra but he refused the offer because he did not want to pass for white.

Benny Carter had left Willie Lewis for a position as arranger for the British Broadcasting Company in England before Willie had started his broadcasts. Coleman Hawkins had stayed in Paris for a short time only and was living in Holland. But he came back to Paris at times and Willie engaged him for a broadcast which passed the 30th of May.

I had seen Hawk when I was young in Cincinnati, had heard him at the Roseland from the Electricians booth and heard him at the Savoy. I hung out in Big John's, Pete's and some other bars where Hawk and his private bottles in each one, and I got to know him well enough for him to know my name and what I did. But at last I was going to play on the same programme with the master and that was a great honour for me.

Willie Lewis asked me to join his orchestra when my six months was finished at the Villa d'Este and I did that in June 1936. Willie offered me 170 francs a day and I could have got ten more from him had I realised the value of money at that time and cashed in the power of my popularity and considering that I was known to be the best American jazz trumpet in Europe.

But I enjoyed working at "Chez Florence" in Willie's orchestra. We started work at 11 p.m. and played until 1 a.m. and then had one-and-half hours off. A French orchestra played during our off time and when we came back, we worked until 5 or 6 o'clock in the morning, depending on how many people that stayed until that time. The good thing about working at "Chez Florence" was that there were no afternoon tea dancing there.

The director of "Chez florence" was Madame Regina and the Maitre d'hotel(head waiter) and second director was a Monsieur Victor. Another good thing about working there was that I did not have to take a bus or taxi to work as it was 12 minutes walking distance from where I lived and 2 minutes to Boudon's cafe.

At the "Chez florence" there was never actually what you would call a show. There were entertainers, and they would have a singer. Apart from that we played dance music - a lot of it was just commercial orchestrations. Often, when I'd take my solo, I'd have to blow into my stand to keep it from being too loud. I always like to blow out, because it's difficult to play with the same intensity quietly. If you feel free to blow, it's easier to get the feeling. I had the same trouble in the Pump Room in Chicago with Teddy Wilson who also had to play at restricted volume. So sometimes I'd turn my back and play. Most nights we'd play a number for the radio and then you could stretch out, but the rest of the time we were restricted.

Looking back now, I think that Willie Lewis's orchestra must have been really quite good. It was quite a swinging band and had it been transported, for instance, to the Savoy, I think that Willie would have done as well as Teddy Hill, when he was there. Willie didn't have any big names but he had good musicians in the band. Big Boy Goodie could swing, and on a good night, Jack Butler could too. Billy Burns was not a great trombone player, but a lot of bands had trombone players who were not great jazzmen. The clientele seemed to like the band. They would even send champagne when they asked for requests. Randolph Hurst used to come often. He and Billy Burns were good enough friends to go out together.

Jimmy Donaghue, Barbara Houtton's brother, also used to hang out with the orchestra. If we would go to a cafe after work, he would often come along. I don't know how interested in jazz he was, but he certainly seemed interested in the band.

The 3rd of July, I had another concert at the Ecole Normale de Musique. Alberta Hunter, the blues singer, Garland Wilson, a pianist-singer, and Chittison with the orchestra of Christian Wagner were the other participants, and the place was packed to standing room only. Alberta Hunter had been in Europe for quite some time but Garland Wilson, who was not a real jazz pianist, played an exciting entertainers type of piano and had not been in France very long. I had seen Garland on the stage of the Apollo in Harlem a few times but never met him until this concert. Christian Wagner was an alto-sax and considered one of the best French jazz clarinetists.

On July 15th, the Willie Lewis orchestra left Paris for a place called [Knukke] Knocke in Belgium, with all the orchestra wives. This was my first time to go to Belgium and it was always thrilling for me to visit a place I had never been before and have time to discover something of that place.

Willie was engaged for 6 weeks to work in the Casino Kursall and [Knukke] Knocke was a beautiful summer resort. The casino was a very large one and we played in a large hall that seated about 1,200 people. It was also the hall where concerts were presented with a big symphony orchestra composed of all the classical professors of music who were Belgium and different well known conductors and opera stars were engaged to appear there.

There was a symphony concert every night and we were on a bandstand next to the stage which the symphony orchestra occupied and across from us was a Swiss orchestra of 9 musicians whose name was the Lanigiro Syncopating Melody Kings. Later when I became better acquainted with these musicians, I asked one of them what the work Lanigiro meant. He told me that it was original spelled backwards.

We played naturally for dancing which did not start until after the classical concerts were finished, around 10 every night. One of the trumpet players in the symphony orchestra became interested in the way I played. He had never heard a jazz trumpeter in person and I had to explain the points of improvising to him. He would listen to me almost every night and stayed a long time after the other musicians he played with had left. He told me that for certain numbers in the classics he changed mouth pieces and was quite surprised that I didn't change mine and played high notes and low ones on the same mouth piece.

We stayed in a big hotel named the Trianon right on the beach when we arrived in Knocke but later found a pension that was not as expensive as that one. A pension is a hotel where the clients have room and board. This hotel was named Derby and it was 5 minutes walk to the casino and the beach.

Most everyone in the orchestra and their wives rented bicycles and we would ride to Zeebrugge, Brugge, a jewel of a town, and Sluis, Hollande. We visited the World War I museum and monuments along the coast of the North Sea and got plenty of exercise riding to different places and going to the beach also.

I was never a heavy beer drinker but I drank less alchohol during our stay in Knocke than at any time after I learned how to really drink. There was a cafe in the casino building down stairs under the terrace of the casino that served good German beer called Dortmund and after every set, most of us made a bee line for this cafe which was called Berry's.
Monsieur Berry looked as though he was Hitler's twin brother. The same little moustache and he combed his hair in the same style as Hitler. He was a very nice person and really enjoyed our company.

Johnny Mitchel, Burns, Joe Hayman, Ted Fields and myself were the most regular customer, of Berry's cafe and we must have drank at least a gallon and a half of Dortmund between us every night. I was actually getting a kick out of beer for the first time in my drinking life.

Louis Vola had played bass with Willie in "Chez Florence" but Willie engaged a Cuban bass player named Jose Riestra for the Knocke engagement and I forgot to mention that Bobby Martin had left when I joined Willie. I could understand a little French by now, but Riestra didn't speak English and his French had a Cuban accent which was very hard for me to dig. He was a fine solid bass player and a wonderful person.

The band had ordered a uniform of white suits before we left Paris which we received two weeks after we had started at the casino, and the first night we wore them, it seemed as though those uniforms lifted our spirits sky high because we played better than we had been it seems to me. Willie Lewis did most of the singing in the band, but I featured in a number called "The Music Goes Round and Round" because it was a number that tells about what happens on a trumpet when the valves are pushed down. I played and sang this number better than I ever had and made a bis (encore).

We played two weeks in the big hall and then went downstairs in a smaller club called the "Pingoin". Adelaide Hall did an attraction. The band also sang some spiritual numbers with Willie always singing the lead. Willie had a wonderful baritone voice and sang with great power. The "Pingoin" was more suited for a jazz orchestra than the big hall upstairs, but we had success in both places.

Benny Carter had a vacation from his job in the B.B.C. so he and his wife Inez came to Knocke, but Benny was on holiday and never sat in with the band although he came to the club often. Another famous

Negro woman who was an opera singer and had sang in the casino was Miss Catherine Yarbo. I saw Catherine when she did Aida in Knocke and she was a great artist. She had her vacation after playing the casino and stayed in Knocke for two weeks. She did not know how to ride a bicycle so she and another woman friend of hers rented a four wheeled pedal contraption and rode to Sluis or Seebrugge with us.
We finished at the Pingoin the last of August and Willie had a two week engagement in Den Hague at a dance hall called the "Tabarin".

Willie Lewis and Chittison had continued to live in the Trianon Hotel in Knocke and the day we left for Holland as Den Hague was not too far from Knocke, Willie hired a bus to take us there and we were all to meet in front of the Trianon. Instruments were packed in the bus and the baggage also and everybody was there except Chittison. Willie went back into the hotel to see what had happened to Chit and found out that the hotel owner would not let Chit leave because he had not paid his rent during the 6 weeks he had been there.

I don't know how this could have happened unless Chittison had arranged to pay at the end of the season, and when the time came to pay it, he pretended he didn't have the money. I know that Willie paid him every week the same as he did for the rest of us. So Willie paid the bill for Chittison and I also know that Chit never paid one franc back to Willie. And Chit was not a gambling man although we would all shoot some craps now and then and Chit did also. But he was not the gambling type that went in the gambling rooms of the casino and played for big stakes. I was to find out some other little mean things about Chittison's character later.

We started in the Tabarin the 1st of September until the 15th. Holland was very nice and I had never seen too many bicycles before. Couples rode together holding hands and parents had their children on them in little seats attached over the rear wheel. There were delivery

bicycles, flower pedlers on bicycles and people even moved their furniture from one place to another on bicycles. At lunch time and evenings when jobs were finished, the traffic was thick as flies in an open garbage can on a hot summer day.

The dance hall closed at 1 a.m. and at 1.10 a.m. there was no one in the place except the orchestra and other personnel of the place. I never saw people leave a place as fast as they did in Holland but later I found out that there was a law in that country that when the last dance was finished no one was allowed to linger a while except the musicians and personnel. Even a musician's wife could not wait in the place for him if for example he had to change clothes. And if a musician had made a date with a girl, he had to rush like hell to put his instruments away and get to her as he could because she would not wait for him outside.

I always believe in testing the national drink of any country I went to. So in France it was cognac and in Belgium they drink more beer than any other drink. In Holland I found out that the national drink was Bols which is less heavier than gin but looks like gin. We were allowed to drink on the bandstand and sometimes I had as many as six glasses at my side but the size of the drinks were not very large and three glasses was just a good drink to me or any other billard drinker.
The Tabarin was a very nice place to work and the hours were from 8 in the evening until 1 a.m. and no matinees, not even Saturdays and Sundays.

After we finished in Holland we had two weeks before going back to "Chez Florence" in Paris, so Beezie and I decided to spend a week in Brussels because we could not visit it when we were in Knocke as I was obliged to work every night. It was a very nice city and had the privilege of being known as the little Paris of Europe.

We came back to Paris and lived in the same building on rue de la Tour d'Auvergne. I had a lot of trouble with taxi drivers when I lived on this street. I couldn't speak much French and like many of the lazy

type American musicians in Paris at that time, I didn't try too hard to learn the language. Sometimes when I wanted to take a taxi home, I would have to ask three or four drivers before I could find one that understood me. And I would say the name of the street to him the same as I had said it to the others and by luck he would understand. But it was one of those things that if a foreigner didn't or couldn't pronounce a word with a certain accent, the taxi driver would not try to understand.

Willie started working at Chez Florence again and not long after we had opened, a violin player named Leon Abbey contacted me and asked me if I would like to go to India with him. I had heard about Leon Abbey in New York because he was the leader of an orchestra that came to Europe a few months before I arrived in the big city and had taken Fletcher Allen, an alto sax player with him. Fletcher had played with Lloyd Scott before I joined the band and the Scott Brothers used to talk about him often. Leon Abbey and Fletcher were in Egypt when I came to France in '35.

This offer to go to India really excited me. The conditions were 50 dollars a week, room and board and transportation from Paris to Bombay and back to Paris. I would have to pay Beezie's transportation and board but that was a small matter as far as I was concerned. The excitement of going to India was all that mattered to me. Other things I would take [them] in their stride.

So I gave my notice to Willie and naturally he was upset because there was no one in Europe that could replace me as far as Willie was concerned. He asked me if I wanted more money to stay with him and I told him that it was not a matter of money but that I wanted to see as much of the world as possible whenever I had the opportunity to do so. I suggested as a replacement for me either Frank Newton or Jack Butler with whom I had gigged with and knew quite well. The musicians that hung out at the Rhythm Club called Jack "Tonics" because he always talked about the tonics in musician harmony.
Before my departure, we had a recording session with Willie Lewis's band the 15th of October 1936.

Leon Abbey had gone to Chicago and came back with a tenor player named Antony Cosey. The 21st of October we left Paris for Venice, Italy where we took a boat for India. The other musicians were Arthur Lanier, alto and singer, Ollie Tines, drummer, Emil Christian, a white trombone player who had played with the Original Dixieland Band and had lived in England and France a few years. The pianist was Charlie Lewis who had come to Europe with Leon.

We passed through Switzerland which was a beautiful country and arrived in Venice the 22nd of October and that was where the trip started to get interesting. I had read some of the history of Venice and its canals and it says that there is no other city like Venice. We went from the railroad station to the pier by taxi gondolas and watched the way the gondolier guided the gondola and the traffic on the canals. It was a real sight to see. From the pier there was a launch that took us to the ship we were to sail on, which was named Victoria. It was a very nice ship but there was one bring down. The men had to be in a cabin together and the women in another. The only two couples were Leon and his Italian wife and Beezie and I. On the boat we met an English singer who was going to India to sing in the Taj Mahal Hotel which was where we would be working also. Her name was Aimee Denton. The men had a cabin with five berths and the women had one with four.

The weather was beautiful in Venice and we left the port in the afternoon. The following day we rented deck chairs and I began to get better acquainted with the musicians whom I had not known much about before. This was Leon's second time to be engaged at the Taj. Charlie Lewis was known as "Dizzy" and "Dizzy" called Leon "Dog". We started calling Cosey "Bags" because he had a ruptured testicle which really showed, but it didn't seem to bother him physically. He in turn called everybody "funny looking", even Beezie and Leon's wife who's nickname was Boop and they were both beautiful.

We arrived at night in Port Said, Egypt and went ashore for a few hours as it was early evening and the ship would not sail until that night through the Suez Canal. The Canal is 87-and-a-half miles long and took at least 12 to 15 hours to traverse. Egypt was the starting point going to the Far East and there were so many sights that we saw for the first time to indicate to those that had never seen the likes of it to let him know that this part of the world was the land of the Pharaohs. To our way of thinking, the men were wearing Grandfather nightgowns and the women wore long black robes which covered their faces to that only their eyes showed. This was another world.

The shops were beautifully oriental with so many tempting things to buy but I was not looking for souvenirs at that moment. There were sidewalks cafes, the same as in France, and that was the only link between Eastern and Western ways that did not surprise us. Not all the males wore gowns and some of the women did not cover their faces, but the real natives did and that was exciting for anyone who had never seen it. One guy really knocked us out. We were sitting at a sidewalk cafe when someone happened to see this fellow coming along. There was no traffic on the street and people were walking everywhere. This fellow as about 6 feet tall, real dark and had on what we called a nightgown that was five inches above his ankles, a wide brim straw hat and a pair of black shoes that looked long enough to be skis. He really reminded me of an Apollo theatre comedian and we all almost had chronic spasms from laughing so much at this sight. We decided that we had seen the greatest of all comedy acts and went back to the ship happy as a cow chewing on it's cud.

We awoke the next morning going through the Canal and it was the first time I ever saw a desert except in movie films. Of course there were some small villages and cites along the sides of the Canal and the route went through four lakes. The largest city before reaching Suez, the Eastern gateway of the Canal, is Ismailia and passes Gebel Mariam Lake.

Later the Canal goes into the Great Bitter Lake which is the supposed track where the Israelites crossed the Red Sea from Fayed. The Great Bitter Lake runs into the Small Bitter Lake where the Canal starts again at a town called Geneffe and finishes at Port Tenfik which runs into the Red Sea and where the city of Suez it situated.

There were interesting monuments to see on both sides of the Canal and in some places the sands were so hot that heat waves could be seen raising from them. I saw for the first time camels caravans and Egyptians riding on the rear end of their little donkeys and the whole set up was very exciting. We could not go ashore at Port Tewfik as the ship did not go into the docks but there was plenty of action to be seen. Tug boats coming in and going, some bringing freight to be loaded on the ship and others taking freight away. Launches bringing and taking passengers.

After we left Port Tewfik I noticed quite a number of Arabic people on the lower deck of the ship with what must have been their worldly belongings. Leon, who had made a trip like this before, told me that they were deck passengers. This deck was covered with a canvas cover to protect the passengers from the sun and at night the weather was very warm, so these people who could not afford to travel even in third class cabins, slept on the deck at night, eat in the third class dining rooms and spent the days on the deck.

We met an American white couple who were dancers that were also going to Bombay to work at the Taj Mahal. They were known as Tracey and Hay. The fellow was Sid Tracey and the woman was Bessie Hay. The 28th of October we arrived in Aden, Arabia and went ashore with Hay and Tracey. We took photographs posing with camels that didn't have a life that was easy like those in the zoos. These camels had to work. We posed with shark teeth and with the natives. We had stopped the day before at Massawa which was Italian Eritra but there was not a large port there and we could not go ashore.

The whole voyage was wonderful and I felt as though I was living in wonderland. We arrived at Bombay the 2nd of November, ten sailing days from Venice. We were met by the manager of the Taj Mahal Hotel who was a Mr. Faletti, an Italian who was a naturalised English citizen, and two Negro musicians who were living in India and were going to play with the Abbey band. One was Cricket Smith, a trumpet player and the other was Rudy Jackson, an alto sax man. Cricket and Rudy had come to Europe in the early 20s.

We has seen many exciting things in the port towns we visited but Bombay gassed them all. The taxis were opened top five passenger cars, mostly American made, and I could see in front, on the sides and from the back without any difficulties. There were so many sights to see that I almost had a sore neck turning it so much from the time we left the port until we reached the Taj Mahal Hotel. One sees different events in newsreels and also movies about India which are very interesting but when you see these things with your own eyes, for a person from another part of the world, its fantastic and hard to believe that you are not in fairy land and it's only a dream.

The "Taj" was a very large and beautiful place which sat on a street overlooking the bay. The front faces the city and I learned later that the architect that drew the plans for the hotel commited suicide after the hotel was completed because the back of the hotel was built facing the bay and it should have been the opposite.

I had a very large room assigned to me in the hotel until other lodgings could be arranged. The bed was very large also and had cheesecloth curtains on the four sides which was to keep the mosquitos from having a good time when you went to sleep at night. Mr. Farletti presented us to the assistant manager who was an Indian named D.R. Banerjee who was to look after us personally.

On the left side of the Taj facing the bay was a monument called the Gateway to India and to the left of that was a smaller hotel owned by the Taj direction called the Mayfair. I also met a pianist and accordionist called Teddy Weatherford. Teddy was an American Negro who had travelled over most of the Far East and had a big name amongst the early jazz musicians before I came on the scene. Teddy had been in India quite a few years and was very popular with the English dignitaries and others in the Bombay High society.

The next day we started rehearsing the show which included six acts with a troupe of English girls and a tap dancer named Rosalind Wade. A French trombonist who had been in Bombay for sometime was added to the orchestra which made ten musicians in the orchestra. We opened a couple of days later and everything went fine. Arthur Lanier sang ballads and we formed a quartet with Leon, Ollie Tines, Lanier and myself to sing variety numbers. The job was not hard because we worked 4 nights and 2 matinees a week.

The management found two apartments for us. Leon with Boop, Cosy, Lanie, Beezie and myself stayed in a six-room apartment called Moby Mansion. Charlie Lewis and Ollie Tines were in an apartment not far from where we lived with their Anglo-Indian girl friends whom they had met during their first stay in Bombay. Cricket Smith and Rudy Jackson lived with their Anglo-Indian women. Leonard, a French trombone player who had been added to the band, had been in India for some years and lived with some friends. We also had a servant (all men servants were called Boy) to clean our apartment and run errands.

Some of the acts that we played in the Taj did not have their music arranged to suit the formation of the orchestra and had no parts for trumpets. So they gave Cricket and I violin parts to transpose. I was not up to date on transposing because I had never had to do it, but Cricket could transpose as if it had been actually written for a trumpet

in B Flat. He showed me the way it was done but a musician must be trained to that type of situation and I was very slow at transposing. So Cosy who could copy things from records and write them, wrote my parts in the keys they were supposed to be in and I had no troubles after that.

Cricket had always been a first chair man and had come to Europe with Sam Wooding's orchestra in the early 1920's. Sam Wooding was the first Negro leader to bring a Negro jazz orchestra to Europe although Jim Europe, who was the leader of the 365th Engineers band during the first World War, was recognised as being the first Negros to play jazz in Europe in 1917. Jim Europe played marches, but in a ragtime way, as they were played by the marching bands in New Orleans when they were returning from the funeral of some lodge member.

But Sam Wooding had an orchestra that played dance music and was composed of 12 or 14 musicians where the parade band of Jim Europe had 30 or more musicians as the usual type of parade bands. So it was thusly, Sam Wooding was recognised as being the first Negro jazz orchestra to invade the European continent. Cricket and Rudy Jackson had played in Wooding's orchestra and they were both fine musicians. I played second parts in the brass section and taking the jazz solos. Cosey took the hot chorus on tenor and Leon had some on violin. The trombone player Leonardi was a straight man and played only what was written, but he also played violin which was nice for some of the acts we accompanied.

Teddy Weatherford accompanied Aimee Denton in a room known as the Harbour bar and Teddy also did numbers on the accordion. On very special nights, Teddy did a few numbers in the room where we played which was a very large dining room and dance hall combined. On Saturday and Sunday afternoons, we played matinees in a smaller room but matinees were not very popular at the Taj.

Although we were in an appartment where there was a kitchen, the only time we used it was when we wanted some real southern fried chicken or other home style food. Otherwise we ate at the Taj. But the food we were

served was never very well seasoned and was not the same as that which was served in the main dining room. The Indian employees ate in the same dining room as we did but they had special food cooked in curry.

The head waiter was named Peter and like most of the waiters he was from Goa which was a part of India governed by Portugal. We told Peter that we liked curried food better than what we were getting and when they had some left over, Peter looked out for us and curried food was never wasted.

One thing I had a hard time to get used to was Lizards. They were everywhere and in the best hotels and houses. In our place they were almost as thick as flies, our beds had screens to protect us from mosquitos, but there was no protection to keep lizards out of the house. They were about two-and-a-half inches long with tails almost twice as long as the body and are known as wall lizards. Whenever we did use the stove in the kitchen, we had to light it and leave the oven door open so that the lizards would get out before it got too hot, and we did not want any fried lizards in our baked macaroni!

I drank less alcohol in India than I was drinking in Europe and I suppose the desire was less demanding because of the climate, although hot climates have been known to make alcoholic wrecks of many men. We had plenty of canned beer that was furnished to us by the hotel. For a woman, Aimee Denton could down a few. Leon liked a taste of gage now and then and Charlie "Dizzie" Lewis liked his juice although he did not drink too much while we were in Bombay.

But one day Dizzie got on a bender and bought a python from an Indian who had a street act for tourists which was a battle between a snake and a mongoose. So Dizzy bought a python and took it home. His girl friends Ivy was not at home when he arrived. In fact no one was there and the juice started getting Dizzy down, so he got on a bed with the python and went to sleep.

When Ivy did come home, the sight that she saw sent her out of the house screaming like mad. Charlie was lying on his back with his mouth wide open, the python was coiled around his body and it's head was five inches from Charlie's mouth. The alcohol scent from Charlie's breath must have paralysed the python to the point that it could not squeeze the life out of Dizzy. Ivy went to get her brother to come back home with her and with the help of some other friends, they got the python into a cloth sack and gave it to the zoo.

It is not possible to write about all the sights I saw and the things I did beside playing music in India because this is a book about my life with a horn and a limited account of the places I've been and musicians I've known and some of those that I have worked with. I wouldn't have missed the opportunity to go to India even if Willie Lewis had offered me five times more money than he was paying me before I left him. I had a horn and would travel as far away as places were, the places I wanted to see the most.

Christmas came and it was the first time I spent a Christmas Eve that I didn't have to wear an overcoat. The whitest thing about that Christmas Eve was the white suit I wore when I went out in the afternoon. We went out often between mid-day and 4 p.m. which was the hour that most people took their siesta. The Indians had a saying that no one went out during those hours except Englishmen and damn fools. Too bad we were not Englishmen.

The Taj was jumping Christmas Eve and Christmas night also, but the biggest ball was New Year's Eve, 1936. The room was filled with English dignitaries, diplomats and Maharajahs. Some brought their families. I saw two Maharajahs that I had seen in Paris, "Chez Florence". One was the Maharaja of Cochin, the other was the Maharaja of Kapurthala who took his European gals with him where ever he went. There were about 6 or 8 of them.

There were some young prince that came and stood near the band stand to dig our jazz like the jazz lovers did at the Savoy. Later in the night when it came time to push the old year out and welcome in the new one, they started throwing cotton balls at us and we threw them back at them. Everybody let their hair down and started having a ball.

Mr Faletti had allowed us to invite our wives and girl friends to a bar that was in the back of the main dining room. Beezie, Boob, Ivy the girl friend of Charlie Lewis, and Ined the sister of Ivy who was Ollie Tine(s) girl friend and their brother who was about 17. They could hear the music from the bar but could not see what was going on in the main dining room.

We finally had a break and went back to the bar and Ivy's brother came to me and pointed out a fellow sitting at the bar and said that he had insulted Beezie. Then the three girls said that they were sitting at the bar when this guy comes in and started asking the barman, who are these bitches, get them out of here, they stink.

So I went to the bar and asked this jerk what was the idea of insulting my wife and the girls that were with her? He started to puff up and asked me who the hell I was. I swung a right to his chin and that knocked him off of his stool. Cosey was standing near and the blow glanced and caughted him on the jaw but it didn't hurt him.

This bastard went and got Mr Faletti and told him that I had hit him and he should get rid of me. Falletti told him yes, and now you come with me because you've had enough to drink. This guy turned out to be the American vice-consul and was known to raise hell when he started juicing and nobody liked him. Faletti and everyone else that knew about this ass were glad that I had put him in his place. I was sorry that I didn't break his neck.

The morning passed and we still had a good time and went into the year of 1937 in the groove. I even took a couple of puffs from Leon's peace piece pipe cigarette to celebrate in New Year. Later in the season, there was a big diplomatic ball at the hotel and the vice-consul came. And he stayed the whole night. He gave me a look as if to say that trumpet player must be out of his mind.

Our music was jazz even though played quite commercial at times because played for a public that were European or had those kind of ideas, and the Taj Mahal hotel and even the Greens across the street catered to that select clientel. Naturally our type of music did not appeal to the average classes such as the Hindus, the Untouchables and other sects. So I met only two Anglo-Indians who were interested in jazz. I remember that one was named Ruby and he played Alto-sax. I never heard him play, but he and his buddy used to come to the hotel often in the afternoon after we had lunched and asked us questions about jazz music and musicians that they had heard about.

Sometimes when I would be taking my afternoon siesta I would hear some Indian music on someone's gramaphone and it was great music. They had their type of jazz which included a great soloist on instruments of which I did not know the names of and favorite singers. I suppose that (I had) been an arranger I would have taken more interest in the Indian music. But I did listen to those sounds coming from someone's appartment and get my kicks. I'm sorry that I did not buy even an instrumental or vocal record. But I did spend a small fortune in films and I didn't have an expensive camera.

One night we played a big party given for Ali Kahn, the son of the Aga Kahn. This party was on a boat and was catered by the Taj Mahal hotel. I think that it was the birthday of Ali but anyway the diplomats, Maharajahs, Maharanies and Bombay high society were there. The boat

sailed out into the bay and after dinner Ali Kahn wanted to take his clothes off and dive in the bay from the highest deck and swim around the boat. It was said that that was high delight whenever he went out on a boating party. But he was restrained that night because it was rumoured that there were sharks in the bay and they could have been attracted by the lights of the boat although we did not see any.

Another wonderful thing about that night is that during one of the intermissions I was sitting on an upholstered bench near the bandstand and a beautiful blonde-haired lady was sitting on the same bench and she started talking to me. What the conversation was I don't remember but I remember this lady was very nice. Later I excused myself and got on the bandstand. Someone asked me if I knew who the lady was that I had been talking to and when they told me I could have been knocked over with a feather. She was the English wife of Ali Kahn who became Princess Ali Khan and the mother of Prince Karim the present Aga Khan. At that time, she had not been married very long to Prince Ali.

The six months in Bombay passed very fast and on April the 27th 1937, we left India on the Conte-Rosso which was an Italian boat headed for Venice and another world. Teddy Weatherford had never been in Europe and had decided that he was coming back with us. Charlie Lewis brought his girl Ivy back with him and we landed in Venice the 8th of May and the next day we were in Paris. The trip was great coming back the same as it had been going, but Beezie and I had a cabin to ourselves on the boat.

In a very short time Leon landed a job in a night club at Place Pigalle, but I didn't care much for the place and the band seemed to have lost something in it's style and gayety, so I gave my notice to Fess and rejoined Willie Lewis.

Willie had succeeded in getting Jack Butler in my place when I left for India but he was pleased to have me back in the band again. Willie had added George Johnson to the sax section and with me re-joining the orchestra, that made it eleven musicians and the only all-Negro American Orchestra in Europe. Wilson Meyers was on bass. I don't remember who Meyers came to Europe a second time with but he and I had been in Lucky Milliner's band together in Monte Carlo and Paris.

Willie's orchestra was working at the Ambassador which was a part of the Ambassador Theatre across the street from the American Embassy at Place de la Concorde. Shortly after I had rejoined Willie, Teddy Hill and his band came to Paris with a Cotton Club Revue and played quite a few weeks at the Moulin Rouge at Place Blanche. The revue was staged by Clarence Robinson who was very well known in Harlem for staging shows in the Cotton Club, Connie's Inn, the Lafayette Theatre, Harlem Opera House and the Apollo Theatre.

Teddy had changed a few musicians since I left the band in 1935. Bob Carroll, ex-Redman alumnus, was on tenor, having replaced Chu Berry; Wilbur de Paris had been added on trombone, and a young 18-year old trumpet played named John Burks Gillespie whom the other fellows in the band called Dizzy. Dizzy had replaced Frank Newton who had come in the band after I left.

My recording activities started the 7th of July when I recorded with Dicky Wells' Orchestra which included Bill Dillard, Shad Collins, who had replaced Roy Eldridge, Dicky, Django Reinhardt, Richard Fullbright on bass and Bill Beeson on drums. We recorded the "Bungle Call Rag", "Between the Devil and the Deep Blue Sea" and "I got Rhythm", which later
became collectors items.

The session was supervised by Hugues Panassie and it was another first in jazz because it was the first time a group of that type had recorded without piano accompaniment and also the first time that three trumpets and a trombone had been recorded in that manner. Dicky Wells did the arrangements. Dicky and I did three other numbers without the other two trumpets of which "Hangin Around Boudon" became the most popular.

With Django playing the kind of rhythm guitar that only he could play, we did not miss the piano. Bill Dillard has a soft and mellow tone and could take very nice choruses although he was considered a first chair man. He was a first chair man and one of the finest around New York.

[the] Shad Collins was the hard blow type who was influenced very much by Roy Eldridge style. My style which had been influenced by Armstrong was now very personal, not too loose, not as soft as Dillard's and very flowing, sort of like a country stream flowing down to some distant river. I never could really write an article on my style, so I'm quoting what some critics have said about my style when I say it was a flowing style!

I think the record of the three trumpets may have even been better if Dizzy had been included because the sound of four trumpets playing and phrasing the way we did those numbers had not been recorded in those days. But it seems that most of the musicians had something against Dizzy because he was young and maybe a little wild to their way of thinking. I never heard Dizzy play then and I saw the show a couple of times. There were not many solos because the band accompanied the actors and only played an overture number before the first and second part of the show.

After a few weeks at the Moulin Rouge, the Cotton Club show moved to the Ambassador Theatre which was next door to where we were playing and sometimes I would see Dicky Wells coming from around the back of the building and he told me that he had been back there listening to our band because he could hear it better than from the side that gave onto the street.

The Cotton Club Show left for England and Willie Lewis' band left for another summer season in Knocke, but George Johnson did not go with the orchestra. I suppose that Willie had engaged him only for the Ambassador job. It was only during engagements at the summer resorts such as Knocke and Ostende that Willie Lewis' orchestra played tea dances or matinees every day. But it was a pleasure to work in the best Negro orchestra in Europe and although we stayed up late most every night, I and some of the other musicians found time to go bicycle riding, swimming and still be fresh and ready for the afternoon job. Jack Butler and I along with his wife Raye and Beezie shared an apartment on the side street across from the Kursall.

Ray Ventura was the leader of the biggest French jazz orchestra in France and he was engaged to play upstairs in the large hall of the Kursall. Ray had an orchestra of about 16 or 17 musicians and an American girl singer whose name I remember as being Betty. Ventura had a real show band, but he also had the best musicians in Europe from different countries. One outstanding musician in the orchestra was a French trumpet player named Philippe Brun. Philippe had spent a few years in England and was influenced by Armstrong but with a little of his personal feeling about how jazz trumpet should be played. He was way out in front of any of the other European trumpet players.
When we played the matinees the place was never crowded as it was at night because the weather was so beautiful that most of the vacationists spent the afternoons at the beach. Some spent it in the

gambling halls of the Kursall. But we always had a nice crowd outside. The Penguin Club was on the street level of the Kursall and the windows and doors were wide open. Our music could be heard blocks away. As I said before, we always had an audience outside in the afternoon and I remember one little fat boy about 15 years old who never missed a day. He must have known many of the numbers in our repertoire as well as we did.

One day I was out riding the bicycle with some of the gang and I was going along a very speedy pace. There are special sidewalks along many of the roads in Belgium and Holland for bicycles but in some places these special roads for bicycles come to an end and you are riding on regular road again. That was the case that day but after a little while I saw that the bicycle road started again. I was going so fast that I missed the entrance and when I realised that I was going to fall, the first thing I thought about was to protect my lips. I fell with both hands covering my face but my upper lips received a small cut on the side near the middle where I place my mouthpiece. My face was also scratched near my right eye and I could not work for two days.

After six weeks in Knocke we went to the Ostende Casino for two weeks. Beezie's daughter Joan who was 4 years old was living with her father in New York and Beezie received a letter saying that someone in Joan's father's family had some incurable illness and they were going to send Joan to us. Joan was due to arrive a week before we finished at Ostende, so Beezie came back to Paris a week before me.
We went into Florence for a short stay because Willie was engaged to play at a pavillion for the great Paris fair of 1937.

In October I recorded with Alix Combelle whom I spoke of before as being one of the first French jazz musicians that I became acquainted in 1935. The pianist was a New Yorker named David Martin who's family had a music school on 136th Street between 7th Avenue and Lenox. Dave

accompanied quite a few classical musicians and singers and was in Europe at this time accompanying Eddie South who was known as the "Dark Angel of the violin". Dave was also known as a jazz pianist and that was the reason he was on this date which was recorded under the name of Combelle. Wilson Meyers was on bass, Roger Chaput guitar and Jerry Mengo drums. We recorded four numbers of which "Hang Over Blues" was my composition.

"Hang Over Blues" was just a name that I decided on and not because I had a hangover. Another number was recorded but never issued. It was "Sometimes I'm Happy". I never found out why it was never issued and have no idea what it really sounded like. This Combelle record was recorded the 4th of October 1937.

The 18th of October Willie Lewis and his orchestra recorded six numbers with the full band. The 12th of November I recorded under my own name with Stephane Grappelli, Joseph Reinhardt on guitar, Wilson Meyers and Ted Fields, drums. Grappelli surprised me by playing piano on some of the numbers. Whenever Hugues Panassie asked me to record I seldom asked who the other musicians would be unless I was asked to choose them. And that was the reason I was surprised when I arrived at the studio and I knew the instruments that everyone played that were present. So I asked who was going to play piano and Hugues said Stephane. I had no idea that he was playing piano. But he was as good an accompanist as Dave Martin as far as jazz was concerned.

November the 19th I recorded "Bill Coleman Blues" accompanied only by Django on guitar which was another first for Hugues Panassie because it was his idea to record just the two of us for one number and it was the first time a trumpet and guitar had been recorded on a jazz record. The other five numbers recorded on that date had Christian Wagner clarinet and alto, "Big Boy" Godie tenor and clarinet, Emil Stern, piano, Lucien Simoens, bass, and Jerry Mengo drums.

After the engagement at the Paris Fair, Willie Lewis and orchestra were engaged to go to Alexandria, Egypt and this was as thrilling as the trip to India. I had seen Egypt for a few hours going and coming from India and now it was possible for me to spend some weeks there. I was now a papa because Joan was with Beezie and I. The musicians that were married took their wives with them. But Jack Butler's wife had gone back to the States and "Big Boy Goodie" was a batchelor. Willie Lewis was married also but his wife did not go to Eygpt with us.

We left Paris for Marseille the morning of the 13th of December 1937. As the ship we were sailing on, the Champollion, did not sail until the evening of the 13th and we had boarded the ship in the afternoon, it was decided that we would spend a few hours seeing Marseille. The wives went sight seeing together and the men did the same. It is not possible to say how many cafe's or bars that we (the men) stopped in, but when we returned to the ship, I was really sailing before we left port.

A half hour away from Marseilles the sea became very rough and little Joan got sea sick. The ship was doing everything except flying and with all the juice in my stomach that I had consumed, the pitching and lurching of the ship became too much for me and I became sea sick for the first and only time in my life. When Joan saw me giving up everything that I had downed earlier in the afternoon, she asked me in a very pitiful but cute voice, 'Are you sick also Daddy?'

We arrived in Egypt, Alexandria, the 17th of December and had rooms reserved in the Hotel Syracuse. Again I was thrilled by the way the real natives dressed, the women wearing long black robes from head to foot and black veils covering their faces. There were hundreds of little donkeys and carts everywhere and most Egyptian men, even those dressed in European or Western clothes, wore tabuck It was a thrilling and fantastic as India although the styles in native ways of dressing were not similar.

We always knew that Willie Lewis got quite a lot of money for the band and that was normal and correct because he did the business. But somehow we learned that he was getting much more than we thought he was and he had not offered us anymore than we made in Europe. So one night we had a meeting with Willie and told him that we knew he was taking advantage of us and we wanted a raise. Willie started to cry and deny the fact but he had forgotten that he had told me and maybe someone else that he could cry real tears anytime he wanted to.

He tried to convince us by saying that he would bring his contract the next night and we could see how much he was making. But we were wise to that trick and told him that if he didn't consent to give us a raise then and there, we would not come to work the next day. He finally gave in and admitted that he had lied about the money he was making, but everything was alright the next day and Willie never cried any more of the crocodile tears again as long as I was with his band.

When we finished at "Monseigneur" we had a few days to wait before the ship that would bring us back to France sailed from Alexandria, so Burns, his wife Louise, Beezie and myself visited Cairo. We made a visit of the Sphinx and the Pyramids of Ghizeh. It was a dream that came true because I had studied about Egypt in school and it was a big part of the holy land that I had learned about in Sunday school. It was like living in another world which in reality was another world and days gone by when our guide explained to us the meaning of the designs in the tombs of the Pharaohs that were buried near the Sphinx. We also climbed up the largest Pyramid in which a certain Pharaoh and his Queen had their tombs.

We visited the most famous Mosques of Cairo and rode camels around the Sphinx and Pyramids. We visited the first Memphis in the world where I saw many small Sphinx and a huge statue of who was perhaps the better known of all the Pharaohs in the history of Egypt.

We left Egypt and arrived back in Marseille the 30th of March 1938. Passed through Paris on our way to the Hague where Willie had one month's contract in the Tabaris which was my second time to play in Holland. And every night there was [were] at least ten glasses of Bols around my music stand and I don't remember every buying that many at any time.

Bobby Martin, the ex-Willie Lewis trumpet man, had gone to the States and come back to Europe with an orchestra composed of Glyn Paque (alto), Johnny Russell (tenor), both of whom I had worked with in Benny Carter's band in 1933, Ernest Purce (alto), Ram Ramirez (piano), whom I had seen with Garnet Clark in the "Apple", Kaiser Marshall, the ex-Fletcher Henderson drummer, and Ernest "Bass" Hill on the bull fiddle. Jack Butler, Billy Burn, Johnny Mitchell and myself joined Bobby's band for a recording session which took place in Hilversum in April. We recorded "Crazy Rhythm" and "Make Believe Ballroom". I never was able to put my hands on this record and I've never run across anyone that has or had it in their collection of records. I wonder if I had a solo on both of the numbers or only one. On May the 4th I recorded again in Hilversum with the Willie Lewis Band.

When we came back to Paris at the end of May, Willie didn't have a job for us to go on until [Knokke] the middle of July in Knocke. Oscar Aleman was the leader of an orchestra in a dancing hall on Rue Fontaine. "Spider" Courance had left the Villa d'Este where he had continued to work after I left there to join Willie Lewis. Oscar asked me if I would care to work with him until time for me to go to Belgium and although I didn't care for the type of music Oscar was playing as it was mostly Latin-American music, I accepted the job because it was something to do to keep my chops up.

Valada Snow, the third woman that I had heard play trumpet, was in Paris working as an attraction in some club and the manager of the also hired her to come in and do an attraction for 20 minutes. When I first heard Valada and I was an amateur horn man, she was waiting, but
now it seemed as though she had lost something although she still blew strong.

The 13th of June I recorded with Eddie Brunner who was a Swiss tenor and clarinet player and a damn good swing man. Alix Combelle and Noël Chiboust were the two other tenors and Eddie blew clarinet on most of the numbers we recorded. Chiboust had played trumpet before switching to tenor and he and Combelle were the best French tenor men [in France]. The rest of the orchestra was composed of Herman Chittison (piano), Oscar Aleman (guitar), a bass player named Grasset, and Tommy Benford on drums. I knew Tommy from New York. He was a swinging drummer.

Oscar's orchestra became sadder and sadder to me every day and when Willie's gang finally started in Belgium again it was a couple of weeks before I could get really in the groove. And I realised the saying that if you put a good apple in a barrel of bad ones it eventually turns bad. Oscar's band didn't swing and after playing two months with him, I couldn't swing for a long time regardless of how hard I tried. But I kept fighting and finally got myself back in the groove.

Jack Butler was not content to be just a member of the singing trio we had with Wilson Meyers, although we did our numbers in the Pengoin and they went over big. One afternoon Jack told Willie that he wanted to sing a number alone. He had been studying voice with some teacher in Knocke and even had a pianist who may have been the teacher to accompany him. He sang an Italian song the title of which I or no one else had ever heard.

I know that I did not have a great voice but Willie Lewis did. He had a wonderful baritone voice with plenty of power behind it. But Jack sang through his nose and most everybody in the club that afternoon was going into hysteria from laughing when Jack started singing his song. And the saddest part of the whole thing was that he was supposed to be singing in Italian. One of the waiters spoke Italian
but he couldn't understand one word of what Jack was saying. Well, after that, Jack didn't ask to do a number anymore.

One night at the Pingouin, Jack Butler had a dispute with Willie Lewis and when Willie went into the men's room Jack followed him. Willie was washing his face and as he bent over the wash bowl, Jack hit him. But the blow didn't hurt Willie and he didn't make any attempt to fight back.

We finished the season with two weeks at the Casino of Ostende in September, as we had done the year before, and Willie announced that he was not going to lead an orchestra anymore. But when we arrived in Paris Willie told me that he would contact me in a few days. Ted Field and his wife Evelyn decided to go to the States. Willie did contact me a few days after we returned to Paris and told me that he had a job to open in a big dance hall called the Coliseum.

Willie engaged Tommy Benford as a drummer. Also another trumpet player who had been in France for a long time who's name was Theordore Brock and a tenor man who was living in France for years named Bernard and was said to be the wealthiest Negro American musician in France. I never found out where Brock or Bernard were from in the States or who they have come to Europe with. I should have been a little more nosy than I was, but I never did ask other people many questions about themselves.

We opened the Coliseum in October with a French orchestra on another stand and there were about 30 dancing hostess's engaged for men who came alone which was run on the taxi dance plan, but we did not play like the New York dancing school bands had to play. Willie also raised my salary to one thousand francs a week which was quite a good salary in 1938. The band now had two tenors and two altos. Big Boy Goldie was not with the band and Fletcher Allen had been hired in his place.

Fletcher had worked with Freddie Taylor and left to go to India with the first group that Leon had taken to Bombay. Joe Hayman was still there. The other changes were Brock in the place of Jack Butler and Benford in the place of Ted Fields.

Jimmy Monroe, who was the brother of Clark Monroe who had a famous club in Harlem, was in France because his wife Nina Mae McKinney who had starred in the first all-Negro movie produced in Hollywood "Halleluiah" was working in London, but Jimmy could not get permission to stay there and could only visit there for a few days at a time.

Jimmy opened a club in a small street called Cite Pigalle. Spider and his wife lived in this street and also Joe Hayman and wife. Bob Greir, another American Negro who had been in Paris for some time, was Jimmy's partner and the club, which I was told had never been a success for anyone that had ever tried to run it before, became a big success and meeting place for most Americans that were in Paris, and there were plenty of them. The club featured the latest jazz records and became a rendezvous place for American Negro artistes and their French friends.

One night I came home from work and Beezie was not home. We had put Joan in a private school a little outside of Paris shortly after we came from Belgium. Beezie didn't come home until about 8 o'clock that morning and when I asked her where she had been, she told me she was at Jimmy's place with Mae and Spider. I never cared much for Mae after the night I came home when she and Spider, Beezie and I were living together in the same building and Mae had made Beezie drunk by giving her cognac and wine and telling her that she would not be hurt.

I didn't raise any hell because Beezie came home that late that morning but warned her not to let it happen again. Beezie and I had our ups and downs. I was very jealous and reproached her to have become too independant. We also had disputes about Joan. I thought she was too hard with the kid and she said I was too soft with her. Joan didn't get along too well with her mother.

Two nights later I came home and there was no Beezie, and this time she came home about 4 a.m. I didn't say anything to her and the next day I packed all my belongings and took a room in a hotel not far from the Coliseum.

When the news got around that Beezie and I had separated, many of the friends that we knew asked me not to leave her stranded over here. Every week I gave her an allowance. When she didn't come for it, I took it to her. At times I wanted to go back to her but I felt that we would not get along as long as Mae seemed to have an influence over her.

Meantime, I received a letter from the director of the Taj Mahal hotel in Bombay asking me if I would accept to come there alone to join an orchestra they had engaged which included Cricket Smith and Rudy Jackson. Ollie Tines, the Leon Abbey drummer had returned to Bombay because the climate in Europe was not good for his health and he was also in love with an Anglo-Indian girl there. So I suppose he was in the orchestra also.

I had really enjoyed my stay in Bombay and I suppose that if I had been offered the opportunity to go back there with a group formed in Paris, I may have accepted. But I didn't have any desire to go there alone and it was not because I was afraid of anything. I refused the offer.

In December, Mr Pastraudis, the owner of the Monseigneur in Alexandria, Egypt, came to Paris and contacted Burns to form an orchestra for his place. When he did not want to take Willie Lewis again, I never knew, unless that he had contacted Willie and he could not get out of the contract he had at the Coliseum.

Some of us had began to get a little fed up with Willie and Burns knew who they were. So he told us about the Alexandria deal and the loot was good. We therefore decided to form a group and keep it a secret. We had a meeting in Burns's hotel suite and planned everything. There was

Joe Hayman, Herman Chittison, Fletcher Allen, Burns and myself. We contacted "Spider" Courance who was still working at the Villa d'Este and Burns knew a drummer from Holland who was a Negro born in the Dutch West Indies. His name was Arthur Pay. Pastraudis said that there was an Italian bass player already in Alexandria.

We left Paris by train for Italy the 5th of December 1938 without telling anything to anybody and sailed from Genoa the following day, on the Italian liner Esperia. On board I met the leader of a Cuban orchestra whom Pastraudis had engaged as an Argentina Orchestra. He was a violinist named Bernardo Alemany. We had a wonderful trip but when we arrived at Alexandria we could not leave the boat because Pastraudis did not have the working permits for us. But he was a big man in Alexandria and he told us that he would arrange everything. We stayed on board and the ship sailed for Haifa and came back to Alexandria the next day. Pastraudis had the permits and everything was in the bag.

Before leaving Paris I gave Mae enough money for Beezie and Joan to go back to New York. Mae was coming to Egypt after "Spider" got settled there. She told me that Beezie was out of town, staying for a few days with a sick friend.

We had met a Belgium woman named Madame Piers who managed the Pingouin in Knocke. She had gone to Egypt when Willie Lewis went there and acted as his secretary. She did not stay in Egypt and was back in Knocke when we did the 1938 summer season. But she had fallen in love with some fellow in Egypt and came back to Alexandria after the season in Knocke and was working for Pastraudis. She became our manager when we started working in the "Monseigneur".

Our salary was three Egyptian pounds a day for each of us and that was more than we had made with Willie Lewis in that country. It was also a big salary for those times. Fletcher Allen was a good arranger and

after a few days of hard rehearsing we had a nice repertoire and we also had some head arrangements. We incorporated the band and took the name of Harlem Rythm Makers. Jazz had not been very popular or well known in Egypt until Willie went there and his band made a big hit.

So when we returned with a less commercial band than Willie had, we made a big hit with the clientele of the Monseigneur. Many of the young jazz lovers, who were mostly from rich families, came to hear us at least three times a week. There were many rich Greek families in Egypt and also many rich young Egyptians whom we became well acquainted with. There was one American girl that I remember well because her father was the United States' Ambassador. Her name was Nancy Fletcher and she usually came to the Monseigneur with some rich Greek fellow whose first name I still remember.

We wore a grey suit uniform for the afternoon matinees and tuxedos at night. Every night the band got better and I became the featured singer. My voice was not great but I had more nerve to try and sing a song than the rest of the fellows. One night we were singing like mad on a number and when I finished my two choruses, I finished on a high note and Arthur Pay (who was an amateur drummer) stopped right after I took my horn from my chops. We all wondered what was wrong because the number was not finished. I asked Arthur why he had stopped and he said: "Man, you were blowing off so I thought it was the end when you made that high note."

In the room where we worked at night there was a young fellow who was the cashier and this fellow liked to hear the "Donkey Serenade" which was a number we played but didn't care much for it. This fellow was a very talented designer and would make a different design of an ass and send it to the bandstand by a waiter or give it to one of us when we passed his desk after an intermission. He was such a nice fellow and really loved our music, so we played "Donkey Serenade" at least once a night although this fellow would ask for it two or three times a night which was too much serenade for a Jackass.

Eventually we received news that Willie Lewis had put a complaint against us to the French Labour Government for leaving without giving a notice and we could not come back or would not be permitted to enter France for five years. But that did not worry us because we had a fine jazz orchestra and everything was going swell for us.

One young Egyptian jazz fan that we became well acquainted was called Mimi and his parents owned a very large farm on the outskirts of Alexandria. Mimi's father was a minister in the Egyptian government and was away from the farm quite often, and ever so often Mimi would give a party which would take place in the afternoons. There were two cabarets in Alexandria that engaged European girls as entertainers and Mimi who was a sort of playboy also, would invite some of the girls to those parties and we all had a good time.

The biggest honour and the most celebrated occasion we experienced was when our orchestra was engaged to play for the wedding reception for the marriage of Mohamed Riza Pahlevi, the crown Prince of Iran (who became later the Shah of Iran) and Princess Fawzia, the sister of King Farouk.

The wedding and reception took place in Cairo on the 15th of March 1939. Unfortunately the reception did not take place in the Palace of the King which would have been very exciting to have visited a part of. But it was in a very large mansion near the centre of the city. The orchestra was placed on the landing of a large staircase just a few steps down from the room where the reception took place.

We didn't play dinner music because we were not a dinner music playing orchestra but we played softer than we usually did. After the dinner and a few drinks, the reception began to get gay. Confetti and cotton balls were passed out and we were included in the fun because Farouk and some of the other Royalties started throwing balls at us and we threw balls at them. Later we were asked to come up to the floor where the reception was held to play a special jazz number
for the newly weds and the rest of [us] the royal household. So now I could say that I had played for some crowned heads of Egypt and bald heads of Europe.

The 4th of April we were engaged to play in Cairo again for a ball given by the Women's Health Improvement Association at the Shepheard's Hotel which was the largest and most expensive hotel in Egypt. The ball was given under the patronage of King Farouk. Bernardo Alemany and his Argentinians, who were the second orchestra at the Monseigneur, alternated with us for this affair.

Pastraudis closed the Monseigneur in August for the whole month. We went to the beach most every day and enjoyed the vacation. Mae Caurance had come to Alexandria a month after we arrived there. She and Edgar were living in the Syracuse Hotel where I had stayed my first time in Egypt. Eventually there was a three-room apartment on the ground floor of the hotel, so Joe Hayman and myself moved in with Mae and Spider. Later there was an apartment on the top floor of the hotel which was the eighth floor. Mae did the cooking and we shared the expenses.

Burns bought a white packard sport car with a rumble seat from Pastraudis and we went to Cairo a few times and visited the first Memphis in the world. During the vacation Pastraudis decided that he didn't like Arthur Pay, so he had him put out of the country. Arthur went back to Holland. When we started again in the Monseigneur we had an Egyptian drummer named Francois. His parents must have been French and he was born in Egypt.

As Egypt was a protectorate of England, it was normal that there were many English familes of the Royal British Navy. We made the acquaintance of four soldiers; two of them played music in a military band and the other two were jazz fans.

A.J. Henderson, known as "Ginger" because of his red hair, played trumpet and Teddy Hill was a drummer. The other two, Henry Campbell and Nick something, were just pals of Ginger. Henry Campbell played tenor-sax. They loved our music. Ginger was not a jazz trumpet player but Teddy Hill was the best drummer in Egypt and we really enjoyed when he would come around and sit in with us. There were many bands in Europe and the U.S.A. that would have been happy to have him as a drummer. We invited Ginger to sit in also and he called himself our second, no-solo-taking trumpet.

We also made friends with a couple of Egyptian military aviators and some coast guards officers. After we became well acquainted with the coast guards officers, they used to give us big pieces of hashish and told us how they got it. There was plenty of hashish smoking in Egypt. Women were not allowed in Egyptian bars of sidewalk cafes. But everywhere, but I never found out if there was a law against it or only a law against smuggling because these coast guard officers told us that whenever they caught someone trying to smuggle in hashish, they would take a big portion for themselves and turn in a certain amount as evidance against the prisoner. Maybe they sold some to other people but they would give it to us.

We had a band valet whose name was Hassan but we called him Sam. In return he had a name for each of us because some of the names were too difficult for him. I was Gee-Gee, Burns was Mr. Eat for what reason I don't know, because Burns was not a big eater. Edgar Courance was Auspa. I don't remember the names he gave to the others.

Whenever we received a big hunk of Hashish from our friends, we would have Sam come to our place to prepare it because there is an artistic touch that must be employed to prepare a hubbly-bubbly pipe and Sam knew how to do it. It did not became an
every day habit with us to smoke hashish but it was kicks to get high on it now and then.

The attitude of Pastraudis towards us began to change because we noticed that when he was standing at the bar which faced the bandstand in the room where we played in the afternoons, he would be talking with someone with his personality smile on his face: and when he looked at us on the bandstand he had a look of hatred and we found out later that he detested us.

After having Madame Piers and Arthur Pay put out of the country, he pulled a dirty trick on Fletcher Allen for no reason that we could see. Fletcher had been living with an Austrian or Hungarian girl for a long time but never married her. He name was Elsie and Fletcher had brought her to Egypt. Pastraudis knew that Fletcher and Elsie were not married so he had her deported. That hurt us almost as much as it did hurt Fletcher.

A few months after Elsie left, Burns's wife Louise received a message to come home as quick as possible. Louise was from Holland or Belgium. Burns decided to go with her and started making preparations to leave. Naturally he wanted to sell the car he had bought from Pastraudis and Pastraudis knew that this was going to happen. So he arranged things in a way that no garage owner would buy the car from Burns and he was obliged to sell it to Pastraudis for about a third of the price he had paid for it.

An Armenian trombone player named Gielaby replaced Burns. Of course there was a small difference in the band now as far as the punch we had when we first started at the Monseigneur because we had an Italian drummer in place of Arthur Pay, an Italian bass player and an Armenian trombonist. But the front line was as strong as ever with the three saxophones, Chittison and myself, and we still had the favor of the public.

One afternoon Spider got drunk and he always had a bad temper when he drank. I was his best friend and we had known each other for years. But one night we had both been drinking. It was in Paris; we were having a good time with Beezie and Mae and we were making the rounds of a few bars. In one of them, Beezie and him were playing and Beezie accidently hit Spider in the mouth. He wasn't angry about it because they were playing.

Later, we were in a bar called "Sans Souci" at rue Pigalle and Spider began to get nasty with me and accused me of hitting him on the mouth. I kept telling him that it happened when he and Beezie were playing in another bar and we had some more drinks. Later he started accusing me again and the next thing I knew I was getting up off the floor.

Spider had hit me on the chin when I was not expecting anything like that from him and I wasn't looking at him at the moment. My head just missed a radiator by the wall and I was stunned for a couple of seconds. I got up and started at him and he grabbed me and started crying and saying he was sorry. A couple of policemen that were standing outside of the bar came rushing in and asked what the trouble was and we pretended that we were only playing. I didn't have any bad feeling against Spider despite I was hurt, so we left the "Sans Souci" like the two friends we were.

This afternoon at the Monseigneur, Spider was drunk and in an ugly mood. He sat on the left end of the stand which was one foot high and there was a young English fellow that came to the place quite often who was sitting at a table at the corner of the stand, on the side where Spider was sitting. He liked our music and I had talked with him a few times. He had one foot on the stand and for some reason Spider didn't like it. So he told this officer to take his foot off the bandstand. The rest of us had no idea of what was happening and me the least of them because I was three
chairs away from Spider on the right side of the band.

Suddenly there was a big confusion and I saw this young man standing up and his face was bleeding. He had not moved his foot when Spider asked him to do it and Spider had hit him. The fellow was ready to fight back when someone jumped between them. We were all quite disgusted with Spider because of what he did was really uncalled for. The young man left and we continued to play.

But when Pastraudis came in, someone told him what had happened and he fired Spider for two weeks and told him that he could not come back to work until he had begged the fellow's pardon. It happened that this young man was in the English Army and stationed in Cairo.
