Pastraudis told Spider later that he would be obliged to go in Cairo on a certain date and apologise to the young officer in front of his commanding officer and pay his doctor's bill. So for two weeks we played without a tenor and Spider didn't misbehave after that when he got high.

Hitler had been causing troubles in Europe for a few years and September the third the war was declared on Germany by France and England which cooked our goose for coming back to France even if it had been possible. Pastraudis really jumped on the chance of taking advantage of us by cutting our salary to one pound a day. That didn't kill our spirits and I suppose he was deceived by that. Once he had invited us to his home and now he was giving us dirty looks.

The end came in December 1939 when Pastraudis said that he would continue our engagement if we accepted to work for 90 shillings, which was 10 less than a pound. We didn't know what future laid ahead for us, but we had taken all that was possible from Pastraudis and that was the last straw. As we
could not go back to France and all of Europe was at war except Italy and Switzerland, Pastraudis said that he would pay our transportation to Italy as he was not obliged to pay it to the U.S.A.

He held all the high cards because of his dealing with the British army which made him a highly respected business man. I was never a person that looked worried about a rainy day and I spent my money as if it grew on trees. But after my salary was cut to one pound and I was 5489 miles from New York, I started to economise a little and saved a few pounds, just in case push would come to shoving. It finally came.

We were supposed to leave Alexandria at the end of December. Meantime, we were offered a job in a new club that was due to open the first of January 1940 but Pastraudis had obtained our deportation papers and the owners of the place that was to open in January did not have the power or the pull with the government to combat Pastraudis' decision to put us out of the country.

From Italy we would have to pay our fare to New York and that would have left me and perhaps some of the rest of us without a penny. Spider would have to pay his way and Mae's fare also. So we decided to go see the American Ambassador to try and arrange a deal wherein we could work our way back to New York on one of the many American Export Line ships that came often to Alexandria.

We never got to see the Ambassador who was a certain Mr, Fletcher, the father of the girl who came often to the Monseigneur. However, we managed to see the vice consul and when we explained our case to him, he told us that there was nothing they could do for us because they (the American Embassy) were there in the interest of Ford Motors, Standard Oil and other big American concerns and that we boys should have been prepared for
the events that were facing us. That I'm certain would not have been the case had we been white.

The day before we were to leave Egypt, Spider, without any of us knowing about, went to the Italian Embasssy and explained to someone there that we were being put out of the country and our transportation was paid on the Italian Line who would be obliged to support us as long as we were stranded on their line. We would not have been allowed to get off the boat in Italy if we did not have the passage paid to another port.

Spider also explained that there was a place opening that would engage the orchestra and had agreed to pay the rest of our transportation from Italy to New York but they could not get the permission from the government. So the Italian Embassy got busy but we didn't know the results until the next day when we were at the docks getting ready to board an Italian boat for Naples.

The only one that remained in Pastraudis' favour was Herman Chittison and we didn't know about it until we were all at the dock except Chit, when the news came that we were being permitted to stay in the country for two months and we must go immediately to the working permit office.

When we arrived there, the owner of the place known as the Carlton that wanted us to work for him for two months was there. There were five of us left from the original seven of the "Harlem Rythm Makers" and the Carlton's management had received the permission for the five of us to stay in the country. But Chittison had not come to the dock to leave with us and we didn't know where he was.
So a detective was sent for and told to find Chittison. A
half hour later Chit was in the office with us and was told that the five of us had received permission to work in the Carlton.

Chit was in love with an Egyptian girl and had made arrangements with Pastraudis unbeknown to us to stay in Alexandria. He was satisfied to stay because of his love life, but I'm not certain if he was happy to have to work with us. The morale of this story was that someone had as much if not more power with the government administration than Pastraudis and I suppose he must have turned green when he found out that we have been permitted to remain in Alexandria after he had wanted us expelled. I never saw him again and never wanted to.

We engaged a white drummer named Bob Haye but we had no bass. We also had to play for five acts, an Italian dance team, a Spanish dance team, a Hungarian dance team, a girl that did a Hula dance, one that danced Gypsy style and another that danced Spanish Flamenco style. Mae had sung with a trio for a while in Paris and she didn't have a bad voice. So she was engaged as singer. We had managed to recuperate the same appartment we had before. Our salary was the same as the one pound we had at the Monseigneur but the Carlton's management accepted to pay the rent for us and it was a good deal.

The clientele at the Carlton was 100 per cent English and at that time the 'Lambeth Walk' song and dance was very popular. So for two months we had to play 'Lambeth Walk' at least three times a night.

Everything went fine and the 25th of February we left Alexandria on a small Italian ship called Egeo. We stopped at the Island of Rhodes which we had time to visit. The next stop, [was] Oireens, Greece and we visited Athens. It was a three-day trip from Alexandria to Naples and we were obliged to stay in Naples

five days before we had a ship to New York. We met an Italian sailor and a civilian who became friendly with us and showed us around the city, took us to some restaurants where we could eat good and not pay too much. The sailor went AWOL and spent every day with us. We had to report to the American Embassy where our passports were cancelled for any further trips to Europe. Some jazz fans got the news that some American Negro jazz musicians were in town so they came to see us and one of them invited us to his home which I remember was on a hill which overlooked the bay and the down town section of Naples.

We left Naples the 5th of March 1940 on the Italian liner Saturna and the trip was eleven days. We jammed most every night with the musicians that played in first class and they were really happy because it gave them a chance to get some ideas about jazz, which they liked but seldom had a chance to play or listen to, except on receords and in some clubs in New York where the ship would stay for three days, to take on supplies for the return crossing back to Naples.

At one time in Paris, some musicians were on the snook kick. (cocaine) Snow is jive language for heroin. Heroin was sniffed in the nose the same as people back in ancient times used to sniff snuff. A certain musician that I knew very well was using it and one night he tried to get me to take a sniff but I wasn't taking any chances on trying any form of dope. I smoked a little gage now and then but I was afraid of anything else except alchohol, so there were no dice.

But perhaps it was because my love affair had gone wrong that made me decide to buy a package of snow before I left for Egypt and I remember that I was so afraid that the customs agents going through Switzerland or coming into Italy may come on the train and perhaps search me or my luggage that I hid the package under the mat in the vestibule of the coach we were in. We

arrived at the station in Genoa, Italy and after going inside the Station and everyone was off the train, I pretended that I must have forgotten something on the train and went back to recover my snow.

Many months after we had been in Egypt, I remember the stuff and before we left I looked everywhere for it because I really did not want it to be found amongst my belongings when I arrived in New York but it was impossible to find.

I had a turtle neck sweater that I had bought before I left New York in 35 that had a zipper up collar and two pockets with zippers on them. I had not used this sweater during my stay in Egypt but one day on the Saturna way out in the Atlantic, I decided to put the sweater on. And as I was strolling along one of the decks and put a hand in one of the pockets, I felt something like a piece of paper and when I pulled it out and looked at it, I realised that it was the package of heroin that I had looked everywhere for in Egypt. I stayed gay for the rest of the voyage but I never touched any after that. And it wasn't bad.

There were three days during the crossing that were real rough because the ship was crossing the Gulf Stream in the Atlantic and that part of the Ocean is always rough. People were sea-sick and vomiting everywhere. The dining room was almost empty for those three days, but no one in our group suffered and we were present for every meal. It is said that one should not drink too much liquid on a voyage when a ship is rolling up and down and from side to side. The weather was not stormy but the ship was doing everything except standing still. I would stop at the bar on my way to the dining room and have two or three grappas, the well-known Italian alcohol, before each meal to give me a good appetite.

We arrived in New York the 16th of March and after being away four years and six months, it was almost as thrilling to return to the Apple was it had been the first time I came there in 1927. The only hotel in Harlem that was well known to me because of the publicity it had received from the Basie recording, was the Woodside on Seventh Avenue and that's where I went. Thanks to the management of the Carlton in Alexandria who had paid our fare from Naples to New York, I had one hundred dollars when I landed. That wasn't much money, but at least I could make it last until I found work which was not to difficult as I had not been away long enough to be forgotten.

New York was still having winter weather and there was snow (the real thing) on the ground. I arrived at the Woodside and paid a weeks rent in advance. After installing myself in my room which was quite a deception from what I thought the Woodside would have, I came out and headed straight for the Rhythm Club. Some of the musicians I had known for years greeted me with joy, and others that I had also known for years greeting me as if I had been coming to the club every day for the last four years and six months that I had been away. But what the hell, that's the Apple.

I stayed one night in the Woodside because Beezie had found out by some means that I had returned and where I was staying and she came with Joan to see me. We patched up our differences and I moved to the place where she was staying which was on 154th Street up on a hill in a section that was known as Sugar Hill. It had more class than down in Harlem and I was very satisfied with the surroundings and very happy that Beezie and I were together again.

I had not got a divorce from my first wife Madelyn and my alimony case was still pending in the domestic court. My mother had written me once and told me that Madelyn had come to visit her in Cincinnati when I was still in Europe and said that she would not

press charges against me if I came back to the States. Nethertheless one day a detective came to my house with a subpoena for me to appear in the domestic court. I went with the detective and was locked in a cell in the Court House until my case was called. This was the second time I heard the klink of a jail door closed on me. Eventually my case was called and Madelyn was not there, so the judged dismissed the case and it never came up again.
The Golden Gate ballroom was a new dance hall for me. It was at Lenox Avenue and 143rd Street, just two blocks from the Savoy and was a couple of doors from the old Cotton Club.
The first time I went there, I heard the big band of Coleman Hawkins who had returned to the States from Europe in 1939 and it was a fine band.

I had not heard the recording the "Bean" did on "Body and Soul" but I had heard about it. Naturally it was Hawk's biggest hit and when he played it this night, it made chills run up and down my spine. Hawk had come back from Europe and let everybody know that he was still the master of the tenor sax and had lost nothing by being away for a few years although it was often said that a musician usually lost something if he stayed in Europe too long. Hawk was the great Hawk he had always been and playing better than in his Fletcher Henderson days.

Another night I heard Benny Carter's big band which was great also. Benny never had a bad band if it stayed together a few weeks. Some nights the two bands would be Hawk's and Benny's and that made for a battle of alto and tenor sax with honours being distributed even.

Teddy Wilson was not with Benny Goodman and had formed a big band also which played certain nights as the Golden Gate. This was a very interesting orchestra because all the musicians were new to me except Teddy and Adolphus "Doc" Cheatham, one of the
trumpetists. I later found out the personnel of this band.

The musicians in Carter's band were Joe Thomas, Shad Collins and Russell Smith, trumpetists, and Benny also played trumpet and alto sax. The trombone were Sandy Williams and Milt Robinson. The sax section included Benny, Carl Frye and George Dorsey on altos, Sammy Davis (not Junior) and Stafford (Pazula) Simon, tenors, Sonny White, piano, Ulysses Livington, guitar, Hayes Alvis, bass, Keg Purnell, drums, and Roy Felton, vocalist.

The Coleman Hawkin's orchestra was composed of Joe Guy and Tommy Lindsay, trumpets, Earl Hardy, trombone, Eustice Moore, Jackie Fields, altos, Ernie Powell, tenor, Gene Rodgers, piano, Charles Smith, bass, Arthur Herbert, drums and Thelma Carpenter, vocalist. The only musicians in the band that I had known before going to Europe were Jackie Fields and Gene Rodgers.

Teddy Wilson's orchestra had Adolphus "Doc" Cheatham, Carl(Baura) George and Harold "Shorty" Baker in the trumpet section. Jake Wiley, Floyd "Stumpy" Brady, trombone, Rudy Powell, alto & clarinet, Pete Clark, alto & baritone, George Irish and Bob Carroll, tenor, Al Casey, guitar, Al Hall, bass, J.C. Heard, drums, and Jean Eldridge, Vocals. Buster Harding was arranger and second or stand-in pianist. The only ones in this band that were not new to me were "Doc" Cheatham, "Stumpy", Brady, Rudy Powell, Pete Clark, and Al Casey, and of course, Teddy.

One of the first things I had to do upon my return to New York was to be registered in the musicians union because I had let it drop in 1936. It costed me fifty dollars. There was a union in Paris, France, but hardly any musicians belonged to it.

Things did not seem to have changed too much musically since I'd left. As far as trumpet players were concerned, even Dizzy Gillespie had not changed too much. He was still coming up. He had not, as yet, acquired a reputation. He got his name 'Dizzy' because he was a little wild, but apart from that people didn't consider him as any more than just another trumpet player. He didn't really start to emerge until after

he had left Cab Calloway. I appreciated the playing of Shad Collins and Roy Eldridge, but I didn't even hear of Kenny Dorham until he came over to France in 1949 for the Jazz Festival. I think at that time, Roy was still the 'king'.

The fourth of April, I recorded with Joe Marsala and his Delta Four, a session that was supervised by Leonard Feather. I had met Leonard in Paris where he came a few times to listen to certain jazz musicians as he was a critic of jazz music and wrote for the English musical paper 'Melody Maker'. Leonard had gone to New York at the beginning or shortly after the war started in 1939 and was later to become one of the editors of 'Down Beat', which was the best jazz magazine in the States at one time. Leonard also played piano and composed numbers.

With the Delta Four for this recording session, there was Pete Brown, Carmen Mastren, Gene Traxler and a singer named Dell St. John. Joe Marsala played clarinet and was well known by the white jazz musicians all over the States. Pete Brown, I had known for years and the first time I heard him play was at the Savoy with a relief band. He played alto sax and his style was very original. He played very staccato in an abrupt, disconnected manner which was opposed to legato and was the swingingest alto player I ever heard. Carmen Mastren and Gene Traxler were white, and along with Joe Marsala, they were the first white musicians that I ever recorded with in the States.

Carmen was also well known in the jazz field as was Traxler and they were both musicians with plenty of class. Dell St. John was a Negro girl who had a fine voice and could sing the blues in a style that was strictly Dell.

Shortly after the recording with Joe Marsala. I joined Benny Carter's orchestra replacing Joe Thomas and the line up remained the same as it was when I heard Benny at the Goden Gate. In fact, it was at the Gate where I joined the band and we also played at the Savoy on different nights. The 20th of May, 1940, the band reocrded.

When I joined Benny, the only musicians that I knew well were Shad Collins, Russell Smith, Sandy Williams and Milt Robinson. The rest had come to the scene while I was tooting in Europe. But I soon became well acquainted with the others and Ulysses Livington lived not far from me at 155th Street and St. Nicholas Avenue, so we became very good friends.

Benny's band was great to work for. He would get close to his musicians, talk with them, and go out drinking with them. The fact that he could really converse with them and that he also knew how to put a band together meant that in many ways his bands were excellent. He could take a band, and in two weeks you would think that the guys had been playing together forever. Besides being a clever arranger, he also knew how to explain what he wanted. The only problem with his bands was that they somehow never seemed to manage to swing very much. His arranging seemed to be too melodic; the orchestrations were sometimes too heavy and symphonic for the kind of swing which Count Basie and Andy Kirk achieved.

There was a bar called "Fat Mans" just under where Ulysses lived. Fat Mans' was Charles Turner and he played bass in Marion Hardy's Alabamians, the band that Cab Calloway came to New York with, and whom I played opposite at the Savoy with Scott. Fat Man and Eddie Mallory, a trumpet player with Hardy's band, had opened the bar together, but Fat Man eventually bought out Eddie's interest and was the sole owner. It was a very modern bar and became quite a hangout for musicians that mostly lived in the neighbourhood.

To name a few, there was Billy Taylor, the bass player, his son Billy, Jr., who also played bass, John Brown, a bass player, Jonah Jones, the ex-Stuff Smith and Cab Calloway trumpet man, Doles Dicksens, bass, Slick Jones, drummer on many Fats Waller recordings, Al Hall, bass, Gus Askins, trumpet, Leonard "Henn" Davis, trumpet, Bobby Sands, ex-Claude
Hopkins tenor man and the great Coleman Hawkins as well as Benny Carter.

The Golden Gate closed and the band worked a few weeks at the Savoy. Benny engaged Vic Dickenson in the bone section. He had been in Count Basie's band and told me that Besie had told him to take a rest because he was hitting the bottle too heavy and his playing was getting a little too sluggish. But within two weeks, Basie recalled Vic and he left Benny which Benny knew would happen. But Benny and the rest of the gang enjoyed listening to Vic for the short while he was with us.

A few months after I had returned to the USA, Louis Armstrong was playing a week at the Roxy Theatre downtown on the 7th Avenue and 50th Street; and I went down to catch the show. Pops had taken over the Luis Russell orchestra and as I knew all the musicians, I went backstage after the show to say hello to them. I had seen Pops plenty of times, and he had a photo with him, Zilner Randolph and myself that was taken in Cincinnati in 1935 when I was a fugitive from the New York domestic court.

But I wanted an autographed photo of Gate so Higginbottom took me to Louis' dressing room and I asked Pops for a photo. He said 'Sure, Gate, I'll give you one. What's your name?' I told him Bill Coleman.
In August, Benny accepted a job in a dance hall at Coney Island, an amusement park in Long Island, New York, a suburb of New York City, and we played a month there.

A very good friend of the orchestra was a rich young man named John Hammond who came quite often to the Savoy and was the sponsor of Count Basie and was responsible for Basie coming to New York. I had known John for quite sometime and he had also put Charlie Christian in Benny Goodman's orchestra.

One day I received a message from John saying that Teddy Wilson no longer had a big band but was forming a small group to go into a place called Cafe Society down in Greenwich village, a section in lower down town on the west side of New York, and John wanted me to join Teddy because he liked my solo work and probably thought that I'd be happier in a small group where I had more liberty than in a big band, which was true.

I liked working in big orchestras because of the harmonious sounds of the different sections working together and especially with three trumpets cutting riffs through an arrangement like a knife cutting through a tender steak, but I had a desire to work with a small group in a club, which was something I had not done before, so I gave my notice to Benny and joined Teddy.

The drummer was a fellow named Yank Porter who had worked a long time at the Harlem club and I had known him for years. Benny Morton was the trombonist, Jimmie Hamilton, a clarinetist whom I didn't know before, and Al Hall, whom I had seen in Teddy's big band, was the bass player.

This club, which was actually called Cafe Society Downtown, was at Sheridan Square and was owned by a man named Barney Josephson. The manager was Harold Johnson and a great barman called Lew. I will mention why Lew was a great barman to me later. There were four acts in the show and I know that three of them were discovered by and sponsored by John Hammond.

Boogie Woogie was popular and John had put it together the three greatest exponents of that style of piano playing. They were Meade Lux Lewis, Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons. But the Cafe only Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons were working as a team, and there was a great blues singer named "Big" Joe Turner whom the two boogie woogie pianists accompanied. And the three of them would really rock the joint every night. And they could drink plenty of booze and carry it well.

Another act was called the Golden Gate Quartet. Their names were Bill Johnson, Clyde Redick, Wilson and . They had a style of singing gospel songs which I had never heard before. In fact I didn't know anything about gospel singing except what I had heard in Baptist churches. But this was more like Holy-Holy singing to me, because it had a jazz rhythm and these fellows slap their thighs with their hands in four-four rhythm; and Yank accompanied them on drums with wire brushes on the snare drum and the joint kept jumping.

The other act was a young woman named Hazel Scott. Hazel was a classical pianist who would play a classical number as it was supposed to be played, and then do the same number in jazz. She was well trained and was also an arranger and jazz singer. Yank also accompanied her with wire brushes. In fact he played only wire brushes which sometime didn't give the band the push it needed on certain numbers.

We didn't play loud because it was not necessary. Teddy had a soft when touch on piano, Benny Morton was at his best/playing not too loud and so was I. That was the big difference in playing in a big band and a small combo. In a big band you must blow loud and my ideas and technique were not as good when I had to play loud. Hamilton had a nice soft sound on clarinet and was really an admirer of Benny Goodman. So Yank's brushing style was nice for the band except as I mentioned before, it didn't always give the band a certain push on certain numbers. Al Hall was a solid bass player.

Yank Porter had worked at a Cafe before. Teddy went in and as Yank was very well liked by Barney Josepson, Teddy was obliged to use him. And John Hammond had made pressure on him to hire me, although I had worked with Teddy in Benny Carter's orchestra, I know that he had another trumpet player in mind when I was pushed on him.

Teddy was quite a nice person but I soon found out that he had a sunny character because we used to play a certain number in which he would play his solo in a minor key and the number and other solos were in major. I liked the way Teddy made it sound in minor and one night I asked him if I could play my solo also in minor. He told me yes, but after I had taken my solo, he did not play his, and then I knew that he didn't like it because I had played it in minor. I never asked to do it in minor again.

We never played behind Hazel when she did her act, but one time I suppose she wanted to see what quality the band really had because she made an arrangement on a song that she wanted us to accompany her [on] and she had it in the key of A, which put me in the key of B, which is five sharps and which is a key that is not often used in jazz. We rehearsed the number one afternoon and she put it in her programme that night. We played it down perfectly, but Hazel never called the number again. What a funny bird!

I said I would explain why I thought Lew the barman was a great person. Barney was a real liberal boss and a communist. He gave us a special price for drinks and it was Lew who served us. Al Hall and myself were the heaviest drinkers in the band. In fact we were the only two in the group that drank. Other than Yank, who smoked cigars, we were the only two in the group who smoked cigarettes. The popular drink at the moment was rum and coca cola and Lew was very heavy-handed with us when we went into the bar for a drink. He would put so much rum in the glass that there was hardly any place left for the coke. Of course Lew didn't serve the clientele in this manner but he liked performers and that's why he was a great barman to me.

The 4th of October, I recorded for a singer named Eddy Howard and the group included Benny Morton on trombone, Edmond Hall clarinet, Bud Freeman, a popular white tenor man, the famous Charlie Christian on guitar, Billy Taylor, Sr., Yank Porter, and Eddie Gibbs on guitar. The 9th of December was a date with Teddy Wilson's orchestra for an ex-Benny Goodman singer named Helen Ward with George James, a baritone sax player, and Eddie Gibbs added to Teddy's group.

In December 1940, Barney Josephson branched out and opened a Cafe Society Uptown on East 58th Street, and it was a real plushy joint. The Cafe Society Downtown was not a very large place, and there was only one small dressing room for musicians and entertainers. But at the Uptown, the whole building was occupied by the club and there was a big dressing room for the two bands, the Golden Gate Quartet and the Boogie Woogies. There were at least 4 other dressing rooms quite large and they were all on the third floor.

The club featured Teddy Wilson and Eddie South's orchestra, the Gates, the Boogies without Joe Turner, Hazel Scott and a comedian named Penner. Eddie South was a violinist known as "the Dark Angel" of that instrument and had been trained by some of the finest violin professors in Europe and especially in Hungaria. He was a classical musician that could play jazz also and had recorded some duets with the famous Stephane Grappelly in France.

Eddie had the bassist Dole Dickens, a fine classical and jazz pianist named Stanley Facey and the well known drummer Gordon "Specs" Powell to accompany him. Eddie was one of the attractions in the floor show and also played for dancing when we had our intermissions.

The club jumped from the opening night on and the clientele (customers) was of a higher society class than that at the downtown club which was in the Village, a part of New York that was considered to be the little Paris in the Apple, at least the left bank of Paris.

Lew the barman was now the head barman as it was necessary to have two men behind the bar, one to prepare drinks for the clients that were ordered by the waiters for people seated at the tables and one for those to be served at the bar. Most every night for the first show which went around 11 o' clock, the place was so

crowded that there were tables on the dance floor and there was just enough space to push the two baby grand pianos against the bandstand for Pete Johnson, Albert Ammons and Hazel Scott. For the second show at two o'clock, there were less people but still a good crowd and the show could be put on in the middle of the dance floor. The Golden Gates had to squeeze in between the two pianos when they went on for the first show.

We didn't do too much drinking at the bar because we had spacious rooms upstairs where we coudl play cards with Pete, Albert and some of the Gates when we had our rest periods, and we formed a club composed of those that liked a few tastes every night and bought our bottles of Kick-a-poo joy juice at a whisky store near the club. But if a friend came in or a client who admired a cert_ain musician invi_ted one of us at the bar, we accepted.

After a couple of weeks ef everything going well, Barney began to be Mr. Josephson because of the success of the Uptown Cafe Society. He put up a sign in our dressing room which specified that no sideman in the orchestras would be allowed to sit at a table with a client. The only exceptions were for Hazel who was the star of the show, Teddy, Eddie South, and of course, the comedian. As a rule, Pete and Albert always went upstairs after their numbers because they preferred to enjoy themselves talking, telling jokes and drinking with the rest of the cats.

But I refused to obey the sign whenever someone asked me to sit at their table or have a drink at the bar and so did Al Hall. Barney was a liberal downtown and had not made any difference about who should do what when the club was opened uptown and I felt that I was as much a gentleman as far as the clients were concerned as Teddy, Eddie South and Barney himself. And Barney never said anything to Al and I if we accepted the invitation to sit at a table when we were invited or to have a drink at the bar when it was offered to us. It was the idea behind the sign that I could not accept. If in the beginning a rule was made which did not allow any of the employees to sit at a table or drink at the bar and it applied to everyone. I would have accepted the rule the same as anyone else.
I mentioned before that Eddie South was so well trained on his

instrument that I doubt that he had ever made a mistake during his long career as a violinist. But one night he was playing a classical number that had a passage of eight bars for violin alone and Eddie made a mistake which those that heard it dismissed as something that could happen, but was not supposed to happen to a great performer like Eddie.

The next night Eddie did the number again, which was a number he did in his attraction set and he missed in the passage at the same place again and that did bug him, because it was a number he had played many times and had never missed a note before, and I suppose many others that witnessed this incident really felt sorry for Eddie and he became very upset because he had the passage two consecutive nights. The third one it was the same, and we all knew that now he was fighting with the passage and that's what he did for almost one week. When he did at last conquer, he played the number a couple of nights and I never heard him play it afterwards.

We worked at the Uptown for one month and left for a two months engagement in Chicago, at the Ambassador East Hotel which was one of the finest hotels in the city. We were to play in the Pump Room where only one other Negro orchestra had ever played and that was John Kirby's "biggest" little band in the world. I had heard many of their broadcasts and had never before heard six instruments that sounded like ten. Kirby's band had played in many places where Negro musicians had never played before and the "Pump Room" was one of them.

Teddy engaged his favourite drummer J.C. Heard, who had been a member of Teddy's big band, and added George James on baritone. This made the front line four horns, trumpet, trombone, clarinet and baritone sax. The baritone gave the band a heavy sound and the arrangement that Teddy made along with some that he had arranged made us sound quite big also.

For this job we had white cut-a-ways made in New York, and everything we wore was white from collar and bow tie down to socks and shoes. Only Teddy wore a black cut-a-way. I had never been in Chicago before this time and enjoyed the idea of going there
although I did not have the same enthusiasm about going there as I had when I first came to New York, and I had heard many nice things about Chicago.

Chicago was George James' home town and Teddy had been around there for a few years. Benny Morton had been there a few times also. Most of us stayed in a hotel on the South side which was the Harlem of Chicago. We were there for a few days before we were to start working in the "Pump Room", so we reported to the musicians union to receive our transfer cards and were told by secretary that a transit musician was not allowed to stand up and acknowledge applause if they were introduced in a public place.

As the Ambassador was in an exclusive part of Chicago and quite a distance from the Southside, it was necessary that we had transportation. Teddy bought a new car, Jimmy Hamilton bought one, and J.C. Heard bought a second-hand Cadillac, which was in good condition. George James rode with Jimmie, Al, Bennie and myself rode with J.C.

We had to do a musical show at a certain time every night and the number Teddy had chosen for me to feature was Gershwin's "I've Got Plenty of Nothing". We did our feature numbers on the dance floor in front of the band. The bandstand was very nice and Teddy's piano was on the floor with the band behind him.

There was also three nights a week when we had to broadcast. We could not blow very loud except during our show and for the radio, so Bernie and I played muted except for those two occasions. And I used to turn my back at times when I had a solo on an up tempo number, and blow at J.C. who sat in back of me. It may not have looked very nice but there is a certain amount of push in fast numbers that made it almost impossible for me to play if I had to hold back and use a mute at the same time.

One night we were playing "Sweet Georgia Brown" and on the last chorus, J.C. was really pushing and the number was swinging more that night than ever before. I had a feeling that I could never have had if Yank Porter had been on drums. So I turned towards J.C. and blowed the way I felt and ended on a high F.

When we came off the bandstand for an intermission, Teddy told me that I should not play high notes in that place, and I replied by saying that I didn't see anything wrong with it because I made a high note, and told him that no one ever said anything to him about playing high notes on the piano. He didn't like what I had said, and never said anything about the notes I made after that.

There was a small hotel on the Southside that had a club which featured small combos and was open until the wee hours every morning. There were also musicians playing in most of the bars and Chicago was jumping. Al and I were drinking buddies and we used to go to this hotel most every night after we finished at the "Pump Room" which was at 2 a.m. The club was managed by a dancer called Broadway, whom I knew in New York. Roy Eldridge brought a band in during our stay in the city and I met his drummer whose name was Kansas Field. I became better acquainted with Kansas later when he came to New York.

We had Monday nights off, and one Monday night, the orchestra of Count Basie played a dance at some large hall which gave me the opportunity of hearing Basie in person for the first time. When I was in Egypt, I had rented a big radio and had heard a broadcast of Basie for the first time. I had not heard of the band before but I immediately recognized Dickie Wells. But being able to hear the band and see it for the first time was real kicks and I'll never forget the impression I had listening to them.

At the same time, when I heard the Basie broadcast in Egypt, they had played a number called "Sweet" and Sentimental" which featured a tenor sax who sounded very much like Hawkins. I later heard this same number on a large speaker in a theatre one afternoon during the intermission between pictures but never found out who the tenor was. There was also a fine clarinet solo on the tune. So when I caught the band in Chicago, I asked Dickie who the tenor was, and he told me it was a fellow named Hershel Evans and that he was dead.
["Blue and..."]

J.C. had a radio in his car and one night as we were coming from work, we caught a broadcast of Duke coming from somewhere in California. They were playing a number called "Flamingo" and a male singer was singing it. This fellow really had a wonderful

voice and Duke's band was sounding great as usual. But it was the singer that had really captured our attention. At the end of the number, the speaker announced that we just heard a new voice of the/Duke Ellington orchestra, Herb Jeffreys singing "Flamingo".

We always changed from our white uniforms after we finished a night and had a room in the hotel for that. And every two weeks we had them cleaned. A quick cleaner near the hotel would pick them up on a Monday and they would be ready for us when we returned Tuesday night. J.C., Al, myself were about the fastest changing members of the band, because sometimes we would arrive a little late dressed in our regular street clothes about 10 or 15 minutes before starting time. But three minutes before time to hit, we would be on the band stand in our pretty white cut-a-way uniforms and ready for the night.

We finished at the "Pump Room" the last of March and I came back to New York with Beezie who had come to Chicago to be with me the last two weeks. It was understood that we were to go back to the Cafe Society Uptown within six weeks time, so during the wait I did a few gigs.

One day I was standing on the steps of the house where I lived with my landlady and Beezie when a car drove up. Two fellows, one small and the other quite big got out of the car and asked if they could speak to me. We walked a couple of doors from my place and the little fellow asked me if I knew a woman named Sally. I said that I didn't, because I knew right away what the deal was about. Then they showed me a photo of Teddy's orchestra. The little guy told me that Sally was his wife and she had told him that she had been in Chicago with me. He also showed me a letter she had received in Chicago which was unsigned and said that it was from me.

But I had a shoe to fit his foot because I pointed to Beezie and told him that she was my wife and that she had been with me in Chicago. That I could prove by her that the handwriting was not mine. If it had not been for that I suppose I would have gotten a good beating from the big fellow who must have been the small one's strong arm man.

But this woman had been in Chicago with Al Hall who had been going with her for a long time and I did know her. What made me angry was that her husband found a letter written to her by Al and a photo of the orchestra, and when her husband had asked her who she was with in Chicago, because he knew she had been there, she had said she was with me to protect her lover, and that could have cost me my life if I hadn't had proof that the letter was not written by me. I did not blame Al for what this woman had done but I told him that it did not make me happy.

Two weeks before we were to go back into the Cafe Society, Al came to my house and told me that he and I would not be included in the orchestra when it opened. He had gone to see Teddy and had given him his notice and told him that I would not be in the band either. I promptly went to see Teddy to have the news directly from him and he told me that Barney Josephson did not want Al and I in his club anymore. I was very angry about the turn of events, because I had not accepted or tried to get another regular job as it had been certain before we left Chicago that I would go back to the Cafe with Teddy.

I told Teddy to tell Barney that I had lived many years before I ever worked in his place for a few months and that I would not die if I didn't work in his place again. If Al had not come to my house and told me what was happening and I had not gone to see Teddy, I could have reported to the musicians union after Teddy had started in the club and he would have had to pay me two weeks salary because he had not given me a two-weeks notice. But as I had gone to Teddy and he told me within the two weeks limit that I would no longer be with the band, there was nothing I could do. And now I'm happy that I didn't have the opportunity to take Teddy to the Union because I had never had to do that and the only benefit I would have gotten would have been two weeks salary and a lost friendship, although Teddy and I never were great friends. I liked and always did admire him from the first time we worked together in Benny Carter's orchestra.

Timmie Rosenkrantz, who had come to New York in 1933 and eventually became to be known as the "Barrel-House Baron", had married a Negro girl named Inez Cavanaugh whom I had known for quite a long time, and they opened a record shop on St. Nicholas Avenue near 147th Street. I started making the shop my hang-out and soon after that, Timmie asked me why I did not form an orchestra and he would manage it. I mentioned in this book before that Timmie was a real Danish Baron whom I had met at the Empire Ballroom in 1933 when I worked there with Benny Carter.

Timmie was in the know as to what was happening in the jazz w world and knew the onwers of most of the clubs uptown and downtown So we talked about the band I should lead for a few days and then started to put the idea in action. Harry White, an ex-Cab Calloway trombonist, known as "Father" White, was also known as a fine arranger, but he had become an alchoholic victim, and was not in demand at the time. He started hanging out in Timmie's record shop also, and when we had worked out the details of my orchestra, Harry agreed to be the arranger.

We contacted a pianist named General Morgan and his first name really was General. He was a fine pianist. Arthur Herbert, who was an Ex-Coleman Hawkins drummer, Franz Jackson, a tenor man and Herb Fleming on trombone are the only known members of the orchestra that I can remember. "Father" White was living in a back room of the record shop and Timmie was feeding him and also gave him a little drinking money. The shop wasn't doing too well, so not much money was coming in, and we musicians weren't working, so we had nothing to offer in the way of money to pay for the arrangements.

But things were going along nicely at the rehersals and one day, I think that Timmie or Inez hit the numbers for five cents and decided to have a little party for the band. Timmie had been speaking about a famous dish he used to cook called Danish meat balls, or fish balls, and he cooked some for the party. They were made with fish and mixed with mashed potatoes and served with a white sauce, and they were very tasty, to my surprise.

After two months rehersing, Timmie told us that the next week we would have an audition at Kelly's Stable, which was well known jazz spot on 52nd Street between 6th and 7th Avenue. Kelly's Stable was a jazz club long before the Famous Door and a few other 52nd Steret joints became famous. The next rehersal, Franz Jackson did not show up, and the one after that, also. We had no idea what had happened to him, so we engaged a clarinetist named Eddie Williams and on th e following Tuesday night, we went to the Stable to do the audition. Now I remember that the bass player was a young bassist named Benny Moten.

Generally an audition was done in the afternoon, but the two owners of Kelly's Stable whom I only knew as George and Nick, wanted us to audition when there were people in the place, in order to obtain the reaction of the public to our playing. There were two other orchestras auditioning that night and one of them was under the name of Franz Jackson. He had pulled a dirty trick on me by accepting to play with me until he found out where and for whom the audition would be, and then form his own group and undermine me for the job.

By the time that each orchestra had played four sets, it was time for the place to close. I had made auditions with other orchestras, but this was the first time I did one which was similar to a night work and was not paid for it. But musicians have always had to do many things that were not kosher in order to land a job, so the ordeal was sort of normal.

As Timmie was my manager, I didn't ask any questions to George or Nick, but when the night was finished, Timmie told us that the prospects for landing the job looking good but the owners would like for us to come back the following week, and do another audition under the same conditions, which meant nothing for us, but something for the place, if you get what I mean, as Fats Waller would say....

Fortunately the musicians were not difficult, although we were mostly all experiencing rather difficult times, so we were willing to come back the next week for another try at getting the job. We returned and things were the same as the Tuesday night before except that Franz Jackson and the other orchestra that were there the week before, were not there and two other groups were making the audition with us. When the night was finished, Timmie told us that he was supposed to call the owners in a day or two to get their decision.

A few days later, Timmie called and then told us that George wanted us to come back the following week to do another audition and we froze. We had become aware to what the jive was that George and Nick were putting down.

The two groups that played there every night were off on Tuesdays and these guys had worked out a scheme wherein they would have three groups come in on Tuesdays nights under the pretext of auditioning for the job, and [since] auditions did not pay anything, they were having one night a week of free music and making a nice profit,. Nice work if you can get it.

Soon after that, Timmie, was in no condition to go anywhere else to try and get us a job because his face broke out with some kind of infection and as I was not the go-getter type, the band never got it's foot off the ground and that was my only venture in the band leading business in the States. I suppose that I was just not born to be a leader in those days.

Then I started hanging around the Rhythmn Club again and managed to pick a few gigs with Kaiser Marshall, the first well known drummer of the Fletcher Henderson orchestra. And there was a little fellow who played alto sax not very well who was named Leon Gross, but all the musicians called him Bossman, who got quite a few gigs also. Times were difficult as the Depression was still on in the USA, and musicians accepted jobs for whatever price they could get.

Kaiser called a dollar a potato and when he would ask me if I would do a gig with him, he would explain that the job only paid three potatoes. And there was a saying amongst musicians that if you did not want the gig, there was a boy around the corner that would accept it. And I was one of the boys around the corner....I did quite a few

gigs with Kaiser and Bossman. The bands were usually good musicians and there were never any hard arrangements to be played because there were always different musicians for each gig except for two or three regular musicians that Kaiser and Bossman could depend on being free at any time to accept a gig from them.

Sometime during the late spring, Sidney Bechet had come to live on the street where I lived and he happened to get a place just across the street from me. We knew each other casually, but eventually got better acquainted and Beezie became quite friendly with the girl Sidney was living with. Gigs were coming in, less and less, so in June, I decided to apply for my social security, which was everyone's perogative that belonged to the Social Security, and everyone that worked had to have a card.

In order to receive benefits from the social security, it was necessary to report to the bureau nearest to you, and there was one not far from where I lived. I applied and had to report for five weeks before I could get a check for 25 dollars every week for a certain length of time. One could not actually call this a benefit from the government, because a certain amount of money is taken out of one's salary every working week, and it is one's privilege to apply for and receive a certain amount when they are out of work.

During this procedure, Bechet, as every one called Sidney in New York, had applied for a summer session job at a place called Camp Unity which was 70 miles from New York. The Camp was run by the Communist Party, and was known to be very liberal concerning the social mixing of races. I had been aware of the existence of this camp from other musicians that had done a season there. Bechet asked me if I would do the season with him and naturally, I accepted. The regular season was for six weeks, starting the 15th of July, until the first of September. But the camp was open on weekends before the regular season started.

Bechet arranged for us to get free supper which was offered to us. The salary was 25 dollars for the weekend, room and board included from Friday evening until Sunday evening. We played Saturday afternoon and night and Sunday afternoon which gave us the opportunity to be home Sunday night.

I've forgotten who was engaged as pianist, but Manzie Johnson was the drummer and Wellman Braud was on the bass. The first weekend passed without any incidents; but the second one, Bechet was not satisfied, because Manzie had met a white girl and was accompanying her around the camp. Bechet gave Manzie hell for no reason because there were plenty of mixed couples, white men with Negro women and Negro men with white girls, all over the place. But Bechet didn't want any of the musicians congregating with white girls because he thought it would jeopardize the job for him.

Then he got into a big dispute with Braud because he had defended the rights of Manzie. As for Manzie he had taken the whole thing with discretion, but Bechet had really spoiled the second weekend by his stupid reaction as to what was permitted and what he didn't want the musicians to do at the camp.

The next week, my day to report to the social security was changed from Thursday morning at 11 o' clock to Friday morning. Tuesday of the same week, Bechet hit the numbers for a few cents and loaned me a dollar without me asking for it, but it was to chip in on a gallon of wine. We had been taking a bottle with us the last two weekends, because there was no bar at the camp, and cheap wine was the only alchohol beverage that we could afford.

Thursday afternoon, I went over to Sidney's house and told him that the day for me to report to the social security had been changed to Friday mornings. We had left for the camp the two last times at 11 a.m. and we were supposed to leave same time on this Friday. I explained to Sidney that this was the last time I was to report and then I would be receiving my check every week. With 25 dollars for the weekends at Camp Unity and 25 that I would get from the social security, it would make 50 dollars, and I had intended doing it that way until we started working regularly. I would then stop [reporting to report] at the social security.

After explaining the matter to Bechet, I asked him if it would be alright for me to come to the camp later in the afternoon as there were buses that passed near the camp, leaving New York every two hours.

His reply was that we all must leave together. I said: "But Sidney, we don't have to play that night and anyway, I would be there before supper time." But he would not consent to my coming a little later and insisted that I leave with everyone else.

I always had very little patience with someone who was illogical, so I lost patience with Bechet very quickly. I told him that I was going to stay to report to the social security at the time I was supposed to report. He told me that if I didn't come along with him, and the rest of the musicians, he would take me to the union. I told him that he could take it to the Federal court if he wished to do so, and started to walk out of his house, when he called me and said: "And another thing, give me my God damn dollar!" And I gave him his God damn dollar, because I had not spent it, and that was the last of Sidney Bechet for me.

I collected my social security, did a few gigs until Leon Abbey, whom I had gone to India with and who was now in New York, offered me a job at the Ubangi club which was now down town in a basement at the corner of 52nd Street and Broadway. This was the hardest job I ever had in New York. The band was small, consisting of piano, drums, trumpet, tenor sax, bass and violin. There was a relief band lead to a wonderful flautist named Albert Soccaras. At one time, Soccaras had been a member of Chick Webb's orchestra. He was the first flautist I ever heard that could make a flute sound like a pipe organ playing in the lower register.

Abbey's combo was the band that had to accompany a big revue and the violin was no help because there were only two instruments that could really play loud. They were the tenor and trumpet. We started at 9 every night and there were no nights off. We played dance music and two shows a night. The relief band played one hour after the first show and an hour before the second one. We finished the night at three o' clock.

One of the last acts in the revue to appear before the finals was called "the Beach Combers" and it was really a wild act and one of the best I've ever seen in a night club. They were two people, a man who's make up and costume made him appear like a fellow who had been ship wrecked on a deserted island, and a girl whom he had presumably found there, and at the end of their act, he was horse-whipping her. They wanted their music as loud as possible and the arrangement had been made for an orchestra with no less than three trumpets. This number was so loud that I never heard what Leon Abbey was playing in it. And after having played many acts and music for the chorus girls, who were real girls at this Ubangi Club, when it came to the last eight bars of "the Beach Combers" act which was the hardest of all the acts, my lips would be so tired that I just could not bring the number to a close the way it should have been.

And every night, I would hear this fellow saying "That God-damn trumpet player" when he came off the floor and to him I must have been the lousiest trumpet player in the world. But one thing I know and that is that they had the hardest act that I ever tried to play in a small band that had to play to revue which should have been accompanied by a large orchestra. I was asking forty dollars a week and I really earned my pay.

A very nice trumpet player named Archey Johnson was in the relief band and after a few weeks of fighting the music of the "Beach Combers", I told Leon that I couldn't take it any longer, so it was arranged for Archey to take my place and I would play with the relief band. The salary was five dollars less than I had before, which I thought was not correct, because in the other band the work was harder and worth at least fifteen dollars more than I received in the relief band.

I never knew how Archey made out with the "Beach Combers" act because I was never there until the last of the final act was being played. But Archey didn't stay in Leon's band very long and when he left, two trumpet players were engaged. They were Russell Gillon and his buddy Reese. They were both nice young fellows and both play-boys, so it was possible that Leon had hired Russel and he in turn had arranged to divide the salary in order to be together. Otherwise, why had Leon not hired another trumpet to help me when he knew that the job was too hard for one trumpet? Two new orchestras were hired after a couple of months and I started giging again.

In August I was contacted to do a two-weeks tour with Claude Hopkins, the pianist who had been quite a popular bandleader at the Savoy and the Arcadia ballrooms. Claude had no regular orchestra now and most of the musicians were engaged at the Rhythmn Club. Those that I remember on the tour were Ernest "Bass" Hill, Joe Jordon known as Pokey Joe on trumpet. Joe loved to play poker and that's how he became known as Pokey Joe. Joe Hayman was on alto. Also Norman Thronton and Lem Johnson was the tenor man. Lem was also a very good blues singer. Another trumpet player was E.V.Perry. Pokey Joe was a very nice first chair man and so was Perry.

The most amusing thing about the tour was that Claude had engaged a small bus that could carry about 20 people. It was large enough for us because we were about 14 including the girl vocalist. Everytime we came to a hill that mounted for a quarter of a mile or more, the damn bus couldn't make it and we all had to go out and push it. Sometimes we had to stop pushing for ten minutes to get our breaths and Pokey Joe always had a pair of dice with him so the guys would take their minds off of pushing the bus and shot craps for ten or fifteen minutes. I filmed them in the act because I always had my movie camera on a tour. I bought my first movie camera in the Hague in Holland in 1937.

When the bus was rolling, there was a poker game going on until we reached our destination. We played some dates in Maryland, Delaware and Washington, D.C., where we played a river boat dance which was very agreeable at night, because the weather was about 110 in the shade during the time we were there. We stayed in D.C. for a couple of days before the tour ended. I've experienced having to push a car on different occasions on a tour, but this was the first time I helped push a bus and everyone taken it more so as a joke and not a drag.

Beezie and I had not been getting along very well for quite some time and we finally separated. The last week of September, I was engaged by Andy Kirk to replace a trumpeter named Clarence Trice. The position was not to be permanent but I stayed with the orchestra for four months and enjoyed every moment.

There were only three musicians in the orchestra that I knew slightly and they were Harold Baker, trumpet, whom I had seen with Teddy Wilson's big band, Henry Wells, trombone, in Lunceford's orchestra and Edward Inge, ex-Don Redman clarinetist. The rest of the member were Harry Lawson, known as "Big Jim", Ted Donnelly, trombone, Johnny Harrington and Buddy Miller, alto-sax's, Dick Wilson, tenor. Floyd Smith, guitar, Booker Collins, bass, Mary Lou Williams, piano, Ben Thigpen, drums and June Richmond, vocals.

I had however seen Andy Kirk and his "Clouds of Joy" quite a few times when he had a male singer named Pha Terrell with him and had also admired the piano playing of Mary Lou Williams who played strong swinging piano like a man. I soon found out that Mary Lou was a fine arranger also because there were quite a number of compositions in the Kirk book that were written and arranged by her and they were swinging stomping arrangements.

"Big Jim" Lawson was a quite fellow who was quite big and must have weighed at least 200 pounds but he was solid and not fat. He could drink a lot and never show it, and was about the loudest blowing trumpet player I ever heard after Ted Colin. But he had a wonderful tone and although he could blow loud, it was not blasting.

Harold "Shorty" Baker was about four-feet ten and had one of the biggest sounds I ever heard from a trumpeter and he could blow quite strong also. He had a very personal style and was an all around trumpet player. I thought that I could blow fairly loud but I really had to put everything I could into my horn to be heard in the section. Ted Donelly and Henry Wells were nice trombone players and the reed section was quite strong. Buddy Miller played most of the first alto parts and Johnny Harrington played third alto and clarinet. I knew Johnny's brother, who had been in Horane Henderson's college orchestra in Wilberforce, Ohio and was also an alto sax man. Everyone called him Jew Harrington. I never knew the reason and dont remember his first name.

Edward Inge I knew quite well because I had talked with him many times in Big John's bars and made some Redman recordings with him. Inge was a fine man who was always very conservative and never seemed to get excited or upset about anything. He was really the type of person that had complete control of himself at all times. He also played second tenor sax in some of the arrangement but he featured on clarinet.

Floyd Smith was well known for his 'Floyd's Guitar Blues' which he did on a table type Hawaiian guitar, and he was quite a funky guitar player on other numbers. Booker Collins was a solid bass man with a very nice charactar and Ben Thigpen was a nice drummer.

June Richmond had been in the show at the Harlem Club where the Benny Carter band had played in 1933 and I had seen her later at the Lafayette Theatre. June was quite heavy and must have weighed more than Big Jim although she was just a little taller than Shorty Baker. But she didn't need a microphone or loud speakers to be heard when she sang. June had a voice like an opera singer, but she could swing a number like Ella Fitzgerald and the band didn't have to play soft for her. She also did comical numbers and could do almost anything with her voice.
The first date I did with the Band was at the Howard Theatre in Washington, and as we were obliged to rehearse the show as soon as we arrived, I didn't know any of the band members.
Cont...

But I was playing the third parts and Harold Baker was a big help in directing me as to what would take place in certain parts. The arrangements were not really hard but very effective and I did a fairly good job the first day and as the week continued, I became better acquainted with the musicians and things went very well afterwards.

I had heard about Dick Wilson being a great tenor player before I joined the band and he was considered on a par with Hershel Evans. To me, his tone was not as heavy as Hershel's, but his ideas were great and he was a hard swinger. Dick was a very heavy drinker, I soon found out, because he and I became great friends within a few days after I joined Kirk. Big Jim would drink and eat, and so did I. But Dick ate almost nothing and his drinking did not show in his playing.

There was a liquor store near the theatre that gave credit to the people working at the theatre and there was also a joint across the street from the stage entrance that sold juice and stayed open all night. I hung out with Dick in this place after our last shows unitl I could not keep my eyes open and would leave him there almost every morning. I lived at a boarding house just in front of the theatre. When we closed at the Howard, I had a liquor bill of forty-five dollars and the salary for the week was eighty five. When the taxes were taken out the salary was about seventy dollars and I had spent most of the money for drinking in one week than I really imagined could be possible because of Dick Wilson.
Cont...

The next week we opened at the famous "Door" on 52nd street for one month. The Door was not a very large place but it did good business because the customers never stayed very long and the drinks were quite expensive, which was normal and correct for a place that presented first class orchestras and attractions. Of course the customers did get the "rush your drink" treatment, because the waiters would take your drink aways before it was finished if you didn't keep an eye on it. The turn over for the club was very profitable.

Andy Kirk was a gentle leader who had once been a baritone sax player in some orchestra around St. Louis or Kansas City, so I was told. He was very patient with the musicians but no one gave him much trouble except Buddy Miller who would get drunk occasionally and could not do his job correctly.

Being new in the band, I knew nothing about this, until one night at the famous "Door", after an intermission, he had met some trampy looking girl in the White Rose bar around the corner from the club on 6th Avenue and gotten drunk and brought this chick back to the club with him. Before the intermission he seemed to be alright, but when he came back, he could hardly stand. Buddy was also a quiet type of fellow and a fine first alto man. Andy told him very nicely to take the rest of the night off because he was not able to play anymore.
Cont...

Dick and I were in the White Rose after every intermission. They had a free snack table in this bar which at one time there were a few hot dishes to choose from, but people started to abuse the hospitality and now there were only cold cuts, cheese and crackers. Of course you had to buy a drink or drinks to ride this gravy train. Dick and I paid our dues every night.

Shortly before we finished at the Door, Dick became ill and was taken to the Harlem Hospital. No one thought that his sickness was very serious and all agreed that the rest would be good for him. Al Sears was engaged to sub for Dick and he had a style that suited the band. I knew Al many years before, having met him and Sy (Melvin) Oliver in Zanesville, Ohio, when I played that town with the Scott band before we went to New-York.

After the famous Door gig, the band hit the road which was customary for the Kirk band and the first date was at an amusement park for one night in Montreal, Canada. It was considered a usual habit for the band to make a jump of 500 or more miles from one place to another in a bus and play only one night. I had done plenty of one nighters with Clarence Page, Wes Helvey and Scott, but they were seldom over a couple of hundred miles.
Cont...

I would pick on a little pot now and then, and before we left for Canada, I had bought six sticks of some stuff known as "Red Cross". I had met a young man in Chicago who was known as Bob Red Cross when I played the Pump Room with Teddy Wilson and Bob was a pot seller who rolled his stuff with an end on the paper that allowed a smoker to get the value of every grain.

When we arrived in Montreal, I stayed in a room with Ted Donnelly and before going to work that night, I put the sticks of Red Cross in a dresser drawer. But after the dance, I met some people who invited me to their house for a few drinks. I got high and slept there until around eight o' clock that morning and when I returned to the hotel, the bus was ready to leave. Ted told me that he had packed my things, so I had a cup of coffee while we were waiting for someone else to come and when we left, we were almost to the border when I realised that I had left my six sticks of Red Cross in the dresser drawer of the hotel and I hadn't had one puff of the stuff which all the cats that picked up considered to best reefers that could be found.

Our next date was in some town in Delaware, two nights after the Canadian date, and as we were obliged to pass through New York City, I decided to stop there and visit Dick Wilson in the hospital and rejoin the band the next day.
Cont...

The next day I rejoined the band and after the gig in Delaware, we went into the Pearl Theatre in Baltimore for one week and then hit the road for some dates in the real South. It was my first time to as far south as Nashville and Knoxville, Tenessee, Atlanta, Georgia, and Birmingham, Alabama.

We were paid eighty-five dollars a week when we worked theatres and sixty-five in a club. But on the road doing one-nighters, my salary was seventy dollars a week or ten dollars per diem which in Latin means per day and in the music game it is known as per-rater or ratter. That works out to seventy dollars a week if you work seven nights. When I made five nights, that was a good week.

I had heard many true stories about things that had happened to Negro musicians in the South and was being careful that nothing would cause me any trouble. But the night we played Knoxville, something happened.

Ted and I were rooming together again and a couple of local musicians that he knew came to the dance. When the dance was finished, we got together with these two musicians in our room and started having a beer drinking party.
Cont...

When I arrived at the hospital after checking into a hotel it was past the visiting time. I explained at the reception desk that I was a musician friend of Dick's and that I was passing through town and would like to see him for a few minutes. The nurse in charge told me that a lot of people had told her the same thing. I told her that it was not possible because a lot of people were not musicians and they did not know Dick Wilson. So she allowed me to visit her.

There must have been at least 30 beds of sick men in the ward where Dick was and one of the nurses' led me to his bed. He was really happy to see me because he had no real friends in New York and therefore no one had visited him. He told me in a voice that was just a little above a whisper that his feet had swollen up and been opened to drain out the liquid substance that caused the swelling in his feet.

His voice was weak but he seemed to be alright otherwise. He also told me that they gave him a shot of whiskey every day, but only one, and if he could find some one that would get him a pint, then everything would be alright. The real trouble with Dick was that he had not eaten a good meal in such a long time that alcohol had taken his appetite. He actually wanted me to say that I would bring him a bottle of juice, but that was out of the question.
Cont...
A girl that worked in the bar of the hotel was serving us in our room and we were getting more and more groovie with every glass.

Finally, the girl came in with another order of beer and some of the fellows started playing with her, and had her on the bed. Naturally, the chick jumped salty and the fellows stopped pretending that they were going to rape her. She took away some empty glasses and later on, she came back and accused someone of taking her ten dollars from her apron pocket, and she wanted it back, or else she was going to call the police.

I knew that I had not taken anything from her because I had not put my hands on her, and the guys who had been wrestling with her, claimed that they had not taken the money. Nobody was guilty and twenty minutes later we were looking in the mugs of two red-faced cops. I realized that I was in the deep South when one of them said: "This gal says that one of your niggers took ten dollars from her, and we's a tellen' yah that if the nigger that took it don't give it back, we's gonna take youse all to jail."

And that's where they took us because no-one would admit that they had stolen the ten from the girl's pockets. Ted and I had around the same amount of money on us, because we had not been paid for the week. At the police station, we were searched and I had seven dollars and a small pocket knife. When the police man behind the cash desk saw the small knife that I had, he said, "Darn nigger, you ain't got damn near nothing." They were used to taking long switch blade knives from Negros when they were arrested.

But there I was, in jail again and I had not done anything wrong. And I don't know if ten dollars was found on the other two guys, but I knew that Ted Donnelly didn't have any more money than I had because he had been searched before me. One thing he did have was a long knife and no one said anything when it was taken from him.

For some reason, I did not give any thought as to what would happened the next morning when we would be taken to court. But we were not taken to court, and I've always thought that something was phony about the deal every time I think about it. The next morning about 9.30, we were taken out of our cell, and brought to the desk of the police station and given all our belongings except our money and told that our trial would be heard two days later and they were keeping our money as our bonds.

The reason I say that I think something was phony is because Ted and I had told the policeman at the desk when we were questioned, that we were a travelling orchestra and they must have known that we were leaving town that day because the orchestra bus was waiting when we came out. Floyd Smith got a real kick of what had happened because he has an 8mm camera and caught us coming out of jail. And I had heard the clink of a jail house door closing behind me for the third time in my life. I never heard any more about the affair.

After a few other dates in the deep South, we came to Raleigh, North Carolina. As we had arrived a night before we were to play a dance there, I met some fellows in the hotel where I stayed and they invited me to go to a club that was on the outskirts of town. I had a ball, but when we came back, to town in the wee hours of morning, the fellow that was driving the car didn't stop at a cross section marked stop and a motorcycle policeman saw us. I was sitting in the back seat behind the driver and when the policeman came near to the car, I was almost certain that I was going to hear the clink of a jail cell door closing behind me again.

But to my surprise, the policeman was nice for a Southerner. He was leaning inside the car where the window was down by the driver, and the driver was looking straight ahead because he had been drinking the same as the rest of us and it could have been real bad for him, had the cop smelt his breath.

When the policeman would ask him a question or tell him something, the guy just answered "Yes, Sir", and "No, Sir". Finally, the cop told him to come to the court house the next day and I breathed a sigh of relief because I would not have to spend another morning in jail.

The next night, we were playing the dance and the musicians union delegate came to inspect our cards. I recognised him as being the policeman that had stopped the car I was in the night before. When we had finished a set and we were showing him our cards, I asked him if he was the policeman that had stopped a car last night because the driver had not stopped at a crossing and he said yes. He told me that the fellow driving the car had come to the court house and was fined a light sum. Then he asked me why didn't I say the night before that I was with the band that was going to play the dance and he would have let the driver go without having to come to court. But I didn't know that he was the union delegate, so I wasn't saying anything unless I was asked a question, which was not the case.

And on that night, we received word that Dick Wilson had died and suddenly all the spirit went out of the band, and I never heard the "Clouds of Joy" (as Kirk's band was known) play as bad as they did that night. And then I started to feel a little angry with all of them, except Al Sears, because they had known Dick much longer than I, and I was the only one that had made and effort to see him, and did see him, before he passed away.

After some dates in a few other Southern cities, we played a night at the Golden Gate Ballroom in the Apple. Buddy Miller was not there when started the night. The other orchestra was a pick-up band under the leadership of Loon Cross known by all the Rhythm Club fellows as Boss Man. Loon had an alto man with him that I didn't know and Andy asked him if he would play a set with the band until Buddy came.

Buddy played most of the first alto part and this fellow was reading them as though he had been playing them for years. When Buddy did show up, he was too drunk to play. Andy asked Boss Man's alto player if he would finish the night with the band and he accepted. Andy fired Buddy then and there and when the night was finished, the other fellow accepted to stay with the band. His name was Ben Smith, and he and I became quite good friends.

We left New York that morning after the dance, for Pittsburgh where we played that night and from there we went to Detroit in the Paradise Theatre. Then we played a breakfast dance at the Grey Stone Ballroom, an afternoon dance in Toledo, Ohio, and a night dance in Wheeling, West Virginia. We arrived there an hour late because it was quite a long jump from Toledo to Wheeling.
Cont...

We played a week in a dance hall strictly for whites in St. Louis, Mo. and I had the feeling that I was making a pilgrimage when we came rolling into town because I had heard much talk about St. Louis being a swinging musical town and the fine jazz musicians that came from there. The dance hall closed early enough for me to be able to make the round of some of the clubs. But time had caught up with St. Louis and although I heard some swinging cats and jammed with some of them, I didn't distinguish any difference in a good orchestra there and a good one in Cincinnati, Chicago or New York.

But I spent a nice week there and saw four people that I had known before. One was George Hudson, the trumpet player, that I had met on my first trip to Buffalo and later saw him in Omaha, Nebraska, when I met Lester Young. Una Mae Carlisle was playing in a club in St. Louis. I had known her from a club in Harlem and she was also in Paris in the 30's when I was there. Another person I saw whom I had met before was Rasol Saddler, the wife of the saxophonist Clo Saddler, whom I had met when I came to Paris, France, the first time with Lucky Millinder. And there was also a girl (chorus) named Betty who had been a girl friend of Lincoln Mills, the trumpeter I had worked with in Benny Carter's orchestra. Hazel told me that I could find Clo at the musicians club but I never got around to going there.
Cont...

I was in St. Louis on Sunday the 7th of December, 1941, when an extra edition of newspapers came out with the news that the Japanese had bombarded Pearl Harbour, but I really got the news from Al Sears who came to my room in the Booker Washington Hotel and told me that he was going to have his family leave New York because he though the Japanese may bombard the Apple next.

During the week, Harold Baker, who was Mary Lou's ole man, had a dispute with Mary and gave Andy his notice and said that he was going to stay in St. Louis. I think that he had over accepted to work with some orchestra.
