So Andy had contacted his booking agency which was Joe Glaser, the one that booked Armstrong also, and asked Joe to send him a trumpet player to replace Harold. Two days before we closed, a trumpet player named Howard McGhee arrived. Andy called a rehearsal for the next afternoon and when I arrived, McGhee was there, but he was not warming up his instrument or his chops, but was playing piano, and he really could play the box.

Then arrived the day for us to leave St. Louis and Harold "Shorty Boo" Baker had changed his mind and couldn't stand to let his sweet Mary Lou leave him, and it seems as though Mary Lou may have left the band if Andy hadn't agreed to take Shorty back. Andy didn't want to lose Mary Lou, so he was stuck with four trumpeters because McGhee had been sent to him by Glaser and he was obliged to keep him.

The bus driver stopped a few miles outside of St. Louis to gas up and I wanted to take a look. So I went inside the station and asked one of the attendants if I could use the toilet. From inside of the station, one could see when cars were coming from either direction and this fellow told me that I could go in the toilet, but not stay very long. I wasn't supposed to be seen coming out of the toilet by a white customer.

We played a one-nighter in Little Rock, Arkansas, and then on to Chicago where Kirk had a month engagement at the Grand Terrace which was one of the biggest and best known clubs in the city. One night, Tiny Bradshaw came to the club with a.....

party and sat with his back to the band and didn't speak to anyone in the orchestra. He certainly knew me because we had worked together in Luis Russell's orchestra at the Roseland, and he must have known Andy Kirk. But Tiny had had success as a band leader who played mostly in the Southern States and success had gone to his head.

A few nights later, Duke Ellington came to the club with a party and danced with a woman. As he danced and passed in front of the bandstand, he smiled and nodded at each member of the band as we smiled and spoke to him individually. That was the difference in a great person that is someone and Tiny Bradshaw who was nothing to compare with Duke but thought that he was God Almighty.

I didn't have the opportunity to visit any other clubs in Chicago because they were closed when we finished our nights. After two weeks in the Grand Terrace, Andy gave me a two-weeks notice because he wanted to add a second trombone. I had not been engaged by his agency and the brass section was not balanced with one trombone. Henry Wells had left the band before we came to Chicago, and not long after the first of January, 1942, I was back in the Apple again.

I had not been with Kirk's orchestra a very long time, but I did enjoy every moment of my stay. It was probably the kind of band that he'd had for years back. It had the real Kansas City feeling, which a lot of the bands in the East did not have. Benny Carter certainly did not have it, though possibly Teddy Hill came closer to it. It's difficult to define what the Kansas City "feeling" was. The only thing I can say is that their approach to jazz was centered on "swing", which was always the first consideration. Naturally, the arrangements reflected this, and this was the quality which Benny Carter lacked. His jazz had more of a classical feeling than the stomping Kansas City sounds which bands like Andy Kirk produced.

I started getting some gigs and some of them were with the great Fats Waller who was doing theatre dates of from one to three days in small towns in the States of New York, Massachusetts, Connecticut and New Jersey. Dave McRae, an alto player, was the one who engaged some of the musicians for the big band that Fats was using: Jack Butler, Johnny (Bugs) Hamilton, Fats regular trumpet man and myself, were the brass section. Herb Fleming on trombone, Cordic Wallace, bass, Al Casey, guitar, Arthur Tappier, drums, Bob Carroll, tenor and another alto player that I've forgotten his name.

Fats was a natural hit everywhere we played. As "Bugs" Hamilton had been with Fats a long time, he was normally the leader of the trumpet section because he had parts that he played when Fats only used a small combo. He would give Jack and myself the solos that he didn't care about playing. Sometimes when his lips were not feeling too strong, Bugs would ask me or Jack to take a solo in numbers that he enjoyed playing.

We enjoyed the solos also, but when Bugs lips felt alright the next night, he would play the solos again. Jack and I decided to do something about that. The next time Bugs asked one of us to take his solo and we knew the reason he wanted us to do it, we told him that we were not going to take them one day and he would take them only when he felt good. After that, Jack and I had solos which we were featured in, in every theatre we played.

These gigs were on a weekly basis and sometimes there would be periods of two or three weeks that Fats did not use a big band, but whenever he did the same musicians were usually available. We had a few days once up state in New York and Fats was suffering with the gout in one foot. His doctor had advised him not to drink any whisky but told him that he could drink a little wine every day. So Fats had a gallon of muscatel in his dressing room every day.
We played this town for three days. He would invite the musicians to drink with him, but he drank most of the gallon.

When I was working at the Ubangi Club with Leon Abbey, a fellow named Rodger Kramer arrived in New York from Egypt and came to see me at the club. I had met his brother Leon Kramer in Alexandria, but Rodger said he had been in France singing with Arthur Briggs, having arrived in France about the same time as I arrived in Egypt. He said that he was going to change his name from Kramer to Ray and he wanted to form an orchestra with my co-operation.

We were still working on the project while I was gigging with Fats and in July I was contacted to replace a trumpet player in Noble Sissle's orchestra who had joined a U.S. Navy Band. And again the first appearance with the orchestra was at the Howard Theatre in Washington D.C. There were two things that were different however, with playing the Howard with Andy Kirk and the same theatre a few months later with Noble Sissle. First the band didn't swing and secondly, I did not drink the way I had when I went there with Kirk and was Dick Wilson's drinking pal.

There were fellows in the orchestra that drank and I was advised by a few of them that Sissle didn't like to see them doing it, so when they drank, they did it in an undercover manner. I knew quite a few of the musicians in the band because I had worked with them at one time in other orchestras and on gigs.

The trumpet section had Wendell Culley, Clarence Wheeler, George Wingfield and myself. Ben Whitted, Don Pasquale(altos), Chester "Butch" Burrell and Herb Fleming, trombones, Teddy Giles, bass, Harvey Brooks, piano, Wilbur Kirk, drums, and Olivetto Miller, harp. Sissle thought he was a singer.

I had seen Sissle in some shows that he had been co-produced [of] and in which he had a principal role and although the shows were good and some of them had played in theatres down town, his acting was always corny to me. And as he had no real jazz feeling his type of orchestra was commercial but sad commercial.
There were some excellent musicians in the band, jazz wise and classical, but Sissle possessed such bad taste to my estimation
in music, that it was true the saying that a band is not better than its leader.

It is difficult to know why Sissle's band did not swing better than it did. Even though the musicians were not the greatest, the rhythm section was not bad, and it seemed to me, that the band ought to have sounded better. I think a lot of it was because Sissle (i)id not want a swinging orchestra - I don't think he really knew what swinging really was. It seemed crazy to take a society band into some of those dance halls. He had lousy arrangements, and the band never did anything. When the people danced, they never seemed to be as happy as they were with an orchestra like Kirk's. The orchestrations were just stock numbers. There were a few good stock numbers, like "Night Train", which Benny Carter used to play, but Sissle had stock numbers that didn't mean a thing. Meanwhile, he would direct the band, and on a few numbers, he would sing. He was a very poor singer also. To me, he was a theatre man who got the chance to form an orchestra. But anyway, I was out of work, having left Andy Kirk in order to be able to come to New York, and so I joined the band for that reason, but it was never a very happy experience.

One night at the Howard Theatre, time had been called for the show to get on and I had a small bottle of juice from which I was going to take a drink. I was in the back of a curtain when I saw Sissle coming out of his dressing room. So I waited until I thought he was on stage and took my bottle out of my hip pocket to take a swig when Sissle stopped around the curtain and saw me with the bottle up to my mouth. He went back on stage and when I came on the bandstand, he told me so that all the other musicians could hear him that if he ever caught me drinking on his bandstand, he would send me back to New York immediately.
That made me dislike him more than I had before because I had not cared much for him even before I was engaged in his orchestra.

When the week was finished in Washington, we left for the South, my second time to go deep into it. We played some of the place I had been with Kirk and finally came to Florida, a State I didn't see with Andy. We stayed a couple of days in Miami.

On our way to play a dance in Fort Lauderale, the bus stopped for a red light in downtown Miami, and a white sailor standing at the corner must have recognized or thought that we were an orchestra. He/ asked where we were playing and someone told him. He said that he would be over to hear us and asked the name of the band. This was a Negro dance we were playing and a few minutes after we opened the dance, the sailor came in and stood near the band.

He was the only white person there but no one said anyting to him and he seemed to be enjoying listening to the music. About 15 minutes passed when he came in two white policeman who walked up to the sailor and asked him what he was doing there. He answered them that he was listening to the band and they told him that he could not stay there because this was a Negro dance and white people didn't go to a dance that was not for white people.

When we played in Orlando, Fla, we met a very nice white fellow who owned a five and ten cent store. He was saying: 'Yes, sir' and 'No, sir' to us. The reason is that he was from the North and he has a certain respect for us and he was happy to see us in his store.

But when we spoke to and talked with a Negro soldier who was from the North and stationed at an army camp near Orlando, he was not happy to be in the South. There was a curfew for Negro soldier and they had to be back at their camp or off the streets by 9 pm.

We played a dance in Tampa, Fla, and this night Sissle must have known that George Wingfield and I were drinking on the stand but he could not afford to make himself ridiculous by trying to find out if it was true. George was and had been for a long time a very heavy drinker and he had drank so much in days gone by, that he looked as though he was always pickled.

George and I would take turns in sending the band's valet to buy a bottle of bootleg whisky from a fellow who was doing business right in the hall, and then, we would have the valet to buy us each a bottle of cocoa-cola which we would drink half and then have the valet put sole of the whisky in it. Sissle was suspicious but he didn't say anything and some of the other fellow that liked their juice were doing the same as George and I because that was an old billiard drinkers trick known by many musicians.

I was surprised though to see Earl 'Inky' Tremble in Tampa. The last time I had seen him was in 1955 when I was in Cincinnati and we played together in Paige's orchestra. Inky had joined some unknown orchestra because nothing much was happening for him in Cincinnati. He was gone South with this band and was now making Tampa his home. Our band was leaving that night or morning after the dance but I had time to have a few drinks with Inky and some of his musicians friends before we left for Jacksonville, Fla.

After Jacksonville, we played an army camp which was a benefit performance. My salary with Sissle was the same as I had with Andy Kirk and the conditions were the same. Seventy dollars a week per rata. When we arrived at this camp we asked for a place to wash up and refreshen ourselves. I had my shaving kit with me and Sissle didn't have his razor and wanted to shave himself. I told him that I could let him use my safety razor which I did.

I finished washing up and left Sissle in the washroom. We did the show and when it was finished, I asked Sissle what he had done with my razor and he said he had left it in the wash room and didn't even thank me for the use of it. When I went to get my razor, I found
it on one of the wash stands full of hair. He had not cleaned it and that caused me to dislike him more than I had before.

The army camp filled the bus with gas and we left for Atlanta, Georgia. We did a lot of night travelling and I could not sleep in a bus without drinking, so I was always ready for those night rides. The bus pulled into a gas station early in the morning and it must have been the stopping of the bus that woke me. I went into the toilet at the side of the station and when I came out, I began to get thirsty for a nice drink of cold water and I mentioned this to one of the musicians who told me that there was a water fountain inside the gas station.

I went in, saw the fountain and started to drink. Some of the others were drinking cokes or eating candy and there was only one man serving. I drank and drank and the water tasted so good that even when I had had enough, I decided to take a few more swallows for a good measure. At that moment someone tapped me on the shoulder and when I looked up, it was Sissle. He said: 'The man behind the counter is talking to you.'

I turned to face the fellow and he said with his cracker accent: 'Boy, don't drink out of that fountain! That fountain is for white folks, use that dipper up there.' I looked up on the top of the fountain and there was a dipper that looked as though it had been on a city dump for ten years before someone found it and put it on top of the fountain for Negroes. To use the dipper, first you had to be black, second you take the dipper, press the button that sent the water up to the mouth piece and hold the dipper under the mouthpiece that the white folks drank from. I said excuse me and went back to the bus without bothering any further about drinking some more.
But one thing I can say about the fellow. He called me Boy and not nigger and he didn't seem to be upset about what I had done. I asked the bus driver where we were and he told me, Athens, Ga.

After playing Atlanta, we went to Augusta, Ga, for two days. Herb Fleming and I were walking in the centre of town, window shopping, and saw a pullover sweater in a store window that pleased me, so I went in and asked the price. Eventually we each bought one and when we had paid for it the salesman asked us where we were from? We told him New York City, and he said that he though we must be from up North because the coloured people in Augusta never came in the shop. We knew the reason but we didn't tell him.

A few more dates in Tennessee and North Carolina and then a week in Detroit at the Paradise theatre where I gave my notice to Sissle because I had had enough of his band. I would have considered staying longer if he had offered me a raise but he would have preferred cutting off his right hand than to ask me if I would stay for a raise in my salary.

In the meantime, I had been receiving letters and telegrams from Rodger Kay asking me to hurry back to New York because he was going to take a combo into a new club and wanted me to join him. I played my last job with Sissle in Louisville, Ky. and taken an early morning train to Cincinnati, where I stayed a couple of days to visit my parents and the rest of my family. Saw a few old friends and returned to the Apple.

Things had happened quite fast and unforunately for Rodger. He had formed an orchestra with a white drummer, Jim Chapin, a Canadian pianist whose name was Bill something, a well known white bassist named Sid Wales and Jem Davis, an alto man that had a style on the order of Pete Brown. Lem and Pete both lived in Brooklyn.

The trumpet chair had been left open for me and the band had worked in the club two weeks before I returned. The club was located at 152nd East 55th Street. But Rodger Ray was not there because Sid Weiss had pulled a trick on him. Rodger's voice was not as good as he thought it was and when Sid heard him sing, and he knew that Rodger did not belong to the musicians union because he was not a musician, he reported him and a union delegate came to the club and told Rodger he could not work, because he was not a member of 802.

Sid promised Rodger that he would take charge of the orchestra until I arrived and Rodger was supposed to have his salary collected by Sid and given to him because he was the one that had found the job and formed th band.

and formed the band. But as Rodger could not go into the local, the owner of the club cut his salary off completely. The club was run by a fellow named Oscar who had been the head waiter at Cafe Uptown when it opened in 1940. The orchestra was playing more commercial numbers than jazz because that was what the owner wanted. Business was not good and within two weeks after I had joined the band, the place was closed. We did a radio show/that was the end of Rodger Ray's dream of being a singer and band leader.

I gigged and did many Sunday afternoon jam sessions at Jimmy Ryan's and few in Boston at the Ken Club. Once in Boston I jammed with Pete Brown and another time with Coleman Hawkins. The sessions at Jimmy Ryan's which was across the street from the Famous Door and the three Dances on 52nd Street, were presented by Milt Gabler who owned the Commodore Record Shop near the Grand Central station on East 42nd Street.

Jack Crystal who worked in Milt's record shop was in charge of the session which featured many well known black and white musicians: Art Hodes, Pee Wee Russell, Bobby Hackett, George Wettling, Rod Cless, Sid Catlett, Hank Duncan, Sandy Williams, Wild Bill Davison and Oran "Hot Lips" Page to name a few that participated in these sessions which really jumped. There were always two bottles of whisky furnished by Milt to get the sessions in a swinging mood. The closing number was always 'Bugle Call Rag' and I'm certain that there were never so many different bugle calls played in any other club in the world as were played in Jimmy Ryan's.

One day, Al Hall came to my house and asked me if I would like to replace a guitarist named Billy Moore who was sick in a hospital. My brother(who was a tailor) and I were sharing a three-roomed furnished apartment on 161st Street and I had not seen Al for quite some time. He told me that he was working at the Cafe Society Uptown with Billy Moore and a pianist.

I was surprised because Teddy Wilson had told me two years before that Barney Josephson had said that he never wanted Al and myself in his place again. I accepted to replace Billy until he came out of the hospital and that night I met the pianist. His name was Ellis Larkins, was from Baltimore and had been studying at Julliard music college on a scholarship he had won in his home town.

Teddy Wilson was still in the club with Joe Thomas on trumpet John Williams, bass, and Sid Catlett, drums. I don't remember who was playing sax, but Benny Morton was still with the band. The show had Hazel Scott, the Golden Gate Quartet, two sisters who danced East Indian dances named the Craft Sisters, Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons, the two boogie woogie pianists. With our trio of piano, bass and trumpet, we took care of the dancing. It was the first time that I played with only a piano and bass. Our salary was sixty-five dollars a week, and Billy Moore was getting leaders fee. He had been playing Ellie Larkins loss because Ellis was now in the music field and Billy had Ellis under his influence which enabled Billy to take a part of Ellis's salary, plus leaders fee, before he was taken ill.

After two weeks, Barney was satisfied with the trio as it was, Teddy and his musicians enjoyed us, and we went well with the customers, so Billy Moore was out and I was in. We decided to split the leader's fee between us, and that made each of us have 80 dollars a week. When the last show went on at 2 a.m., we were finished for the night, so we were able to be at the White Rose Bar at 52nd street and Sixth Avenue, before the musicians on Swing Street finished. That was our hangout, and the night was never complete if we missed going there. The other musicians told us that we had a position and not a job because they didn't finish work until four in the morning. They came into the bar when they had their rest periods and the bar closed at four also.

A couple of months after I had been working at the Cafe [B.] Society, Hazel Scott went to Hollywood to play in a movie, and Barney went also, because he was Hazel's manager. His brother Leon was directing the club. Mildred Bailey was engaged to sing, while Hazel was away. One night, a young Swedish fellow whom I had not met and drank with in the White Rose, came to the club, pretty well pickled. Time came for the last show, and as I passed the bar, this fellow was sitting there and invited

me to have a drink with him. I ordered something, and then I had to go to the toilet, which was on the second floor. I asked this fellow to hold my horn, and also asked him not to try to blow it, he was quite high, and I wanted to be certain that he would not create a scandal.

When I came back, Leon was furious. The Golden Gate Quartet had gone on while I was in the toilet. I was told that the only sound in the place was the song the Gates were singing when suddenly, there was a blast that almost gave some people in the place a heart attack. Leon blamed me for leaving my horn with this fellow, and told me I was fired. I told him not to yell at me, because that's what he had done, and if I was fired, to give me my two week's salary, because no musicians that belongs to the Union can be fired unless he is given a two week's notice or paid for the two weeks then and there. Ellis Larkins was nervous and thought if was the end of a trio, but I came to work the next night, and Leon didn't say a word about what happened the night before.

But when Barney came back, Leon told him that we had a run-in, and asked me what happened. I told him my side of the story, as I didn't know what his brother had told him. The only thing that Barney had to say is that he thought I was a little too continental. What I think he would have loved to have told me was that I had too much nerve and pride for a Negro. But everything went smoothly afterwards.

World war number two had been going on for nearly two years in America. The trio was beginning to become popular, and we co-starred with Hazel Scott after her return from Hollywood for a benefit to buy watches for the Soviet Army, which had taken place at Carnegie Hall the 11th of April, 1943. The trio did a few numbers and for the finale, we were joined by a trombonist named Frank Orchard, and the trumpetist Jack Butler.

One night at the Club, just before we took the stand, Ellis in the process of lighting a cigarette, burned a finger on his left hand, and was not able to play. Someone called Mary Lou Williams, who was not working, and asked her if she would replace Ellis for a few nights, and she accepted. But in the meantime, we had to go on, because Teddy Wilson had finished his set. So we asked Sid Catlett to play with us until Mary Lou arrived. That was a unique replacement for a piano, but with Sid on drums, and Al Hall being the solid bass player that he was, the piano was hardly missed, and it's too bad that a recording of the set that Sid did with us could not have been made of that session. Mary Lou arrived during the first show, and played with Al and I for four days, and it was a real groovy, because Ellis was a nice smooth pianist but Mary Lou had more feeling for jazz, a heavier touch and could swing more than Ellis.

Quite a number of musicians were in the army on navy bands, and as salaries were going up in many jobs, we figured that it would be the right time to ask Barney for a raise. Barney told us that he thought we deserved one, but he didn't say he would give us one.

A few nights later, a guitarist named Gene Fields came to the Club, but we thought nothing of it because musicians came in often to see and listen to the musicians working there. Tony Pastor, who had taken over the leadership of Artie Shaw's orchestra when Artie split, came in a few times. Also, Lena Horne, when she was singing for a while with Charlie Barnet.

When we received the next pay check, there was a message in it, telling us that we had two more weeks in the Club. Barney thought that we deserved a raise, and he raised us out of the joint. Later, we learned that Gene Fields had replaced us, but we didn't hold any animosity towards Gene, because it was the same like it was played in the music field, and we still had a ball while we were at the Cafe Society Uptown.

On June 15th, there was one of the biggest concerts ever given anywhere at that time. It was in Philadelphia, and was sponsored by Sammy Price, the boogie and blues pianist, and Dan Burley, a reporter for a Negro newspaper in New York, "The Amsterdam News", who was also a pianist and exponent of a rhythm called scuffle. They formed the Basin Street Swing Club and for this session which started at 1.30 pm and finished at 6 pm, part of the line-up was Sidney de Paris, Chelsea Qualey, Jack Butler, and myself, trumpets. Benny Morton, Brad Gowans, Sany Williams, Wilbur de Paris, trombones. Pee Wee Russell, Edmond Hall, Milt Mezzrow, clarinets, Eugene Cedric, tenor sax. Al Hall, Jack Bland, bassists, Danny Alvin, Sid Catlett, drums, Art Hodes, Dick Carey, Ellis Larkins and Sammy Price, pianists. One Newspaper said that the personnels read like a "Who's Who" in jazz. The session was played by forming three orchestras with those musicians and it was a jumping afternoon in Philly.

It was in December 1943 that I made records with the great Lester Young. I had first met him when I was on tour with the Ralph Cooper orchestra in 1932 in Denver, Colorado. We were playing a theatre, and after finishing that, there was a dance. After the dance, the musicians came to the place where we were living which was known as a popular musicians hangout. The band that had played for the dance was the Blue Devils, with whom Lester Young was playing saxophone. We started a jam session, and that was when I first heard Lester play. At that time, he didn't sound extraordinary. He had a nice sound, but I had no idea that he would later on become the great star. Perhaps he made a lot of progress since the first time I heard him.

When I came back from Europe, I met Lester again when he was playing with the Basie band. We got to talking. Then later on after he left Basie and had his own group, he came to play the Apollo Theatre with his group, while we were playing the show, and we renewed our acquaintance once again. It was shortly after this that the chance to record came up. I never knew exactly how it came about. Possibly, Buck Clayton, was not available.

I remember that the session was very informal, more of a happy get-together. There was no system for working things out. We all decided that if something was good and could be of use, and did it that way. Of course, he was featured more than anyone else, as this was supposed to be his group.

Even in those days, he was drinking quite a lot - he liked gin mostly - but I never saw him over-juiced. The only time I saw him stone cold sober was during the last few days of his life. He was then at the point when he had lost all his appetite. His playing had declined, he hardly had the strength to play at all. A few days after that, he went back to the States, and died about three days later. So that was my association with Lester Young. There were no jam sessions like we used to have in the 30's. Perhaps Lester used to go some place to play, but I never went with him. In fact, in the 40's, even jamming came under the control of the Union. You were paid to jamm; there were official jam sessions at Jimmy Ryan's on Sunday afternoons, but it was illegal to go out and jam like we used to in the old days.

A club in the village called Tony Pastors started giving Sunday afternoon jam sessions, which were presented by Frank Newton, and some well known names assisted at these get-togethers. Sessions were jumping also in the Village Vanguard, Eddie Condon's club and Nick's all situated in Greenwich Village.

The owner of the Village Vanguard, Max Gordon, and a naturalized Frenchman named Herbert Jacoby opened a swank club at 152 East 55th Street, the same address as the club that Rodger Kay had put a band in and the joint folded shortly after I joined the band. This club was called the Blue Angel and it clicked with the high society the first night it opened. Our trio, which was known as Ellis Larkins' trio, was engaged along with a singer, Madame Claude Alphand, whom I was told, was the wife of the French ambassador to the USA. She sang her songs in French. The other attractions were the Bernard Brothers who did pantomine comedy, and a coloured girl singer from Canada who's name was Gwyn Tines.

This was the easiest job I ever had during my many years as a jazz musician, and the 52nd street musicians were really jealous because we didn't start working until 10:30 pm and if we went to the White Rose, which we did almost every night when we finished at the club, we were there at 2 am. We played a set for one hour and the attractions went on at 11:30. Madame Alphand had her own accompanist and the Bernards didn't need/for their act. We accompanied Gwyn who sang five numbers. There was a commercial pianist who played popular tunes between shows and....
We would play a short set before the second show and accompany Gwyn in a few more numbers and the night was finished for us.

Gwyn was a very nice looking brown skin girl who must have weighed about 120 pounds, but she would drink like a fish and never was tipsy. She also smoked and it never bothered her voice which was fine and jazzy. I don't think she ever made any records. We treated her like a little sister and when the club closed for the Christmas and New Year holidays, which was very rare in the night club business, Gwyn cried on our shoulders because she would not be with us when the club opened again.

After New Year's Day, when we started again, the attractions were the same except for a girl singer named Evelyn Knight. Evelyn was white and came from Washington DC. Her manager was a commander or had been in the Navy. We soon found out that Evelyn didn't have a great bit of experience because she would skip measures in some of her songs. She began to like us very well because we were able to follow her when she missed the timing in a song and after a few weeks
of working with us, she became more confident in her work and made less mistakes.

Eventually Evelyn was engaged to do a radio show where Paul Whitman presented an artist every week. I was told that Whiteman also owned some stock in this radio station. Evelyn wanted us to accompany her, but someone at the radio couldn't stand to see three negro musicians accompanying a pretty white woman on that show because it was a broadcast done in a studio where the public were invited to participate.

So the pianist, bassist and a trumpet player from Whiteman's studio orchestra came to the Blue Angel anonymously for a few nights to listen and try to copy the way that we played behind Evelyn. I heard the broadcast because it was before I went to work. Evelyn skipped a measure in one of the songs and the cats accompanying her didn't know how to cover up for her. It must have been embarrassing for all that were concerned in front of a radio public.

Later during our run at the Angel, Evelyn received an offer to do a broadcast once a week for thirteen weeks on station W.J.Z. providing that the programme passed the test demanded by who ever was sponsoring it, which we never found out who it was. We were accepted and the programme went very well. Evelyn was very pleased and so were we because the loot we received was not bad and gave us extra pocket money.

But the success for us didn't last very long because when we appeared at the studio for the second week's broadcast, we were given notice that our services would not be required after one more broadcast. We were told that the reason was because the broadcast was a special programme that was heard only in the South and it would be relinquished if it was known in the Southern States that Evelyn Knight was white and the musicians negroes.

Each programme was recorded and we heard the first one which to my ears was great and there were no skipping of measures when Evelyn sang. But I never believed the story that the programme would be relinquished if it was known that negro musicians were accompanying a white singer. Someone at the radio station just didn't like the idea and thought it was too good for Negro musicians, so a white trio
was taken from the studio band and they copied the way we accompanied Evelyn from the recordings that were done during the three broadcasts we did and Evelyn did ten more broadcasts without us.

One afternoon, I had a dispute with one of the co-owners of the building where my brother and I had an apartment and it finished with him on the floor where I had knocked him. He had me arrested and I heard the jail door clang shut behind me again. I didn't know anyone to go my bail, so I missed a night at the Blue Angel. Russell Gillion was a fellow I could always depend on to replace me, as he had done a few times at the Cafe Society Uptown, but I didn't have his phone number with me when I was locked up. The next day in court I was fined ten dollars for assault and also had to move from the apartment. But I didn't regret what I had done because this fellow seemed to have a dislike for me because I was a musician and was always finding ways to irritate me and I had taken as much as I could from him.

After quite a few months at the Angel, we began to feel that we were liked well enough and popular enough to ask for a raise in salary and we did ask for it. We got exactly the same answer from Jacoby that Barney Josephson had given us when we asked him for a raise. Jacoby said: You boys deserve a raise and we thought the matter was settled. We did not speak about the amount because we thought that it would be at least five dollars each.

One night shortly after we had asked for the raise. Herman Chittison came to the club and when we received our pay envelope at the end of the week, there was a two-weeks notice which stated that our service would not be required after two more weeks. Chittison had taken a trio in after we left and had a very nice guitar/with him who's name was Everett Barkedale.

We started getting some jobs from the Joe Glaser booking agency and once we had an afternoon party to play for a very wealthy family by the name of Managers who owned the hotel Astor. The party was in honour of a son who was a medical ensign in the Navy and all the young men who were invited were in the Navy also.

During one of the times that we had stopped to have a few drinks, we got into a conversation with an ensign who told us that he was from New Orleans. He told us how much he liked our music and talked about the times when he and some of his relatives and friends would go places on Saturday nights to watch 'the Oxford Greys' sing, dance and listen to them play. I didn't grasp his meaning of 'Oxford Greys' for a long time, and then it came to me that he was talking about Negroes!

We later worked in a very large bar in Newark, New Jersey. The bar was circular and the bandstand was in the centre of the bar. New Jersey is full of crackers and as there was a white girl singing with us, some of them didn't like the idea and spoke to the manager about it. So we worked there for one month and quit the job, as we personally didn't care much about working there.

Then we were engaged to work in quite a nice place a few miles from Philadelphia and Ellis Larkins came to the job an hour late the first day, with his clothes looking as though he had slept in them for a month. The boss was not too happy about the beginning and neither were Al and myself, especially the way that Ellis was looking. Al's parents lived in Philly so we stayed with them. Ellis would take a train back to New York every morning and one to come back to the job. He was drinking like a fish and looking like a bum. We talked to him about his appearance but it went in one ear and out the other and we were given our notice after the first week. That was the end of the trio.
Al and I started rehearsing with Mary Lou Williams who had enjoyed the way we sounded when she replaced Ellis at the Cafe Society Uptown.

One day we were rehearsing at Mary Lou's apartment and Irving Randolph, the trumpet man known as "Mouse", came in to ask me to replace him at the Cafe Society Downtown where he was working with Edmond Hall, clarinetist. Mouse lived in the same building as Mary Lou and his wife was not feeling too well so he didn't want to leave her alone that night. I was not in a mood to want to play at the club that night and told Mouse that I didn't want to go back in that place again. Then I reconsidered and promised that I would replace him and be on time.

After the rehearsal and I was on my way home, I bought a pint of whisky, which I decided to take with me to the club. I had dinner in a restaurant and came home to change clothes. I opened my bottle and took a good taste from it and then put it in my trumpet case. Where I was living was a good 15 minutes walk to the 8th Avenue subway and when I came out to go to the gig, it was raining cats, dogs, and little fishes. I rushed to a taxi stand not far from where I lived but there were no taxis and after waiting in a doorway for a few minutes and no taxi came, I decided to walk to the subway.

When I arrived there, my feet were soaking wet, my pants were wet up to my knees, despite of having a raincoat on. I also had a straw hat and water was running through it down my neck and back. It was impossible for me to go play somewhere and have to sit for hours in wet clothes and wet feet. So I called the club, got Ed Hall on the other end of the line and told him what had happened and that I was sorry but I couldn't come to work under the circumstances.

Then I returned home and decided to take a hot bath to keep from catching a cold, open my bottle of juice and enjoy myself reading my papers until I got sleepy. I took my bath, but when I opened my trumpet case to take my bottle out for a nice big swig, the bottle was empty. What a bring down that was. The cork stopper had come out and the juice had dripped out in the rain. There was not one drop in the bottle and that was one of the worst nights of my life. The liquor stores were closed so I couldn't buy another bottle. Mouse didn't believe my story when I told him what had happened, but I was the loser of the deal because I didn't make the gig and so didn't get the money and I had paid for a bottle of whisky from which I only had one small taste from.

After a few rehearsals with Mary Lou, we recorded for a small company called Asch records. One of the best numbers of the six we recorded was 'Night and Day'. The three of us had put our ideas togeher and Mary Lou wrote the arrangement. Another one I liked very well was 'You know Baby' which the composer Frank Lewis cooperated with Mary Lou and gave me a few extra bucks to sing. But my voice was under-recorded because Asch thought that I was singing too loud. His studio was quite small and so was his sound cabin, and he almost faded me out completely on the singing chorus. Two versions of this number were recorded by us.
These recordings were made in August 1944, and later Asch recorded two numbers with the singer Josh White and the line-up was Mary Lou, myself, Eddie Dougherty on drums and Jimmy Butts on bass.

September found us rehearsing with a show that was to make a propaganda tour for the re-election of President Franklin D.Roosevelt. Jack "the Bear" Parker was added on drums and the trio became a quartet. The other members of the troupe were Will Greer, who was well known in the Broadway Theatre circuit for the role he played for years in Tobacco Road, Roland Smith, a singer well known in Europe and high society clubs in the States; the late Woodie Gurthie, who was a guitarist and folk singer, well known in his profession; Woodie's partner Cisco Houston; Jack de Merchant, a singer, Laura Duncan who had sang in many negro shows that played in Harlem and on Broadway; Bernie Hern a comedian; William Korff; Daniel Nagrin; Helen Tamiris; a classical dancer, Princess Orelia; and Pedro who had a fine Cuban dance act.

The name of the show was People's Band Wagon, and was produced and directed by Edward Royce whose wife was a classical pianist and accompanied most of the acts. The show was composed of jive, satirical skits, dances, songs, and political pep-talks, stumping the nation for President Roosevelt. That's what one newspaper critic wrote about the show.

When we hit the road and played Boston, the show was picketed and there was an effort made to close the show. There was almost a panic in the theatre when someone shot off a bunch of fire crackers, but the show continued.

We were doing one night stands and played Chicago, Indianapolis, Milwaukee, Minneapolis, St. Louis and some cities that I've forgotten as we were moving around so fast. The last performance was in New York city the 30th of October at Manhattan Centre. The show was a big success everywhere and Adam Clayton Powell Jr. made a speech at Manhattan Centre before the show started which put everybody in high gear. And Mr. Roosevelt won the election which made all of us feel as though we had a big hand in his Victory.

December 15th, 1944, Mary Lou recorded three numbers for Asch with seven musicians which included Coleman Hawkins, Claude Green, clarinet, Joe Evans, alto sax, Eddie Robinson, bass, Denzil Best on drums and me. Then there was another session with Jack (the Bear) Parker replacing
Best and Al Lucas in place of Robinson on bass.

We had a real fine trio because we rehearsed well and the arrangements that Mary Lou did were in the groove. Meantime, Al Hall was engaged for the radio show of Mildred Bailey and that was the reason he was not on the last Asch sessions.

We heard that Mary Lou had been offered a job at Kelly's Stable for the trio at a salary of five-hundred dollars a week. Al and I were expecting to get a hundred and fifty a week and Mary Lou would have two-hundred because she was the leader of the trio arranger. But nothing happened and we never knew if the rumour was true because we didn't ask Mary Lou about the deal. So we were rehearsing with no work in view and the trio drifted apart. Later I heard that we were supposed to have gone into the 'Downbeat Club' on 52nd Street if Mary Lou could get her 802 Union card, as she was on transfer and could not take a regular job until she became a full member of 802.

Mildred Bailey was featuring one or two known musicians on her weekly show and as she knew me, I was asked to do a number one week. I wanted to do "Russian Lullaby" and asked Mary Lou to make a lead sheet of the arrangement we had recorded for the staff arranger of Mildred's show. When the day came for the rehearsal, Al had seen his part of the music and told me that it was not arranged in the key we recorded it in which was 'C' for the piano, and the arrangement was in 'F'. The director of the orchestra was Paul Baron who was a well-known conductor and arranger also. When I told him the number was not in the key I was used to playing it in, he told the musicians what key they should transpose it to, and that was all. Those studio musicians are the best and in the orchestra, there was Charlie Shavers, Roy Eldridge, and a well-known studio white trumpeter named Jimmy Maxwell. Teddy Wilson was the pianist, Al Hall on bass and Specs Powell on drums. The rest of the musicians, I didn't know. That night when it came my time to go on, I was at ease because the number had gone down at rehearsal as if it had been written in the key I was familiar with. I have often wondered what Mary Lou's idea was and what could she have been thinking about when she made the score for me to play that number!!
Came Christmas and the New Year of 1945, and John Kirby contacted me for a gig. There were a few changes from the original musicians

that had helped make Kirby the biggest little band in the world. In place of Russell Procope there was George Johnson, Bill Beason was the drummer and Ram Ramirez had replaced Billy Kyle. When we arrived at the place we were to play (which incidently was a concert) Buster Baily and I found a quiet place and he instructed me on how some of the numbers went. Of course, everything was written and no one that didn't have some experience in reading music could make it in that band and many others for that matter.

I made out alright and a few days later, Kirby asked me if I would like to go to California with him and that was another case of "had horn and would have travel". I had never been in California. I wasn't working and had no great love in New York to hold me there, so it was 'California, here I come' for me.

It was not possible to have pullman service at the time because they were reserved for military personnel and transportation of wounded soldiers and sailors, so we had to be content with making the 5-days trip in reclining seats. We left New York in February, and I really enjoyed the trip because I alwayd did get a kick out of travelling and I had never been further west than Denver, Colorado. I got my one and only view of Las Vegas one night when the train stopped there for about 45 minutes.

There was not much we could do on this long trip because there was no lounge car where we could play cards or some other games. Some of the stops in different cities would be as long as two or three hours, and there we had a chance to buy some juice which we would pass around amongst us and pray that we had enough to last until the next long stop. We bought quite a number of paper bag lunches as it would be hours between stops and there was no restaurant car on the train. There was a war going on and the most comfortable and convenient trains were for government use.

Kirby was engaged to play a month in a place called 'Burton's Lounges' and Burton's was one of the two clubs run by Negroes in Oakland. For one week, Buster Bailey and I got together on the Kirby book which I must admit was one of the toughest that I ever had to tackle. One of the thughest numbers I ever played was the arrangement of "Whitman Stomp" by Charlie Dickson, the Fletcher Henderson banjo player. But most of the numbers in Kirby's book were arranged by Charlie Shavers and Charlie was as touch an arranger as Dickson. But at the end of the week, I could play some of the numbers without looking at the music.

We played a matinee every afternoon from five to seven, and from ten till two a.m. every night. There were plenty of sailors in town, because there was a naval base near Oakland. So the town and the joints were jumping. The prostitutes were getting rich and hinkty. Even those that looked like Wolephant had their asses on their shoulders. Wolephant is the name Arvell Shaw, the bass player, called ugly chicks, a mixture of wolf and elephant.

Kirby had a contract at Burton's for only one month, so when our time was up, he had not received another contract but promised us that he would have work for us in a few days because his agent was working on a deal. It came through - Kirby told us that the band had a gig in some town about fifty miles from Oakland.

But Bill Beason had gone back to New York without saying anything to anyone or giving Kirby a notice. However, Kirby found a guy to replace Beason and we left for the gig in two rented cars. Kirby drove one and Burton the other (Burton had arranged the gig). Kirby had the instruments in the car he was driving and the drummer. Ram, George Johnson, Buster and myself were with Burton.

Burton wore very thick glasses and as we were going to the gig, he told us that he had been drafted in the Army but was discharged because of his eyesight was bad and one night, he had driven a truck into one of the barracks on the Army post. It was beginning to get dark and we noticed that whenever a car was coming at us from the opposite direction, Burton would slow down from the 45 miles an hour he was doing. I began to believe Burton's story about his discharge from the Army and didn't feel too secure with him.

The gig went down well enough because of the drummer being new and not acquainted with the arrangements. It was not the best performance that the Kirby band could do, even with me being there a little over one month.

We packed up and started back to Oakland following the car Kirby was driving. Kirby could drive and before we had gone one mile, we couldn't see his tail lights. Burton was rolling along at the exhausting speed of about 20 miles an hour and it was a good thing he was not going faster because suddenly we were off the road, leaning to the right at a ten degree angle. Burton had managed to stop the the car and when I looked to the right there was a river about three feet from where we were sitting.

We got out of the car on the left side and Burton got it back on the road. Everybody was really worried now. Ram was sitting in the front seat with Burton, Buster on the left side, George in the middle and me on the right. We were rolling along at a fast twenty miles again and suddenly we felt the car jumping as though all four tires had gone flat. I sat up to see what was happening and saw that we were on a rail road track. We were actually going along on the track. George and I looked back at the same time and saw the big headlight of a locomotice and George had opened the door of the car before I could move and was ready to jump when we saw the locomotice/standing still. It was a good thing it wasn't moving, because if it had, this story would never have been told. How Burton happened to get on the track is a mystery that I or the rest of us could never solve. That was the most miserable night I ever had in a car.

Jack McVey was a tenor sax man in San Francisco who was very well known on the West Coast. He had a band in a place called Jack's tavern and for his first anniversary there, the owner celebrated with a turkey dinner and cocktails starting at two p.m. The John Kirby orchestra was invited and it was really a ball. A jam session was really the order of the afternoon and McVey started it rolling with Cappy Oliver on trumpet, Chuck Bailey, Raborn Tarrant, and Frank Clarke, the bass playing brother of Kenny Clarke. Then the Kirby band played some numbers after which the two bands joined together for a super jam session. The cocktails were wonderful, the turkey was fine and the music was great. I sort of fell in love with San Francisco because of that swinging party.

Our next move came a couple of weeks after we finished at Burton's lounge. We were engaged to play in San Diego at a place called the Silver Slipper. We left San Francisco on a train that carried no heavy baggage and only went to Bakersfield from where we took a bus to arrive in San Diego. The trip was beautiful and we were in San Diego early in the afternoon. We went to the Silver Slipper which was in the down town section of the city but the club was a run down joint. We had to wait there until our baggage arrived as they were sent by another train.

Eventually I got the urge for a drink and the bar in the joint wasn't open. So I came out and saw a bar across the street. But for some reason I didn't want to cross the street so I walked to the corner but there was no bar. I decided to walk to the next corner of the same street but no bar, so across the street I went and found a place at the bar where no one was near me. Things were real quiet in the bar but I didn't pay much attention to that. I stood at the bar for about 4 minutes and the barman passed me a few times. Finally he came and asked me what could he do for me. I said, give me a drink of whisky with a beer chaster, but he told me: You've had enough to drink. This surprised me and I told him that I had not had anything to drink and that was why I came in there.

He just looked at me and said: I don't care what you say, I said you've had enough to drink, and then it hit me: I said: Oh! you mean that you don't serve coloured people in here. He said: I'm not saying that, I'm only telling you that you've had enough to drink.
Then I realized the reason for the silence when I came in.Everybody in the place was eyeing me and listening to what was being said between the barman and I. So I said 'Thank you' and walked out.

I was surprised because I had been in plenty of bars in downtown Oakland and nothing like that had happened and perhaps that was the reason unbeknowing to me at the time that I didn't want to go across the street to that bar. That caused me to dislike San Diego and the atmosphere at the Silver Slipper didn't help me to like the town either, because the people in general were not very friendly.

Benny Waters, the tenor sax man that I had worked with in Charlie Johnson Small's Paradise orchestra, was leading a quartet in a cabaret that was strictly for white, but he told me that I could come to hear him, but I would have to sit on the bandstand. I had not seen Benny for years and was surprised to see him so far away from the Apple. I went to see him between one of our sets one night as the place where he was working was one very near the Silver Slipper which should have been called the 'Dirty Slipper! Benny's wife was playing piano, but I don't remember how the band sounded, although I do remember that Benny was blowing a lot of alto and tenor.

We finally finished in San Diego and came to Los Angeles where we stayed in a hotel on First Street and San Pedro which I was told was the Japanese quarters before the Second World War began or before the Japanese bombarded Pearl Harbor. After a few days, the hotel started jumping because some of the musicians from Eddie Heywood, Jr.'s orchestra were staying there and Buster Bailey and myself got together every day with Emmett Berry the trumpeter and Keg Purnell the drummer. Eddie Heywood was at his height and playing in a club near the hotel we were in.

Buster found a place where it was possible to buy one or more sticks of gage and I did the same thing. Keg liked a taste also, so between us we had some gage and juice every day. The government narcotic agents, known as 'G' men, were very hard on marijuana in California, which made it very dangerous to be caught with it and we were really taking a chance because every door in this hotel had a ventilation opening which could not be blocked or closed up in any manner, so the smell of anything that was not natural air could be distinguished if someone happened to be passing at the time when a stick was being smoked. It was said that an agent was living in the hotel, but nothing happened to us.

After a week in Los Angeles we went to work at the Plantation Club which was a few miles outside of the city limits. The jumpingest part of Los Angeles for Negros was around Central Avenue. But it was only possible to get a taxi from the railroad station to your destination when you arrived in town, because of the war conditions. It took such a long time to get to Central avenue from where we were living, by any other means of transportation except private car, that most of us had no desire to go to that part of the city.

Kirby hired a big car to take us to the plantation which I remember as taking about two and a half hours to get there. And that was how I saw Central Avenue, because we passed there going and coming from the Plantation. On the bill with Kirby's orchestra was T-Bone Walker and Betty Roché, the ex-Ellington singer. I had heard of T-Bone, but never seen him in action and I must say, that he was the best blues singer to accompany himself on electric guitar that I've ever heard. And Betty was still a great vocalist. Kirby had hired a white drummer who was not bad, but I don't remember his name.

There were four people in Los Angeles that I had known back East: Herb Fleming, who was the trombonist in my unsuccessful adventure as orchestra leader, Inez Cavanaugh, the wife of Timmie Rosenkrantz who had been my manager, and Zutty Singleton, who had come to New York with Louis Armstrong and stayed there for years before going West. Also Benny Carter, my old boss and friend from way back. It was certainly nice to see someone that I knew from New York which was back home to me.
We worked two weeks at the Plantation, and then a lay off. I was beginning to get lonesome for New York and felt as though I was farther away from there than when I was in Egypt.

Kirby got a gig in some town near L.A. to do a concert which also featured T-Bone Walker and Red Nichols with his Five Pennies. I used to buy records by Red when I was still an amateur and I picked up a few things from him although I didn't strictly go for his style.

T-Bone drove me, Buster and someone else to the gig and we smoked some gage going. I got more of a kick out of hearing Red Nichols for the first time in person than I did from the old records I had of him. Red had been living in California for years and was almost a forgotten legend.

T-Bone went on before us and when we closed the show, he had left and gone back to Lost Angeles. We had to get back the best way we could and I put T-Bone on my S--T list, even if he was a good blues musician.

We did at least three broadcasted live radio shows for the Armed Forces which were M.C'ed by Ernest Whitman, an actor whom I had seen many times at the Lafayette and Apollo Theatres and these shows were also recorded on V Disc. I heard quite a few V Disc later, but never one that the Kirby band did.

The 30th of March, 1945, I did a recording that gave me one of the greatest thrills of my life. Coleman Hawkins had come to Los Angeles and was working at Shepp's Playhouse on First Street, just around the corner from my hotel. He was engaged for the recording date and the rest of the line was Buster Bailey, Benny Carter, John Kirby Oscar Moore, Nat 'King' Cole, Max Roach and a girl singer named Kay Starr.

Al Hall had introduced me to Nat Cole a few years before, and also Oscar Moore, who was Nat's guitarist. They were playing at Kelly's Stable then, and had not become very well known. I had never heard of or met Max Roach, and Kay Starr was a west coast singer that I had not heard about also. We recorded four numbers, and one included "Stormy Weather", which Kay sang, and "If I Could Be With You One Hour Tonight". I had recorded with Benny before, and Coleman Hawkins in 1943, but this recording intrigued me more than the others, because I was recording for the first time with two great musicians together, Benny and Coleman Hawkins. And I got some kicks from hearing Nat and Oscar playing for the first time, and the drumming of Max Roach sent me also. Kay Starr was a fine singer who had a real jazz feeling that one associates with a Negro girl singer. The session was a gasser.

A few nights later Kirby was engaged to do a concert along with some other musicians at the Philharmonic Opera House in Los Angeles. This must have been at the beginning of Norman Grant's presentation of jazz at the Philharmonic which became famous in later years.

Coleman Hawkins asked me if I would work a couple of weeks with him at Shepp's PlayHouse. Howard McGee was supposed to have come to Los Angeles with him, but did not show up when Hawk started. I don't remember any of the other musicians that were in the group, but it was another great moment in my life to be playing a Club date with the one and only Hawkins, and I enjoyed every moment of it.

Hawk was an easy man to work with, but difficult to get to know. We'd talk if we were in a bar or someplace like that, usually about cars or other musicians, but he was very much a lone wolf, so we never spent much time together off the bandstand. I did not get to know him well enough for him to invite me to his house. I did invite him here to dinner in Paris, but otherwise I never got to know him better than a lot of musicians you would meet in the Rhythm Club. He was very self-sufficient, he would talk to you at the bar and you could offer him a drink, but he would never offer you one. On the bandstand, he was very easy to work with. He'd call the numbers for the set, but if there was something you did not know, he would quite happily play something else.

Hawk and I were playing in the lounge room and upstairs was a cabaret with a big band, chorus girls and comedians. One night during our break, I decided to go upstairs and have a look around. Suddenly, my eyes fell on a trumpet player whose looks astonished me for a moment. This fellow looked enough like Claude Jones, the trombonist, to be his twin brother. The only difference I saw was that this fellow was smaller than Claude. Claude Jones was a fellow that was very light skinned and had lost all of his hair when he was quite young from some kind of sickness he had suffered. He had no eye brows and wore horn rimmed glasses. And this fellow looked, as I've said before, like the spitting image of Claude Jones. He also wore the same type of glasses as Claude. I found out that his name was Monty Easter.

When the two weeks with the Bean (as Hawk was also known) were finished, he asked me if I would like to stay longer, but Kirby had received an offer to play in a white club in Baltimore. I was lonesome for the Eastern part of the country, and Baltimore being only a few hours by train from New York City, I was happy to be going away from Los Angeles. So I refused Hawk's offer, and a few days later, we were on a train bringing us back East. Fir the first time and the last time in my life, I saw some parts of the state of Texas because we were on a different line from the one that we had taken to go to Oakland. It was a beautiful sight to see so many of the foot)(hills and mountains. Many of the landscapes reminded me of some that I had seen in hundred of western movies. I had my movie camera, but no films as they were impossible to obtain, because the firlm companies were supplying films for government needs only, so I missed getting some wonderful shots that would have been pleasant souvenirs.

The trip was five days coming to Baltimore, the same as it had been going to California, and when we arrived, Kirby had hired a local pianist and drummer for the club job. There was a white girl named Ginger in the floor show, and she was the first woman I ever heard play an accordion. I had heard Buster Moten, the brother of Benny Moten playing a piano accordion, and he would really swing on it. Ginger was not a jazz accordionist, but she played a nice commercial style. We often played black jack between sets, and she liked to play the game with us. And that was something to think about, because Baltimore was a Southern city and negroes and white people
(***Ram had left the orchestra after the plantation dates)

had very little to do with each other socially speaking. Some of the customers and especially many of the men that came to the club have wanted to hang us if they had known we were playing cards back stage with a white woman.

Monday was our night off, so all but the two local musicians would grab the first morning train for the Apple. I had a girl friend named Irene Henderson, and I would spend Mondays with her. The second Monday, we had free, and spent it the same as the first one. But when we arrived at our Hotel in Baltimore that Tuesday afternoon, Kirby told us that the job was finished. He didn't give us a plausible reason, and some of us pushed the matter because we were not very keen about the job from the first night we worked there. So it was back to Irene and the Apple, and that was the end of the John Kirby band for quite a while.

By this time, the Bebop movement was catching on, having started on 52nd Street with musicians like Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie. There were only a few big bands going, mostly playing theatres. The Ballrooms were still open but usually had small combos. Even the Savoy Ballroom was no longer a place which interested me. The atmosphere was no longer the same. Things were bad economically, and they were starting to tax the dance halls very heavily after the war. Also, Bebop was hard music to dance to, a fact which a lot of people didn't like about it. The problem was the way the rhythm sections played. It didn't give you a danceable beat; it was just music to listen to. I did get to know Charlie Parker in New York, but we were not great friends. I knew both he and Miles Davis from 52nd Street, because I used to hand out there quite often. At that time, I liked his playing because he was blowing more or less in the style of Dizzy Gillespie - not so good, but along the same lines. Later on, I saw them both again at the Jazz Festival in 1948. Even them, we never had any conversations about music.

The only interesting thing musically that happened for me on during the next few weeks was a concert/the 9th of June at the Town Hall. This concert was presented by my old friend Timmie Rosenkrantz, and the line up was another who's who inthe jazz world. Red Norvo had an orchestra composed of Joe (Flip) Phillips, Shorty Rodgers, Aaron Sachs, Eddie Bert, Remo Palmieri, Teddy Wilson and Slam Stewart. A fellow named Fran Warren did a voice and drum solo. Don Byas and Slam Stewart did a couple of duets. Erroll Garner had Don Byas, Slam and Specs Powell in a quartet. Billie Holiday did two numbers. Stuff Smith's trio was composed of Billy Taylor the pianist, and Ted Sturgis on bass. I did two numbers with Billy Taylor and Ted. Teddy Wilson played solos without a rhythm section and there was a jam session with every tub taking part.

In July, I was engaged by George Johnson to play one month in the Savoy in Boston. A nice blowing little fellow named Johnny Hartsfield was the tenor man and Red Richards was the pianist. Both of them had been in New York for quite some time, but it was the first time I had met them. Johnny was a nice guy until he had taken a few drinks, and then he was a little devil. We all sat down to play except George, and the bass player, who was a fellow from Boston. One night, Johnny had had a few tastes and he would start worrying about his wife whom he had left in New York. When he got in that mood, he was subject to do disagreeable things. This night I saw him measuring the distance between his foot, which he had crossed over one leg, and the music stand, which had quite a few arrangements on it. I knew that in a few minutes, he was going to kick it over and that's exactly what he did after thinking it over for about 4 minutes. His parts flew in every direction. Naturally, George didn't like it, but he didn't give Johnny hell, because he understood Johnny's character.

I had been to Boston a few times before. Once for a week with Ralph Cooper, another time ona jam session at the Ken Club with Hawk and once with Benny Carter in 1941, and also Andy Kirk, but it was not a city that amused me. About one week after we were there I decided to have a tooth next to the middle one on the right side taken out, and a new one put in, because this one had rotted away until it was only half a tooth. Some one gave me the address of a Negro dentist in the center of town who had many white customers and was considered one of the best dentists in the city.

So I went to him and he started working on my tooth. In fact he took it out and told me to come back at a certain date, which would be a couple of days before I would finish at the Savoy. He said the gum would have to heal before he could install a false one. I had no trouble blowing my horn because I blow from the middle of my mouth and this tooth that had been extracted was on the side. Finally, the day came for me to go back for the big deal, and when I arrived at the dentist's office, he told me that he had noted the date I was supposed to come back and that he could do nothing for me until a week later. I told him that I would be leaving Boston in a few days, and did not want to go back to New York with a tooth out. He gave me the address of another dentist and said he was certain that this person could take care of me.

So I went immediately to the address and this dentist looked to be about 70 years old. His office and equipment looked about as old and out of fashion as the man himself. But I wanted the tooth put in, so I decided to risk the chance that everything would be alright. He took a fitting of the tooth/where the crown would be placed, and the size of the tooth to be put in, and I went back to him the next day to have the tooth put in. That night I could hardly play anything, and the last night was almost as bad. What this dentist had done was to put the crown on crooked and the right front tooth was sticking out about a fraction of an inch farther than my left front tooth, and that disarranged the position of my mouthpiece when I would blow. And it was quite a few months before I became accustomed to playing the way I had played before.

When I returned to New York, I stayed with Irene for a while and then found a room with a tenor player named Bobby Sands. I knew Bobby when he played with one of Benny Carter's first orchestras, and later he was with Claude Hopkins orchestra.

Bobby was a Batchelor and had a four roomed apartment at Amsterdam Avennue on 161st Street. I had lived in that neighbourhood before and liked it very much. Leonard "Ham Davis, the trumpet man I spoke about when I first played the Savoy ballroom, lived in this building also. I did a few gigs with Bobby and some jam sessions around town. September 23rd, I was back at Town Hall for a concert called BIAJ which was presented by Specs Powell. BIAJ meant 'Best in American Jazz' and the musicians that performed were Buster Bailey, J.C. Heard (drummer), Al Haig, piano, Al Hall, bass, Stuff Smith, violin, Pete Glover, bass, Freddie Jefferson, piano, Teddy Wilson, piano, a percussion duet on tom toms by Coker and Cimber, Frank Newton, trumpet, George Wettling, drums, Hal Stein(a 16 year old saxophone virtuoso), Charlie Parker, alto-sax, Bill Coleman, trumpet, and Four Chicks and Chuck, a vocal group who were stars on the Kate Smith Show. The town Hall concert of Timmie Rosenkrantz was eventually issued on an album, but BIAJ was not, and I think that it should have been because the concert was as interesting musically as the first one in Town Hall.

One night in October, I was coming out of one of the Clubs on 52nd Street and met a drummer named Herbie Cowens, who was known to meet musicians as "Kat". Herbie asked me if I would like to go to the Phillipines and maybe Japan. I didn't think that he was serious, but I told him 'yes' and gave him my address. A few days later, I received a message from Kat saying that the first rehersal and general meeting would be the 12th of October. I arrived and saw my old friend Edgar 'Spider' Caurance, Ernest 'Bass' Hill, Ben Smith, who had left Andy Kirk's orchestra quite some time ago, and a pianist I had never met, whose name was Eddie Allan. We were told by the assistant director of U.S.O. Shows engaged in New York that our salary would be $95.00 per week, which was equivalent to the salary of a Colonel at that time. We would receive this aount until we left for the road and then we would receive only $25.00 per week, and $70.00 would be put in the bank, making each one have an account. This was the best salary that I had ever made, and we rehearsed for six weeks. Exactly what I did with the money, I cannot say, except that I had a good time.

If I was behind in my rent which happened now and then, mostly then, I was able to pay it up and if I had anything in the pawn shop which also happened sometimes, I was able to get it out of hock. And I suppose the White bar at 52nd and 6th Avenue and also Beafsteak Charlie's bar got a good taste from me, because they were the places where I spent many moments that were not lonely ones and spent lots of loot there also.

During the six weeks we rehearsed we had to take a health examination which Ben Smith did not pass. Therefore, Herbie had to replace Ben and I felt sad about it because we had been together in Andy Kirk's orchestra and besides being a fine musician, he was a great person whom I had plenty of fun with. "Kat" engaged an alto player named Curby Alexander. We had to be inoculated against smallpox, Typhoid-paratyphoid, tetnus, typhus, cholera, yellow fever, and on the physical examination card in miscellaneous, it is marked plague. These shots were really heavy loads to carry, and we started taking them the first week of rehearsal, and the day after any one of the inoculations, my arm would feel as though I had a ton of lead tied to my wrist, and I could not put it down. And there was no drinking of kick-a-pee joy juice for at least two days after each shot.

Willie Bryant, the exband leader and show man, was the Master of Ceremonies for our group, whose unit number was 789. The girl singer engaged was named Melrose Colbert and whom I found out later was Ray Nance, the Ellington trumpet and violin virtuoso's first wife. She was now his ex-wife. I had never heard of her before, but she had a fine voice. The comedy act was Henry Matthews, known as Shorty and Alfred Chester, known as Slick. He was the straight man and Shorty was the comical one in the act. There was also a dance team known as Millie and Bubbles. They were married and their name was Martin. Martha Cooke known as Martha Please was an acrobatic and fast tumbling artist.

The last two weeks of the rehearsals, I worked two nights a week at the 3 Deuces and 52nd Street with George Johnson who replaced the two bands actually playing there on their nights off, which one had on Monday and the other Tuesday. Monday was always the day that I was inoculated, and my arm would give me hell Monday and Tuesday nights. And not being allowed to drink alcohol because of the shots didn't give me much inspiration to play, but at least I tried. The second and last week, one night I blacked out for at least a second after some choruses on a number and almost fell on my face.

Then suddenly, I had to go to the toilet and when I arrived there, I taken off my coat and I felt so weak that I could hardly hang it on the hook behind the door. After about five minutes sitting on the throne, my strength came back to me, and I was able to finish the night.

We were given army officer's uniforms with short jackets and the night of November 23rd, we left New York for San Francisco by train. This time, I was amking the trip from New York to California in style because I had a pullman berth and ate in the dinning car as this trip was sponsored by Uncle Sam who had priority for everything possible. From San Francisco we were to fly to the Phillipines. We were booked in a hotel in San Francisco to await the plane flight to the Phillipines and Joe Louis happened to be in the city and was staying in the same hotel. We had an interview with one of the leading Negro newspapers and made some photos with Joe. I was shaking his hand on one of them and asked the photographer if he would send me a copy. I gave him the number of our unit and APO address. I never received the photo or a copy of the interview which I was promised.

From the day we arrived in San Francisco, we were on alert which meant that we should be ready to leave at any hour, but we stayed in Frisco for one week. Spider Courance and I had a connecting room and during the week, we each drank at least a quart of whisky every day. I became quite friendly with Curby Alexander whom I had not known before he was engaged to replace Ben Smith. Curby was a billiard drinker also and could take it better than Spider, and we often drank from each other's bottle. I was so busy drinking and having a ball otherwise that I did not visit one jazz club during the week.

Eventually, we were notified that we would be leaving for Hamilton Field the next morning at a certain hour. Hamilton Field was a military air force base near Frisco, and the morning that the air force came to get us, Willy Bryant was missing. He had taken a train back to New York when he learned that we would be flown to the Phillipines... We stayed on the base that night and the next day we were briefed on how to use a Mae West (safety belt) if something went wrong and the plane would have to ditch (come down) in the Ocean.

That afternoon, we boarded a C-54 and this was a flight for our unit only. We were 12 people with a crew of 4 in a plane that could carry 60. Our first stop would be at Hickam Field in Honolulu, 2091 miles from San Francisco. This was the first time that any one of us had flown in a plane and the pilot told us that we would be flying for

14 and a half hours before landing at Hickam field. We didn't have anything to drink other than water because alchohol was not allowed on the air base or military planes, but we played black jack and visited the pilot's cabins. That night we ran into some stormy weather which had the plane flying in most every position except upside down, and the only person that became air sick was the hostess.

Every U.S.O. unit had a number and name. Our group was known as Drum Boogie number 789. We arrived in Honolulu the next day and Bubbles Martin was not feeling well, and went to see a doctor at the Hickam Field Base Hospital. He was put in bed and we were told that we could have passes to go into the city. That was quite alright with me because I had heard so much about Honolulu's Hawaii and wanted to see what it was like, although I didn't expect to see the chicks in grass skirts and I didn't see any. We had no idea about how long we would be in Honolulu, but the troupe could not go or leave one of its members behind. So it happened that we stayed on the island for a week.

We were given a pass every day and the second night, we found a dance hall that had some jazz musicians playing there. The next night we had our instruments and jammed until the joint closed. There was an alto player with the band that looked exactly like a musician named Durante whom I had seen at the Savoy ballroom with an orchestra known as the San Domingo Serenaders and he played exactly the same style.
