But this fellow denied that he had ever been in the States at all and he was not a Hawaiian. But he was a fine musician.

I saw Pearl Harbour and Wakiki Beach and jammed every night until Bubbles was well enough to continue the voyage. The public of the club was made up of natives and they liked jazz very much. They were used to it and we had a ball. We left Honolulu for the Philippines. There were stops in Kwajalein, an island in the pacific ocean and Guam.

On the 12th of December, we arrived at Nichols Field in Manila, and were driven to our headquarters in an army weapon carrier. I happened to be sitting at the back end of the truck which had a canvas top and when we arrived in the city the sight that hit my eyes was like a nightmare that had become real. In the middle of the city some buildings were standing but without roofs or windows. Others were leaning against others that were standing, but looked as though they would fall any minute. The destruction was horrifying and it was difficult to imagine that such a terrible catasrophe could be possible.

There were not many U.S.O. shows in the Philippines when we arrived and the place where we were billeted was quite nice and not too far from the center of the city. We stayed there for 5 weeks playing camps nearby and it was wonderful the way we were received. Those soldiers had not seen many shows from Stateside as back home anywhere was called.

One day while walking downtown, I was surprised to see an ex-bandleader of mine. It was Teddy who had an orchestra in the Savoy Ballroom when I came to France in 1935. Teddy told me that he had done service in Europe and was supposed to have been discharged and sent back to New York from Germany but he had a run in with an officer and told him that he had been manager of a club in New York which seemed to have been a better position in civil life than the officer had and this officer arranged to have Teddy sent to the Philippines instead of being discharged when he was supposed to be. But Teddy was on the list to be sent home in a few days when I saw him.

I became acquainted with some Philippine musicians but how this happened, I do not recall. However, it happened and one who played trombone called himself Felix the Cat. He had played in Japan before the war and told me that he had been associated with an American trombone player known as Slick. I had known Slick also because he had been in Cincinnati for a while and he also played trumpet. He was the first trumpet player I had ever known that played trombone or visa versa, But I never knew his real name.

Felix played with an orchestra, all Philippines, that had 16 musicians. And if you closed your eyes or only heard them playing if you were coming into a dance hall, you would bet your bottom dollar that it was the Glenn Miller band playing an engagement while passing through Manila. The only weakness was in the solos. But the sound was there.

We were invited to a few local spots where they would play now and then and I would sit in with them a few times. They gave me all the brass solo parts and I gave them everything I could because I was really getting my kicks playing with a big band and hearing good harmony, accompanying me. And the musicians were getting their kicks listening to me because they had no soloists of any value in the trumpet section and it pleased them to hear something played as it would have been in the States by jazz musicians or on records.

We played some camps far away on some other islands which included Clark Field Batan and Subic Bay. When we returned to Manila the 2nd of January 1946, we were billeted in a large camp which had formally been occupied by a military service known as Sea Bees. There seemed to be hundreds of U.S.O. shows there, and the camp was jumping. We were about five miles from Manila but there were plenty of little shops near the camp where whisky was sold and whisky was plentiful and cheap. Curby and I became drinking buddies and the hot weather did not have any bad effect on the 2 or 3 fifths that we drank every day.

There was gambling in the upstairs recreation room and jam sessions downstairs. Jessie Stone, the composer of Idaho had a band which included Franz Jackson on tenor and Louis Bacon on trumpet, Otis Johnson, an ex-Luis Russell trumpeter and Fess Williams' son Rudy were with the group. The Jeeter-Pillar orchestra of St.Louis fame were there, and one of the trumpet players was a fine solo man named Sam Massenberg who had been a member of the Savoy Sultans. The bass player with the Jeeter-Pillar group was Carl Pruitt who was well known around the Apple. Jeeter-Pillar and an all girl orchestra from California who were white were the only orchestras composed of 16 or more musicians. Nelson Williams, another trumpet man who had been discharged from the army some months before we left New York was also with a group.

There were two Broadway hit shows with lots of girls at the camp. One was "Gingham Girl" and the other was "Meet me at the Astor". Many of the actos were show people that had come out of forced retirement and were very happy because the pay was good and the food was not bad except on Sundays. And the only thing bad about food that day or any Philippine holiday was the chicken.

Cock fighting is a big sport in the Philippines and there was an arena very near our camp and I saw many of those contests which were very cruel but veryfascinating. The camp's personal which was adminis-tered by the army, had an arrangement with the administration of the cock fight arena to buy the loser of a match because a cock fight is going on until one is killed. Cocks are trained for quite some time before they fight and I suppose they become as tough in character as a prize fighter. So the loser of the fight was the meat we ate on Sundays and holidays, and it was so tough that anyone who had false teeth had to eat only vegetables on those days.

Otherwise the food was good, the days were hot and the nights were just right for sleeping. The men and women had different sections and even married couples could not live together. The housing was a wooden floor and the frame work of a large room with no walls and a canvas top roof. There were four army cots in each corner and one could get a mattress and clean sheets from the supply commissioner. A mosquito net was a necessity and flit guns were also supplied because the mos- quitos were malaria carrying insects in the Philippines.

The camp personals such as commander, guards, chef cook and directors of different departments were all white and all in the military service. The servants were Philippines and when we came to the camp there was a sign in the men's latrine in one corner that read: for Philippines only! Of course, we sat anywhere we chose and after a few days, I noticed that the sign had disappeared. The young Phili- ppines had gotten enough of being segregated in a latrine in their own country and it was because of us that they realised that they did not have to accept those southern U.S. habits. And there was not ano- ther sign put up to replace the one that had been there before and those cats sat anywhere and no one said anything to any of them.

One afternoon, we were jamming in the recreation hall and a soldier came in that I knew. His name was Stanley Facey and at one time he had been the piano accompanist for Eddie South who was known as the "Dark Angel" of the violin. There was another soldier with Facey who had a trumpet and they both had come tothe camp because they had heard that it was possible to blow there.

So Facey sat down at the piano and this trumpet player sat on the piano and they began to play along with the rest of us that were jamming, But the picture started to change real soon because these two cats started playing so much piano and trumpet that everyone else just wanted to listen. And the more they played, the better they seemed to get. I knew that Stanley was strong in the classical field but it was the first time I had ever heard him play jazz and he was wailing. His skirt was soaking wet and he looked as though he had been under a shower and had forgotten to take his shirt off.

The trumpet player had a style that seemed to be a mixture of Charlie Shavers and Howard McGee but it was not as hard as Charlie's and he had plenty of feeling and ideas galore. After about two hours of jamming by Facey and his fine trumpet player, I was able to get

into a conversation with the latter. He told me that his name was Thad Jones, and his brother was Hank Jones, the piano man. I had heard of Hank Jones but not met him. Hank had the reputation o being a fine accompanist and a great soloist. I later discovered that the reputation of Hank was not a conjectural narrative but a comformity.

Thad told me that he and Facey were in a U.S. army show that Thad had arranged all the music for. I had the feeling that Thad was going places after he would be discharged from the army and a few years later, that premonition came true. That cat played too much horn at that time to not have been better known than he was,.

I've seen Thad quite a few times since those days and he always mentions to someone around whenever we meet that our first meeting was in the Philippines.
I will never forget that day when he and Stanley Facey came to our camp and blew everybody out.

After a few weeks at this camp, one of the best straight men in show business joined our group. For the sake of those that don't know about show business, or never saw vaudeville, a straight man was one that assisted the comedian by asking him a straight question and getting a comical or double meaning answer to make the audiance laugh. Johnny Vigel was this fellow's name, and he was well known in Negro Theatres from coast to coast. Alfred "Slick" Chester was another well known straight man who had been engaged to manage our troupe. Every show had it's manager and Willie Bryant was supposed to have been the straight man with us. But when he cut out in California because he didn't want to fly to the Philippines, Slick had substituted for him until another straight man could be sent to join us.
One army camp that we played, not far from our camp, was where the Japanese general Yamashita, who had lead the invasion of the Philippines was hanged.

Some weeks passed and a big U.S.O. show was arranged in the largest stadium in Manila with the participation of all the U.S.O. groups that were assembled in the area. Kirby Alexander had lost face with Herbie Cowen and Herbie had Kirby sent home. There was no replacement for Kirby, so there was only Spider and myself in the front line.

The big night came and there were two weapon carriers that came to pick up our group. I could never understand the reason for this because there were not that many people in our show to make it necessary to have that much transportation. I don't remember who else left before the carrier that I was in, but when we arrived at the stadium, the others were not there. The different shows were going on to do their bit, and we were waiting and wondering where the others could be. After two hours, the others came but without Herbie. There had been an accident and Herbie was injured. We were told that Herbie was sitting near the front in the vehicle which had seats running length-wise, and had his arms stretched out along the upper part of the seat, which had the form of a bench. The driver of the vehicle ran into a truck that was carrying some lumber which was protruding from the rear and a board came through the windshield and almost tore Herbie's right arm off.

So there was no show for us and I foe one had really wanted to play that night because there must have been at least 20 thousand people in the stadium. It was an affair staged by the American government, and there was no entrance fee to be paid.

Herbie was placed in the best army hospital where we visited him a few times before he was sent home. He had the best of medical care possible and was told that the arm could be saved and he would be able to play again.

We began to wonder if we would be sent back to the States before our time of six months had terminated. We were supposed to go to Japan after our tour of the Philippines and I really didn't want to miss out on that. And we were saved by Henry "Shorty" Matthews, the comedian, who had had a little experience playing drums. All we wanted really was someone that was able to keep time on the drums and we were still in business.

Eventually, the exodus for Japan started and it seemed that every other day a group was leaving the camp and we were staying on to wave goodbye to them. We were almost the first group to come to the Philippines and almost the last to leave. But the time finally came and the 26th of April, we left Manila on the s.s. 'Octorasa', a small military transport steamer for Japan, and arrived at Yokohama, a few days later.

In Tokyo, we were lodged in a building called Honcho House in a part of the city that had not been to badly bombed out and for the first time since we had arrived in the Philippines, we were not living in a camp. But we were still sleeping on army cots which were quite comfortable when one had a mattress to go with it.

We were served meals by beautiful Japanese girls in native dresses and the food was like it would have been in a fine hotel, and not an army camp, although the food in the camps was not all bad, except for the cocks that lost the fights, on Sundays and holidays, in the camp near Manila.

One large room in Honcho House had been transformed into a movie hall and the first night we were there, a film called "Lost Weekend" was shown. I've seen films and more films that I shall never forget and the same thing goes for many actors that make them. But there is a special reason that I shall never forget "Lost Weekend" and the featured actor whose name was Ray Milland.

When we left the Philippines, I didn't think it would be necessary to take at least a small supply of Kick-a-poo-joy juice with me. It was possible to get beer on the boat, but I was never a great beer drinker, although I did drink it now and then as a chaser. When we arrived in Japan there were no little or large shops anywhere that one could buy a bottle as had been the case in the Philippines, and that night, as I watched Ray Milland drinking in bars and at home, I knew where, he had hidden a bottle that he could not remember where and he almost tore his place apart looking for it. I almost went crazy for a drink and would have been willing to pay as much as 5 bucks for a sip, but no one had a drop, or if they did, they were not letting it go. What a miserable night. And I didn't have a drink until we played the first base a couple of nights later. After the show we were invited to a Colonel's quarters, and I kept calling him Major, because of the eagles on his shoulders.
"Shorty" Matthews had begun to play drums not badly and our show made a hit with the soldiers and the Japanese personals that worked at the different camps.

Tokyo,like many other large cities,had its red light districts, and it was the most beautiful one I ever saw. When I was a kid in Cincinnati, there were certain streets where the prostitution business bloomed and it was the same in the other cities. But in Bombay and Egypt, there were special district. In Paris, they were called brothels and there was no particular street or district where they would be located. The districts in Bombay or those I saw in Alexandria and Cairo were like cities within a city. The one in Tokyo was similar in area to those in Bombay and Egypt, but it was so beautiful. There were individual houses that were typical to paintings I had seen of Japan and the girls were really something to write home about. It was more like a fairy land than a whore house district, and it was hard for a guy to make up his mind which beauty he would care to have.

There was no cabaret life in Tokyo for American service men or personals. And if there was any night life for the Japanese, it was off limits to Americans. Tokyo had been pretty well bombed in certain districts, but there was plenty of every day activities around the Ginza which was in the center of the city and the most famous boulevard in town.

As there was a shortage of cigarettes in Japan and we were allowed to buy a certain amount of cartons a week from the P.X.(post exchange), there was no end to the wonderful Japanese souvenirs we could have in exchange for a few cartons of cigarettes. I bought many nice silk typical robes and other souvenirs for my family and special friends back home. I had also acquired quite a few from the Philippines because the same conditions existed concerning cigarettes as it was in Japan.

I met at the Honcho House, a very famous Broadway and Harlem comedian who did a one man show act. His name was Johnny Huggins, and I had seen his act many times, and had the honour of playing for him one week at the Lafayette theatre. Everyone that knew Johnny called him "Banjo", because he used the word in association with almost any conversation he had on any subject. If he disliked something, he would say: that banjo is out of tune, the strings are broken, or it sounds bad, and many other expressions concerning the instrument.

Johnny was a black faced comedian which was the kind of act presented by Al Jolson and Eddie Cantor. But "Banjo" was a light brown skin Negro and did a pantomine act of a singer which was original and amusing. A trumpet player would stand on stage near the wings and use a plunger to get a wa-wa effect which coincided with the lip movements that "Banjo" did in his impressions of a person singing a song. I had not known him personally until we met at the Honcho House. We were together quite often in Tokyo, and I was very proud to have been one of the many trumpet players capable of accompanying such a fine comedian and person as Johnny "Banjo" Huggins.

The 25th of May 1946, we received the last oversea pay which was 375 yens that was equal to 25 dollars, the part of the salary we received each week away from home. May the 31st, we boarded the s.s. 'Marine Serpent', another military transport ship for home. I had visited Kamakura not far from Tokyo and saw the largest statue of Buddha in Japan. I was happy to have spent some time in Tokyo, but there was a certain joy in knowing that in a couple of weeks I would be back in the Apple again.

Jessie Stone's group, the "Gingham Girl" and "Meet me at the Astor" troupes were going home on the same boat, and every night, there was entertainment abroad in the mess hall after the evening meals. We arrived in Seattle, Washington, the 6th of June, and left there the 8th by train. Arrived in New York the 13th.

I had not room reserved when I arrived in New York and I had not stayed in contact with my ex-girl friend Irene, whom I probably could have stayed with for a while. But Louis Baken came to my rescue. He had a 3 room apartment on 147th street, and told me that I could sleep in the front room on a folding couch until I found a room which I did after a few days. And Baken would not accept one penny from me for the days I stayed in his flat.

For some weeks I roomed with a woman named Mrs Fips on St.Nicholas Avenue. at the corner of 153rd street. Coleman Hawkins lived not far from me on 153rd street and also a bass player named John Brown. Whenever Illinois Jacquet came to New York, he stayed at this place and Mrs Fips always had a room reserved for him. Her son's name was Bobby and he knew many of the younger musicians and people in show business. It was Bobby who introduced me to Babs(Lee Brown) Gonzales.

One day, the landlord of the house where I had lived with Beezie on 154th street came to see me and told me that he had a room to rent and I jumped at the opportunity quicker than it takes to say'Jack Rabbit', because this fellow and I had many things in common which I had discovered when I lived in his house before Beezie and I separated. His name wa s Earl Norman and his wife's name was Stella. I really felt at home with these people who were more like a brother and sister to me than my landlord and landlady.

Sy Oliver had left the orchestra of Tommy Dorsey for whom he had been the arranger after he had split from Jimmie Lunceford and it must have been around the middle of November, 1946, that I heard through the grapevine that Sy was forming an orchestra and would be auditioning musicians at a rehearsal studio on Broadway.

The audition had not started when I arrived, but there must have been at least 60 musicians in the studio. Sy lived not far from me on St. Nichols Avenue and we had met many times, mostly on the corner of 155th street, and St. Nichols Avenue in front of "Fat Man's Bar".

Sy picked certain musicians to go on the bandstand and I was among the first group. After going down a number, Sy asked some different musicians to come on the stand,but told me to stay there. This procedure went on for an hour or more, and when Sy finally decided on the musicians: he really wanted, which I'm certain that he had an idea in advance about the ones he really wanted before he auditioned the others, I was still there.

When the band started it's first engagement in the Zanzibar club at 48th street and Broadway, the line up was Bill Coleman, Lamar Wright, Sr., Lyman Vunk, Sreets Reed(trumpets)Dickie Wells, Henry Wells(no relation of Dickie)Gus Chappell, Bill Granzow(trombones)Eddie Barefield(also sax-clarinet) George Dorsey(alto sax) Freddie Williams, Gail Curtis(tenor-sax) Williard Brown(baritone sax) Billy Kyle(piano) Aaron Smith(guitar) George Duvivier(bass) Wallace Bishop(drums). Four of the musicians were white. Lyman Vunk, Sreets Reed, Bill Granzow and Gail Curtis.

To my knowledge, it was the first big band to play a night club in New York that had Negro and white musicians. The first parts in the trumpet section were divided between Lyman and Lamar who were both fine musicians. I played the 4th part and had all the jazz solos. Lyman and Lamar also blew very loud, but never out of tune and I had to blow my lungs out to be heard when we were doing section work, because I had been playing in small groups for 5 or 6 years and gotten out of the habit of blowing loud. I even developed lip trouble and had to be replaced by Buck Clayton, who enjoyed playing with the band to the extent that he was not happy when I came back after a lay off of 10 days.

It was a swinging band because Sy knew how to make a band do that and he knew how to arrange numbers in a swinging tempo. He also bought arrangements and George Duvivier was an arranger in the Sy Oliver medium. Very few big bands used guitars in the rhythm section anymore except for Count Besie. But Sy had one which was a big help to the section and kept it from being jumpy or instable otherwise.

The only musicians in the band other than Sy that I had known before were Dickie and Henry Wells, Eddie Barefield, Lamar Wright,Sr., George Dorsey, Billie Kyle and Wallace Bishop. I had seen Freddie Williams but did not know him very well. Aaron Smith and I became quite friendly, and we used to have a few drinks together in the Turf bar which was down stairs under the Zanzibar, when we had our intermission. Sometimes we went to Beafsteak Charlie's on 50th Street near Broadway, where many musicians hung out.

One night I told Smittie as most everyone called Aaron, that I had been in Europe during a certain time and had recorded with a guitarist named Django Reinhardt and I was surprised when he told me that he knew of Django and considered him the greatest improvising guitarist that ever lived.

A real genius, which he was. From that night on, Smittie began to call me "Mighty" and I suppose it was because he appreciated the fact that I had been fortunate enough and capable of recording with such a great musician as Django.

George Duvivier and Smittie had been friends for many years and Smittie told me that he was the first one to give George lessons in harmony. George was not a drinking person, so he did not have the same thing there in common as did Smittie and I. And speaking of drinking, Lyman Vunk could drink us all under the table and walk a straight line from Central Park to Times Square. He and Lamar had their bottles and a glass on the bandstand quite often. Lamar or Limmie as some people called him was not a heavy drinker, but Lyman after we finished our work at 3 in the morning, would go to a bar on 7th Avenue near 52nd Street called Charlie's Tavern, and drink until closing time.

We had a show to play twice a night, The first one at 10:30, and the other at 1:30 a.m. There were chorus girls, singers and the usual cabaret routine, but one of the stars was a comedian known as Dusty Fletcher whom I had seen many times. But the act that he did was very funny and sometimes, above the heads of some of the clients, because it was typical Negro comedy, and the Broadway cabaret cliental were mostly well-to-do white people. Dusty proved one thing in his act, and that was the statement many white people made when they would tell a Negro that they knew his people. They did not know them as well as they thought they did.

The highlight of Dusty's act is when he arrives home drunk and has no key. He rooms with a friend named Richard, and they are both so poor that they only have one suit of clothes between them. When one goes out, the other has to stay home. When Dusty discovers that he has no key, he calls out, 'Open the door, Richard'. There is no response, and then Dusty says, 'I know he hasn't gone out, because I've got on the clothes,' after which he starts to climb up a ladder, singing "Open the door, Richard". Where did he get the ladder? He had it with him when he was thrown out of a bar for not buying the drinks which he said was nonsense because everybody else was buying, so why should he?
We all got kicks out of Dusty's act, but it knocked Lyman out every night.

Django came to the States to do some concerts with Duke Ellington, and was to appear in one at Carnegie Hall. We had an hour intermission and there was a small group whose leader was Claude Hopkins, that included Greely Walton, who played the intermission, and after the last show; Greely and I had worked together in Luis Russell's orchestra.

I decided to go and see Django for a few minutes as Carnagie Hall was only a few blocks from the Zanzibar. When I arrived, the atmosphere back stage was not very brilliant, and I was told that Django had not shown up for the concert. I was disappointed because I had visioned a happy but short reunion in which I could perhaps persuade Django to come to the Zanzibar and meet the musicians I was working with, after he had finished his concert.

Later I heard that the reason Django did not show up for the concert was because he happened to meet Marcel Cerdan, the French boxer, and as he was lonesome, he was so happy to be able to speak French that he started drinking with Marcel and forgot about the concert. However, it was said that Django did arrive later, but had no guitar and was not dressed formally for the concert.

We recorded for a new record company called MGM which I think was affiliated with the movie company. This date was with the band and there were numbers where some vocals were done by Sy and Dickie Wells, Henri Wells and the whole orchestra. Sy was keen on the 'Glee Club Style' of singing and knew the technique of it. He had done it with the Lunceford orchestra successfully and on a few numbers with the Dorsey band. There were two other dates for MGM and one was with the comedy team of Buck and Bubbles whom the orchestra accompanied only. I've never seen this record listed in any discographies or And in any record shops./I don't have the first ones that were issued in which I have a very nice muted solo on "Slow Burn", a composition and arrangement by Billy Moore.

After two months at the Zanzibar, we finished in January 1947. As a rule, bands usually stayed in clubs of that standing for months no end and in some cases for years, as Dule Ellington did at the Cotton Club in Harlem. Charlie Johnson at Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson at the Roseland Ball room, which was a rare occasion for a dance hall, and numerous other orchestras that stayed in cabarets for six months and sometimes years.

There was another recording date before the band left the Zanzibar, but I don't remember if it was for MGM, but I do remember a couple of numbers we recorded. One was titled, "You can't tell the Depth of the Well by the length of the Handle on the Pump", a very long title, eh what! The other was "Bingle, Bangle, Bungle", and the words referred to a monkey who did not want to leave the jungle because modern civilization was too wild for him. I never saw or heard anything about that recording after it was made.

The 24th of January, 1947, we went into the Apollo theatre in Harlem which was headlined by the orchestra, Jackie Mabley, the woman comedian and the four Ravens who were a popular singing group. The Apollo changed shows every week. The band had taken on some new members and was now without any of the white musicians. Wallace Wilson and Frank Galbraith had replaced Lyman Vunk and Skeet Reid. Ernie "White Folks" had replaced Gale Curtis. Ernie was called "White Folks" because he looked like a white man, but like Willie Bryant and Willie Smith, the alto man of Jimmie Lunceford fame, he was proud to be negro. Fred Robinson replaced Bill Granow in the trombone section. Billie Kyle had left the band and was replaced by a young pianist named Buddy Weed and James Crawford did the week in the Apollo in the place of Wallace Bishop who had left the band also.

In February we played two weeks at the Savoy, but the joint didn't send me the way it had done when I was there with the band of the Scott Brothers. Later in February, we went to Boston for a one nighter and played a battle of music with the Jimmie Lunceford band. This was really a challenge to Sy because he would have the chance of showing his ex-boss what a good band he had built in a few months time. But the honours were equally divided and both Sy and Jimmie, as well as members of the two orchestras were satisfied with the results.

Jimmie had some musicians that had already made good names for themselves and some that were to become better known later. Those that were better known in the jazz world at the time wre Edwin Wilcox (piano) Albert Morris(Guitar) Charles Parham(bass) Earl Carruthers (baritone sax) Joe Thomas(tenor sax) Omar Simeon, a great New Orleans clarinetist and Russell Bowles(trombone). Those that were to become better known later were Joe Wilder(trumpet) Rennald Jones(trumpet) and Albert(Al)Grey(trombone). The other members were Joseph Marshale (drums) Mushiclata Hasashaion(alto sax)Robert Mitchey(trumpet).....
Russell Green (trumpet) Alfred Cobb (trombone) Nick Brooks (vocalist) and Kirtland Bradford (vocalist).

In March, we hit the road and one of the nighter we did was in Cincinnati. Sy was known there because as a young arranger, he was with Zack White's orchestra in Cincy for quite a spell. Naturally, I was known there because it was where I was raised and started my musical career. I taken Smitte home with me and my ole man and he became good friends from the beginning of their acquaintaince, and Dad made us some of his famous dixie rolls before we left. Dixie rolls was a sort of home made biscuit made with yeast and were eaten hot with the butter oozing out of them. They were great with sausage, mashed potatoes and gravy, and my Dad was really a champ when it came to making them.
Most of my old companions came to the dance which was in the Hall on central avenue where I had heard Louis Armstrong playing once when I was four blocks or more away from it.

From Cincinnati, we went to Dayton for one night and then to Detroit for a one week engagement at the Paradise theatre. The pit band who played one number before the show and one after, was lead by Buddy Bowen, a sax alto man, whom I had met in New York when he played for a while at the Savoy with another orchestra that I don'tt remember the name. Buddy was also the walking delegate for the musicians union and the trumpet player was Georges(Buddy)Lee, whom I had played with in Wes Helvey's orchestra in Cincinnati. I mentioned Buddy Lee before as also having played in McKinney's Cotton Pickers orchestra. In the show was a singing group known as the three Blazers whose leader was a brother of Oscar Moore, the guitarieet in the Nat "King" Cole trio, and was also a guitarist.

Another act was the Will Mast/en trio of whom the youngest in the act was Sammy Davis Jr. Sammy was unknown at that time, but he was responsible for the success of the trio, because he was a fine singer and tap dancer. His uncle Will Mast/en, and his father, Sammy Davis Senior, were the members of the trio. Sammy used to call me BeBop, but I certainly wasn't playing that style.

After the week in Detroit, Sy hired a bus to take us to Gary, Indiana, for a one night stand. Before we arrived in Gary, the windshield of the bus blew out. I never knew the reason it happened, but there it was, all shattered to hell, but we made it to the gig. Then the bus driver went over to Chicago whichis not far from Gary and had a new windshield put in and returned to Gary 1 a.m We were leaving that morning for Indianapolis after the dance. The bus driver who was a white fellow was a jazz fan and instead of getting some rest after driving so long, wanted to listen to the orchestra because he had never heard it.

The dance lasted until 2.30, and by the time we had packed up, loaded the bus and had a snack, it must have been 3.30 when we hit the roat for Indianapolis. I usually had to have a few shots under my belt before I could go to sleep, and after we got started, it was not long before I went to sleep. I can't say how long I had been sleeping when I was awaken by a strange quick movement of the bus. I had an idea that the bus driver was sleepy and decided to watch his reactions. I sat in the middle of the bus by a window on the left side. Everyone was sleeping now, except me,and the chauffeur. Suddenly, I felt the bus jerk and I immediately got up and went up to the bus driver and asked him if he was sleepy. He said 'yes', he did feel a little sleepy, so I asked him why didn't he pull over to the side of the road and sleep for a while? He said that he knew a place where one could get food and coffee that stayed open all night which was about seven miles away, and he wanted to get there and have some coffee to keep himself awake. So I stayed beside him and talked to him until we reached the all night restaurant. And we arrived in Indianapolis safely.

After a few more one nighters, we returned to the Apple, and April the first, we recorded again for MGM. A few days later, we went to Chicago for a week at the Regal theatre, after which we played a dance in Minneapolis with the Bazors as an added attraction and a dance in some town in Ohio. In Minneapolis, I was aurprised to see Earl "Inky" Tremble, the sax alto man that had played with Sy in the Zack White orchestra and the Clarence Page orchestra with whom I had played before going to Europe. I had last seen Inky in Tampa, Florida in 1942. How he happened to be in Minneapolis, I neve r learned, but he told me that things had not been good with him and he had not played sax for a long time and was working in a garage.

In Ohio, Frank Galbraith met some friends he had known for a long time, and as Sy didn't have any more jobs for a while, Frank stayed in this town. He was the first person that I ever knew that called everybody "Baby". If something was wrong, for example, a certain phrase in an arrangement, and Frank felt that he knew how it should go, he would say to the one that did not grasp the idea: "No Baby, it doesn't go like that." At one time, only a girl that a fellow may have liked, was called "Baby", but now, anyone - in the entertaining world especially - may call his colleague "Baby".

June the 27th, we played the Apollo again. Pearl Bailey was the featured attraction and Cosy Cole had a revue of dancers and Tom-Tom players. I had been in an Edgar Hayes band that played some theatre dates in Atlantic City, New Jersey, Pennsylvania with Pearl before she became a big star in the early 40's. Bill "Bojangle" Robinson was the star of the show. Now I was hearing Pearl as a big star, and Sy's band was breaking a record by bearing the only band to play a return engagement in the Apollo within six months after the first one. Frank Galbraight had come back and Wallace Wilson and Arthur Trappier, one the ex-Fats Waller drummer had replaced Wallace Bishop.

Sy was quite a difficult leader to work with. He didn't have the same hospitable feeling that Benny Carter had. He's one that considers musicians to be like children - he's the father, and your're the kids. He actually used to address us as "You Kids" sometimes. He didn't mean any harm by it, it was just his way of behaving. He was a good ground man on trumpet - not a lead player, but a good second or third trumpet player that didn't take too many solos. His playing was rather in the style of Bubber Miley, but he was an excellent arranger. As a result, it was a really good band with a lot of good musicians in it. At first, it was a mixed band, but when we finished at this club, then we had to revert to being an all black band, because some of the white musicians didn't want to leave New York. We didn't travel too much, but we didn't want to leave New York. We didn't travel too much, but we were out of New York sometimes, and most of the white guys were studio men.

There was not much booking after the Apollo date, but the band rehearsed once a week anyway. One day, we were rehearsing in the hall next door to the Lafayette theatre and suddenly, Sy stopped the rehearsal and started to make a speech about something. Then after, he started to ask the musicians what they thought of him? Different ones said this and that, but not all of us said what we though except Ernie Powell. Ernie had been in the army with Sy who was a sergent and was director of an army band in which Ernie was a member. So Ernie told Sy that he thought that he had an army sergent complex...we finished the rehearsal but at the next show, there was no Ernie Powell. And the band didn't last very long after that. The last date I played with Sy, was a small combo gig in the Blue Room of the Radio City building at 49th street and 6th Avenue.

I had a few gigs now and then which were mostly then and was getting behind in my rent. But the Normans never bothered me about that and sometimes, I would borrow a few dollars from them because they knew that When I made a gig, I would pay my rent and give back the money I had borrowed. Earl Norman, my landlord and I had built a large table in his basement on which we were going to realize our dream of havin' some miniature electric trains. Earl was an automobile mechanic and a damn good one. He also knew many things about electricity. One night, we were in the basement, and we were talking about work, so he asked me ff I knew Earle Howard. Earl was a pianist called Nappy, and I had met him during my first few months at the Savoy when he had a relief band there.

I told Norman that, and then he says that Earle Howard was the head red cap at the Pennsylvannia railroad station and asked me why didn't get a job carrying bags. He told me that in a very polite way and I told him very politely that I didn't like to carry my own bags and had no eyes for carrying those of other people. Many New York musicians had done it, but for the time being, I figured to make it in the music game, even if there was not much on the rail for the lizard.

So on November 21st of '47, I went into the 845 Club in the Bronx with a small combo lead by Billie Kyle. We were all ex-Sy Oliver members, except Charlie Holmes, the alto sax man. Freddie William was on tenor, George Duvivier on bass and Wallace Bishop on drums. The 845 Club was the only Negro night club in the Bronx

which was not very famous as a night club district but this club did a very good business. The featured, at different times were: Derby Wilson, a fine tap dancer on the Bojangle side, June Richmond who had gone back to her singing act after she left Andy Kirk, Willie Bryant, who was the perm ent Master of Ceremonies, Jackie Mabley, the woman comedian and George Kirby, an imitator of voices. A relief trio was lead by an organist named Lawrence "88" Keys. There was also a chorus line of six girls.

I had met George Kirby in the Philippines the same time as Thad Jones because he was in the same army with Thad and Stanley Facey and had entertained at our recreation hall when I heard Thad playing so much horn. George did an imitation of Joe Louis after he had won a fight and radio announcer would aks Joe to say something to the listeners. Joe had a very southern accent and George imitated him perfectly. One night, Joe Louis came to the club, but George didn't want to do that part of his act for fear of insulting Joe perhaps. But all of the show people were around him and kept shouting for the Joe Louis bit, and finally George did it, and Joe Louis who seldom laughed at anything did so that night.

We stayed in the Club until the last of February 1948, and than it was back to giring for as many potatoes as I could make where ever it was. From the time that I had done my first gig which was with a pick up band that played a white dance somewhere in New Jersey under the name of Fletcher Henderson which was in 1929 and up to 1948, many strange things had happened.

The most embarrassing gig I ever went on was a pick up band that played in Atlantic city under the name of Duke Ellington. This must have happened around 31 or 32 and I made the trip with "Spider" Caurance who still had the same model 'T' Ford that he had bought before I left Wes Helvey around 1926. Spider had old types onthe car, and it was a very hot day when we left New York.

He must have had 10 blow outs and the inkertubes had more patches on them than flies in ano open sugar barrel. I thought we'd never make it to Atlantic City on time but we did. The dance was on the pier in a place that was usually reserved for the white public but this night, it was for a Negro dance. The band was under the leadership of Benny Carter but I dont remember who the other members were except Cour//ance and Mack Horton on trombone.

We got on the bandstand and after a couple of numbers, some cats standing close to the bandstand who knew the personnel of Duke's orchestra started asking very loudly: "Where is Johnny Hodges? Where is Freddie Jenkins? Where is Barney Bigard?' and so on... When Fletcher Henderson had a pick up band playing under his name in New Jersey, he did come on the gig and direct the musicians for a while, but Duke was in New York at the Cotton Club and no one in the orchestra resembled Duke. What an embarrassing night.....

I had been in touch by correspondence with Charles Delaunay of the Hot Club de France who told me in a letter that he was trying to arrange something in Paris that would bring me back there. Charles had been in New York shortly after my return from Japan. I had met him and told him of my desire to come back to France. He told me that things were not the same then as before the war, but if I wanted to give it a try, he would see what he could do, but he wouldn't promise anything.

It was at this point that I decided that I would go back to Europe. I felt that I would have a better chance to make a living, and I'd always been in love with the European atmosphere. You could go where you wanted to go, and spend your money where you liked. There wasn't the prejudice that you had in the States, and it was my idea of living. I decided I was going to stay. I felt that if I came to Europe I would probably be getting a second chance at life. I wasn't down on the thought that nothing in New York was happening for me. I just instinctively felt that once I got there, things would be better, and I think it has. I feel free in a way that I wouldn't have if I had stayed in America. Also, I have always loved to travel, even in beat up old bus, when its a hundred and ten degrees in the shade, driving across Cansas. It was amusing, and I find that travelling still is.

One letter I received from Charles that had no date, mentioned that he almost had a contract for me to play with Charlie "Dizzy" Lewis and "Big Boy" Goudie but he didn't mention where. The next one was dated the 7th of October and mentioned that he was on the verge of getting me a contract in a new club that was going to open and asked me if I was still interested. I wrote immediately and told him, I was and also would agree to the conditions which were not bad.

At the time, I was rehearsing with a group of musicians of whom I can only remember one musician who was Austin "Slim" Moore, a trombonist. I had known "Slim" a long time. He was about 6 feet 4 and weighed 190 or perhaps 200 pounds, and was a long way from actually being slim. The pianist-and leader was a pianist who lived on 135th street between a couple of times a week and we had done a couple of gigs together. Most of the cats were beginning to dig the modern jive and I remember the first one of those numbers that I was introduced to, was BillysBounce and Slim was going all out for the style.

I had mentioned to some musicians that I may have a chance to go to Europe and when this pianist got the news through the grape wine, I was excluded from the rehearsals. In November, I had some luck and hit the numbers twice for 5 cents and again for 25 cents the first of December.

Oran "Hot Lips" Page taken an orchestra into the Apollo for one week and had asked me to join the band. I refused because I was expecting a word from Charles any day telling me that everything was set and I didn't want to be tied up in any circumstances.

On the 10th of December, I received a cable saying that a plane ticket was waiting for me at the Air France office..I was to leave the 12th. I could have made the Apollo gig for Lips but I didn't know things were going to happen the way they did. I did not have time to tell most of my friends that I was leaving but they knew I was expecting to leave. Even my girl friend Irene didn't know I was leaving so suddenly, and only my brother - Roger Kay and his girl friend Nancy, also the Normans and some of the others that lived in the house knew about it.

I bought a bottle of whisky, my brother came to the house and I was packing all night. I didn't realize I had so much this and that until then. I had told the Normans that I was going to Europe for 3 months, but I had decided that I was going to stay even if I had to drink muddy water and sleep in a hollow log. That's why I was taking everything I owned with me. But there was a surprise waiting for me when I arrived at the Air France office and terminus. I had $100.-- of excess baggage. I was under the impression that I could take what I had because I had inly traveled by air when I went to the Philippines, and on a military plane where there was no limit to the weight of one's baggage. I was unaware of the weight allowed on a commerical flight, but when I found out what it was and how much it would cost me, I was almost floored, because I didn't have but a few dollars over a hundred.

But what saved the situation was an announcement that the flight would be delayed an hour because of motor trouble or something. So I grabbed a taxi, went back to the Normans, had the taxi to wait for me, made some quick changes and taken only the things that would be necessary for a few weeks, jumped back in the taxi and made it back down to the Air France office on 5th Avennue in time for the bus going to the Airport. My brother didn't come to the bus terminus because he had been up all night with me while I was packing and the only people to see me off was Rodger Kay and Nancy. I said goodbye to New York and though about an old world war(first) song I heard when I was about 15 which said: "How're you gonna keep'em down on the farm, after they've seen Paree?"

The flight was 15 hours and there was a stop in the Azore Island somewhere for more than an hour early the morning of the 12th which was Sunday. When we arrived over the French coast, it was raining cats and dogs,as the saying goes. Arriving at Orly near Paris, it was pouring down little devils and pitchforks. A young man was waiting for me at the airport. He presented himself as Serge Griffin. I was expecting Charles Delaunay to meet me because we knew each other and it was he that had arranged a contract for me to come to France. Serge brought me into the city, but with the weather being what it was, nothing looked beautiful. I was told that I had to do a concert that afternoon and it was 1 o'clock in the afternoon already! I was not disturbed very much about who I would be working with or how it would go. Somehow I was feeling confident, so happy to be able to play in Paris again after 12 years.
The last concert I remember doing in Paris was the 3rd of July, 1936. I left Paris in December 1938 for Egypt, and now it was 10 years later that I was back again.

After having a meal in a restaurant near the Opera, a place that I was very familiar with, Serge took me to the theatre where the concert was to take place. It was not far from the Opera either, and I found out the name of the theatre was Edouard the 7th. The musicians I was to do the concert with were there, and I was presented to them. A couple of them spoke english, and that was a big help to me because the few words I had known in French, I had forgotten them all, except 'Yes'(in French, 'oui').

But what surprised me most of all was that these fellows were all young and not one was over 30 and they knew most of all the jazz standards and classics' that I knew and some modern ones that I didn't know. So there was no sweat getting a programme together. But I could not remember the musicians' names, so when we were doing the concert to a full house, I presented the pianist as Barney, the saxophonist as Mike, the vibraphone player was Joe, the bass player John, and the drummer - Rodger. Another surprise was how hip these fellows were to the styles being played in the U.S.A., and they were not at all behind times as I had sort of expected the French Jazz musicians to be.

And I was also surprised at the large following that jazz had as compared to the public that afternoon in the theatre. I suppose I was better known to the jazz public here than I realized I was, because I had never had such a warm and enthusiastic reception. I was happy about the way the musicians had supported me, and after the concert, my old friend Maurice Cullaz and his wife Yvonette, whom I had known very well since 1935, came backstage to greet me. I was surprised to see the wife of Frans Jackson whose name is Maxime who came back stage to say 'hellow'. She had been up in the Scandinavian countries, and had stopped in Paris a few days before going back to the States. Maxime was a singer.

When all the greetings were over, Charles taken me to the hotel where a room had been reserved in the neighbourhood of Montmartre which I was familiar with. He left me and I was on my own. The hotel was called "la Bruyère" and was situated on the corner of a street by the same name and rue Pigalle, not far from the Hotel Eden where I had stayed when I came to Paris in 1935. After unpacking my bags, I decided to go out especially to Boudon's and the tabac at the corner of rue Fontaine to see if I could find any old familiar faces. The only one I found was a barman in tabac (cafe where they selling tobacco, and who are just called "tabac"), that I had known before and he could speak a little English. I learned from him that "Big Boy Goodie" came around to the corner on a certain day. I was happy to be in Paris again, but started feeling little lonesome for some of the old gang that used to hand around there. The corner had lost it's gaitry, but it had not changed it's looks. I eyeballed Boudon's for a while, but didn't see anyone I had known before, so I went back to the hotel and relaxed.

A few days later, I rehearsed with the musicians. I learned that Serge Griffin was the accountaſnt for the Edouard 7th theatre, and I also got together on the names of the musicians which was not easy for me to do. Barney, the pianist, was Bernard Peiffer. Mike, who played alto sax, was Michel de Villers. Joe, the vibe player was Geo Daly. John, the bass man was Jean Bouchety, and Rodger, the drummer, was Roger Paraboschi. But it was quite some time before I could pronounce those names correctly.

Bernard Peiffer had a very personal style, and sometimes, he could do a good imitation of Erroll Garner. But when he got excited his taste was bad and he seemed to be giving instructions on how to break a piano up in public without using an ax.

Michel de Villers had learned a lot from Charlie Parker records, and played the style well. His only draw back was that he didn't read music. Geo Daly was considered the Lionel Hampton of France. He and Peiffer did a Hamp and Milt Buckner act on the piano with Geo (pronounced Gee-o) doing the one finger bit like Hamp, and that always pleased the audiance. Jean Bouchety was a fine bass fiddle man, arranger and pilot. But I never knew if he had flown a plane during the war. Roger Paraboschi played solid drums which is all that a good jazz group needs.

Eventually, I ran into "Big Boy" Goddie, who had spent the 2nd world war years in South America. I also later saw Arthur Briggs, who had been in a concentration camp after the Germans occupied Paris. Briggs told me why the few of the old gang that was still in Parid did not hang around in Boudon's anymore. The owner had collaborated with the Germans, and had denounced some Jews and Negros. I had been eating in the place, but went somewhere else after hearing what Briggs told me.

I heard that Rex Stewart was in Paris, but didn't see him until two weeks had passed as I didn't know where he was living, I happened to be sitting at the Omnibus café at Place Pigalle, and Rex came alone. He had come to Europe in 1947 with a group that included Sandy Williams, ex-Chick Webb trombonist, Vernon Story, a tenor sax man. Don Gais, piano, Johnny Harris, alto and clarinet, Ted Curry, drums and Honey Johnson, a vocalist. He used an unknown French bassist.

It seemed like old times seeing Rex, whom I had not seen for quite a long time. He gave me his address which was on rue Washington near Champ Elysees, and invited me to dinner. While in Paris, he was going to a cooking school and said that he would let me know when I should come to his placefor dinner.

I was being paid by the week but was only working Sunday afternoons, because the new club that I had been engaged to play in was to be in the Eduuard 7th theatre building and had not been finished to open when I arrived. I had not heard any outstanding trumpet players or musicians, except the ones I was working with during my first two weeks in Paris.

Thirteen days after my arrival in Paris, Christmas came and then I got the blues, because I had not made the acquaintance of anyone that may have invited me to join them in celebrating the holidays, and the few people that I knew were spending that time with their families. So I passed the time in a bar at the corner of rue Fontaine and rue Douai, owned by an ex-prize fighter named Roger. The same thing went for New Years. I drank 1948 out and 1949 in. Roger's place was my hangout, and although I could not speak very much French, and he spoke no English, we made ourselves understood.

One night just before Christmas, I was in this bar and somone tapped me on the back. I turned to see who it was and had a great surprise when I looked into the face of Joe Turner, the pianist. Joe had been in France and other parts of Europe before the last war, and we had met in Boudon's many times. He was surprised to see me also, because he didn't know that I was back in France. I had not seen him around New York for quite a while before I left. It certainly was nice seeing a fellow musician from across the pond that I could talk some trash with, and we really dished the dirt that night. Joe told me that he was on his way to Budapest, Hungary, because he was married with a Hungarian woman and had a daughter whom he was forced to leave there during the war. The next time I saw Joe, it was in Switzerland a couple of years later.

One Sunday afternoon, ther was a concert at the Eduoard 7th theatre which featured Rex Stewart, myself and a French trumpetist named Aimé Barrelli. On the bill which taken place the 13th of February, were some other French musicians that I had not known. Maurice Meyunier, Alf Masselier, Claude Marty, Joan-Claude Forebach and Eddie Bernard. Barrelli was a fine trumpet man and I was told that he was the best in France. I believed it when I heard him play, for he had a big sound, technique and a touch of Armstrong in his phrasing. Maurice Mennier played nice clarinet, Alf, for Alfonso, bass, Jean Claude Forenbach a Hawkins style tenor. Eddie Bernard was a lover of Fats Waller, James P. Johnson and a swinging cat. He spoke very good english. The concert terminated with a jam session after which we all went to a cafe for a much deserved drink. I had a few.

When I arrived in Paris, I had exactly one hundred dollars but as Serge had advanced me some francs on my weekly salary, I didn't have to change any dollars and decided to buy some American Express checks. But I kept delaying this procedure and when I went out, I would hide the money somewhere in my room so that if something happened when I was out, the money would not be in my pockets. One day, I decided to have a blue suit cleaned and gave it to a cleaning place on the rue Pigalle. Two days later, I was looking for my dollars and realized that I had put them inthe watch pocket of the blue pants I had given to be cleaned. I went to the shop and tried to explain the situation, but they didn't understand me or pretended they didn't. So I went to Charles Delaunay, who published the Jazz Hot magazine and had his office on rue Chaptal not far from where I was living and told him the story, and asked him to come with me to explain to those people what had happened. But it was hopeless, because they claimed that they had not found the money which did not surprise me, because I knew that honesty was one thing and money (any kind,anywhere) is another.

I seemed to have had a losing streak for a certain time because shortly after the loss of my money, I lost a slave bracelet that was given to me by the U.S. Coast guard Training station in appreciation for a concert I did at the base in St. Alban, New York, with the Ellis Larkins trio. There was an all girl orchestra on a tour in the Philippines by the name of Joy Cayler. I spoke to Joy before when mentioning the different groups that were doing U.S.A. shows. I became quite friendly with the first trumpet player in Joy's orchestra whose name was Flo Dreyer. They were still touring when I returned to the States and I used to send Flo 'Down Beat' magazines and other journals concerning jazz musicians. So Flo sent me a nice Zippo cigarette lighter from Hong Kong. It was in a silver casing with a dragon trimmed in gold, a trumpet casing with a dragon trimmed in gold, a trumpet impression also in gold and my name inscribed.

One night, I went to the club with some of the musicians from the Eduoard's band and after a few drinks, I felt like blowing, so I joined the musicians that were playing and I happened to have my axe with me. I felt like smoking also so I lit a cigarette. I never laid a cigarette on a piano or anything else that tood the fisk of being burned, so I took my lighter and laid it on the piano and put my cigarette on it when I was blowing my horn. I never saw the lighter after that.

Not long after the beginning of 1949 in January, the club that I was contacted to play in was opened. Don Byas had come to Paris a few days before. I had known Don Byas in New York and was also supposed to have been in the band that Don Redman brought to Europe as it was Timmie Rosenkrantz that was responsible for the tour and he asked me if I would like to come to Europe again, even though he knew I wanted to before he asked me. But I was not in the Apple when the band was formed, Timmie didn't know what to reach me and therefore, I missed out a second time being in Don Redman orchestra.

The 14th of January, Byas and I recorded four sides for a label called Jazz Selections and the 5th we recorded five numbers for Swing label using the musicians of the Edouard's band except for Michel de Villers. This was my first recording date in France since 1938 before going to Egypt.
I think that Don had been in Paris before because he came to Spain with Don Redman's orchestra in 1947, and had toured Europe with that band.

Don was engaged to join the Eouard's band and we opened the club with Louie Williams as an added attraction. Louie was from the dance team of Pops and Louie. I had known both of them when they were kids dancing with the Whitman sisters show. Pops was the son of Alice Whitman who was a great top dancer and had taught both Pops and Louie how to dance. Louie also sang very well.

The club was very nice and rather exclusive as it was not in a basement as most clubs were. But it didn't stay open long, although it was successful, because they didn't have a licence to sell liquor. There was a bar in the theatre owned by the management which had a licence and the management thought that this licence was suitable for the club also. But the law didn't go along with that.

I moved from the hotel Bruyère to another one on rue Henri Monnier in the same district. I t was a family hotel where I could at least cook my breakfast. This I did on a one burner alchohol stove, and ate my evenings meals in a reataurant.

But the management were not sitting on their bunns and we were booked for some concert tours. We played the most important cities in France, playing to packed houses. The reception of the public was great, the applauses terrific, atomic wrote Louis Fritch from Strasbourg. Some jazz fans were following the band from town to town. We had little sleep and lots of drinks. I doubt that now such enthusiastic atmosphere could be recreated.

Besides France, we did concerts in Belgium, Switzerland and Germany. I had been through Switzerland a few times going to and coming back from India and Egypt, but this was the first time I was playing in Switzerland. It was in Zurich that I met a man who later became a great friend of mine, Johnny Simmen. He knew more American jazz musicians than I ever knew existed. And there were very few that he didn't have records of.

We were the first foreign musicians to play in Germany after the war and the public had been starving for some jazz music as played the way we did. Jazz had been forbidden in Germany by Hitler. Our first date was for the German radio in Wuppertal and the director of the jazz department was Dr. Dietrich Schulz-Köhn who was a jazz enthusiast that I had met in Paris before the war when I was with Willie Lewis. Neither of us had forgotten the meeting because we saw each other often during the week that he was in Paris.

I had seen the ruins of Manila after the bombings it received during the war and it looked like a flower garden compared to what the allies had done in Germany. But the radio station was booming and a few buildings were untouched by bombs.

Inez Cavanaugh had been engaged to make the German tour with us as singer. We gave a concert in Dusseldorf, Dortmund and some other places before landing in Hamburg where we did five concerts to packed houses of not less than 2000 people at each performance. And what surprised me was to see many elderly white haired people, mean and women in the front news of the hall which was the Musikhalle which in turn was the Opera house and the largest one in Hamburg. I was told later that the management had vowed never to rent the place again for a jazz concert because the people in the balconies were stomping and applauding so hard after each number that they thought the place would cave in.

Hamburg had been hit quite hard in some parts by the bombs but there didn't seem to be a shortage of food and alchohol at that time at least in reataurants and cafés. There was a district called St.Pauli which was also known as the Ripperbahn and this was the jumpiest night life district that I ever saw. I never frequented the strip-tease joints in New York and only went to a burlesque show which was the ancient name for Strip-tease, once. That was a theatre in Broadway and the admission price was reasonable. But when strip-tease went into clubs where Kick-a-poo joy juice was served, these places became sucker or clip joints. If you went into one in New York or Place Pigalle in Paris with fifty dollars or any reasonable amount of money, you were subject to come out broker than the ten commandments.

But these places in the Ripperbahn were not clip joints. The shows were quite amusing and the girls were nice, although some of them were not extraordinary good dancers. In some of the places, big bands were engaged. The musicians were not paid very well and they worked from 8 o' clock in the evening until 5 in the morning. One place had booths with telephones in them and engaged many girls to sit and drink with the men customers that came there alone. If a guy saw a gal in a booth on the other side of the room who was alone and he wanted to talk to her and buy her a drink, all he had to do was look at the number of the booth which could easily be seen, pick up the phone and ask for the booth he wanted. The girl would answer and it was her move to accept or refuse.

Another place that was different from the strip-tease places had a regular show-and as an added attraction it featured girl wrestlers. But they were dirty wrestlers because they wrestled in mid. Another place which was very large, featured a tyrolian orchestra and served nothing but beer in clay mugs. There were big german women dressed in native costumes that served the beer and they could serve six mugs or more with one hand. Beer was not expensive and this place was always crowded with people of a certain age who seemed to have a ball. The orchestra leader would invite someone to come on the bandstand to direct the orchestra and when the number was finished, the person would have to pay a round of beer for the orchestra who was composed by about 20 men. It was very amusing and I enjoyed the happy atmosphere of this place. The Ripperbahn in Hamburg was the only place we visited in Germany that was jumping.

The only bringdown we experienced was when we left Hambourg to go to Bremen. The international trains were nice and comfortable because they had 1st and 2nd class coaches as well as 3rd class. But to go from Hambourg to Bremen, it was with a local train that only had 3rd class coaches and very old ones. It must have taken us 8 hours to get to Bremen because the train stopped at almost every house along the way. There was only 70 miles from Hambourg to Bremen but we could have arrived there with bicycles before the train did if we had left at the same time. It was daylight when we started the trip and not warm at all because it was still winter. The month of January to be exact. When night came there were no lights in the coaches and we almost froze before we arrived in Bremen.

We did a good concert however, and after we finished some people invited us to a cabaret for some drinks. We were in this place about 10 minutes when some American military M.P.'s came in. Don and I were the only American civilians in this place and one of the MP's asked to see our papers. We showed our passports to them, and then we were told we could not stay there because it was off limits for Americans. I knew that in certain places where U.S. soldiers were stationed that there were certain night club districts that were off limits for military service, personals, but I didn't think that the rule applied to civilians.

So I told this M.P. that I was going to see about it. He said, 'Alright, you can see about it now' and told Don and I to come along with him. Don said that there was no need for him to come along because he had not said anything but the M.P. said, 'Yes, you come along also'. We were taken in a jeep to the military headquarters and after waiting for half an hour, we were finally questioned by an officer who told us that when a place was off limits for Americans, it meant soldiers, sailors and civilians. That was the end of that, but Don was really salty with me.

Back in Paris, my regular handout became the Omnibus Café in the Place Pigalle, which was a one minute walk from the hotel I was staying at on rue Henri Monnier. Many French and Martinique musicians met on the square at Place Pigalle every evening around 6, which is known as the apertif hour. It was also where musicians were engaged for gigs the way it was at the Rhythm Club back home. I met some musicians I had known before the last war at Place Pigalle.

Django, his brother Joseph, Louis Vola ex-bassist of the quintet du Hot Club de France, Alix Combelle, André Ekyan and some Cubans, one named Raoul and Humberto Canto who played bongos and danced. Humberto could not speak very good english, but I would understand him and we became good friends. He was very folly fellow. There were also two Algerian fellows that I became quite friendly with. One was named Mohammed Hamida, but I called him "Monsieur Chemise" because he admired the shirts I wore. Chemise in french is shirt in english, and Mohammad called me also Monsieur Chemise as eyeryone called Robert Horton the trombone man "Mack" because everybody was Mack to him.

The other Algerian was called Pépé and he spoke good english. After a few times talking with Pépé, I figured I knew him well enough to ask him if he knew where I could get some gage. I was never an addict but I liked a little taste now and then and Pépé said he knew something. He asked me how much I wanted and as I didn't know how it was sold here, I figured that three thousand francs would get me a few sticks, so I told him to bring me enough for that amount. The francs was worth 350 frs to a dollar. I didn't give Pépé the money because I didn't know him well enough to take a chance like that.

A few days later, there was a knock on my door and when I opened it, there was Pépé with a big package wrapped in newspaper. I asked him what it was, and he told me it was the stuff I had asked for. It was still on the branches. I paid him and then opened the package when I was alone and it looked as though Pépé had brought me a whole tree without the trunk. I was expecting some stuff already cleaned, which I would only have to roll and stick when I wanted it. But I had to go out and buy a sifter and do the job of separating the seeds and other parts from the goody.

It taken me a whole afternoon to do that, and when it was finished, I had a mountain of gage. I had bought a pair of shoes not long before this and still had the box, so I filled that and still had more. I filled another box about half the size of the shoe box and put some in a newspaper package. Then I became scared and started to wonder if Pépé had brought me all that stuff to get me in trouble with the law. I wondered where I could hide the stuff and the only place I could see in the room was the top of a cabinet where I had my clothes hanging. I stood on a chair and looked on top of the cabinet and saw that it

was the ideal place to conceal the stuff for a special reason. I said before that this hotel was a second rate one, although my room was nice for that type of hotel. The bed was clean and sheets were changed every week. The maid cleaned everywhre except under the bed and on top of the cabinets, so when I looked on top of the one in my room, there was dust thick enough to plant potatoes. I took my boxes and the package, put them on top of the cabinet and covered them with dust. Then I breathed a sigh of relief and said to myself: if 'Johnny Nab' comes to search the room and finds the stuff on top of the cabinet covered with dust an inch thick, I wouldn't know anything about it. I had regular visits from Hunerto and would give him enough to make a few sticks every time he came. I also gave little Louie, the dancer, some a few times, and the stuff lasted me for about two years.

The Edouard's band, Don Byas and myself were still doing concerts and in April, we went to Knokke for three days at the casino with a big show. This was the 16th, 17th and 18th. The show included the orchestras of Bernard Hilda and Maurice Toubas. They were both known as high society orchestras in Europe, and we took care of the jazz department. Other acts engaged were the Nicholas Brothers - dance team- Rosario and Antonio, famous Spanish couple, Borrah Minevitch's Harmonica Vagabonds, the well known Bluebell Girls from the Lido, and the very famous french artist of music hall fame and films - Fernandel.

The war had not changed naything in Kokke since I was there the summer of 1938. Everything went well until the last night when Don Byas went into one of his acts after the last show. Of course, we all had quite a few drinks and were feeling no pains. I had already left the casino when thiks incident happened, but I was told by one of the musicians that Don was high and in the process of changing his clothes, he decided to chase one of the Bluebell girls that had passed his lodge when the door was open. But he was chasing this girl in his shorts only, and Mr. Nellens, the director of the casino happened to be in the hallway of the dressing rooms. He gave Don hell and that killed the chance for us and the band to have a summer season in the casino of Knokke.

The big thing in jazz from the 8th of May until the 15th was the jazz festival that Charles Delaunay organized in collaboration with Frank Bauer, Eddie Barclay and Jacques Souplet. Sidney Bechet and Charlie(the Bird) Parker were the stars, but there were other musicians that were already in the limelight, whose names were to become much better known than they were in 1949. The American musicians presented at this festival were Bechet, Parker, "Big Chief" Russell Moore, Oran "Hot Lips" Page, Kenny Dorham, Tommie Potter, Al Haig, Max Roach, Miles Davis, Jimmy McPartland, Ted Dameron, Kenny Clarke, Georges Johnson, James Moody, Richie Frost, Don Byas and myself. This was an international festival with musicians from six european contries including France. England was represented by the orchestra of Vic Lewis and Carlo Krahmer. Belgium was Toots Thielman's trio. The National all Stars from Sweden, Hazy Osterwald with E. Hollenhagen from Switzerland and France was represented by Aimé Barelli, Hubert Rostaing, André Ekyan, Jack Dieval and his trio, Jean-Claude Forenbach, Leo Chauliac, Lucien Simoens, Hubert Fol, the Junior all stars Michel de Villers, Maurice Meunier, Geo Daly, Bernard Peiffer's trio, Claude Luther, Pierre Braslavsky and their orchestras, the College Rhythm orchestra, Jean Bonal and Bernard Hullin.

Jazz was jumping in Paris that week at the Salle Pleyel and jazz fans from different countries (mostly those who had musicians that were favoured in the places they were from) were here to take in the festival and all the jazz clubs were jumping and especially the club St. Germain des Pres on the left bank of Paris, because the American musicians and some from other countries would go jamming after the nightly concerts or on nights when they did not have to appear with Rostaing(clarinet) Braslavsky(clarinet) Bechet (soprano-sax) Byas (tenor) Tommie Potter(bass) Moody(tenor sax) Osterwald (vib) "Lips Page"(tp) Max Roach(drums) Miles Davis (tp) Barelli(Tp) Bill Coleman(tp). I don't believe a session like that every happened before or after in the Salle Pleyel and I'm certain that a good time was had by all. Musicians and the audience.

One day during the festival, I went to see "Big Chief" Moore at his hotel. Russell is a real indian and the only one I ever knew that played jazz. I didn't know his weight exactly, but roughly guessing, it must have been at the time about 350 pounds. I tqas about 12:30 a.m. when I knocked on his door and he was still in bed. When he asked who was there. I told him and he said:'Just a minute'. I was waiting almost 10 minutes before he finally opened the door.

When I walked into his room, I saw the reason it had taken him so long to come to the door. His bed was about two feet wider than an army cot and the springs and mattress were about five inches from touching the floor. It must have taken "Big Chief" five minutes to get out of bed and five others to put his bath robe on.

Another day during the week of the festival, "Big Boy" Goodie came to my hotel with some people from Switzerland and introduced me to them. One fellow's name was Peter Wydler and the other was Felix Debrit. "Big Boy" had played in Bern, Switzerland, with Glyn Pacque, the altoman I had worked with in Benny Carter's orchestra 1933 band. Pacque is mentioned in this book back in 37 or 38 and he had been able to stay in Switzerland during the war.

Peter and Felix were jazz fans and Felix advised the owner of a place in Berne called the 'Chikito' as to what jazz men should be engaged or contracted for the place. Felix wanted me to form an orchestra for an engagement in the Chikito, but he had an idea about certain American musicians whom he was in contact with, being in the orchestra. I had no great desire of becoming an orchestra leader, but "Big Boy" was helping Felix push me by telling me how nice it was to work in the Chikito. I told Felix that I would think it over and promised to keep in touch with him.

Don Byas, myself and the Edouard's band were no longer being booked by the Edouard 7th theater group, but someone, maybe Delaunay got us a job playing at a left bank bank club called the "Vieux Colombier" which didn't last very long and the band broke up after that engagement.
I did some gigs with different musicians and later wne into the "Reve" a dance hall in the Rex theater building with Charlie "Dizzy" Lewis who had also engaged George Johnson on alto-sax.

After a month at the "Reve", I worked a couple of weeks with a fellow known as Cuban Pete at the Ambassador where I had worked with Willie Lewis after I came back from India in 1937. Pete was an Algerian but most people didn't play an instrument but he was as smooth operator and had collaborated with his pianist and had published some music under his own name. The music that Cuban Pete's orchestra played was Cuban style with not a touch of jazz and I had to wear the Cuban type of shirt that all Cuban and many Martinique orchestras wore, and as a uniform, I didn't care for it, and I was missing the good ole jazz rhythm, so I didn't stay with Pete very long.

I was supposed to have played a concert in a town called Limoges with Edouard's band and Don Byas before the band broke up, but missed the gig because I thought that I knew how to get the railroad station we were to leave from with the metro.(subway) I did get to the station which was gare d' Austerlitz, but too late for the train the others had taken because I went the wrong direction inthe subway.
