No one I came in contact with at the station could speak english. I tried to find out if there was another train later that would get me to Limoges in time for the concert. I understood there was not so I tried to engage a car, to take me there, but that didn't work out. I missed the gig. A few days later, I was contacted by a jazz fan named Jean-Marie Masse from Limoges who was the president of the Hot Club there. I explained to him why I did not make the concert and he understood. He told me that he would arrange for me to appear in Limoges and a few weeks later, I went there alone. The nights of the 11th and 12th of June, 1949, I played at a place called Sully which was a night club in Limoges. I was accompanied by a guitarist named Bob Aubert whom I had met before in Paris. Jean Marie Masse, drums-to my surprise, because he had not mentioned before that he was a dnummer. The pianist and bassist I don't remember who they were, but they were frin the region of Limoges.

I stayed with Jean-Marie whose wife's name was Paulette, They had a daughter named Sylvie who was 5 years old and one about 2 years old called Agnes. Jean believed in eating good and his wife was a very good cook. I had some french food that I had never heard about and that sent me. Little Sylvie, I adopted as my little mamma, because she was with me all the time I was awake and would get me a glass of cognac or whatever I wanted to drink wheever I asked her. I let her blow my horn and she really got a sound out of it the first time she tried blowing a trumpet. I spent two fine days in Limoges and was forgiven by everyone concerned with jazz in that town and I've been a great friend of Jean-Marie Masse and his family ever since then.

I was so happy about being in France that I celebrated every day with a fresh bottle of cognac which I kept in my room and was drinking 15 to 20 glasses of cognac in bars and sidewalke cafes. But after a few weeks, my lips began to get dry and I could not play the way I was supposed to. I knew that it was from drinking too much, and although I was never drunk, I knew I had to stop drinking until my lips became right, and I did stop for at least one month.

Kenny Clarke who had been working in the orchestra of Tony Proto, a french altoist, and Lobo Nochio, a singer, formed an orchestra, and I joined it. Lobo had been in the army, was dischraged in Europe and had settled in Paris. In the orchestra was Byas, James Moody, Hubert Fol, Nat Peck, an American white trombonist, Jay Cameron, another white American, who played baritone sax, Pierre Michelot, a fine French bass player, and a few more French musieians whose names I don't remember. An English girl named Anabella Ross was the female vocalist. Annabella became very well known later as Annie Ross of the Dave Lambert, John Hendricks, Annie Ross trio.

We were engaged to work at Frisco's International Bopera House in Montmartre on rue Notre Dame de Lorette. I became acquainted with Frisco in 35. At one time, he had a club in London and had come to France in the 20's. I was not supposed to stay with the orchestra very long because I had been engaged before to go to Nice for two weeks in a place called Club St. Germain des Mers, which was to open in late July by Sarge Griffin and the director of the Edouard 7th theatre. In August, I was to join the orchestra of Jack Dieval to play the month in Geneva, Switzerland, at the Grillon dancing.

In Nice, I worked with Bernard Peiffer, Huber Fol who had been in the Clarke-Lobo orchestra. Hubert told me that the later orchestra didn't last long because Frisco wanted the French musicians to continue to play when the Americans would take a rest and the place was not going to well as far as business was concerned. Kenny and Lobo did not agree with the way Frisco wanted the band to play and that didn't help either the situation, so the band broke up after a few weeks.

The other musicians in the Nice deal were Jack Smaley on bass, and a young white American drummer named Richie Frost. Jimmie Davis who was known as Jimmie "Lover Man" Davis because he was one of the co-composers of the famous song, "Lover Man" was engaged as an entertainer. Another singer engaged there was Monique Davis who was French
and the wife of Pieffer.

I had been introduced to Jimmy by Beezie in 1940 because they were both from Leonia, New Jersey, and she had known him a long time before we met. Jimmie sang and accompanied himself on the piano. He had been a warrant officer in the army and came to France after his discharge.

In Geneva with Jack Dieval was Kenny Clarke on drums, Paul Vernon a French tenor man, Emmanuel Soudieux, also French, on bass, and an American Negro singer, named Arstella Whitter from Rochester, N.Y.

Arstella had presented herself to me after a concert at the Edouard 7th theatre, my first or second one, and told me that she knew a little girl in Rochester whom I called my niece but she actually was not related to me. I never knew how Arstella happened to come across to France,and as a singer. I had never heard of her in the States, but she had a nice voice in the style of Ella Fitzgerald, when she sang sweet numbers.

Paul Vernon I had met soon after I came to Paris. He played tenor in the style of Dexter Gordon whom he admired with a little mixture of Prez(Lester Young). As for Jack Dieval, he was a good business man who probably had classical training on the piano and came into the jazz field because he liked that type of music and especially the blues. He was avery good accompanist. Soudieux was one of those solid bass players whose interest was not in being a soloist, but backing up instrumental soloist with the correct bass chords and big sound. Kenny Clarke, known as Klook, I've mentioned before, and he was not a new comer to me or anyone else, that is,or was a follower of jazz and its history. We made quite a hit with the public and had some nice arrangements which included a few numbers that I sang alone and with Arstella.

Felix Debrit who had asked me in Paris when I met him during the festival about leading an orchestra in the Chikito came to see me in Geneva, with Johnny Simmen. Johnny came along to help Felix persuade me into taking a group into the Chikito and they succeeded. I accepted the offer. Not because I wanted to be a leader. I never felt as though I had the qualifications to be one, but I decided to give it a try.

Felix told me that he was in contact with Ernest "Bass" Hill and Norman Lester, a pianist, both of whom I knew. "Bass" and I had been in a Benny Carter orchestra together, also in the Philippines. Norman I had known for years, but we had never worked together. Felix was also in touch with an American tenor sax man named Fred Palmer, who was in Italy. I didn't know this fellow, but was told that he had been a member of Noble Sissle's orchestra at one time. That was no worhty recommendation to me, but it was Felix who was really forming this orchestra that I was to lead. "Bass" Hill and Norman Lester had been in Europe before and their desire was to come back again. As "Bass" had been in contact with Felix and Felix was an advisor to the owner of the Chikito concerning jazz musicians and orchestras, he had proposed these musicians plus "Big Boy" Goddie and myself and the owner had accepted the proposition. "Big Boy" had been in the Chikito in an orchestra lead by Glen Pacque who had managed to make his home in Switzerland near the beginning of the second world war.

After I had finished at the Grillzon dancing with Jack Dieval, we did a radio show in Lausanne, and I was invited to spend a few days with Johnny Simmen, whose real name is Hans George Simmen, and his wife Lisette, who dosen't like her real name, which is Liza. I had met them, Johnny's sister, her husband and a girl named Bettina Blockinger, the first time I did a concert in Zurich with BonByas and the Edouard's band. After the concert, I had been invited to Simmen's home and enjoyed their company intil the wee hours of the morning. Johnny had a collection of records that was second to the collection of Hughes Panassié, which ran into thousands and included most everyone that I had made. During my visit with Johnny and Lisette after the Dieval deal, every night we had a record session of recordings I had never heard by musicians known and unknown to me. And what's more, Johnny knew the history of all those musicians including mine and could tell me when and where they were born, the different orchestras they had played with, those that were still living and what most of them were
doing at the present time.

When I came back to Paris near the end of September, I contacted a West Indian drummer named George Smith whom I had met before and asked him about joining the orchestra for the Chikito as a drummer was the only musician missing in the line-up. He accepted and I wrote to "Bass" Hill and asked him to start collecting some music in New York. When I received an answer from him, he told me not to worry about music because Norman Lester was an arranger and would take care of the repertoire.

Buck Clayton had come to Paris with an orchestra which included Merrill Stepter, a trumpetist I had known a long time and Wallace Bishop the drummer. I recorded with Buck and his band the 23rd of November, 1949, which included a French personal of Alix Combelle (tenor sax) Armand Conrad (tenor sax), George Kennedy (alto-sax), André Persiany (piano), George Hadjo(bass).

We did six numbers in which one featured the three trumpets on "Sweet Georgia Brown" and one featured Buck and I on a number we called B.C. and B.C. and it's very easy to see the connection between the title and the two of us.

"Bass" Hill and Norman Lester arrived in Paris a couple of days before we left for Bern which was the 24th of November. Fred Palmer came in from Italy and we opened in the Chikito the 26th with nothing but head numbers. I had, however, bought some music stands with my initials B.C. on them, but Norman had not arranged anything before leaving New York, and I had not picked up on any orchestrations from publishers in Paris because "Bass" Hill had told me that Norman would take care of that end. I had made my first mistake as a band leader by depending on the word of someone else and not preparing for the event myself.

& So there we were, with these nice looking stands of light/dark blue with golden sprayed B.C. on them and not the first sheet of music on them. But we made out alright because the one thing that Norman Lester knew was any number that was ever popular in jazz and most of them that were not. He also knew the original keys and the names of the composers. I had never played a gig with Norman, so I didn't know what style he played until we rehearsed the day before we opened at the Chikito. He played a Fats Waller stride style which I would say included some James P. Johnson, or Lucky Roberts or a little
of Willie "the Lion" Smith and he did a good imitation of singing like Fats.

George Smith was an up to date drummer who could not have been in France more than a couple of years before I arrived in 48. He liked to do singing imitations of Louis Armstrong which didn't sound very good to me. "Big Boy" Goudie had a very personal style on tenor and played very good New Orleans style clarinet. "Bass" Hill was always known as a solid bass man and had played with many of the big named bands in New York. We had been together in the Philippines. The weakest man in the band was Fred Palmer who had no style on tenor and no voice for singing. I had also engaged Arstella Whittier as vocalist because it was stylish to have a canary as girl vocalist were sometimes called.

Other than the fact that we had no music on the stands, we still made a hit with the public at the Chikito. Later Norman Lester wrote some original tunes which actually had no swing possibilities and although he was a good piano man, he was not an arranger. But we played the tunes every night because I was a begger and had no choice.

"Willie the Lion" Smith came to Europe during this time and his tour brought him to Berne. There was a jam session every Saturday and Sunday afternoon at which I would invite the local musicians to participate and the joint would jump during these sessions. The first of December, Buck Clayton and George Johnson along with the "Lion" (who was giving recitals in Switzerland at the time), were invited to the session. Merrill Spepter was also there because Buck was engaged to play a ball in a hotel that night with a group lead by Glyn Pacque. George Johnson had come back to Europe in 1949 and was living in Paris. The 'Lion' was real groovie and we all had that New York jam session feeling, so it was the jumpiest session of all at the Chikito.

I taken the occasion to ask "Buck" if he would make me some arrangements, but for some reason which I never found out why, he never did any for me and he was engaged through the influence of Felix to come to the Chikito quite a few times and play with my orchestra.

On Christmas and New Year's day, Felix invited us to his country house in a place called Lugnorre which was about 50 miles from Bern to spend Christmas day. This was just a party for me and my musicians along with a few friends of Felix and his wife Liza, but only Norman Lester, "Bass" Hill and myself were there. We had taken some juice with us and Felix had plenty of white wine which is a famous party drink in Switzerland and we really bent elbows that day and night.

My engagement at the Chikito was to finish at the end of February 1950 and we were now within a few days from closing. The night of the 23rd a sweet looking Swiss girl was sitting in the balcony of the place. The Chikito was built in a circular form with a balcony that went around the place and the dance floor was down a floor below with tables around. There were tables in the balcony also and as I came by one of the tables going down stairs toget on the band-stand, this sweet looking Swiss girl asked me for an autograph. I gave it to her and then asked her if she had come to the Chikito alone. I didn't speak much French and she didn't speak any English, but we made ourselves understood. I found out that she was not from Bern and was not staying until the night was finished. I asked her if she could have coffee with me the next day at 2 PM, and she accepted.

She came the day after and we got along very well between the little French that I spoke and making signs with out hands. She told me that her name was Lily, that she was Swiss and that she was a jazz fan although she didn't know too much about jazz musicians at the time. She had come a few times to the Chikito and was crazy about the band.

We met a couple of times after that and I managed to make her understood that when I finished my contract at the Chikito, I would play a concert in Olten an the 3rd of March with Buck Clayton. As Olten was not far from the place where she lived, she say she would come to the concert.

I saw her one more time before leaving for Rome. We were starting to be in love with each other. She was a nice looking brunette, sweet and witty with a pleasant personality. She had told me that she was married, but was not happy. I told her that if she would have been free, I would have ask her to come along with me. She answered that she may do it later.

I did not want to be the cause of her breaking up her marriage, but she said that things had been bad for quite a while between she and her husband, and she was intending to get a divorce anyway. I had no idea what the future would hold for us and we parted, promising that we would write to each other. I gave her the American Express Company as my address. Lily had started to take English lessons, and was trying very hard to make progress.

Felix had become my manager and had contacted a hotel in Rome where I was offered a six weeks engagement. During my stay at the Chikito, I had met an American army in Germany and this man got me an engagement to play for the Army's first year celebration of their headquarters in Heidelberg. Felix was with us the day we arrived at the headquarters which was the 4th of March. I was commended by a Colonel who seemed to be a nice person. He invited Felix, myself and the fellow that got me the engagement(whom he knew) into his office and asked me if I would be willing to but my price for the date because his budget was not what it should be. I was not happy about this and told him that I would have to take the matter up with the musicians. We talked it over and decided that there was not much we could do otherwise, so we accepted the cut which was fifty dollars less than the contact was called for.

The Colonel was satisfied and then taken us on a tour of the kitchen where we saw at least ten big refrigerators that must have been seven feet square and six feet high, all packed with food. He promised us a fine meal when we would be finished that night. We had a snack before we started. The affair taken place in two big halls. We played in both of them alternating with another orchestra.

We were playing our last set of the night around 3 in the morning and did some numbers that were more spectacular than we had done the whole night. This Colonel had been juicing it up the whole night and when he heard us do these numbers, he wanted us to go back to the other hall and do them again. I refused because we had started the job on time had taken a cut in the salary and I thought that we had done our good deed for the day. So this bastard ordered every refrigerator locked up and told the kitchen personals not to give us anything to eat. I regretted having accepted to cut the price of the contract, because after all, the money was not coming from his pocket as the affair was really sponsored by the U.S.A. army, and he must have put those

fifty dollars in his pocket. Even the fellow that had gotten the engagement for us and was a friend of the son of a bitch, couldn't make him change his mind about giving us a meal. We slept on empty stomachs that morning because no restaurants were open in the city when we returned to our hotel.

The 11th of March, 1950, we left Berne for Rome and that was a thrill for me because I had learned the history of this great city in school, and had heard about its beauty with all the ancient ruins from the times of the Caesars, and now I would have the opportunity of seeing those things.

George Smith left and band after the Heidelberg deal because he was obliged to respect a contract he had made for the Cigalle, a jazz cafe in Paris. So Felix had asked an American drummer named Benny Bennet, to join me in Rome.

Benny was a Negro who looked more like a suntanned South American. He had gotten his discharge from the army somewhere in Europe and stayed in Paris. We had taken a night train from Bern and arrived in Rome the 12th and were taken to a hotel not far from the hotel Bernini-Bristol, where we were to work.

The next day, we had to give an audition forthe director of the hotel. He started to make a stink because the drummer I had was not the same as the one on a photo that had been sent to him. Felix explained the reason for the change in drummers which I could not understand would make much difference, as long as the rest of us were the same as on the photo. I had gone to all the music shops in Bern long before we had left there and collected as much music as possible, so when we opened in Rome, my band stands were not bare.

The opening was on the 16th of March and we followed a big radio band with singers which was about 25 musicians and singers altogether. This big package was lead by Armando Trovafoli who played piano and I was told that he was the best arranger in Italy. And here I was with my five musicians and one girl singer, trying to please a house that was accustomed to the sound of a big orchestra and a group of singers and accustomed to the sound of comercial music. It was quite a snobbish audience, some women were using lorgnette to look at the band. The big band didn't have to use sonorisation but it was a necessity for us, and the loudspeaker were terrible and badly regulated. My efforts or I should say, our efforts, didn't last very long because we were told on the second night that the next night would be our last one.

The next day I taken Felix and "Bass" Hill with me to the American Embassy and we told the lawyer of the Embassy about the affair. He told us that he didn't think there was much we could do and that a contract with anyone in Italy was not worth the paper it was written on, but he would see what he could do. That same afternoon, I received word that we could work an extra day, but the management would not pay our train fare which we had paid from our pockets from Bern to Rome. So we finished on the 19th of March and that was that. It was a sad situation to be in, in such a beautiful city, but it really didn't worry me.

A Roman jazz magazine called 'Musica Jazz' had this to say about my Bristol-Bernini engagement: "The month of March had brought us a very big deception. One of the most famous trumpetist in the history of jazz had been engaged to play at the Bernini-Bristol and had brought with him a combo of fine jazz musicians of good reputation. But what happened was that Bill was fired after only three days and for what reason? The band had refused to play the Harry Lime theme, tangos and Italian commercials. What kind of band was that? Were they not to please the public and play their request?..... So all the people who liked jazz and were overjoyed to have for once the occasion to listen to a good jazz orchestra were more than disappointed because many of them did not have the chance to hear the band.

Norman Lester had won a law suit for some sort of accident he had in New York and the thousand dollars which was waiting for him in the States had him in a pretty bad mood most of the time. He had learned about winning thecase not long after we went into the Chikito. And when he would get in those moods, an arguement about one thing or another would take place between he and I, and he would ask me to give him the music he had written. The next night he would come to work feeling good and pass the music out again. One night he went through this routine and when he brought the music back the next night, I wouldn't play any of them because I had picked up on some music as I mentioned before. And I never played his numbers again. So he was not sorry when the Bernini-Bristol deal finished and he left as soon as he could to get back to New York.
The rest of us had decided to stay in Rome and play by ear, which means take a chance on something happening.

One day, I received a letter from Lily saying that she was coming to Rome. As it was written in French, I could not read much of it, but I thought I understood what day and the hour she would arrive and I intended meeting her at the station. A few days later, I was coming from the American Express Company and happened to look into a taxi that had stopped and who should I see but Lily! I was surprised, because I had not been expecting her at that time. What happened was that I had mixed up the time of her arrival with the date and the day and I was not at the station to meet her when she arrived. She had been very upset because she did not have my hotel address, having only one address, the one of the American Express Company, and it was sheer luck that we met in the street.

I became acquainted with an Italian name Sergio Sangiorgi whom I later found out was a count and a lover of jazz. I also became acquainted with a bass player named Carlo Loffredo who was president of the Hot Club of Rome and did a concert with the Roman New Orleans Jazz Band of which he was a member. This happened the 10th of April, and featured Arstella Whittier, Big "Boy" Goodie, Armando Travaioli without his big band and Ivan Vandor, a soprano sax man and member of the Roman New Orleans Jazz Band. There was also a Spanish tenor man named Salvador Font Orofitg.

Fred Palmer could speak the Italian language quite well and he made the acquaintance of an impressario who had nothing but ideas and this fellow told Fred that he was going to put on a show and wanted to use us. So we started rehearsing at Count Sangiorgi's home with a Martinque musician named Edouard Pajaniandy whom I had met in Paris. He had left an orchestra called Fanfan, who was played at the night club "Rupe Tarpea" in Rome and "Big Boy" had taken Edouard's place in that orchestra. We had an Italian drummer, pianist and an Italian alto player named Al Melili whom I had known in Egypt. Pajaniandy also played alto and clarinet. I had let Fred Palmer take charge of everything because he could explain things to the Italian musicians. But Al Melili spoke good english.

The day after the concert which was the 10th of April at the Cinema Theatro Bernini(ntohing to do with the hotel Bernini-Bristol) we taken a bus for Naples where the show was to start. Lily had gone back to Switzerland and was to come back definitely to Rome in 20 days. It was the first time I ever waited that long for a girl to come back to me.

We checked into a hotel and Fred went to find his man in order to know what time we would rehearse the show, He came back a few hours later and told us that there was not going to be any show. That was the 11th of March, and we came back to Rome by bus on the 12th. I never knew exactly what happened. Fred paid the expenses for the trip because he was the one that was doing the business such as it was.

I had a room in a place called Pensione Beccari on the via del Tritone and to cut down on expenses, I shared a two roomed bedroom with a hungarian fellow named Pista. Pista was a refugee, and there were quite a number of them-men and women-staying in this pensione. But the day that Lily returned, I moved to another room in the same place. While at this place, I met a West Indian fellow named Stanley Carter. I had heard of him, but never seen him. Stanley played piano and sang. His act was on the style of Morris Rocco, an American Negro who was very popular in the downtown theatre circle of many big cities and white night clubs in the States.

Duke Ellington was on his first tour of Europe after world war II and it was a delightful pleasure to know that he would be coming to Rome during the time I was there. This was in May and Duke played a theatre for 5 to 6 concerts. It was something for Lily also, because she had never seen or heard of a big band playing jazz. The musicians I knew were Jimmy Hamilton, Sonny Greer, Harry Carney, Ray Nance, Al Killian, Russel Procope, Quinton Jackson, Johnny Hodges, the Duke himself, Don Byas who had been engaged to play the trombone parts of Lawrence Brown on tenor because Lawrence had become ill and had to go into a hospital, Nelson Williams whom I had met in New York and saw in the Philippines.

The new musicians that I did not know but had the opportunity to meet were Ernie Royal, a trumpetist, Alvin McCain, a tenor man, Butch Ballard a drummer that Duke had engaged to play the serious drum parts while Sonny featured on certain numbers that called for his showmanship. I didn't know Wendell Marshall, the bass player, but Lily and I went to four concerts and eventually we became acquainted with all the musicians I had not known before and that was the first time that I had heard Duke and his men so many times in less than a week.

Not long after Duke left Rome, Roy Eldridge came for one concert with Benny Goodman. It was a small combo which I did not hear, but I met the drummer whose name was Ed Shaughnessy and we went to the Florida Club to have a drink with he and Roy. They told me that "Toots" Thielemans, the guitar and harmonica player from Belgium was with the group. I knew of "Toots" but had not met him. It was a nice feeling to meet my ole colleague Roy in Rome where we had no idea we would meet when we played together in Teddy Hill's orchestra back in 1934-35.

Most of the refugees were coming from behind the Iron curtain and were artists. One of them whose name I don't remember was doing some booking of artists in different clubs and he landed a contract for Arstella, Fred Palmer and myself to appear as an attraction in a cabaret called Florida Club which was not far from where I was living, so we opened on the 10th of May. The pianist, bass and drummer of the house band accompanied us and we did three times a half hour each night. The pianist and bassist were good musicians but the star of the orchestra was the drummer. His name was Roberto Zappulla and he was only 16 years old. But he played drummer like a professional of 30 years, and he was modern but solid. The orchestra was very nice but played only Italian songs when they were not accompaning an attraction that had their special arrangements. I was the only attraction that played jazz and the musicians loved it.

During the day, Lily and I visited a different place every day and I had a ball filming the ruins and also modern monuments. Arstella did not stay at the same place where we lived. One day, she told me that the had found a place in a family that had a few rooms to rent, and it was possible to cook there. This pleased Lily and I because we were eating in restaurants and starting to get tired of that kind of food every day. The 16th of March, we moved into this apartment on the via Quintino Sella 20. The apartment belonged to a woman of a certain age and her daughter who was about 20 years old and studying medicine.

Lily was born in Neuchatel, Switzerland, but had been raised in Pntarlier, France. She was separated from her husband and was waiting for a divorce. What happened after that concerning our marriage will come later in this book, because I was not divorced from my first wife Madelyn and many moons passed before it became a reality.
The 31st of May, I finished at the Florida club. Meantime,

Count Sergio Sangiorgi had contacted the owner of a casino in Viareggio, Italy and this man came to Rome in June to talk over the prospects of engaging a band for his place and the deal came through. Sergio went to Viareggio every year for his summer vacation, and he was sweet on Astrella also. So if he could arrange for us to go to the casino, he was certain to have some jazz when he wanted to hear it in person and be with Arstella. "Bass" Hill had been contacted quite a while back for a job somewhere in Germany and had left Rome when I was at the Florida Club. So we engaged an Italian bass man and rehearsed at Sangiorgi's home until the time came for us to go to Viareggio. Al Melili, the bass and drummer were the Italian members of the group.

From the time that I had finished at the Florida Club until I went to Viareggio, I didn't have one gig. Lily could speak Italian and one day, when she was in the kitchen, the woman that we rented from, asked her why I did not try to get a job, perhaps as a dishwasher in some restaurant. Lily tried to explain to her that there are times when artist in music and show business had periods when there was no work and don't favour washing dishes or doing other kind of work that is not to their liking. Anyway, I always paid my rent when it was due, so she had no reason to worry about if I worked or not.

June the 29th, we left for Viareggio, That is, everyone of us except Mr. Fred Palmer, who would never take the same train with the rest of us even when we did some concerts in Switzerland after we had finished at the Chikito. He had taken a train before us when we went to Rome and the only times I can remember him ever travelling with the group was when we went to Heidelberg and the bus trip to Naples and back to Rome. He was a strange guy who was playing Mister "BIG" all the time.

Lily didn't go with me because I had a strange feeling about going to Viareggio, so I told her to wait a couple of days until I could see how things would go and if everything was not alright, I would come back to Rome.

We arrived and went to a hotel next door to the Casino. After we settled, we went to see the manager of the Casino to straighten out the hours we would have to play and any other business that had to be taken care of. The first thing the owner did was to pretend that he was surprised to see that the band was not an all Negro group and three of the personnel were Italian.

I spoke no Italian, except for a few words such as "Bon Giorno", "A-Rivederci", and "Grazie", which means 'good day', 'goodbye' and 'thankyou'. So Al Melili was interpreting what the fellow was saying. I told Al to tell this guy that it was not true that he expected the group to be all Negro because he knew that it wasn't when he came to Rome to discuss the contract. What Al told him, I don't know, but I could see that Al was afraid to speak up for our rights, and I figured that if Sangiorgi or Fred Palmer had been there, things would not have happened the way they did.

I knew that Melili had not done much work since he had come back to Italy from Egypt where he had stayed quite a number of years and he did not want to lose this opportunity to work. The results of the discussion was that the man would not pay the same price for a mixed orchestra as he had proposed to Sangiorgi when he was in Rome and to my estimation, knew that the orchestra would not be all Negro. To go back to Rome and do nothing was not my idea of something to do and I accepted the fact that it was better to do the season with a cut of salary than to do nothing at all. But I was getting sick and tired of the Italian way of doing business.

I had received a letter before leaving Rome from Charles Delaunay saying that things were slow in Paris and all the summer resorts and casinos had already been booked for the season. I knew of no other impresarios in Europe. When Mr. Palmer arrived with a later train, I told him the sad news. I sent the next day a telegram to Lily, and told her to take a thing train that left the same time as I had. When she arrived, the first/she asked me to do was to take her to the nearest bar and buy her a drink because she just had had enough money to pay her train ticket and not even 10 lires left to buy some water from the boys who circulated in the train at each stops with water and she was dying of thirst.

The casino was not a real large one but it was very nice and looked more like a rich private home with a very large garden in front. It was surrounded by a high wall, and there was a bandstand in one corner near the street, and that's where we played. No one could see us from the street although we could be heard for quite a few blocks away. The casino was on Viale Carducci, a street that ran along the beach, the whole length of the town which must have been seven or eight miles long. Viareggio is a summer resort, not far from Pisa, and every year, around February or March, a big carnaval takes place there.
Viareggio is on the Mediterranean sea and there was a forest of pine trees called "la Pinetta" that ran through the town and many miles outside of it.

Our opening night was a big success and it was very joyful to be playing out in the open with the sky, the moon and stars above us. There was no canopy above the bandstand and the music did not go straight up to the sky, but I suppose Gabriel could hear what I was blowing. After our first set, I talked with some Italians that spoke english and were jazz fans and were happy to know they would have their favourite music to listen to for the first time in this resort.

After a few days, we started looking for a place where we could have a room and cook our own meals because we did not want to spend the biggest part of our small salary for hotel and restaurants expenses. Eventually, we found a place with a woman who had three rooms to rent and next door there were two rooms in a private home. Lily and I had a nice room in the front. Al Melili had a room alone, the drummer and bass shared a room. Atstella and the pianist took the two rooms next door. Fred Palmer of course had a room in a fashionable hotel.

Lily had volunteered to do the cooking for ourselves and the musicians that stayed in ourplace. We had two meals a day. After a few days the musicians started to ask for spaghetti at every meal before they ate anything else. Once or twice a week was enough for me and Lily. I started to get a little salty later when I realized that my woman was being a work horse for those guys that never offered her a small gift or a-nything, for what she was doing for them. But she had a good heart and as she had volunteered to do the cooking to save them as well as myself some money, she said that she would continue, even though I told her that she was not obliged to do so.

The place where we lived was on the opposite of the pine wood, which was long but half of a mile wide and we could walk to and from the casino in 15 minutes. Sometimes, Lily and I would rent a couple of bicycles and ride around town for hours and then take a nap in the afternoon. Most of the shops and business places closed from 12 noon until 4 PM, because the weather was so hot that the people who were not on the beach, stayed inside their homes until the sun cooled off a little. We also had plenty of time to go to the beach although I was not a great swimmer. We met quite a number of people that we eventually became well acquainted.

We visited Pisa quite often as it was not far from Viareggio. The first time I saw the leaning tower, I could hardly believe my eyes when I saw the angle it was leaning in. It looked as though it would fall over any minute and I suppose that is the impression that anyone would have the first time they saw it.

The owner of the casino belonged to the Communist party and the United States was involved in the war in Korea. Every Week we had to meet with him at least twice because of our salary. The people that cared for jazz music were not very numerous so there was never a large amount of people at the casino. Therefore, the place was not taking in much money of nights and the owner was always behind in giving us our weekly salary which was weak. We would get half of what it was supposed to be at the end of the week and the rest during the middle of the week. And when we went to his office, it seems that that was the happiest moments of his life when he could talk about the difficult times the Americans were having in Korea. And if they lost a battle that made him so overjoyed that I thought he was going to wet his pants. Either Al Melili or Fred Palmer would explain to me what he was saying. But he really got his kicks when something went against the Americans. The whole region was communist but I never had any difficulties with anyone and at no time.

Time passed and the summer season came to a close at the 3rd of September. Fred Palmer had heard from "Bass" Hill in Germany and "Bass" arranged for Fred and Arstella to join whoever it was that he was playing with. I had met some musicians from Pisa who had asked me about doing some work with them in the region. It was Lily that had taken these affairs in charge for me because she spoke Italian and was beginning to pick up on English. So I decided to stay around that part of Italy for a while. The rest of the musicians that had been working with me, went back to Rome.

Lily and I were invited to Pisa quite a few times to have dinner with one or the other of these new found friends and we were treated royally. Some of these places I worked with this group were Calce-Montecatini, Vechiano, Sarzana, Lucca, Bagni di Lucca, Forte Miami and Pisa.
One night we were in Pisa and one of the fellows invited us to have dinner at his place as he was having a party that night. He had

prepared a fried chicken dinner. Our landlady had a little dog named Foufie and we asked our host to save the chicken leg bones for this dog. There was almost a mountain of bones and the next day when we showed them to Fouffie, he ran away so fast that you would have thought he had seen a ghost.

I had agreed to a new contract with the Chikito starting the 1st of December, 1950, so we decided to go to Paris to engage some musicians. We left Viareggio the 6th of October and arrived in Paris the next day. It was quite a thrill for Lily because she had never been to Paris and it was a pleasure for me to show her around this wonderful city. Paris has so many places to go and things to see, which is always amazing and I got as much kicks out of showing Lily what I knew of Paris as much as she got learning about the city.

A few days after we arrived I was contacted to make a five days tour with a small variety show called Radio Cocktail 51. The three Peter Sisters who were a very popular singing trio in the States were in France and there were two younger sisters named Edith and Joyce who had formed a singing duo and they were part of the show which included André Salvador, the brother of Henri who was very famous singer and comedian in Europe. I first met the Salvador brothers in late 1935 at the Villa d'Este when they were about 17 and 18 years old. They both played fine guitar and used to join us for a jam session at times. Don Byas was also engaged for the tour as was Lucienne Marney who was famous for impersonating other actors. Also Francis Linel, a singer and comedian. The other musicians were French and lead by a pianist named Henri Lecca.

The two sisters were billed as the Peter Sisters Jr. and their mother travelled with us. Our first date was in Perpignan at the Nouveau theatre the 23rd of October. Then came Toulouse, Castre, Montpellier, Beziers, which was the last date. In Montpellier, Joyce and Edith ran into some racial trouble which I have never experienced in France. They had been booked in a different hotel from the one we were in and when they arrived and asked for their reservations, they were told that none had been made for them. Miss Lucienne Marnay was booked in the same hotel and when she heard that the Peter Sisters were refused a room, she raised hell in French, because Edith and Joyce were not able to do it in that language. When Lucienne got through telling whoever it was at the desk, what she thought of them and what a scandal she would make against the hotel, they found the reservation for Joyce and Edith but quick.

We came back to Paris the 28th of October and did different gigs the 11th of November when Don Byas and myself were engaged to open a new club called the Perroquet. A Hollywood starlet named Marsha Gayle was the directorist of the club which was at 49, rue de Ponthieu in back of the Champs Elysees. Ruddy Castel, a cuban orchestra leader played afro-cuban music while Don and I taken care of the jazz. A young girl dancer in Catherine Dunham's show, that was playing a theatre in Paris, was making her debut as a singer in the Perroquet Club. Her name was Eartha Kitt. Also on the bill was an african dance troupe called Kanois. But the club didn't go well despite it was decorated very nicely. The music and show were good but it closed after a week.
I did a couple of radio shows, one being broadcast to Sweden and a gig in Chalon-sur-Saône and left Paris the 28th of November for Bern, Switzerland.

Fred Palmer was to join me in Bern because he had finished his job in Germany. I engaged a pianist from Martinique named Pierre Jean Louis who had a style of playing that was a little like Theolionus Monk, but with more technique. Pierre was a big fellow who could drink his share of juice and some of mine, but was never drunk and always in good humour. Georgie Smith was back again on drums. A bass player named Alvin "Buddy" Banks had received his discharge from the army in Germany and had come to Paris where I engaged him. "Buddy" was on the Oscar Pettiford kicks and was a very promising musicians The alto player I engaged was also the Martinique musician named Edouard Pajaniandy who also played clarinet and piano.

We opened at the Chikito the 1st of December and finished the 31st of March, 1951. I had a concert in Brussels, Belgium at the Palais des Beux-Arts and played concerts with my group in Geneva, Bienne, Zurich, Neuchatel and Luzern. These dates taken place between the 2nd and 16th of April. I had a contract to play at the cinema Rex in Zurich for 11 days starting the 16th of April. I was having a longer and more successful run with this orchestra then I did with the first one. I had some arrangements that were made by a trombone player from South America named Bill Tamper whom I had met during my stay in Paris after I came back from Italy. I had orchestrations from different music publishers, so my band stands were not empty,as they were the first time I had played the Chikito.

We had played the Jazz club of Luzern the 12th of April and coming back to Bern which was still our jumping off point in Switzerland, I told the fellows that we would play the Rex starting the 16th. Georgie Smith said that he was not going unless he saw my contract. I thought he was kidding because he or anyone else had never said anything like that to me and I had never heard any musician ask the leader to let him see his contract. I ask him what did he mean and he said: 'Put the contract on the table,' which meant that he really wanted to see it. I told him that my contract with the Rex was my business and I was not going to show it to him or anyone else, and told him to think it over and let me know how he felt when we arrived in Bern. When we were there, I asked him his decision, and he said that it had not changed.

I can be just as stubborn as anyone else if the occasion calls for being that way and I told Georgie that my decision had not changed either and that it had been nice knowing him. I knew that Wallace Bishop was in Basel, Switzerland and had heard that he was not working. So I got in contact with 'Bish' the next day and he was free and willing to join me. We opened the Rex and the band sounded better than before, because Bishop had more experience on drums than Georgie Smith, which gave us a different inspiration. There was an Afro-American ballet lead by a dance director named James Fields which was an all Negro troupe.

One day, the manager of the Rex came to me and told me that one of the musicians had come to his office and asked to see the contract. Here we go again. I asked him what did he do and he said that he had let the musician see it. I was mad as hell and told the manager that he should not have done that because my contract with him was a personal matter between he and I, and was no concern of my musicians. He seemed surprised that I had taken that attitude but I made him understand that I was the one that did business with him and not the musicians. I found out that it was Edouard Pajaniandy who was known to be a trouble maker. I had had several disputes with Edouard about different things which he would do to make it difficult for me to get along with him. I told him that if he stayed in my band, that I was going to tell the managers wherever he went that no one that worked in my orchestra had the right to see my contract.

We finished the 26th of April at the Cinema Rex and went to an engagement in Blankenberge, Belgium. Blankenberge is a summer resort on the North Sea and we opened at the Cave du Majestic on the beach, which is very early date to start a summer season and as it was so early, not many places that do business from June till September were open and we only worked the last three days of every week during that time until June.

Bishop received an offer from Switzerland to join an orchestra that was going into the Chikito, which paid him moremoney than he was making, working only weekends, so he left the 20th of May, and I came to Paris to look for another drummer. Fred Palmer left and went back to Italy, so I had to look for a tenor man also. After two days in Paris, I found a drummer who was a West Indian, whom everyone that knew him called "Dreamer". The tenor man I engaged was a Martinique named Andre Siobud. He was a good musician and a nice and quiet person.

The owner of the Cave du Majestic had another place called the Palais d'Eté, not far from the Cave, which resembled a large beer hall. In fact they served more beer than any other drink. Alchohol is not served in most cafes and dance halls in Belgium. This place had two bandstands and engaged attractions. We had to play afternoon tea dances and I disliked that, because we had to play on a bandstand that was in the window near the entrance. There was quite a large terrace with tables, where people could have drinks and then there was the dike who was like a very large promenade in front of us, the beach and the deep blue sea. I hated playing in this window, because it made me feel that we were similar to a circus side show band that had to bellyhoo to the people outside, to get them to come inside. But playing in the cave was nice.

The owner, M. Bonnevalle, also ran a movie house in another town and he was a nice man to work for. As I said before, no alchohol was sold in his place, I mean like cognac or whisky, the strongest thing was vermouth or beer. But there was a liquor store on a street just behind the cave and I had a pint bottle which I would take there and get me juice from a barrel.
Everything went along smoothly until the end of June, and we had been playing every afternoon and night since the 15th that month. Then we found out that the boss didn't have a working permit for us.

Why, I cannot say, because he must have known that it was necessary. Then he tried to get the permits and we found out that he had been in trouble with the government about taxes and had put all of his business in the name of his girl friend whom he had been living with for years. The result was that we were refused working permits, and the 9th of July, we all left Belgium. Buddy Banks had married a Swiss girl, so he went to Switzerland, and I came to Paris.

Home was wherever I hung my hat, and I travelled with all my earthly belongings. When Lily and I got together, she had quite a few things also. We had left a few bags in Switzerland and when the gig in Blankenberge fell through, we decided that Lily should do to Switzerland to get the suit-cases we had left there and I would go to Paris with the things we had with us. I left with 11 pieces of luggage, and when I had to change trains in Brussels for one that would bring me to France, the train was so crowded that I had to leave most of the bags in a corner of the vestibule of the coach I was riding in. I was worried about having to open all those bags when the custom agents would come through at the border. But to my surprise, all they did was to ask for my passport.

I had always lived in the Pigalle section of Paris and as I had given Lily the address of a hotel on a rue Blanche where we had stayed before, that's where I went to await her arrival. Five days after I arrived, I received an offer through the help of Charles Delaunay, to work at the Club Vieux Colombier, a club I had worked for a while with the Edouard's band and Don Byas. This time, it was with a young French pianist named Claude Bolling. I started the 14th of July which is a National holiday in France, and as the club was in a different section of Paris known as the Left Bank, Lily and I decided to move to this side of town. And things were jumping on the Left Bank because there were plenty of students, writers and painters. There were more jazz clubs on this side of town than at Pigalle which was more renowned for strip tease joints. We moved into the hotel Crystal on rue Saint Benoit near Boulevard St.Germain des Prés. The Vieux Colombier was a five minutes walk from the Crystal. And just across the street from the hotel was a club known as Club St. Germain des Prés.

The corners of Boulevard St. Germain des Prés and rue de Rennes, St. Benoit and St. Germain were the most popular corners of the district, and had very large cafés, where the students,artists and friends met.

My favorite café was the Café St. Germain des Prés, and I eventually made many friends there, amongst them quite a number of African students and dancers. After a few days with Bolling, I became acquainted with the name of the musicians. One I knew before was Roger Paraboschi, the ex drummer of the Edouard's band. Jaques Hess played guitar, Maxime Saury, clarinet, Gille Thibault, cornet, Guy de Fatto, bass, and Benny Wasseur, trombone. The style of the band was a mixture of New Orleans and swing. I had heard that Claude Bolling had been a child prodigy, and he was an arranger also, and loved the arrangements of Duke Ellington, regardless of the fact that Billy Strayhorn made many of the arrangements also.

The Vieux Colombier was jumping and the young dancers had picked up long before I came to Paris on how to dance the jitterbug. The African students were the best dancers, but there were some French cats that were on the ball and gave the Africans a tight race. I don't have any idea of how long Bolling had been working at the Vieux Colombier, but his band and I finished there the 2nd of September. Claude was going to work in the club St. Germain des Prés, starting the 17th of September and he made me two propositions. One was to work at the club as an attraction, and the other was being a regular member of the band. The last one was moreinteresting for me, because it paid a little more than the first proposition, and that's the one I went for.

In between the time that Bolling had to wait before opening at the club St. Germain, a proposition came to me to do a 7 days tour with a show that was organized by Jacques Canetti, whc was the booking agent that had booked Louis Armstrong's first tour in France in 1934. It was through the grace of a French drummer named Gerard Pochonet that I got this gig. I had done some gigs with Pochonet before. He spoke very good English and admired American Negro musicians. He was a go getter and nice drummer also. Bill Tamper, the South American trombone man and arranger was also hired for this gig and we played with an orchestra leader named Henri Lecca who was married to a well known singer named Rose Mania. Lecca was also on the tour I made with Don Byas and the Peter Sisters Jr.

The stars of this show were Felix Leclerc, a French Canadian Singer and composer and André Claveau, who was a very popular music hall and radio singer. Another person who was to become a big star later was a comedian named Fernand Raynaud.

Jack Gauthier was quite well known fantasist and singer. Rose Mania was also with the show; a woman named Paulette Lancry and a couple of duettists named Vared and Bailly made up the rest of the show. We played the first four dates in Belgium, then we went to Lille, Roubaix and Bethune. Our success with the public was as great, if not greater than the stars, and we were put under a certain pressure by Rose Mania and Henri Lecca. We went on before Rose and di only three numbers, closing with the Saint Louis Blues. Rose and Henri didn't want the curtains to close when we finished our act, because the public would have asked that we play another number, and that would have made it hard for Rose to follow us. So when we finished, we had to walk off the stage with the curtain open after taking our bows. Pochonet squawked to Henri Lecca about this because Bill Tamper and I squawked to him as we two could not speak good French. In one theatre, it happened. They closed the curtains and Rose came damn near not being able to go on. After that, everywhere we played, the curtains were left open when we finished our last number, and it made us feel foolish to have to walk off the stage when everyone else could have curtain calls when they finished their act.

Felix Leclerc was a very quiet and nice person to be with. Jack Gauthier, gay and full of life but André Claveau was very temperamental and playing big star. The show was often back stage as much as in the hall and it was very funny.

We came back to Paris the 11th of September and I started working at the Club St. Germain des Prés the 17th. Claude Bolling made some changes in his band and a trombone player named Charles Huss replaced Benny Wasseur. Paraboschi was replaced by a drummer named Robert Barnet and a bariton sax man named William Boucaya was engaged in the place of Jacques Hess. Gilles Thibault was out, because Bolling was

using only one trumpet and that was me. The club featured a show with a young woman that recited poetry accompanied by background piano music, an african dance troupe and me doing a couple of featured numbers with the band.

The 9th of November, 1951, I did a recording session for Phillips records CCI of which Jacques Canetti was one of the big directors. I had Bill Tamper to arrange the numbers and also play trombone. The other musicians were Jay Cameron who played alto on this session, but was actually a baritone player. William Boucaya, baritone, Jean-Pierre Sasson, guitar, Guy de Fatto, bass, Gerard Pochonet, drums, and Art Simmen, piano. Simmons

We were all on time for the session except Art. The starting time was two o'clock in the afternoon. So while waiting for Art, Jean Pierre Sasson and I composed a number and called it "Jumping at Pleyel" because we were recording on the stage of the Salle Pleyel. We recorded this number with the rhythm session minus piano and the other instruments.

Art finally arrived about 4, and naturally Canetti and none of the rest of us were happy about this. Art claimed that he had had another recording date that he thought would be finished in time for him to do the one with me. Canetti said that he never would use Art for another session and Boucaya who was doing a lot of studio work said that something like that only happens with jazz musicians.....

One night in November, I was surprised to see Josh White, the popular folk singer and guitarist come into the club. When we had a break, I went to his table. He was with some English people and he had come to Paris from London where he was working, to do a radio show for B.B.C. He engaged me and the band to do his show which was to be heard at Christmas and we recorded it the 23rd of November.

Another night, I met two movie stars who were in Paris either on vacation or to make a film. I was never a nosey Joe or curious as a cat, so I did not ask them their reason for being in the city. They were Shirley Winters and John Garfield. John was a heavy jucier and he slept in a chair almost from the time he came in until the night was finished for us. I had seen him in many films but had never seen or heard anything about Shirley Winters, who was a starlet then. She was a vivacious girl who liked to dance and had a crush for the trombonist who looked like Robert Mitchum.

We also had a visit of Tommy Dorsey one night. I had seen Tommy and heard some of his orchestras in the Apple, but had never met him. Someone asked him to sit in with us and although he did not have his trombone with him, he tried the one that Charles Huss had and found out that it was a good instrument, so he played a couple of numbers with us. I told him that I played in Sy Oliver's orchestra before I came to France and he was quite well pleased to hear that, as Sy had been his arranger for a few years. There was a photographer there that night and we taken a photo of him. I remember one night at a session in Jimmy Ryans when Tommy's brother, Jimmy Dorsey jammed with me and some other cats, so now I had met the two famous brothers.

At times I would have a gig out of town for which I would inform the artistic director of the club, whose name was Guy Masse. In March, 1952, on a certain date, I was engaged by Willy de Cort, president of the Belgium Hot Club to play a concert at the Galeries des Beaux Arts in Brussels. Don Byas and Art Simmen were also engaged for this deal. I don't remember the rest of the musicians. Another organisation had organised a concert with Sidney Bechet and as Willy was the first and biggest organiser or jazz concerts in Belgium, and I suppose he wanted to see exactly how strong he was with the fans, he organised this concert to take place the same night of Bechet's.

A few nights before I was to play in Brussels, some young fellows came to the club St. Germain and asked me if I could be engaged to play a few numbers on a river barge which they had transformed into a club. I told them they would have to get permission from Guy Masse and he gave it. The concert in Brussels was on a Sunday night and this thing on the barge was the following Monday night. I returned to Paris that Monday afternoon and played one set at the club St. Germain. Someone from the barge came to get me and when I arrived there, nothing was happening.

I waited around for quite a while, and after midnight came, I still had not played anything. I decided to take a taxi and go back to the club. When I arrived, Guy was furious because I had not come back in time to do the show. As he had given me permission to go to this gig, I didn't figure that he was expecting me back at a certain time. I finished the night at the club and he told me that I was fired. He just could speak a little English, and his words for telling me I was fired, were that he was kicking me out. When he said that, I told him that if he kicked me out, he would never forget it every time he would get dressed, and have only one shoe to put on, because the leg that he would use to kick me out, would be the one that he would have cut off. And that was the end of the Club St. Germain for me. Actually, I was engaged by Claude Bolling to play at the club and Mass was the director of the club and not the band leader. Bolling should have said something concerning if he wanted to fire me or not. But he was a shy young band leader and was afraid to say anything that may have caused him to lose his job.

Soon after I finished at the Club St. Germain, I received an offer to do two concerts in Berlin and left by train for Hannover the 27th of March. When I arrived in Hannover the 28th, I took a plane to Berlin. There I was met at the airport by some men from the television and two German jazz fans, Hans Blutner and Fritz Krull. They presented me to an American boxer named Tiger Jones who was campaigning in Germany.

I had an interview at the TV and di a concert the 29th with some very good German musicians after only talking over a few numbers I wanted to play. The public was very enthusiastic and I had a great reception.

After the concert, I was invited to the most popular jazz club in Berlin, so I was told. It was the largest jazz club I had seen in Europe. It could hold about 400 people. Hans, Fritz and Tiger Jones went with me. Jones was a jazz fan as so many athletes are. There was a fine guitarist whom I met, named Rediske and I sat in with his group and the joint was really swinging. Tiger Jones could sing and not bad, so he joined the session also. He was well known there because when he was not in training, he was in this club almost every night, I was told.

As this was my first time in Berlin, Hans and Fritz took me out sight-seeing the 30th. The effects of the bombings that Berlin suffered in World War II could be seen everywhere, but the bricks from the ruins were stacked in neat piles and the streets were the cleanest I've ever seen anywhere. I saw the gateway to East Berlin, the Russian war memorial and the stadium where Hitler had refused to shake hands with the great American Negro athlete Jessie Owens during the 1936 Olympic Games.

I did my second concert in a different theatre from the first one and in a different part of the city. There was a German trumpetist on the bill that night who was known as the best jazz trumpeter in Germany. His name was Macky Kasper and he was good. But his main claim to fame was that he could blow loud. He had some "iron chops" as we say in musical terms for a trumpeter. After the concert I went back to the club I had visited the night before and jammed with the cats again. Tiger Jones was also on the scene. The next day, I had a direct flight back to Paris.

In April I did concerts and balls in France and Belgium. The 7th I was coming back when Lily and Jimmy Davis met me at the railroad station. Jimmy told me that he was engaged to do a cabaret scene in a movie being filmed called 'The Respectful Prostitute', from a Jean-Paul Sartre novel. Joe Benjamin, the bass man and Bill Clark a drummer, were in France with Lena Horne, and they were going to make this cabaret scene also. Aaron Bridges was the pianist. The film featured an American Negro Shakesparian actor named Walter Bryant, and an American actress living in France named Barbara Leage.
We did one of Jimmie's tunes called "The blues jumped and got me", and we were only in the studio for two days. The loot was not much but it was fun making the film.

On May the 19th to be exact, I left Paris by plane for Morocco to join Gerard Pochonet, the drummer, Charlie Blareau, bass, Bob Aubert, guitar, a pianist whose name was Armand Borgono, and a tenor sax named Roll Evins. They had been in Casablanca a few days before I arrived. I had done quite a number of gigs with Pochonet in France and it was he that arranged for me to come to Morocco. There was an American white fellow named Glyn ________ who was a singer, and we did two concerts at the Municipal Theatre, the 21st and 22nd of May.

Casablanca reminded me very much of Egypt as concerned the weather and the way the Moroccans dressed. In Egypt, the women wore black djellabas and covered their faces with black veils. Those in Morocco were djellabas of different colours and covered their faces with different coloured veils. You could only see their eyes. There were no difference in the way that the native men dressed in both countries. Some wore djellabas, some were dressed like the men in European countries. The women in Egypt and Morroco who did not cover their faces or wear djellabas were girls that were not married I was told.

The 23rd we did a concer in Rabat and then came back to Casablanca to play as an attraction in a place called "l'As des Clubs"(the ace of clubs). To say a few words about the musicians, I had known Blareau and Aubert in Paris and they were both fine young musicians who played good jazz. The pianist was good also and knew how to accompany a soloist. Glyn was a red head cat that sang a Frank Sinatra style, but I had never met him before.

At the Ace of Clubs, there was a giant size Arab who was the doorman and he spoke very good English. We became quite friendly that night. And as I liked a little taste of gage now and then, and was also aware that I was in a country where I could get some good stuff, I hit on this fellow and he was more than happy to get me a supply. The next night he had a nice package for me and some of the other musicians who also liked a taste now and then were my guests.

May the 24th, we did another concert at the Municipal Theatre in Casa and attraction at the Club where I played also the 25th. The 26th I went to Meknes to play with an orchestra composed of French amateur musicians who were residing in Morocco and some of them may have been born there. The president of the Hot Club whose name was Conrad Matiossek, played trumpet and he is the only one that I remember. Most of the jazz fans were Europeans in Morrocco and as they seldom ever heard many American musicians in the flesh, I drew some nice crowds to my concerts. I went to Meknes from Casa by bus and came back the same way. The things that I saw going and coming from Meknes made me think that I was back in the old biblical days according to what I had read in the bible, of which I read more than half of in my early youth.

I was supposed to come back to Paris from Casablanca the 27th of May but the Air France company had a strike that day and I was obliged to stay in Casa. There was a Martinque trumpet player named Eddie Laspar whom I had known in Paris who was co-director of a club in Casa called Cabane Cubaine. Eddie asked if I would like to do a few numbers in his place that night and I accepted as I had nothing else to do. The musicians were not very up on jazz but I closed my ears as best I could to many of the things that were not what they should have been and had a fairly nice time. Next day, the Air France strike was over and I came back to Paris very pleased to have some agreeable days in Morocco. Ever since my stay of one year and two months in Egypt, I've always had a sentimental feeling about some of those North African countries.

The month of June '52, I did gigs in France and Belgium. Had a few also in July until the 16th when Lily and I left Paris for Chamonix, which is a summer and winter resort. It was a beautiful trip going up in the mountains on a special train for climbing mountains where the tracks seem to never stop going around and up.

Chamonix is a very nice and clearn little town or moreso village and is the centre of all mountain climbing expeditions to the famous "Mont-Blanc" and others that surround the village. I was engaged to work the summer season in a place called l'Outa. A summer season in many places in Europe is usually from the middle of July until the last of August with a few places continuing for two weeks in September.
I had not known any of the musicians I was to work with although

they were from Paris, but they knew about me. The leader of the group was the bass man and there was a guitarist, tenor, pianist and drummer. l'Outa was anice place on the main street of Chamonix and it had a very large park like garden in the back. We were obliged to play every afternoon for what is known in Europe as Tea Dance and we did it in this nice garden. It would have been great if some people had come there. Tea Dancing died during the Second World War, but many people that owned clubs and dance halls did not want to accept the fact that those days of gigolos and tangos in the afternoons were gone with the wind. So we played to the flowers and the tress in the garden every afternoon from 5 until 7 and that was/only drag about the job.
I eventually got to know the names of the musicians but can only remember the guitarist's name which is Harry Katz. His brother married one of the Peter Sisters - Ann.

The pianist was not a jazz man but he could accompany in the old way that pianists did way back when. Harry was a fine guitarist who also played bongos. The leader was a solid bass man but not a soloist which has never been a real necessity to make a band whateve r it is.

We were staying in a hotel where a stream from the mountains passed just under our window. The water was as grey as some days that I have seen and the current was so swift that it sounded like the water that goes over Niagra Falls in a continuous roar. It was beautiful to see this stream coming down from the mountains and going to Lord knows where with such rapidity, but trying to sleep with that continuous roar was impossible. So after a few days, Lily went to a real estate agency and asked if there was a possibility of renting a small chalet somewhere near. They found one for us that had everything that was needed. We were near the same stream that passed by the hotel but it did not roar at this spot and we were about 10 yards away from it with the mountain trains passing 1 yard from our side porch. But that never disturbed us, because they were electric trains and did not make much noise. We named the chalet Billily, half my name and half for Lily.

We went on visits to the Sea of Ice and were happy in our little chalet which was the first time we felt that we had our own blue heaven. All that was missing was Baby, and we found a little cat to take the place of one.

There was only one other place in town that had a group of musicians and that was the Casino. But they were not a jazz group and played the type of music that most groups and larger orchestras were obliged to play in small town casinos. When the public wanted to hear jazz, they came to l'Outa and we had a good crowd every night. There was also a master of ceremonies by the name of Willy Sanders who was also French and he entertained the audience by telling jokes, some that I eventually understood. Harry, the guitarist was the only one in our group that spoke English andhe was a great help to me when I wanted something explained to the other musicians concerning music .

We finished at l'Outa the 24th of August, a little early to finish a summer season that's the way it was there. I had some gigs in the vicinity of a town called Sete in the Southern part of France, but the first one was not until the 29th of August. I was also contacted for a tour of 21 days in Germany starting the 12th of September.

Lily had started to work on a concert tour of France for me, a few months before we came to Chamonix and we decided that there was no need for us to hurry back to Paris, as she could work on the coming tour where she could be away from the noise of a big city and she could concentrate better in our little chalet than she could in a hotel room. I was really surprised to discover that Lily was a woman that had a business head and not knowing anything about jazz until she met me,and after only being in France for a short time, was capable of organizing a concert tour.

I had been a little reluctant at the beginning, thinking it could mean troubles, but Lily had convinced me that it would be interesting work for me and the publicity all over France and Europe would be very valuable. So I got in touch with musicians in New York that I wanted to make the tour with me. My ole pal Dickie Wells on trombone, Tommy Benford, drums, and Jimmie(Slim)Rodgers, an-ex-Benny Carter pianist.

Some people had advised Lily against a tour of the kind she had in mind and one was Charles Delaunay who feared that we would loose money. But we had met a young fellow named Jean-Gabriel Formisyn who lived in Toulouse, when we were there at an earlier date. Jean was an architect and he was 100 per cent for a tour featuring me with my own group and he talked a long time with Lily about it and told her that he could get her some good connections with managers of theatres un many towns, and he was willing to work with Lily to organize the tour. He came to Chamonix for a few days with lots of information and ideas about the tour and also ideas of how the posters should be made.

The 28th I left Lily in Chamonix to continue her work for the tour and I to do my gigs. I had taken my ticket for Sete in Chamonix and had asked information as to what changes should be made, if any, and where. My train left at 5'20 in the afternoon. That was the special mountain train and I had to change to a normal one in St.Gervais. At the station in Chamonix, I was told that I would have to change at another town but they didn't mention at what time. After a couple of hours away from St. Gervais I began to wonder what time the train would arrive at the place where I was supposed to change. I didn't know where that town was located. In France if you don't know what time you are supposed to arrive at your destination or where you should change from one train to another, the trip can be very unpleasant, and especially if a conductor does not pass whom you can ask some information. This was a night train and the trip was a terrible one for me because I was in a compartment alone and not one conductor came through during the night.

I would doze until I felt the train slowing down and then jump to the window to see if we were coming into the place where I was supposed to change. The conductor don't come through to announce the next station as they do in the U.S.A., Switzerland and Germany. So I was jumping up all night until 4 a.m. when a conductor finally came through. He told me that I didn't have to change trains because this one went to Sete directly. The train arrived at my destination at 5'15 a.m. and I was certainly in a bad humour because I had been given the wrong information, and I had not slept the whole night because of that.

I played two dates in Sete, one in a place called Agde, another in Amelie les Bains and two in Perpignan and left there the 4th of September for Paris because I had to see a lawyer there who was in charge of getting me a divorce from my wife Madelyn. I returned to Chamonix the 5th and there was alter from Tommie Benford saying that he could not join me for the tour because he had been playing in the orchestra of Jimmy Arche for a few years and Jimmie would be coming to Europe at a later date so he decided to stay with that group. He was the one that had asked me many months before we had planed a tour to see if I could get something for him to do in France.

The 10th of September, I had to leave Chamonix for Geneva, Switzerland, where I was to take a train for Hannover, Germany to begin the 21 days tour of that country. The concert tour of France was to begin the 13th of October. Lily was to leave for Paris in a few days and would inquire about a drummer to replace Tommy Benford.

The 12th of September, I met the orchestra, rehearsed with them that afternoon and did a concert at the Niedersachsenhalle in Hannover that night. The leader of the orchestra was a trumpet player named Fred Bunge(prounced Bun-gee), Teddy Paris was the name of the drummer and the pianist was Glen Buschmann. There was a sax man, trombone and bass, but I dont remember their names. The group had also a girl singer and another girl that played harmonica, and a master of ceremonies. Fred was considered as the best jazz trumpet man in Germany but after listening to him for a few concerts, I considered him one of the best in Europe. He was much better than Macky Kasper, whom I had jammed with in West Berlin 6 months before. Macky was loud and did not have the finesse, technique and ideas about jazz that Fred had.

Teddy Paris was an up to date drummer that knew how to push a soloist and he put just as much heart in what he played behind me as he did for those that he had been playing with for a long time. I'd say that he was a German Sid Catlett. And Glen was a fine pianist, sort of in a Teddy Wilson style and an arranger also. He and I had a friendly disagreement about a number that I was featuring and he had recently made an arrangement on the number and played it on two of the first concerts we did, before I came on. The number was 'St. Louis Blues'.

Of course I did not play it after the band gad done it, but I told Glen that it was the'St. Louis Blues' even though he called it something else. And anyone that knew anything about jazz would have known it was what they had heard. After the discussion, they did not play it as long as I was touring with them and I featured it again.

The girl that played harmonica was very good and one of the numbers she featured was the version of Harry James "Carnival of red Venice". I regret that I did not mark her name in my little/book because she was the only female I ever heard that played jazz on harmonica.

Fred, Teddy, Glen and the girl singer spoke very good English and I always had one of them to help me choose something to eat in the reataurant and other things that I did not know how to ask for in German. Glen lived near Dormund and the night after we played there, we had the next day off. Glen invited the whole group to his home that day, That is, he invited everyone except me. Perhaps it was because I didn't speak German, and they wanted to have a ball without having to translate things to me.
