We were in a hotel in the centre of Dormund and there was a nice restaurant in the hotel.

When I came down to the restaurant about noon, I had a feeling for my favourite fruit which isham and eggs. But I could not read the menu and the waiter could not speak English or French. Usually, in a hotel as nice as this one was and in a big city also, it would be possible to find someone who could say or understand a few words in English or French, but I was cooked gander that day because no one there spoke anything except German. Eventually, I just put my finer on something on the menu and told the waiter:"Das"...I don't remember what it was, but I ate it. Later, I found out that ham and eggs in German is "chinken mit ei", the same as we say eye in English which means eggs. I had made signs of an eggs and even cackled like a chicken, and granted like a pig, but I didn't get any ham and eggs that day!

And that reminds me of a very funny story about a group of Lindy Hoppers that came to Paris with the Cotton Club Show in 1937. The only thing they learned to ask for in French when they went to a restaurant was "oeufs aux jambon", which is ham and eggs, and that's what they ate two or three times a day, as long as they were in France!

I played 21 cities with Fred Bunge in Germany. Sometimes, we did two concerts a day but in different towns. The last one was Wuppertal the 2nd of October, and I came back to Paris the next day. I enjoyed playing with Fred Bunge and his band and they told me that they had been very pleased to have worked with me.

During my stay in Germany, Lily had sent me a letter, saying that she had engaged Zutty Singleton to make the tour with me, that she was organizing. I was not real happy about the deal, although I liked Face, as he was called by everyone that knew him well. I was certain that he would be a very disagreeable person to get along with when it came to working with him. But we were stuck and needed a drummer, so that was that!

Later, while still in Germany Lily wrote me and said that she had received a notice that Jimmie "Slim" Rodgers had died suddenly. Se had heard about a young Canadian Negro pianist that was playing in a club in Paris and asked Zutty and his wife Margie to come with her to hear this pianist and let her know if he thought the fellow was good and would be alright for our band. Afterwards, Zutty said that he liked the way this fellow played and that he thought he would be O.K. Lily told me his name was Randy Downs. He must have come to Paris either during the time that we wre in Chamonix or while I was in Germany, because I had not known anything about him before that time.
So Lily had a talk with Randy and he was willing to make the tour. She drew up a contract for him and Zutty and they both signed.

A few nights later, Zutty and his wife went back to the club where Randy was playing and his night, Zutty didn't like Randy's playing. It must have been a case of Zutty's gage that convinced him that Randy was alright the first night. But Lily had signed the contract with Randy and we would not be able to get rid of it. She had engaged Buddy Banks who had been with me before, on bass.

Dickie Wells arrived in Paris the 6th of October, 1952. I went to meet him at the station with Charles Delaunay. Dickie had forgot his coat in New York and the weather was quite bad, the day he arrived, so he was freezing.

We started rehearsals the next day. We had also engaged a young French musician from Toulouse, Guy Lafitte. He was 21 years old and played the tenor and clarinet. The previous year, he had made a concert with Mez Mezrow and Zutty and had got good reviews from the jazz critics.

Arstella Whitthers, who meanwhile on the suggestion of Lily, had changed her name for the pseudonyme of Martine Kay, had been engaged for the tour. But a few weeks before, she wrote that she was ill and could not make the tour. Lily tried to get in touch with her immediately as we had started to advertise her, but she couldn't be found nowhere. What had happened was that the girl had fallen in love and would not leave her boy friend for several months. Lily was very sore for business reasons and also because Arstella and Lily had been on very friendly terms, and it was a hard blow for Lily.

Somebody signalled us that there was a singer named Miriam Burton in town. Miriam had been the leading singer in Katerine Dunham's group fo singers and had beautiful suprano voice. She was not a jazz singer really, but on ballads, she was wonderful. So, we engaged her also.

We paid every musician a half day salary for rehearsing. That was a gesture that we decided to do in order to become better friends with the guys. We also put in the contract that everyone would be paid a half day salary whenever we had an off day during the tour. We had hired a bus and the driver was an ex-wrestler named Louis Lamy. He was a great guy and become a good friend and a big help for Lily on the tour. He owned the bus and had some others that he rented for tours.

On Monday, the 13th of October, the first concert was given in le Havre. We were a little bit nervous, but Dickie was not in his usual form. He said that he had caught a cold because he didn't have an overcoat, and had to have some "grogs"(toddy). But we had a nice success and we were preparing for the concert in Paris at Salle Pleyel which taken place the 18th of October.

If we were successful with the Parisian concert fans, we were certain that we would have success in other places. Most of my friends came to the concert and the place was packed. We were more than well received, that is everything we did, except Miriam Burton, who was booed when she started to sing "Summertime". She had had a big success in the other towns we had played before Paris. But the Paris Fans just don't go for singers except for a few big names. However, Miriam was not embarrassed on the rest of the tour.

We played for a big gala at the Hotel George V, the 8th of November, for the League, against racism, and that was the only gala we played during the tour of which we did 43 cities in France. That included every big city in the country, and some that were not so large. Average, we had some good crowd, but after having paid the band, the bus driver, and all the expenses, there was not much money left for us.

The first time I ever saw my name in lights was the night we played in Le Mans, which was the 19th of October, after the Salle Pleyel concert. I was surprised when I arrived at the Cinema Rex in that city and saw "Bill Coleman and his orchestra " in big red lights on the marquis.

The next time I saw "Bill Coleman and his orchestra" in big lights was when we did a concert in Barcelona, Spain, the 19th of November. It was a coincidence that it was just one month after Le Mans, and it was a pleasant sight for me to see. And I was thrilled to have had the opportunity to be the first American jazz man to do a concert in Spain since Benny Carter had done one there in 1936. It was the first time I had set foot in that country, and we were treated like Kings. The two brothers Papo, who were two young boys then, took us out in the city to sightseeing. We didn't have much time, but what we did see, we enjoyed.

The tour also taken us to Belgium for three concerts and 8 in Switzerland, which was something extremely rare for an orchestra to do in that country. But there are plenty of jazz fans in Switzerland, and I was quite well known there. And I'm certain that I'm the only American musician that ever done concerts in 43 cities in France with a group.

The period between the 15th of December and the 15th of January is a difficult one to organize concerts, so Lily had asked the musicians if they would agree to work in a cabaret during that period, at a different price ofcourse; the tour could start again inthe second part of January. We had received an offer for the band to work at the "Chikito" in Bern, Switzerland. Everybody had agreed. We told the musicians that the club would be closed the 25th of December, and the 1st of January, and therefore, we would not get any salary for those two days. Lily had asked Zutty if he wanted a special contract for the Chikito, but he said that it was not necessary, that everything was O.K. with him.

But about two weeks after we were on tour, Zutty went into his act which I was afraid he would do, when Lily wrote to me in Germany and told me that she had engaged him for the tour. I knew he had a reputation for being moody and difficult to work with. He would be at times very unpleasant. It was a pity, because he and Marge were such jolly people when you didn't have to work with them, started to be real drags, staying for themselves, refusing friendly advances. They had an old dog named "Bring Down" travelling with them. It came to the point that Zutty coming in the bus, was holding Bring Down really tight so nobody could pet the dog. Dickie tried to make jokes and bring some gaity in the bus, but Zutty told him to shut up.

Zutty couldn't stand the pianist, and every night was growling about...that sh...pianist. He would slow down the tempo terribly, and if I said something, try to put the blame on Randy. He was making me feel miserable, and nobody was happy about that situation except Randy and Bank who didn't care and were close buddies. Those two were always up to some foolishness.

One night, it was almost 9 p.m., and they had not shown up at the theatre. Somebody told me that they had been seen in an amusement park near the theatre and that they were riding a Merry-go-round. I went to check and effectively found them having a ball on a merry-go-round for kids, wearing two long bonnets, one green, one red.

Zutty started to tell me almost every week, that he wanted to be paid for the two nights that we would not work at the Chikito. And every week, I would tell him that I was not being paid for the two nights either, and I was not going to pay him as a special favour from my pocket.

Dickie Wells and Miriam Burton were not supposed to go to the Chikito with me and our last concert was at Chaux-de-Fonds,Switzerland, the 13th of December. Dickie left for France the next day to go back to New York and Mariam Burton came to Paris where she was living.

We started in the Chikito on Tuesday the 16th, had the Christmas night off. We were paid every Monday night, and our first pay came on the 22nd. It was the 29th when we received our second week's salary, minus the Christmas night that we didn't work. Zutty had asked me to be paid in dollars and that's how I paid him. So this time, when I gave him his salary and he counted it, he told me that it was not the right amount. I told him it was right because we were not paid for the night we didn't work. He was salty as a bag of salt peanuts, but didn't say anything more to me.

The next afternoon, I heard from someone that Zutty had left. I called Mr. Tripet who was the owner of the Chikito and told him what happened. Ofcourse, Zutty couldn't be stopped from leaving the country, but Tripet could have had his baggages held the same as the French agent named Canetti had done to Louis Armstrong in the 1930's when Pops left for New York before playing an engagement, Canetti had booked for him. But Zutty had gotten away too early. However, as he and I were members of the 802 musicians union in New York, I wrote to the Union and brought a charge against him for leaving a job without giving me a two week's notice, and the Union condemned him to pay me two week's salary, which he had to do.

Later, I read an interview that Zutty gave to a jazz magazine that he had been working with me in Europe for peanuts which was to say that I paid him a small salary. He had 250 dollars a week with me which was a good salary anywhere in 1952 and there are musicians in the U.S.A. today that don't make a salary like that for a week's work. And he didn't mention that on the tour he did in Europe with Mezz Mezrow, he only had 200 dollars a week. And that's a fact that I know is true.

When I was in Geneva with Jack Dieval, I had met a young Swiss drummer called Caspoil whose real name was Pascal Jeanmairet. He had left me use his bicycle during my stay of one month, and I rode it around town most every day. So when I found out that Zutty had left, with the help of my friend Felix Debrit, I was able to get in touch with "Casspoil". He was actually an amateur drummer, but he studied the drums and could play very well. As luck would have it, he was free to join and arrived in Bern that afternoon in time for the job that night. It was the 30th of December, and I was very lucky to have found a musician free at that period in the year. And the band played better than it had for a long time because Zutty had been a drag with everyone on the tour and it was nice to see a smiling face behind a set of drums and have them played correctly.

I had signed a contract with Miriam Burton only for the tour because I knew that she was not the kind of singer for a night-club. Miriam knew another American Negro girl that was in Paris with her sister. Miriam knew that she could not be hired for the Chikito, so she sent this girl to see me. Her name was Suzette Aimes. Suzette had a very nice low voice and her approach to singing jazz was quite new and could be compared with the way some of the girls are singing today such as Aretha Franklin, etc. But she was singing in a very unusual key and did not know many standards. In fact, her repertoire was very small. It was easy to feel the girl didn't have much experience, if any, but she was swinging in a manner that Miriam could not have done and Suzette was a quiet type of girl who was born in Harlem and she was easy to get along with. So everything went smooth for a while at the Chikito.

The replacement for Dickie Wells was Benny Waters whom I had worked with in Charlie Johnson's orchestra. He had come to Switzerland with Jimmy Archey, the band that Tommy Benford was coming to Europe with after I had arranged with him to make the tour with me. This orchestra was very badly handled by whoever the agent was that had them to come to Europe and after a very few concerts, they all went back to New York, except Benny.

Benny played alto, tenor and clarinet but had left the Apple with only a clarinet and could not find a decent alto in Switzerland when he joined me. Guy Lafitte was playing tenor, so I didn't need another one. However, Benny fitted into the band very well, and the front line of tenor, clarinet and trumpet was very nice. Benny transposed all the alto parts and the arrangements went down well.

A few days after we started at the Chikito, I got quite a shock when I was called by the manager of the Chikito, and was asked to come to his office because there was some trouble with the Banks. When I arrived I was told that Banks was in the country illegally, and the police wanted to expell him within ____ hours. He had married a Swiss girl when he had worked the Chikito with me the second time I taken a band there and when the job in Blankenberg, Belgium fell through because of working permits, he had gone back to Switzerland, and was living in Zurich with his wife. What had happened was that his wife was a prostitute, and the law found out that he was not working and was living off the earning of his wife, and they expelled him from the country. He didn't tell me this and in fact, he told the owner of the bus, Louis Lamy, we used on the tour, that he was married to a Swiss girl who was very rich, had a big house and a big car, and that her parents owned the famous soup factory "Maggi". Louis told Lily and I the story and asked us if it was true or not? We straightened him out about the affair.

Mr. Tripet had been a colonel in the Swiss army and he could pull some strings with the government when it was necessary to do so, and he arranged things that would allow Buddy Banks to stay in Switzerland as long as I stayed and only if he worked with me. Then suddenly, Banks and Randy Downs got the idea that they wanted to go back to Paris and one week before my contract finished at the Chikito, they told me they were leaving.

Banks had a great influence on Randy who was a fine pianist, but young and easily influenced by a person like Banks,who was also a fine bassist, but wild and irresponsible. We closed on the 15th of January, 1953, and they left for Paris the next day I suppose.

Lily and I also came to Paris to engage replacements for Banks and Randy. I had five concerts booked in Switzerland after finishing at the Chikito and was booked for the month of February in St.Gallen which was near the German border.

I engaged the pianist Pierre Jean-Louis who had worked with me before but it was quite difficult to find a good coloured bass player. The trouble was that the people wanted me to bring an all Negro band. Of course, Guy Lafitte was white, but his dark curly hair and tone of skin could make believe that he had some coloured relative in the family. Casspoil was truly white, but the people insisted to have a majority of coloureds in the band.
I finally met a bassist named Emmanuel Jude whom I had known for a couple of years. I think that Jude was from Martinque as was Pierre Jean Louis.

We did our five concerts and started in the Palais Trischli in St. Gallen the first of February and finished the 28th. We had quite a nice success. That was winter time and we had a lot of snow. It was also carnival time, and that was a big affair for weeks in St. Gallen.

The pianist, singer Joe Turner, was living in Switzerland and happened to be playing in St. Gallen during the time that I was there, and we were able to get together a few times and reminisce about some good ole days back in the Apple.

About two weeks after I started in the Trischli, a fellow came to the boarding house where Lily and I were staying and announced to me that he was a lawyer who had been working with a colleague in Paris who was filling a suit against me for his client Buddy Banks who was claiming that I owed him 6,000 Swiss Francs, about 1800 dollars, for rupture of contract. He was claiming that we had done cabaret work instead of concerts at a lower salary, that the contract had not been fulfilled completely, and that the loss for him was of 6,000 Swiss Francs.

I was really disgusted with the guy to whom I had given a chance to be known in Europe, who had accepted that job in Bern, and who didn't even had the right to set foot in Switzerland to do concerts and was now asking for compensation.

Lily being Swiss knew about some of the laws of that country and told me that we should give all the things that were of any value that we had with us to the owner of the boarding house to keep for us, because whenever a law suit was filed against someone in Switzerland, the law could confiscate everything except that which was necessary for a person to use in his employment. In my case, it was my instrument and clothing. I had a movie camera, a new projector, and a few other things of value, and we gave these to the woman who ran the place where we were staying to keep for us. And a few days later, the lawyer came back with a detective and presented me with a paper which said that anything I had of value could be taken from me and held until my case was settled. I had two rings that were not of any value, but they took them from me. They could not, however, take my watch or my horn, and they didn't find anything else of any value that I did not need to use for my work.

I had an engagement after St. Gallen to work two weeks in St. Moritz. I finished at the "Trischli" the 28th of February and started at the Rosatsch Hotel Excelsior, which also had a casino, the first of March. Suzette and Caspoil had become real tight together, and things were going fine for them. Suzette's sister Dolores who had been a model and who was tall and quite extravagant, was travelling with us, but it was Suzette who was paying for her. Dolores and Caspoil didn't get along together, and sometimes had terrible rows.
For three nights, Benny Waters was high and bugging everybody by talking loud when someone else was talking a solo. He was talking mostly to Suzette who was trying to keep him cool, but in vain.

So after the third night of Benny's foolishness, I asked him if he was drinking during the day in his room and he said he was. I then asked him what he was drinking and he said, it was Pernod. That's a drink that people in France take before the regular working man's meal time as apertif. I had nothing against Benny for drinking because I drank also. But I wanted to find out the reason for him for being so high of nights, and although he played what he was supposed to play correctly, there was something wrong cooking in the kitchen. So I asked him if he drank a lot of it, and he did put enough water in it. He was very surprised when I told him that alchohol of that sort was supposed to be mixed with water and ice. He was driking big glasses of it pure, no wonder he was so high and excited. From that day on, he was cooler and not so very excitable on the bandstand.

One day, a few of us decided to go higher up in the mountains for a picnic in the snow. It was warmer up there where people went to ski than it was down in St. Moritz, and some folks were even taking sun bath. The hotel gave their clients box lunches for picnics and we took a funicular up to a station wherethe skiers disembark. If they care to go higher, there are ski-lifts to carry them to the highest points. There was also a hotel restaurant and chalets near the station.

Our group consisted of Guy Lafitte, his wife, Widy, Caspoil, Suzette and his sister Dolores, Lily and myself. We decided to walk higher up than where the station was situated, to eat our lunch. It was tough in some place as the snow was very deep and after climbing for an hour, we decided to stop and eat. We had bought some soft drinks at the station and really enjoyed the outing.

After a few hours, Dolores, Lily and I were ready to go back, and left the others. There was no fix pathway to come down, so we took what we thought was the right direction, as we could not see the station from where we were. And we ran in quite a bit of trouble. Sometimes we would sink down in the snow knee deep and once Dolores went down to her waist, and if she had been a person that weighed 150 pounds or more, we would have had to scream for help. As it happened that she had a weight of about 125 pounds, I was able to lift her out. That did frighten us, and then we saw a place where skiers had made a route to descend and we came down sliding most of the time. Afterwards, we thought we were lucky, because we would have fallen into a ravine.
Joe Castro

One night a party came to the Rosatsch and a fellow came up to me and said he was a pianist. He asked me if he could sit down in for a couple of numbers and naturally, I did not refuse him. He was an American, and a fine pianist. He told me his name was Joe, and he was in the party with Doris Duke, the five and ten per cent store heiress. I had never heard of him, but I did know who Doris Duke was, and I later found out that he was not only with her party, but with her... Lucky cat!

The waiter that served the party was a young fellow and when Miss Duke wanted to leave and pay him with a check, he would not accept it. When the waiters in this place served drinks, they had to pay them in advance to the buffet from their pockets and collect from the clients afterwards. The name of Doris Duke funnily didn't mean anything to this young waiter and he insisted that he wanted cash. No-one in the party seemed to have any cash with them, so the waiter was obliged to go to the Palace Hotel where Miss Duke was staying to get his money. But he got it.

We finished at the Rosatsch the 15th of March, and went to Zurich to play in a place called Hungaria-Esquire starting the 16th. The Hungaria was on the ground floor and was a large restaurant not very expensive with a tyrolian orchestra and attractions. I was near the center of town and the cliental was mostly people who were passing through town. The Esquire was on the second floor and was a night club with the only attraction being the orchestra. The cliental there was of a higher standing than down in the Hungaria. Every night we had to play for a half hour in the Hungaria and that was a drag for me because I knew that jazz was way over the heads of most of the people there. But we always had a nice round of applauds when we finished, which made me wonder if the public really dug us at times or it they were happy that we had finished. But it really jumped upstairs at the Esquire.

Pierre Jean Louis had to come back to Paris after we finished in St. Moritz, so through Charles Delaunay, I engaged a French pianist named Jean-Calude Pelletier. I had never met him in Paris, although he was in the jazz circle and was a fine pianist with a swinging style, that sometimes on the order of Teddy Wilson in the left hand and Joe Sullivan in the right hand. And still there was a personality of his own in his playing.

We finished the Hungaria-Esquire the 31st of March, and that was the end of that orchestra. But Lilly was preparing another tour for the coming autumn and Benny Waters was going to be included in this tour. We had also landed a return engagement for the Esquire in June and had a contract for the month of August at the Caveau Majestic in Blankenberge, Belgium, where I had been refused a permit to work the summer before.

Lily and I went to visit some friends in Zurich for three days. A certain Mr and Mrs. Harry Pfister. Harry played sax and was an arranger also. I had met his wife Bettina in Paris when she came there with Felix Debrit for the jazz festival in 1949, and Felix talked to me about leading a band in Chikito. After the visit with the Pfisters, we went to visit Felix in his country home near Bern for three days and came to Paris the 8th of April.

I assisted in one of the post picturesque weddings I had ever seen. This happened in a part of Paris known as the Commune libre de la Butte Montmarte which is the surrounding of the famous Sacred Heart Church (Sacré Coeur). The marriage was that of a well known Gipsy Violinist Roman Jacowlew to a Miss Pilar Gonzales, a spanish actress. After the wedding ceremony, I lead a parade of montmartrois and Montmartroises (as the people from the Butte Montmarte are called) are dressed in picturesque clothes from the last century. Dozens of children were following, and I was the only one playing an instrument. The scene was televised and filmed. There were famous moviesactors present, and the best known of them was Luis Marino. Later there was dancing in the street provided by a group of accordionists and also tzigane music. The Mayor of the Butte Montmartre, M. George Giriel, made me an honorary citizen of the Butte.

A few days later, the Jazz at Philharmonic was giving a concert at Salle Pleyel. I knew weeks before when they would be in town,so Lilly arranged for me to give a cocktail party for them at the reception offices of Ricard, the makers of the well known appetizer. Roy Eldridge, Lester Young, Ray Brown, Joe Benjamin and Norman Grantz the organiser of the J.A.T.P. came to the cocktail. But there is a story about this cocktail that was very embarrassing for me.
The cocktail was supposed to start at 6 p.m. and finished at 8, and as I was the host, I was supposed to be there before the guests

arrival in order to greet them. I was to bring Prez, so I went to his hotel around 4 in the afternoon. I was obliged to wait for him to get dressed which he did not rush in doing so. Finally, we were able to get out of his hotel, but he told me that he had promised to bring his wife a singing bird that he and she had read an advertisement about in some American journal.

I knew of a place on rue Scribe near the American Express Co. so I took him there. When Prez saw that the birds were not live but stuffed and worked with a winding up machine, that gave out the sound of a bird singing, he was very disgusted because he thought the birds were live ones. But he bought perfume and different other things, and when we arrived at the party, it was 7:30! Lily was burning angry with me and she really had reason to be. Some people had been to the cocktail and had to leave early. One was my good friend Arthur Briggs. But there were quite a few people there including Richie Frost, an American drummer with whom I had gone to Austria with Jack Doevar's group, Ernie Royal and his wife, Jack Butler, a long time friend of mine, Walter Bryant the leading male actor in the film, "The Respectful Prostitute". Lily finally forgave me and Lester for arriving so late, but whenever she thinks about it even now, she gets salty for a few minutes.

...there was a young trombone player from the British West Indies named Herman Wilson, who had not been very long in Paris and I made his acquaintance with a friend of his named Donald Brown. I was in need of some musicians for my coming jobs in Zurich at the Hungaria -Esquire in June and August in Blankenberge. Donald played bongos and Congo drums, but had never played jazz drums in an orchestra. However, he said that he had a little experience on drums and thought he would catch on to the technique of playing if he was given a chance. So I offered him the chance and even signed as his sponsor for a set of drums. I engaged a French pianist whose professional name was Jack Sterling and his real name was Jacques Sansonet, which is the same, a starling or a sansonet being the same bird. I had been on some gigs at different times with Jack who was quite well known and played nice piano. I also hired a freckle faced Martinque bass player named and with Benny Waters, the group was complete.

The rehearsals went along very well, and Benny made some arrangements to add to those that I had in the books. Everything was cool until the day before we were to leave for Zurich,which was the 30th. A fellow who was also from Martinique came to our hotel and introduced himself, and said that he was a replacement for the bass player. This man's name was Lude. I had seen him around Pigalle, where most of the musicians met, but did not know that he was a bass player until this meeting. Lily and I thought that this was a strange story and we wanted to know if the other guy had taken sick or had an accident. But Lude told us that the fellow was not sick and had not been involved in an accident, and all that he knew was that he had asked him to take his place in my group.

So we decided to go see this cat and find out what his story was. I was upset because he had made all the rehearsals with the band, and the working permits were given individually, so one was at his name. He was also on the photos of the orchestra, that I had a photographer to take, and now he was sending someone else to take his place!

When we arrived at his home, we found out that he lived with his grandmother, and they both seemed upset at seeing Lily and I. His story was that he could not find his passport. But that was a lot of B.S., because he had known for weeks that the job we were going on was in Switzerland, and that he needed a passport that was in order.

After a half hour of watching this son of a bitch and his sad grandmother going through an act of utter despair, pretending to look through closets, in drawers and pockets, we became disgusted with both of them because it was plain to see that this bastard had decided that he didn't want to leave Paris and had engaged his grandma to play the game with him.

So we hired Lude officially, arrived in Zurich the afternoon of the 30th of May, and opened in the Esquire that night. I was the only one in my group that sang and the day we arrived in Zurich, it was raining. I usually wore a French beret, but did not have one with me at the time, my head got wet, and the next day, I was so hoarse that I could not sing: 'Am I born to die?'!; and the manager was not very pleased about no one singing, or I should say, me not being able to sing. I wasn't happy about it myself, but that was an act of God, and I was not able to sing for three days.

The band was not too bad considering that Donald Brown had never played drums before and Lude had not rehearsed with us. The front line was very nice together, and the public enjoyed our music which was our main interest, and after I got my voice back, everything was fine.

The job at the Esquire-Hungaria was a break-in for the orchestra, but we needed an engagement for the month of July to keep us going until August. So Lily decided to go to Germany and try to find an engagement. I was not too hot about her going there alone, but she could speak German and we had the address - a booking agency in Hamburg. She was also going to see a woman who was trying to book musicians, named Marianne Knüppel. I also wrote to my friend Hans Bluthner in Berlin and told him that Lily would be coming there at a certain date and ask him to help her in what every way he possibly could.

A few days after Lily left, a telegramme came to the pension where we were staying, announcing the death of Lily's mother, and this really upset me. The telegramme had been sent first to the American Express in Paris, then sent in Zurich in an envelope, and it would be too late for Lily to attend the funeral. I telephoned to Hans in Berlin, but Lily had already been in Berlin and left for Hamburg.

I didn't know where to get in touch with her. So the only thing I could do was wait until she came back to Zurich to tell her that her that her mother had passed away. My heart was really heavy when I broke the news to her. She left the day after for Pontarlier, where her parents lived, to pay her respects to her mother at her grave.

I had never met Lily's parents, except for some relatives in Neuchatel. Her father and mother had been terribly upset about her decision of getting a divorce. Her first husband belonged to a very wealthy family in Switzerland, and they were very proud of her siutation. Her mother could not understand that she wanted to get remarried with a jazz musician. Having a middle class state of mind, she could not give any real consideration to a profession of that kind. For her mother and father, it was living like Gypsys. In a certain way, she was not wrong about that. She had nothing against me, it was my profession and she would have rather seen her daughter remarried to a plumber.

Lily's trip to Germany didn't bring any result in placing the band for the month of July, but I was contacted by an agent in Holland to do July in Köln, Germany. This fellow did quite a bit of booking in Germany, but he was living very high upon the hog and the money he offered for the job was nothing to write home about. But I accepted it to keep the musicians from having to lay off a month. And I may not have been able to get most of them back for the month of August if I had not found some work for July.

We finished at Esquire-Hungaria the 29th of June, 1953, left for Köln the 30th and started working at a place called Moulin Rouge, the 1st of July. And it was to be an unforgettable, long, endless and unenjoyable month for me. The pay was so low that I was obliged to pay Benny Waters(who was the best musician in the band)two marks more than I was getting.

The first of July was a Wednesday and there must have been a crowd of 10 people that night. And they didn't stay more than one and a half hour because the waiters would stand by their tables, and as most of the people drinking white vine, as soon as a glass was empty, the waiter was filling it up and a bottle can go very fast amongst four or five people. The waiters really rushed the people to drink and the people rushed to get out of the joint and that left us playing for the waiters and the cashier who didn't know the difference between jazz and the tail end of a horse.

I saw the owner of the club once, and that was when we opened. But he was there every night until ten o'clock. The bad business that the place did, didn't seem to worry him. He was the manager of a boxer named Muller who was quite well known in Germany. He would play poker every night in another room until ten, and then he would disappear. The cashier was a woman, and she was in chrage of everything. We worked eight hours and had two fifteen minutes rest periods. And as there was supposed to be continuous music, three of us would play fifteen minutes and we'd alternate in that manner. I would play a little drums with Jack Starling at the piano, and Herman with his trombone. Then Donald Brown, Benny Waters and Lude would relieve us.

The most that ever came to the joint was one Saturday when there were at least 150 of them at 11 o'clock. At 2'30, the waiters had chased them all away, except a couple of fellows at the bar. At 8p.m. when we went to work, the sun was still shinning, and when we finished at 4.a.m., day was breaking, and the only happy things living seemed to be birds that we heard singing. No one ever came to me and told me that they were jazz fans, and I know there were some in town because was a place not far from where I was working called the Tabou and Wallace Bishop, my ex-drummer, was working there with a British West Indian tenor player named Sammy Walker, and some German musicians. And they played nothing but jazz in the Tabou. It was not our music that kept the jazz lover from coming to hear my band. It was just that the people that went for jazz knew that the Moulin Rouge was a jip joint and no jazz fan would have gone there even to hear Satchmo or Dizzy.

But we met a nice young couple who was planning to get married soon, Hildchen and Gunter Kwiatkowsky, who invited us in their parents' home and also introduced us to some of their friends. Sometimes, we were invited by some of them or went out in some keller. Colgone had been very heavily bombed and it was quite a sad sight to see.

Nearly every afternoon, I and some of the other musicians would meet Bishop, Sammy and some of the German musicians at a sidewalk café where we would talk some trash as all cats do when they get together, and one day,Bishop told me a story about Sammy concerning his getting high on a certain German made cigarette. The way Bishop told the tale, it seems that Sammy liked to pick up on some gage now and then, but for a certain time, he had not been able to find the stuff. So he bought a package of cigarette one day, and after reading about the ingredients which were written on the package in German, Sammy was getting his kicks from these cigarettes. But Bishop could not believe that a cigarette of that type would be sold in tobacco stores, and he asked Sammy to show him the pack, which Sammy was delighted to do. It stated that these cigarettes were made from a certain kind of tobacco, and'herein' contains a certain flavour. Sammy had read the word 'herein' and mistaken it with herofn, and his imagination that the cigarettes were loaded was making him believe that he was getting high. His feathers fell when Bish told him what herein meant!

Lily and I were planning another tour of France for the fall and we talked to Bishop about making the tour with us because Donald Brown was not and would not be experienced enough for a concert tour at the time we planned to do it. Bishop accepted. There was an Indonesian bass player working with Bishop named Eddie de Hass whom we engaged also for the coming tour.

The job at the Moulin Rouge was a drag more and more each day. One night there was only one man in the bar, and we were playing as if the place was full. Finally, this fellow left and it was almost 3'30, so I started playing "Goodnight Sweetheart", which was our closing theme. I looked at the cashier to get her reaction, and she was making a sign to me not to finish. I went over to her and asked her why should we continue when there was no one in the place, Her reply was that someone may come in. So we had to stay there until four and continue to play. And you can bet your dollar that she went to the top of my S.... list.
On the 27th of July, we finished at that drag joint and the 27 nights that I had worked there made me feel as though I had been in prison for a year during a term of hard labour!

We left Cologne at 7'20 the morning of the 28th, arrived in Blankenberge at 3'20 that afternoon and started at the Caveau Majestic that night. We were all feeling as though we had just awoke from a terrible nightmare. There were plenty of people, smiling and dancing to our music which made us play with more enthusiasm that we have done for a long time. It was like being in Heaven compared to what we had gone through in the Moulin Rouge in Cologne.

The manager of the Caveau had our permits to work in Belgium this time and we spent a lovely month there. Lily's trip to Germany had results for the band and I received an offer to play the month of September in Hamburg. That was rolling 'em Pete, because four months of steady work was very good for the band. We finished in Blankenberge the 30th of August, left the 31st and started working in Hamburg the first of September in a Dance Hall called Tanz Kasino Faun.

Herman Wilson had worked at the Faun with an American trumpet player named Claude Dunson and Herman spoke good German. The manager of the Faun could speak a little English and a little French also. Claude Dunson didn't speak German or French and I learned that whenever the manager of the Faun wanted Claude to change something, or he had something special he wanted to convey to Claude, he would say it in German to Herman, who would make the translation.

Herman sat on left end of the bandstand, and the manager started giving him messages to give to me. It would not have bothered me had I not known that the manager could speak and understand some English or French. I felt that my business with whoever was in charge of the place was between he and I, and not with my men. So I told this man not to tell Herman or any one else on the band to tell me what he wished from me, and if it concerned something special, I could always bring Lily to his office, and she would make the translation. After that, he never gave Herman any more message to give to me.

When I had spent some days in Hamburg with the Edouard's band which was in 1949, and the first time I had ever been in Germany, a big part of the city was in ruin. When I returned this time, it was a new city and the only places I remembered was the concert hall where I had played in '49, and the director said that he would never let the place again for jazz concerts because people in the balconies were patting their feet so hard that he thought the building would cave in. I was living very near the hall with a very nice German couple. The woman's husband had disappeared during the war, and she did not know if he was alive or dead. Her name was Zimmermann, and she was living with a man named Karl, who was working in the harbour and was a very nice man.

The other places I remembered was the night spots in a district called St. Pauli, but better known as the Ripperbahn. As these places stayed open until the wee hours every morning and I finished at 1'30a.m. I had taken Lily to a few of the places. Claude Dunson was playing in a big German band in one of these joints. One of the places featured women wrestlers in a ring filled with mud. That was really an attraction but quite an ugly sight too.
Another place we visited was a big beer hall that could hold seven or 800 people.

The waitresses were mostly not younger than 40 years, dressed in typical German costumes and they could serve from ten to twelve big mugs of beer by carrying them in their hands and not using trays. The orchestra was Tyrolian and consisted of about 18 people including singers. They had a game which was to invite someone on the bandstand to direct the orchestra which was fun. And when the person who directed the orchestra was finished at the end of the number, be it man or woman, they had to pay a round of beer or Stieneiger(German Gin)for the whole orchestra. I never saw so much beer served in one place before.

There was an English orchestra under the leadership of a trumpet player named Ken Coller and his brother Bill, who was playing at a club near the Ripperbahn. My band and Ken's were engaged to do a radio show which also included an Austrian tenor sax player named Hans Kohler, who was very popular in Germany. Ken played the real old time New Orleans jazz and most of the numbers he played on the show were things that I had never heard played by some of the New Orleans orchestras back home. I remember that they were reading the bible and made a prayer before going on stage.

Hans had his trio and his style was a little like Lester Young and Stan Getz. For a musical variety show, this set up was alright because there was the old style New Orleans music of Ken Colyer, the more modern Middle jazz style of me and my band, and the modern style of the 1950's played by Hans Kohler.

I closed at the Faun the 30th of September and arrived in Paris the 2nd of October. I had been in touch with the trombone player Bill Tamper, whom I had toured with a few days on another occasion, and I had signed Bill for my coming tour to replace Herman Wilson who had stayed in Germany with Donald Brown. Bishop and Eddy de Hass, who later changed his namee for Eddie O'Hare, arrived in Paris about the same time as I. We also had engaged a male singer this time to make the tour as there were no girl singers(American)available here in Europe. This fellow's name was Tommy Brookins and he played enough piano to accompany himself. Bishop and Tommy were buddies who had gone to school together in Chicago.

After seven good rehearsals, we had a very nice repertoire. We accompanied Tommy on three numbers and he did one at the piano which was "black coffee" and I liked this number better than any of the others he did. I don't remember what Tommy had been doing in Europe and I don't remember how I happened to get in touch with him, maybe through Bish. He had a big Cadillac car and a fine blonde Swedish chick. He was going to make the tour in his car which was almost as big as the bus we had for the band, and he has to pay the gas for this big buggy from his own pocket, because the bus had been hired to carry the whole group and there was space enough for wives or girlfriends, and I was not going to pay Tommy's transportation in his private car, not that he had ever asked me anything of the sort.

Most of my rehearsals taken place in the celler studio where the "Jazz Hot Magazine" run by Charles Delaunay had it's office on rue Chaptal, and I was never obliged to pay for the use of the studio and I shall always be grateful for that. And this time, I did not volunteer to pay the musicians for rehearsals, as I did when preparing for my first tour, which gesture was not appreciated by most of the guys. But I kept the rule of paying a half day salary if we had any days off.

But the most important day of the month of October to me was the 8th. That was the day that Lily and I got married. And what a wild day that was. I had gotten my divorce and Lily also. As we were both foreigners in France, we had to run here and there to sign all sorts of papers until the last minute. As we were only staying in Paris for a short time, we had to get an exemption for publication of banms.

This was going to be a strictly private affair. People were believing that we were married already. We had invited only a couple of good friends, Maurice and Vonette Cullaz and Colette Lacroix and a French guy, Sacha Dillot. Sacha was best man and Colette the brides maid. The civil marriage was to be performed at the Town Hall (Mairie St.Sulpice) of the 6th district, which was the district where we lived whenever we were in Paris. A religious ceremony was to take place after at 6 o'clock at the American Church. Lily and I were both Protestant.

Louis Lamy, the owner of the bus we had hired, came to see us about lunch time, then somebody else and about 4 a.m. "Bish" came in our hotel room and started to tell us some story. We were nervous and finally had to push him our of the room, telling him: "Bish, we have got to get dressed, because we are going to get married...." If we would not have been in such a hurry, it would have been comic to see his face!

We arrived at the Town Hall just in time, but realized that we had forgotten about hiring a photographer. Maurice said he was going to try to find one. We went upstairs and Sacha found out that the Mayor who would perform the ritual was a buddy from the war. They started a long conversation about the days they had passed together in the Resistance. Maurice was coming in, time to time, to say he had no luck in finding a photographer.

Finally, the ceremony began without a photographer. At one time, the Mayor said something which I did not understand because my French was no hell. There was a silence and then I decided to say 'oui'(wee in French) and I hit the right note. I was expecting Sacha to give me a hint, as we do in the States, when I was to say 'oui', but that didn't happen so I played it by ear and came out right at the coda.

After the civil ceremony we went to a cafe very near to have a celebration drink and Maurice went in the telephone booth again to try to find a photographer. He finally found one and Maurice told him to meet us at the Church on Quai d'Orsay. He was a newspaper reporter from the States that came to Paris soon after the war finished. He wrote for the 'Chicago Defenser'and his name was Ollie Stewart.

The priest - Reverent William, had insisted of giving us a lecture before the ceremony. He asked Lily if she was aware of the problems created by interracial marriage,especially if we had to go back to live in the U.S.A. 'Yes' said Lily, she was.

Photos could not be made during the ceremony and it was a good thing, because it was possible for Ollie to begin shooting, he had a camera with flashes that every time he took a photo, the flash made a sound like a bunch of small fire crackers up every time he took a photo. But they came out wonderful.

After,we went to have dinner at Leroy Haynes' place, rue Manuel. Haynes made wonderful "soul food" and we had a ball. We decided afterwards to finish that happy day at the Rind Side, rue Dartois. It was a jazz club run by an American named Dick Edward. Lionel Hampton came, kissed the bride and jammed for hours! That was the end of an hectic but wonderful day for Lily and I.

The tour started the 12th of October, with the first concert taking place in Rouen. We did eleven concerts before playing in Paris at the cinema Clunny the 23rd of October. We did an afternoon concert which was recorded by Pathe-Marconi. A funny thing happened on one number which was not aware of, until I heard the record later. Wallace Bishop had a drum solo on "Lover" which we played two choruses and then left him alone on stage. After about five minutes, we would come back and finish the number with him. This afternoon, when we went off stage during his solo, Bish yelled something at us which came out on the record, "Don't y' all stay too long!".....

We did another concert at night and did not have many people. As we were the organisers, we were losing quite a bit of money. When we came out of the hall, we and some of the musicians talked with some friends on the sidewalk and some people who were living above the Cinema came out at the window and yelled at us:"Quiet", "Shutup" "Let the People Sleep!". We didn't move right away and they came back with a bucket of water. Benny Waters, who was just coming out of the Cinema, received the shower, bewildered, not knowing what was going on, and disgusted with us laughing and cracking up!

After Paris, we did thirty three more concerts in France before flying to North Africa to do some dates. We had a concert in Marseille the 27th, and were to fly the 29th for Casablanca. There were two jazz clubs in Marseille that were enemies. So the one who was not the organiser, was trying to make scandal and keep the concert from taking place. They didn't succeed, but they cut the tyres of our bus with knives. All four of it!

The 28th, we were invited to dinner at the home of a girl that was a friend to many jazz musicians. Her name was Simone Manzi, and she had prepared a fine dinner for us, with plenty of drinks and all the works. Before the dinner, Tommy Brooks started to tell me he was afraid to fly and would it be alright if he stayed in Marseille and waited for our return. I jumped sky high and told him that the Casablanca's engagement was abig affair and his name was on the contract. He said O.K. he would come.

In the middle of the dinner, Tommy Brookins asked to be excused for a few minutes. When we finally finished the dinner and thanked Simone for a beautiful evening and left for our hotel, Tommy had not returned. At first, we thought that he has gone to the John and after we didn't see him when we left Simone, we couldn't imagine why he left the way he did.

He was not living in the same hotel where we were because he was another Fred Palmer, and besides, he was very jealous. He locked his girlfriend in the room when he had to go out or when he was going to work. Fred Palmer had done that too.

But I had told Tommy what time he had to be at the airport the next morning, but he was not there. The President of the Hot Club of Marseille was there to see us off, and after a certain time when Tommy was still not present, this fellow volunteered to go to his hotel to see if anything was wrong with Tommy. He called me later at the airport and told me that Tommy had checked out of the hotel and didn't leave any word as to where he was going. Lily and I were very upset. We left Tommy's ticket at the information desk with a message for Tommy to take the next plane and where to contact us in Casa, in case he would show up, but we had a nasty feeling that he wouldn't.

When we arrived in Casablanca, we told the organisers who were waiting for us at the airport that Tommy had missed the plane, but would be coming with another one. But he didn't, and fortunately, the organisers didn't say anything. It was a big deal this night in Casa, because it was a Lion's Club Ball, and they had engaged all sort of attractions. I was the big attraction with a group of real American Indians next. There were some Arab musical groups and dancers. The food was Arab, and it was quite amusing to see those people eating with their fingers.
I had never played at a Ball of this type, and we all had a ball this night. And Tommy Brookins wasn't missed by anyone.

We had to give five concerts in North Africa, three in Morocco. In Casablanca, Rabat and Oran, and two at the Salle Pierre Borde in Algier, Capital and seaport city of Algeria. We had a nice success everywhere and Tommy was not asked about, and we didn't miss him. We had a day off in Algier. Louis Lamy, the owner of the bus we were

Louis Lamy, the owner of the bus we were making the tour of France in, had come with his wife with us in North Africa and we went to visit a place a few miles from Algiers known as a park that had thousands of monkeys at liberty. The 6th of December we flew back to Marseilles.

The president of the Hot Club was there to meet us because he knew when we would return to Marseilles. He gave me a message from Tommy which was that he was waiting for us. I gave him one to take back to Tommy which was that he could keep waiting.

We finished the rest of the tour which was eight more concerts ending in Dijon the 14th of December. The tour had been a booking success for Lily who three years before, had not known anything about jazz and had arranged her first tour one year before this one. Without Tommy the rest of the tour continued to make a hit whereever we played and we could have saved more money than we did if the whole tour had been done without a singer. The French jazz fans and those in many other countries are not too wild about singers in jazz groups unless it's Pops Armstrong, Ella Fitzgerald, or some one in a group that can remind the fans of certain jazz or blues singers. Lily was encouraging me to sing more. I was doubtful because I had never taken me seriously as a singer but after that experience I started to sing more and more.

I had a contract for 10 days as the Casino Rosatsch in S. Moritz. Left Paris the 20th of December and opened the 22nd. Bill Tamper stayed in Paris as my contract was for five musicians. From there I went to S. Gallen, still in Switzerland at the Palais Trischli starting the 4th of January 1954 until the 31st. After St. Gallen, I had the month of February booked in a dance hall in Basel called Singerhaus. This was the only place I had played in Europe where the band was obliged to accompany attraction which was a change that we enjoyed.

Lily and I had made plans to go to the States for two months from April until June. She had never been there and I wanted her to meet my parents. After I closed at the Singerhaus, she and I stayed in Switzerland visiting friends and taking life easy until the 15th of March. We then came to Paris and I did a few gigs until our departure from Le Havre the 1st of April.

We sailed on the Liberte which was a fine ship and we enjoyed every mile from Le Havre to New York. I played a few numbers at the gala nights in each class which takes place on different nights. I had been in contact with Oran "Hot Lips" Page who had engaged a hotel in New York for us. He along with some other friends were at the pier to meet us when we docked at the pier at 6.a.m. the 7th of April. We stayed in the Apple until the 15th and I saw many of my friends, my best pals al Hall and Dickie Wells, and many of my colleagues but we went often to the Metropole bar where Red Allen was leading a band which had Herb Fleming on trombone, Cosy Cole on drums, Claude Hopkins at the piano and Lemont "Benny" Moten playing bass.

Charlie Shavers was leading the other group at the Metropole and the joint was jumping every night. Red featured a song called "Kiss the Baby" and any fellow that was with a woman, Red would ask if she was the baby. If the fellow said yes, then Red would tell him to kiss the baby and he would insist until the fellow kissed the woman. He had me kissing Lily in public at least twice every time we went to the place. Another thing he would do was when a musician came into the bar, that he knew, and he knew many, Red would announce that the band was going to play a number that was arranged by whoever this musician may be. So naturally he played some numbers that were arranged by me.

"Lips" Page who had a son of 15 years old, was remarried with a school teacher, Elysabeth. They invited us for dinner and we enjoyed being with them. Lips was a natural born joker and terrific company. We stayed late and told him that we wanted to get back to our hotel and wanted to look for a cab. He said that it was not necessary. He would take us back as he had a big new model Cadillac but had to go in the street to look for someone who could drive it. We didn't dig it. Why couldn't he drive it himself? He said that he didn't have a driving licence, did not want one because he wanted to be able to drink his liquor the way he wanted to and if he had to drive, that would keep him from drinking. It was typical of him. We loved him very much and it was shocking and painful when we heard that he died of an attack 6 months later.

Lily did not like the city of New York very much. She thought that the hotels and also the streets were dirty, that people were upset with money and talked about it all the time, that Americans were very rude. She couldn't stand racism and so was partial with white Americans. But she loved my friends and the jazz scene.

We left New York by train the 15th of April and arrived in Cincinnati the next morning. My father and brother met us at the station and they were both looking good and happy. Lily made a hit with them the same as she had done with the rest of my friends and I was very proud of her. Later in the day, we went to visit my mother and step-father who had taken Lily to their hearts as soon as they saw her. The last time I had seen my parents brother and sister was in 1947 which was six years before this meeting and we had a grand reunion.

My brother Ulysse was married with a nice widow who had six children. Her name was Zola. My sister Thelma had separated from her husband and was living with my father. Lily and I also stayed with Dad and Lily started

calling him Dad, which he enjoyed very much. We were in Cincy from the 16th of April until the 23rd of May and were invited to parties at least four times a week by friends of my family and some of my old musician friends that included Clarence Paige, his wife Ellen, William Smythe, who was William Smythe who was William Smith or just plain Smittie when we worked together in the old days. My sister and her boyfriend were friends with a young white couple named Bob and Phyl Connors who invited us to their home. Bob was an amateur pianist who dug Dave Brubeck and he was also a photographer. He made some very nice photos of Lily and I.

We were having a swell time and I never once touched my horn because this was the first time I had taken a vacation that I was not forced to take because I didn't have any work. But the time came when we were obliged to get back to New York and spend a few more days there before going back to France. We arrived back in the Apple, the 24th of May and as our sailing date was the 3rd of June, that gave us 10 days to spend with our friends and see my buddies again.

When I was at the Faun in Hambourg, I was contacted by a booking agent with whom I signed a contract to do two and a half months concert tour in Germany. I decided to use an alto and tenor sax directly from New York in place of a tenor and trombone. A few days after we returned to New York from Cincinnati, I went to see Ben Smith, whom I had worked with in Andy Kirk's orchestra. Ben was also an arranger who played alto and clarinet which was the reason I wanted him. But he was leading a combo in the Baby Grand on 125th street and had no eyes for leaving the job.

Then I thought about my ole drinking buddy Kirby Alexander and went to see him. Kirby was in bad shape because he had had no work and nothing in sight. He was separated from the mother of his two children, one who was blind. I knew he really needed help and thought that if he could get away from his misery and be able to blow his sax again, that would start him on the road to a come back. He accepted my offer
and I promised to send him a contract and all necessary information after I returned to France.

A few nights later, after my meeting with Kirby, I was in bar in Broadway where many of the cats hung out and met Jimmy Wright, whom I had worked with in a dancing school many moons ago. Jimmy played tenor and after a few drinks and some chit-chat about days gone by, Jimmy started telling me about how well he was doing and bragging about his Lincoln car. Finally I got around to telling him that I was in the market for a tenor man and told him what it was for. As we had worked together, I figured it would be a pleasure to work with him again. And he, like Kirby readily accepted and I told him that Kirby would be with us and that I would contact the two of them after my return to France. I had engaged an alto and tenor, so the rest of my time was spent enjoying the few days left to spend in the Apple.

We had met Oscar Pettiford a few times and he came to see us at our hotel, bringing my wife big bottles of perfume. He decided to spend the last night with us. That last night on that side of the pond was the most. It started at the Metropole, then we went to Jimmy Ryan's as we wanted to dig the Wilbur de Paris band that was loaded with fellows I had known a long time and had also worked with at certain times. There was Sydney de Paris playing trumpet and bass tuba, which I didn't know that he played. I've seen musicians that played a number of different instruments or doubled on two that were different but Sydney was the only one I ever saw that doubled on trumpet and tuba. Sonny White was the pianist, Wilber Kirk drums and harmonica, Wilbur de Paris, trombone, Omar Simeon, clarinet. Omar was the only one that I had never worked with. It was a really happy sounding group.

When Ryan's place closed, Oscar offered to take us up town to Minton's Playhouse. We had no idea of what group was playing there but that didn't matter because Minton's always had good musicians playing there. And one of my old bosses, Teddy Hill was the manager and I'm almost certain that he was at least part owner of the place. I had not seen Teddy since 1946 when we met on a street in Manila in the Philippines and we were happy to see each other again.

But the surprise of the night and it was an unexpected one, was that Billie Holliday was at Minton's this night. Not engaged to sing there but as a client the same as we were. Eventually someone asked Billie to sing and she did not refuse. I've always dug Lady Day from the first time I heard her, so this pleased me to hear her once again in person. And it was a great thrill for Lily because she liked her records very much and now she could see and hear the Lady Day in the flesh.

Oscar would not let me pay for anything and somewhere during the morning, we had picked up Al Hall who was with us at Minton's. We left Teddy Hill about 6 a.m. and Al suggested that we go to his place for breakfast. We also had with us Joan Hill, who had been my common law step-daughter, if some law of that kind exists. Joan didn't get along too well with her mother, Beezie. She was twenty years old, six feet tall and had a baby of six months, Steve. She left us to go and fetch the baby and said she would rejoin us at Al Hall's place. We had ham and eggs with coffee and other things to eat, but the juice was still flowing as it had been everywhere we had gone that night. Soon the time came for Lily and I to get to the boat.

Al was living on 52nd street not far from the pier, which I think was at 42nd street and Riverside Drive. Lily and I were in a hotel at 25th street and 7th Avenue. We had packed our baggage and had to go and get them with a taxi. There was no need for Lily to go to the hotel with me, so Oscar came along and the rest of the party went to the pier with Lily where

we all met to say farewell. Oscar gave me two of his recordings with his autograph, which are priceless to me. One was an L.P. on Debut Records called "The new Oscar Pettiford Sextet" and features the man himself with Phil Urso, tenor, Julius Watkins, french horn, Walter Bishop, piano, Charles Mingus, bass and Percy Brice, drums. Oscar played cello. The other record was a 45 rpm on Imperial records and has Oscar still playing cello and features Arnold Ross, piano, Harry Babasin, cello, Joe Comfort, bass and Alvin Stoller drums. I wouldn't part with those records for a whole lot of money.

We were on the Flandre, another ship of the French line, very nice but much smaller than the Liberte. It left the pier around 11 o'clock the 3rd of June and after we waved to our friends until we could no longer see them. Lily couldn't take it any longer and went to our cabin to rest her tired body. I stayed up to see the statue of Liberty because I wanted to film it and then I hit the hay for the rest of the afternoon.

The morning of the 9th, the Flandre stopped at Plymouth, arrived at Le Havre around 7 that evening. We had a terrible weather, the boat was shaking like a nut shell and in spite of that we didn't get sea sick, we were glad to set foot on earth. We arrived in Paris at 10 that night. We had enjoyed a wonderful 70 days holiday, including the trip on the Liberte and the Flandre but were happy to get back to our regular routine of living again.

One month later, the 9th of July, I started work as an attraction at the Ringside which was a club on rue d'Artois, near the Champs Elysees, owned by an american Negro named Dick Edwards. Martial Solal, the great French pianist was leading a trio at the Ringside and they accompanied me and a girl singer, also Negro from the States, named Pat Boone.

Martial was actually from Algeria. His style was something similar to Oscar Peterson, with a technique like the great Art Tatum and he accompanied me beautifully, although my style was not as modern as that of Dizzy Gillespie and others of that epoch. I really enjoyed playing with Martial who was full of ideas, very inspiring.

I stayed at the Ringside until the 4th of August and started at a place called Metro Jazz, which became the Trois Maillets (three hammers). This place was on the left bank in the Latin Quarter, near the famous Notre Dame church. I was living on the left bank and the Metro Jazz club was about 10 minutes walk from my hotel. The owner of the Trois Maillets was a lady named Denise Calve who had been an actress. The club was a cellar of the 12th century, very well preserved and had been a prison. History said that the famous poet Francois Villon had been imprisoned there. One floor below, was another cellar with a well, which had been a torture chamber and was now a museum. When a prisoner died after being tortured, the body was thrown in the well and came out into the Seine river, which was running not far from the building.

Jimmy Wright and Kirby Alexander arrived around the 20th of September and also a very well known pianist in the States who had become quite popular in France in the middle thirties. His name was Garland Wilson, known by his musician friends as "Mother". Garland had been engaged to entertain at a famous night spot called "the Boeuf sur le Toit" where he and the well known female pianist, Una Mae Carlisle, had worked together in the thirties until the second world war started.

Jimmy and Kirby were really not overloaded with baggage and to my surprise, Jimmy had no instrument. I said that I had worked with Jimmy for quite a while and knew him well enough to know that he was a big bluffer and therefore his story about a big Lincoln car didn't ring any bells with me.

But I did not expect to see him coming all the way from New York to Europe for a two months musical tour that he was engaged to do and arriving without an instrument. Kirby's luck had been bad but he did have a horn to blow.

There was in instrument company in Paris called Couesnon, and I knew the director Mr. Vincent very well. They were trying to push their horns into the jazz field and I had received a trumpet. They had given Dickie Wells and some other famous American musicians instruments also. Mr. Vincent did not agree to give Jimmy a tenor, but as a favour to me, he was willing to let Jimmy have a horn for a bargain price. I was responsible for seeing that Jimmy paid a certain amount every week which I personally would send to Couesnon.

For the tour, the rhythm section was the same as the last tour, Bishop, De Haas and Starling. I also engaged a girl singer from Trinidad named Cecily Forde who had not been in France very long. We rehearsed for about a week, I finished at the Metro Jazz the 30th of September and we left for Aachen, Germany, the first of October and played our first concert the 2nd in Aachen. We played 70 towns from the 2nd of October until the 15th of December with only six days off.

We were in Kassel the 10th of November when someone in the orchestra had bought a U.S. army paper called Stars and Stripes in which there was an announcement that "Hot Lips Page" had died. I had seen him a few months ago and he was in good health at that time and we had not heard anything about him being sick. To my estimation the world had lost the greatest blues trumpeter who could sing them as well as play them. He also had given Lily and I an autographed recording of his, recorded on Columbia. The titles were "Mis Larceny Blues", Page's composition and "There Ain't No Flies On Me". He sings on both sides and plays these blue numbers as only he could play them.

There were a very few towns that we did not play in West Germany, large and small. We played some concerts for the German public and many concerts were for British military camps. The camps concerts were usually done in the non commissioned officers' (N.C.O.) recreation halls and those fellows really showed us a swell time in every camp we played. They enjoyed jazz and enjoyed showing us how much they appreciated what we had to offer. After the concerts we were offered drinks no end, food for each musician and whoever else that happened to be with us.

We played the last date in Germany the 15th of December in Offenback and arrived in Brussels, Belgium, to prepare for a television show the 18th. Did and afternoon concert in Liege and one that night in Brussels on the 19th. Came to Paris the 20th and that was the last time I saw Jimmy Wright.

He and I had not gotten along the way we had, back in the days when we were with Johnny Monneque. He was wild and undependable. His playing didn't mean much to me. He was putting on a lot of show, almost playing on his back. A few times he refused to come to rehearsals. As we were going to be off a few days during the Christmas and New Year holidays, Jimmy told me that he was going to the States for that period and would come back before the tour started again. I had signed a contract to continue the tour in Germany until the last of January 1955, starting the 8th of that month. I also had a date to play an afternoon concert in Lieden, Holland and the Hague the first of January. I told Jimmy that if he went back to New York he could stay there because I knew that he was not coming back.

I engaged Guy Lafitte on tenor to finish the tour and we did the first concert at a British army camp near Dusseldorf the 8th of January and did 22 concerts in as many places without having one day off. Guy could not remain with me after the 31st because of commitments in France, I had a contract for a return engagement in the Faun in Hamburg and as Herman Wilson, my ex-trombonist was still in Germany and available, I engaged him
to replace Guy. And that gave the group a different sound with trombone in the place of a tenor.

We stayed two months in the Faun which was a record because an orchestra was never engaged to work there longer than one month. At the end of that term, we did the month of April for English troops again, and it was a pleasure to get away from the Faun after two months of working every night although we didn't have a day off during this month either; we were changing towns every day and seeing different things. Eddie de Haas Hass had left the band after we finished at the Faun and I had engaged a French Martinique bass player named Gilbert Fanfant who had been working in a club in Hamburg.

This tour ended the 30th of April in a place called Iserlohn and we all went different places. Lily and I went to Zurich to visit our good friend Johnny Simmen and his wife Lisette. It certainly was a good feeling to get away from travelling and band leader worries for a while. But that didn't last very long and as the ball must keep rolling, when I came back to Paris, I started forming another group to go to Denmark for the month of June.

I engaged on the recommendation of a friend who was a jazz critic, an American Negro saxophonist named Charlie Singleton. I thought this Charlie Singleton was the same one that had written a number that was quite popular in the middle fifties. Unfortunately this Charlie Singleton was a sad rock and roll tenor player and the only thing he had was to grind his body like a snake hip dancer. His playing was nowhere. I never like to criticise a musician but that jazz critic friend of mine really pulled my leg when he said this guy was alright.
The city where we had to play in Denmark was Odense and we worked in a dancing called Ambassadeur. There was a Danish orchestra that was engaged to play waltz and Afro Cuban numbers.

I was featuring a tune composed by Henri Salvador, a French Martinque comedian and fine guitarist and singer. The song was "Une Chanson Douce" which was not meant to be and was not a jazz number, but it was a nice commercial number for dancers. About two weeks after I had started in the joint, I came in one night and this other orchestra, who always started playing before my group did were playing "Une Chanson Douce". I was salty as ocean water because my repertoire was not great as we had only a few rehearsals before coming to the place and I didn't think it was kosher for them to play the number before I had played it. Besides as they were playing together for a long time they had a big repertoire. And what's more is that they had copies the number from me and were now playing it exactly the way we did and before us.

So when the night was finished, I told the leader of the band that I didn't like it and thought it was not fair for them to play that number when they knew it was one that I played and to play it before me. They didn't do it any more but the pianist got mad and never spoke to me again. And I'm still crying in my beer because of that, ha! ha!

There is no need to mention the names of the musicians I had in this group except Jack Starling my pianist for a long time and Cecily Forde the singer. All that I can say is that it was the saddest group I ever had. But I was hooked and often thought about how Jelly Roll Morton must have felt when he brought a sad band to Cincinnati way back when. The booking agency that had engaged me for the Ambassadeur had promised me more engagements before I opened in Odense, but they had let me drop like a hot iron.

We were supposed to do some numbers especially as an attraction for 20 minutes and after we did what we could the first night the manager came to me and asked me when was I going to do my dance number. The agency had told him that I played trumpet, sang and tap danced. The guy was very brought down when I told him that I was happy to be able to walk and didn't know one step in tap dancing.

The job was not hard and especially with two bands. When we started work at 8.30. in the evening, the sun was still shining bright. And when we finished at 1.30.a.m. day would be breaking and the birds would be doing their thing.

Sad as the band was, another agent who was a woman who lived in Copenhagen got me 15 days at the Tivoli Karolinelund amusement park in Aalborg, Denmark and this job was very easy because it featured attractions only and one of the attractions was an American Negro named Freddie Crump who was the first drummer in the world that did a drum act. I had seen him when I was a teenager with Cooper's Black and White show, which I mentioned on an earlier page. I've seen and heard plenty of drummers since those days, but I've never seen one that could do an act with only drums the way Freddie could. He was the first black musician to be featured with a white orchestra. He was known as Rastus at that time and although the name is a drag, he was featured with Paul Whiteman's orchestra. He's been living in Denmark for years and has three daughters that play drums in his act.
A few days before the end of the engagement I started to have a bad case of sciatica. I couldn't walk or stand. I went to work with a taxi and had to sit on the bandstand.

Women are great cigar smokers in Denmark. At least they were at this time and they even smoked them in streetcars and other public places.
