The lady that Lily and I roomed with, was a smoker of big cigars. We had invited my sister Thelma to come to Europe for a vacation and Lily left for Paris to meet her and bring her to Copenhagen where we had decided to stay for 16 days. I had closed at the Tivoli but decided to stay 4 days in Aalborg for 4 days before going to Copenhagen.

Our landlady was nice about preparing my meals and looked after me like a mother would do for her son. So I started wondering what I could give her as a token of appreciation and it finally hit me that I could give

her a box of good cigars. I did that the day before I left and she was very happy about the gift. She couldn't speak English or French and I couldn't speak Danish but we managed to make ourselves understood. Later that day I saw her sitting in her living room smoking a cigar so I asked her if it was one that I had given her and if they were good. She made me understand that it was not and said that she was saving them until some special occasion came along and she would put on her Sunday go-to-meeting clothes and that's when she would smoke one or two that I had given her.
We arrived back in Paris the 24th of August. I started working at the Trois Maillets the 15th of September and my sister left for the U.S.A. the 16th.

I had the privilege of going out of the club now and then to do ates in different places and that was the way I worked until February of 1956. In October 1955, I played a two days jazz festival in Lyon which featured Sydney Bechet, Chet Baker and myself. Sidney was the main attraction because his popularity had grown immensely since 1950 and he was the biggest crowd drawing jazz musician in Europe. At one time, I didn't dig him mostly I suppose because I didn't like the sound of soprano saxophone. But I dug him now and I'm happy to say that he was one of the swingingest cats that ever lived and his inspired many of the younger sax men of today who are playing that instrument now.

The musicians that accompanied me at the Trois Maillets were Michel de Villers, whom I had made my first tour with as a member of the Edouard's band. He was now playing alto and baritone sax. The pianist was Andre Persiany who was known as the French Milt Buckner. We called him Pepe. My friend Guy Lafitte was on tenor. There was Paul Rovere, a fine young bass player and Jappy Gauthier on drums. Lily had been working on another tour of France for a few months and as the club was going to close for the
month of February and I had been working with these musicians for a few months, we decided to use them for the tour with Cecily Forde as the canary.

We finished the 5th of February at the club and did the first concert of the tour at Le mans, where the famour 24 hours endurance auto races are held every year. We did 21 concerts and had three days off during the month. It was a difficult tour because that February broke all records in France for being the coldest of any year known in this country. The bad weather started about 3 days after we did the first concert. In some places we played it was so cold that not more than 25 people were brave enough to face the weather. Theatres were ice cold, water pipes were frozen in hotels. In Perpignan, which is not far from the Spanish border and where it never gets cold as a general rule, we found snow and ice.

We came back in Paris the second of March and flew to Algiers to play a big ball at the Hotel St. George and gave a concert at the Salle Borde the 3rd. The 10th of March I played what was called a New Orleans Festival at the Palais des Sports in Paris which featured bands from several European countries and I met the English trumpeter Humphrey Lyttelton for the first time. I had heard of him as he became England's best known jazz trumpet man after Nat Gonella who was the English Louis Armstrong in the 1930's. Humphrey played and still does play a fine trumpet.

I had an engagement at the Alhambra theatre as a feature trumpetist and singer with Maxim Saury, the ex-Claude Bollong clarinetist who was making a name for himself as leader of a Dixieland group. Maxim had a trumpet player named Jean Claude Naude who recorded some numbers with Maxime and it was difficult at times to believe that it was not Satchmo himself. Naude came closer to getting the same tone as Pops than any trumpet player, I can think of, that copies Pops. And he had the phrasing down pat also.
Also featured on the bill at the Alhambra was a singing group known as the "Double Six" who were something like the American group known as

"the Modernaires". But in this group there was a trumpet player named Roger Guerin who was the best modern trumpetist in France. He didn't play with the "Double Six" but was singing with them to my surprise.

Back to the Trois Maillets, in and out, doing galas in nearly every corner of France, concerts which had taken me to Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and a month's contract in the club "Storyville" in Frankfurt, Germany.

The 4th of February 1957 I left Paris for Italy to do a month's tour that featured Benny Waters on tenor and Albert Nicholas, clarinet Jack Starling, piano Gilbert Fanfant, bass and a German drummer, whom I can only remember his first name which was Rolfie. Cecily Forde was engaged as the singer. We did 21 concerts including two in Milano and played in every important city in Italy and some that were not.

The tour started the 8th of February. There were three booking agents handling this tour, two Italians and one Italo-American. One travelled with us. We were travelling by train. His name was Robert Burnier and we gave him the name of the "Creep" because he was tall, skinny, wore a black overcoat and hat and seemed to be always creeping around a corner like Mack the Knife.

During the tour we were engaged to play a big ball in St. Moritz, Switzerland, for the millionaire shipping magnate Niarkos, who was the brother in law of Onassis, another shipping magnate. The ball was given in the Palace Hotel which is the largest and most expensive hotel in that resort. And we also had rooms in that hotel.

We were on the bandstand which was about 15 inches high and I was standing at the left of the bandstand when one of the male guests came by on crutches. Just when he arrived at my side, one of the crutches slipped and I had the reflex just in time to catch him and prevent him from falling. I was sorry for this after, because the son of a bitch didn't thank me or even look at me. I regretted I had not let him fall and break his goddamn neck.

The tour went well until we played Bari down on the boot of Italy. We enjoyed the different views of the town. The weather was beautiful. We went into a restaurant at the seaside to eat some sea food but the windows were so dirty that we couldn't hardly see the sea...We had a nice crowd at the theater but only men, not one woman.

We played Bari the 5th of March and the next morning we had taken a train back to Milano. In fact Bari was our last date of the tour. Burnier had taken an earlier train back to Milano and left word that he would not be responsible for the transportation of Benny Waters and the drummer Rolfie because they had gone to a night club in Bari after the concert and jammed with the musicians. Our contract mentioned that we were not supposed to play anywhere before or after concerts during the tour without the consent of the office. I suppose that Benny and Rolfie thought that as it was our last date, it would not matter if they had some fun playing after the concert. And it was something that really could not cause any harm if any of us had played somewhere for kicks after the concert.

But Burnier had taken this matter as a chance to have some extra loot for the office, I suppose. I had experienced some rougth deals with Italians before and here it was happening again after the tour having been so nice.

We arrived in Milano the 7th of March and went to the office the next day to straighten out things and get our last pay. At the agency they didn't want to discuss the affair of Benny and Rolfie and one thing is certain, and that is there is no winning with Italian impresarios and very few others.

So we told those three cats goodbye and went to our hotel to prepare to leave Milano the next day. The next morning, rather early, I received a phone call from Burnier saying that he had a good proposition for the band and asked us if we would all come to the office that day. We all had individuals contracts with the agency. We had preferred that way to avoid being responsible if something went wrong with one or several musicians. And also if something went wrong with the organisers.

We went to the office and the proposition was for a big ball the next night, the 9th, at the Palace Hotel in Milano. It must have been a big deal for those three, because they promised to pay the transportation of Benny and Rolfie from Bari to Milano which those two had paid from their pockets. They also offered a pretty nice taste if we would accept to play the ball. So we accepted, played the date and left Milano the morning of the 10th for Paris.

The tour in Holland with the Dutch Swing College Band was in September and this was a real happy tour. This was the drinkingest band that I ever knew. I've heard stories about how the old Fletcher Henderson band guys could drink, but I actually saw how those cats could bend elbows. I couldn't and didn't try to out drink any of them, but I taken quite a few solos with the bottle. What was so amazing about their drinking is that they never let that ignorant oil interfere with their playing and they had a swinging group. They were all great fellows and that was one tour that I shall always remember as one of the most enjoyabl of the many tours I've done during my whole musical career. But let me say that not all of those fellows were heavy drinkers, at least one or two were not.

The rest of 1957 and the first two months of 1958 I did galas, concerts in France with various groups and played in my ole stomping ground home, the Trois Mailletz. There was a five days carnival in a city called Narbonne which I played from the 15th until the 20th of February with a big band under the leadership of Alain Romans. Alain was the owner of a club on rue Colisee in Paris, not far from the Champs-Elysees and he plays piano and also has composed music for movile films. I also did some radio programmes for him in his place. Alain is also the brother-in-law of the owner of the Trois Mailletz, whose name is Madame Calve.

Lily and I had planned to make another trip to the U.S.A. to visit my father, sister and brother in Cincinnati and see some ole friends in New York. We also had a cousin from Switzerland from Lily's side who was
living in Sunbury, Pennsylvania, that we planned to visit.

The first of March 1958, we sailed from Le Havre on the Liberte, which was the ship we had went to New York on, in 1954. I was quite well known on the Liberte by many of the officers who had been on this beautiful ship for a number of years.

The trip was very agreeable from start to finish. We arrived in New York the 7th of March, and to our surprise, our great friend, George Duvivier, the fine bass man, had reserved a suite of two rooms for us in a hotel called Schuyler on 44th St., between 5th Avenue and Avenue of Americas and told us in a kidding way that he would shoot us if we tried to pay for anything other than food that we would need for breakfast. When we arrived at the hotel there was a big bouquet of flowers for Lily, beer, soft drinks, whisky and even a bottle of Pernod for a little French atmosphere. There was also a television set and all this was arranged by George to welcome us to New York.

We stayed in New York for 6 days and heard Red Allen, Roy Eldridge, Charlie Shavers, Buster Bailey, Cozy Cole, Claude Hopkins, Coleman Hawkins, Sol Yegar, Russel "Big Chief" Moore and the bassist, Benny Moten at different times when we visited the Metropole on 7th Avenue near Broadway. I didn't find much change in New York from the last time I saw it, but friends told us that there were improvements in the racial relations.

Our first night in the Apple, we had dinner with a Swiss friend, named Peter Wydler and his wife Othella. I was their best man when they married in Paris, France in 1949. Othella, who was American, was a dancer in Catherine Dunham's show which was touring in Europe and Miss Dunham was bridesmaid for Othella and Peter's marriage.
We had dinner another time with Arvell Shaw and his wife, Madeleine who is also Swiss. With Peter and Madeleine Shaw being Swiss, Lily was with some of her homeland people.

Of course I saw many of my musician friends and buddies because I went to Beefsteak Charlie's bar which was an old hangout for many of the gang that I knew before going to Europe. Some of the gang could be found in the Turf bar on Broadway and I went there a few times in the afternoon.

Oscar Pettiford opened a club on 3rd Avenue East side, called the Black Pearl and I was there on opening night with Lily of course. I heard the trumpetist Ray Copeland and Jerome Richardson, the reed man, for the first time. They were both fine musicians and Oscar found time now and then to knock out a few tunes on the bass. It was a very nice club but I heard that it did not stay open very long.

We left New York by train the 14th of March. George Duvivier drove us to the New York Central station in his Cadillac and we arrived in Cincinnati the next morning. The air conditioning system had been out of order and the heat was unbearable. We couldn't drink because the drinking water tank was empty and nobody came through selling drinks. We were more than happy to get out of that train.

My father and sister had moved from West 9th street where they were living when we went to Cincinnati in 1954. They were now living in Walnut Hills on Rockdale Avenue. My old buddy, Eddie Partridge and his wife Mattie, who was a cousin of mine lived in the same house as my father and Eddie and myself had some drinking good times.

My brother, his wife, an uncle and cousin John Coleman also lived on the hill and not too far from my father. We gave a party, my brother gave one and many of his or his wife's friends gave parties and that's the way our visit to Cincinnati was spent most of the time. My old boss Clarence Page also invited us to his house as did my good friend from way back, William Smith, who was known as "Smittie" and who had changed his name to Smyth. He was a union delegate and still playing piano in clubs. Clarence Page waa still playing also.

We spent a few days in my brother's home and one day we decided to visit my Uncle Ernest Coleman, who did not live far from my brother. As we were a mixed married couple, trouble could be around any corner and it was around one this day. We were not far from my brother's place when it started to rain but not hard. One of my brother's step daughters was with us and we sent her back to the house to get an umbrella.

Lily was carrying a very light coloured handbag and did not want to get it wet. I had on a raincoat so she gave the handbag to me and I put it under my raincoat and held it with one hand. Just as Lily gave me the handbag, a police patrol car was passing and one of the two police saw the action. They stopped the car and one of them jumped out and came beside me. He said: Give me that purse, I saw you snatch it. I said: this is my wife (speaking about Lily) and further more, if I had snatched the bag, do you think that I would stand there and talk to the woman I had snatched it from? Then Lily told him that I was her husband so he asked to see my identity papers and I showed him my passport. Then he asked Lily for her paper, which she gave him after I passed her back the handbag. Her passport was Swiss but written in French and this guy couldn't read it. So again, I asked him if he thought I would snatch a handbag and then stand there.

At that time, the other policeman who was in the car and who was his superior came to join us and asked an explanation. We gave him our passports, he gave a look at it and asked us to excuse them and went on to tell us that there was a lot of handbag snatching going on and they thought that's what I was doing. It was a dumb story and it would not have happened I think, if I would have been white.

We left Cincy the night of April 18th. My father, brother and wife, some cousins and friends came to the station to see us off. I had bought round trip tickets on the New York central railroad line. When we decided

that we were going to visit our cousin in Sunbury, Pennsylvania, I went to the railroad station in Cincy to have the tickets changed to the Pennsylvania line. I was told that it was not necessary to change the tickets because the two lines had merged and the tickets were valuable on either line.

About 20 minutes after the train had left Cincinnati, the conductor came through the coach taking tickets and when he took ours and looked at them he said in a very nasty tone that the tickets were not good for that line. I told him what I had been told at the station concerning the tickets. But he didn't want to hear anything. Then I knew that he was a cracker and could not stand the sight of mixed couples and specially if the woman was white.
He threatened to put us off the train at the next stop which would have been Columbus, Ohio, if I didn't pay the fare, which he said was 50 dollars for each, and he kept our tickets.
He went into another coach and I went in the vestibule to wait for him to come back because I was not going to take his insults lying down.

Finally he came back and I stopped him and told him again what I had been told at the station. He lessened and then he said, as if he was doing me a favor, that he would accept the tickets. But his attitude was different now that there was nobody around to show off.

When I came back into our coach, there was a very handsome young white fellow sitting two seats from us who asked me if he could talk with me for a while. I sat beside him and he told me that he had heard what the conductor had said about putting us off the train at the next stop from Cincinnati. Almost everyone in the coach had heard the same thing because that bastard was talking oud especially for everyone to hear him and I had to tell him that he didn't have to yell at me.

This fellow introduced himself and told me that he was a pastor in a church in Louisville, Kentucky, and Columbus, Ohio, where he lived and that he would invite Lily and I to spend the night with him if we were obliged to get off the train in Columbus. I told him that everything was straight and thanked him for his kind offer. Some other white folks told us also that they did not agree with the conductor's attitude and a man said that he had a job in the railroad company and offered to stand as witness if we had further troubles with that guy.
The deal with the policeman and the run-in with the onductor were the only things that made this visit to the States disagreeable.

We arrived in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, the next day. Our cousin Andre Hoffmann and his wife Denise met us and we drove to Sunbury where we spent the night and the next day, visiting the country. Left Sunbury via Harrisburg for New York which was a three hour trip with the train and had the same suite in the Hotel Schluyler that we occupied before going to Cincinnati. George, again, didn't want us to pay anything. We met his mother, Ismay, and we invited her to come to Europe for the summer. Lily offered her to be her guide in Europe. She took us at our words and came to Paris a few months later.

We made the rounds of different clubs, were invited to parties and dinners, including one that Herb Flemming prepared for us in his Bronx home. We also caught Ben Webster on his opening night at the Village Vanguard. Ben had a fine trio backing him, but the only musician I can remember was Philly Jo Jones whom I had never met before. Later that night, Tony Scott came in and blew some baritone sax and had a gone jam session with Ben who was playing his can-off that night.

Saturday nights there was always a session at Central Plaza on East 3rd street which was run by Jack Crystal who at one time managed the sessions for Milt Gabler at Jimmie Rhyan on 52nd street. Jack was a real friend to all jazz musicians regardless of race or religion and his sessions were often a big help to many of the fellows that played them.
Saturday night, the 26th of April I played this session with Dicky Wells, Eddie Barefield, the great Willie "the Lion" Smith and two drummers, Jo Jones and Panama Francis.

I was on vacation and not looking for work, beside I hadn't blown for quite a while, but I was really happy to have been engaged for this session, which was the only time I really wanted to play during my visit to the Apple. The Lion was a regular must at the Plaza and I was told that he was there for every session. I was happy playing with my ole buddy Dickie Wells and the rest of the fellows and they were well pleased to play with me and to know that I had not lost anything concerning my style and ideas as most American musicians thought would happen to musicians who stayed in Europe a long time.

We met there a nice young man, Doug Hague, who was a great jazz fan and also a jazz critic for different reviews in the States and in England. He was there with his young Italian wife and his parents. Albert and Peggy Hague. They had some juice with them in a bag and they kept on asking us questions about France and telling us how much they loved that country and its way of life. Peggy was of French descendance and vaguely related with a member of the Hot Club de France, Jacques Morgantini from Pau. We became great friends afterwards and still are.

We left New York aboard the Liberte again on the first day of May and arrived in France and back home in Paris the 7th of May. I went back to the Trois Mailletz and did galas. There was a big jazz festival in Cannes the month of July and I was invited the 13th to play a jam session with Sydney Bechet, Roy "Little Jazz" Eldridge, Joe Turner the pianist and Teddy Buckner, whom I met for the first time. Whoever the rest of the musicians were, I don't remember, but they were not Americans.

The 20th of July I did a TV show in Milano, Italy and a concert the 21st in a place in Italy also called Malpensa. Went to Copenhagen for a concert the 30th of August and one the 31st on the Ile of Bornholm, which is a Danish island. In between these important dates, I was working at
the Trois Mailletz and doing galas until I left for Milano the 9th of October to do another tour in Italy.

Burnier, the impresario, was organising this tour with a big impresario from Milano named Ivaldi but we never saw him and Burnier only signed the contract though he said that Ivaldi was willing to sign also. Unfortunately, we did not insist on it and so he never signed.

Burnier had engaged for this tour Albert Nicholas, Don Byas (tenor) who was now living in Amsterdam, Holland and the trio of Michel Hausser which had Ricardo Galleazzi, an Argentinian bass player, who was also a fine trombone man, Dante Agostini, an Italian drummer, who was born in France and had never been to Italy before and on piano.
Michel Hausser was a real gifted vibraphone player and accordionist who was the best vibraphonist in France at that period and his style was formed on that of Milt Jackson.

Pope Pius XII had just died when we arrived in Milano and it was a bad beginning for the tour. We rehearsed at a place called the Arhetusa which was a bar and restaurant on the first floor and a club in the cellar. I had rehearsed and also sat in with the band of the Arhetusa before and the owner knew me quite well and called me "Maestro".

Our first concert was the 11th at the Theatro del Nuovo in Milano. We did a matinee and night concert the 12th at the same theater and the crowds were very small for each concert. The Hausser trio opened the concerts and then accompanied Albert, myself and Don, after which we played a number together to close the first half. It was the same routine for the second and last part of the concerts. Each artist announced his own numbers. Burnier had asked me to present the show but Don Byas refused because he was afraid people would believe I was the band leader, so there was no presentation, just name of the tunes.
We hit the road the 13th and played Bergamo, Brescia, Reggio-Emilia and Bari the 19th. We were travelling by bus this time.

Italy was in mourning for the Pope Pius XII and as not many people came to the concerts, Burnier, who had booked these theaters on percentage was behind in paying us. We all had individual contracts and were not working on percentage with Burnier. We were always hoping that the next date we played after Milano would be the one that would bring our pay up to date and Burnier was hoping the same thing.

After a few days of not getting our entire salary, Dante Agostini started theatening to leave for Paris. After playing Bari, we stopped to spend the night of the 20th in a town called Ancona. We were going to play next in Mestre, near Venice.

About one o'clock in the morning, Michel Hausser knocked on my door in the hotel where we were staying just when I was beginning to sleep well and asked me to come and help him talk to Dante because he had checked his drums at the railroad station, bought a ticket for Paris and was going to leave on an early train.

When I arrived in Dante's room everyone of the group except Lily, who had stayed in bed, was in Dante's room and it had taken a lot of begging from all of us to get Dante to stick with us a while longer, which he finally decided to do. He got his money back for the ticket he had bought and the 21st, the group arrived in Mestre intact.

Don Byas had been practising body building and carried two dumb-bells with him in an airplane bag. They must have weighed about 40 or more pounds. Whenever we arrived at a hotel that was up to date enough to have a porter to take charge of the baggage, Don would tell him to take the small airplane bag and we would all be waiting to watch the shocked expression on the face of the porter when he lifted the bag.

The third day of the tour we had played in Torino and we called that day, Don's day. He had told us that he had stopped drinking since he had gotten married to a Dutch girl a few years ago. By some unknown incident Don happened to come into the same restaurant where Lily and I were having

supper, and after we finished eating Don offered us a drink to digest our food. So we ordered Grapa (sort of Italian brandy gin) and Don had one also. Later when we came to the theater we saw that Don had had quite a few grapas and he was worse than an American Indian when he drank.

During the intermission, Don had gone to the bar in the theater and when it was time for us to start the second half of the concert, Burnier came to me and asked me to go get Don because he was raising hell at the bar.

I went to the bar and Don was acting so crazy that everybody there was laughing at him. I finally got him away and we started the last part of the concert. Don't feature number for the second part of the concert was Laura and, drunk as he was, he was able to play until he got to the coda. It was very special and he had a certain phrase he played before the trio made the last chord with him. But this time Don was so high that he could not find the phrase for at least 3 minutes. He was running exercises all over his tenor, trying to find the phrase. The musicians were waiting and looking at Don as if he was a newly discovered animal that had never been seen before. Dante was sitting with his sticks in the air and Michel Hausser had his mallets ready to hit the last chord. Finally after what seemed like a lifetime to the musicians and we who were listening and knew what was not happening, Don found the phrase, the musicians hit the chord with him and everybody breathed a sigh of relief. But Don didn't take another drink during the rest of the tour.

Other places we played were Brescia, Parma, which was the birthplace of Arthuro Toscanini and the theater we played was exactly like the Scala in Milano but smaller, so I was told. Of course there were some very fine pianos there but the one they gave us to use was an upright because they were afraid that our pianist would break a string or some strings on one of the others. But they did not know or did not realise that most classical pianists can hit on the keys much harder than most jazz pianists do.

The last place we played was Livorno. It was not supposed to have been the last date, but the people were not coming to the concerts because of mourning for the Pope, organisers said. Burnier was getting more and more behind in paying us until we all joined the side of Dante and told Burnier that if he didn't make enough money to pay what he was behind in paying us, we would not continue the tour. He didn't come up with the loot so that was the end of my second tour in Italy.

Lily and I stayed in Milano until the 28th of October. Don had taken a plane to Amsterdam and the next time I saw him, he told me that it had costed him more to take his dumb-bells on the plane than his personal ticket did. The rest of the fellows went back to France
The 31st of October I played in Geneva, Switzerland at the Hot Club's cave and the first of November I started a 15 days engagement in Zurich at the "Mascotte" which was a well known jazz club.

A few days after we arrived in Zurich Lily became very ill and we called a doctor who happened to be a woman. She said that Lily was suffering with a grippal meningitis and septicemia. It was about time for me to go to work so we called a private nurse for the night. We were living in a pension (furnished room). Of course I was worried the whole night. The next day she was taken to a private clinic with an ambulance. After a few days she was out of danger but she suffered with a severe cardiac deficiency caused by a sudden complete lack of potassium. She had to be under oxygen therepy for hours every day and we had to hire a private nurse to be with her night and day. Visitors were forbidden, except me. I came every day and stayed there for hours. But after 15 days I had to leave Zurich because I had dates in Be gium and in France. Lily was feeling a little better and a few days after my departure was allowed to have visits. I knew she would be well taken care of and we had many friends there that would visit her, our good friends, the Simmons, Pfisters and Steiners. Johnny stayed in touch with me concerning Lily's health.

I went back to the Trois Maillets the 2nd of December, 1958. Lily came out of the clinic the 8th of December and as the Trois Mailletz closed on Monday, I was able to fly to get her and bring her back to Paris without missing a day at the club.

I was engaged to play a big gala the 10th of January 1959, which is St. William's day in Gstaad. After St. Moritz, Gstaad is the next most popular and best known ski resort in Switzerland. As in many cases, when I did galas in different places, I didn't know with whom I would be working until I arrived at my destination. And was I surprised when I arrived at the Palace Hotel in Gstaad and found out that I would be accompanied by Fred Bungie and his orchestra. Fred, along with Teddy Paris, his drummer, were the musicians I had made my second tour in Germany with in 1952. So it was a pleasant surprise to see those fellows again and to be accompanied by them. Fred always had good musicians and I knew there would be no sweat that night.

On my return to Paris I met a trumpet player named Mike Wyatt. Mike was an English subject from the British West Indies whom I had met when I arrived in Paris in December 1948. He had been living in Paris for quite a while before I arrived. He was a much younger fellow than myself and we became quite good friends.

But the climax or rather the conclusion to this story is that I never saw Fred Bungie or Mike Wyatt again because they were both killed in automobile accidents, Mike in France and Fred somewhere in Germany.

Since 1956 Lily and I had been living in a small but nice rented apartment in the 6th district and we decided that it would not be a bad idea if we bought a little place of our own. We found a flat at 54 rue Monsieur le Prince (a very pretty name to my estimation) which was the house where a famous writer, philosppher and mathematician named Blaise Pascal had lived. A votive tablet is still on the front of the building.
We had this place decorated to our taste and it became a beautiful little two room apartment with kitchen and bath. And it was also the first home that I ever owned.

Not long after we moved in, I was engaged by a piano company of Zurich, Switzerland, named Jeklin, to do a tour of Switzerland, Austria and Germany with the Tremble Kids Orchestra whom I had recorded with in November 1957 in Zurich for Pathe-Marconi. Albert Nicholas and Joe Turner the pianist who was living in Switzerland, were also engaged for this tour and it was a real happy swinging deal.

I left Paris for Zurich the 27th of February rehearsed with the orchestra the 28th and we did our first date the first of March in Lugano, in the Italian part of Switzerland. Other places we played in Switzerland were Bellinzona, Ascona, Grenchen, Winterthur, Basel, Luzern, Schaffausen, Bern and Uster. The pianist with the Tremble Kids Orchestra was a young Swedish fellow named Ola Ringstrom who had a good swinging style.

The leader of the band was a clarinetist named Verner Keller. A good and lively musician. The trumpet man was named Oscar Klein and he also played guitar. Oscar was a real solid dixieland trumpeter and his style reminded me very much of Wild Bill Davison. I never knew Oscar's nationality but I think he was from Austria. Rolf Eizmek was the bass man and Charlie Antolini was the drummer and he could swing. I give the reader of this book the privilege of choosing whatever nationality they may think these last two musicians were.

The tour of Switzerland finished the 10th of March. The 12th we were in Wuppertal, Germany, the next night in Dusseldorf and the following night in Dortmund. From Dortmund we jumped to Linz in Austria the 15th followed by a concert in Vienna the 16th and the 18th in Salzburg.
We left Salzburg the 19th and went back to Germany where we did a concert in Bielefeld the 20th. There was a four day lay-off, so I came
to Paris to spend them with my Baby. Rejoined the group the 25th in Wisbaden, did another concert in Dusseldorf the 26th, Hannover the 28th and finished the tour the 30th in Bremmen.
It was really one of the most enjoyable tours that I had made in Europe because Joe Turner always kept it happy with jokes and other crazy things that only he could do to be the life of the party.

Went back to the Trois Mailletz the first of April and that was no April fool joke. The 15th of May I flew to Portugal for one week with some French musicians to play a ball for the university of Colmbra and also a concert for the students. The students of Colmbra have a very original uniform, black with a lot of colorfull ribbons. They were lively and noisy and we had great fun. I had spent a few hours visiting Lisbonne on my way to New-York from Egypt when the steamer I was on made a few hours stop there. But this was the first time I had ever played in Portugal and also have the chance of seeing what some of the interior was like. I enjoyed what I saw and had a very nice time there.

I came back to Paris and the Trois Mailletz the 22nd of May. Life was great. We had our little appartment that Lily had furnished in a very beautiful way. No more hotel or old furnished places for us. We started to invite friends and give parties. One of them, we shall never forget.

There were many G.I's in Paris as SHAPE was in Versailles, a few miles from Paris. Lily and I became friends with an Ex-G.I. named Robert E. Lee. who was a coloured man and quite a character. Lee could get things for us from the P.X. that we could not get in shops in Paris or if it was possible in shops, it costed less in the P.X. So we became better friends with Lee who was engaged to a pretty blonde German girl named Freia.

Lee and Freia got their marriage papers and as they were living in a hotel room, we offered them the use of our appartment to have their wedding reception. We asked Lee how many people he was inviting and he said about 15, which would be quite a crowd for our small place. Lily
prepared plenty of food which we offered and Lee took care of the drink of which there was plenty.

After the wedding at which there were about ten people, the reception started about two o'clock that afternoon. Soon the 15 people that Lee had invited were there and about 30 others. How we got all those people in our two room apartment is still a mystery to us. And what a wild crowd! The party went late. We had to put the people out because I had to go to work. Lily who was feeling sky high came with me. She said, she would take care of the mess later but when we came home that night, she just fell on the bed and went to sleep.

The next morning we were supposed to go at the airport Orly to meet George Duvivier's mother, Ismay, who was coming to spend her holidays with us. We woke up late and we tried to get by telephone information about the arrival of the plane. The looks of the living room and kitchen was terrific, glasses, ashtrays, bottles, plates, all over.... Lily had such a hangover that she could hardly think. And then suddenly, someone rang at the door. It was Ismay who was frantic and asked my help to deal with the taxi driver. She could not speak a word of French, had no French money and had heavy suitcases in the taxi. We apologised to her and explained what had happened.
Lily who really could not pull herself together, went back to bed and Ismay and myself started to wash the dishes!!!!

I was going through the same routine of leaving the club to do galas and concerts and coming back again at the Trois Mailletz. Max Jones, reporter of the English Jazz journal "Melody Maker" had called me in an article "The man from the Trois Mailletz". Many people started to believe that it was my club. But it was not and the 15th of June 1960, Madame Calvé, the owner of the place announced to me that my service would no longer required after the 15th last of that month.
She had the violinist Stephane Grappelli as another attraction since

a month. She always resented when I was leaving the club for a day or two to do a gig although I was always careful not leave too often. She had agreed that I could go at least twice a month but sometimes, Lily who had become friendly with her, would ask her to let me go for something special and interesting for me.

The French musicians at the Trois Mailletz had been trying for a long time to concince Denise Calvé to get rid of me. They were quite nasty and jealous of my success as an attraction. They had been playing dirty tricks on me.

I was naturally salty with Madame Calvé for three reasons. First, there was no contract between us but we had agreed that if I wanted to leave or she wanted me to go, we were supposed to give one another a month's notice but she was giving me two weeks.

The second reason and a good one, was that it was in the middle of the summer and it was much too late to get an engagement anywhere for the rest of the summer. In fact I had been refusing different propositions because of the Trois Mailletz. And contracts for summer engagements are always done 4-5 months in advance.

And the third reason was that we had taken a mortgage when we bought our appartment and we were still paying for it. We had nothing in advance and we were terribly worried. We had no idea where or what we could do to make some loot before the concert season started in November.

Lily decided to send some letters to different places and some friends to see if something could happen. A few days later we received a reply from our good friend Jean Marie Masse of Limoges with some good news. I had worked quite a few galas with Jean who was doing a summer season in a resort at Royan on the Atlantic coast, not far from Bordeaux.

Jean had spoken to the owners of the place where he was working and convinced them that it may be a good idea to have me there for a few days in July and they agreed. The loot wasn't much but they also offered me

room and board for Lily and myself. As a beggar, I couldn't be a chooser. I had a good paying gig in Brittany in a place called Douarnenez the 16th and 17th of July. Lily had taken a train to Royan from Paris and met me when I arrived the afternoon of the 18th. The name of the place where Jean was working was "Cafe de l'Hotel de Ville". It was a brasserie-restaurant and was owned by two very nice people Marcelle and Charles. They had a terrace in front, where we played. We immediately attracted a lot of people and Marcelle and Charles asked us if we could stay as long as possible in August. As we had found a few gigs for the second part of August, we agreed to stay until the 15th. The second and third of August I had an engagement for the first festival of jazz in Complain-la-Tour in Belgium sponsored by Joe Napoli who at that time had a booking agency in New-York. At the same festival there were Petula Clark and Charles Aznavour who did not have much fame at that time.

Lily remained in Royan and I came back after the festival of Complain-la-Tour. People had been missing me and had been screaming my name in the street in front of the Cafe de l'Hotel de Ville. We liked the place, having plenty of good food and drinks. I weighed 150 pounds until I went to this place. When I left there I was hitting the scales at 170 pounds and looking almost as round as Jimmy Rushing. And Lily was almost looking like Ella Fitzgerald.

Although Lily and I were salty at Madame Calvé because of the deal she pulled on me, we started to be happy about the way it turned out because I started getting more and more gigs that paid me twice as much for one night that what I was making in her place in one week. So the matter of the fact is that she really did us a favor. And the rest of the year finished with me doing concerts and galas, here there and everywhere in Europe.

In April 1961 I was engaged for the month to appear in Barcelona, Spain, in a club known as the Jamboree Cava. I was the first American jazz musician to be engaged in this club, which was the first jazz club

ever opened in Barcelona. I remember that the pianist was called Sandy but I never learned his real Spanish name. All of the musicians were Spanish and they were not too bad at playing jazz, considering that there were very very few places where jazz had ever been played in this country and therefore the musicians there, that went for jazz, had very few occasions to play and experiment with the kind of music they enjoyed.

There were two tenor men in the group I worked with. One was known as Pocholo who also played clarinet and was very popular with the jazz fans. The other tenor man was Salvador Font whom I had jammed with in Rome way back in 1950. The jazz fans in Barcelona were mostly the rich people because they were the ones that could afford to buy jazz records and there was quite a large number of them. But there was also a crowd of young epople, students, writers, painters. The owner of the place, Mr Rossello had asked a group of those young painters to decorate the Jamboree to their own taste and he had given them for salary 600 Cuba Libri (rum and Coke). So the cave was decorated in an amusing and colourful way with paintings on the walls and foot prints on the ceiling. Of course the group was coming every night to hear jazz and drink their salary.. Cuba Libri were jumping, the Maitre d'Hotel, a swell guy named Angelo, was keeping account and the atmosphere was very gay. We made quite a lot of good friends, Ruis, a young leftist poet and painter, François Ferrer, chemist and painter and many others. I enjoyed my stay there very much. I also did quite a few afternoon concerts with the band in some of the surrounding towns and the public in those places were very enthusiastic.

In June I was contacted to play at the "Vieux Colombier" in Juan-les-Pins, the club that Sydney Bechet made famous some year before. Badel, the owner, who also owned the Juan for the month of July and August. He was a slick guy and it was very hard to get a decent salary from him. His idea was to have me to play with a bunch of young French
amateurs who had formed a group not long ago. He wanted me to try to repeat the same experience that Sydney Bechet had made with Claude Luther and his group.

Coming back from Belgium and going to another place I just had a short time to audition the group and rehearse two or three well known standards. It didn't sound too bad but I wasn't very enthusiastic. Badel had left before the end of the rehearsal without even waiting for my decision, taking for granted that it was alright. The fellows were very young and very anxious to get the job so finally I accepted the deal.

Lily and I had decided to buy a second hand car. Albert Nicholas had a Volkswagen "Coccinelle" which had once belonged to Kenny Clarke and as Nick wasn't working very much at that time, he wanted to sell it. Neither of us could drive but we decided to take lessons in Juan-les-Pins. We asked Albert if we would accept to drive us there and we would pay his expenses and his fare back.

So the 29th of June we left Paris with a big load of luggage, our cockatoo named Coco and our Persian cat, Princess. Both animals were scared to death in that car and Coco was repeating non stop "bonjour Coco, ca va Coco?" Princess was mewing. Albert was driving at the speed of 50 miles an hour. We tried to find an hotel room in different places but all the hotels were packed so we had to make the trip non stop except for meals. When we arrived on the Cote d'Azur, Nick was so tired that he was falling asleep on the wheel.

We had a very good friend, Leopold de Lima e Silva who was the son of Mistinguett, the famous Music Hall star. Leopold had inherited from his mother a very nice house with a big garden. It was called the Bungalow and was situated at the Cap d'Antibes, between Antibes and Juan-les-Pins, a 10 minute walk to the "Vieux Colombier". The house was separated in two flats, one was empty and Leopold had proposed to us to live there for a very mild rent and of course we had accepted with joy.

The day after our arrival, I had rehearsal with the band and it was terrible. We tried for two hours to rehearse "Caravan" and another number but it was must impossible. Most of those kids couldn't read, and they had no experience at all. It would have taken weeks to try to teach them to play correctly a dozen numbers. I went to see Badel and told him to look for another band. He wanted to put the blame on me because I had accepted to play with them in Paris. I wanted to put the blame on him because we had told him many time that it was a mistake to engage amateurs just to save money and that I had accepted against my better judgment to play with them because he had put a strong pressure on me. I had to play three days with these boys and finally we had the luck to find some nice French musicians who were already in Juan-les-Pins. One was Nino Ferrer on bass, Peter Giger (swiss) on drums, Sephane Guerault, sax-clarinette. A pianist named Raymond who was playing in a bar located behind the Vieux Colombier, also accompanied us and the group at last sounded very nice.

Every night before my first passage, a group of young rock and rollers were playing for a half hour. It was the beginning in France of the rock and roll era. This group was called the "Chaussettes Noires" (black socks) and featuring a young singer named Eddie Mitchell.

So every night we were going through the same routine. A crowd of about 100 very young teenagers was waiting outside of the "Vieux Colombier". At 9.30 the waiters were letting them in without paying entrance fee. I was even told that at the beginning, they were paid a small fee. They would stand against the walls and they started to shout hysterically: we want "the Chaussette Noires". The group began to play encouraged by frantic shouts from their supporters. After 30 minutes and many loud requests to come back, the band would leave and the waiters would rush the crowd of youngsters out and I had to come on with my quartet and play for the paying guests. Fortunately there
were some jazz lovers there too and we had our success also, but quieter.....

Juan-les-Pins had become very well known for its annual jazz festival. It was the second year that the festival was presented and the orchestras of Ray Charles and Count Basie were the big attractions. It was also the first time for Ray to play in Europe and the first time I ever heard him and saw him. He had a small group with two trumpets, three sax, bass and drums and the Raylettes. He sent me with his style of playing and singing and the arrangements were swinging like mad.

As I was already in Juan-le -Pins, one of the organisers, of the festival, a Monsieur Souplet whom I had known for a long time, wanted me to play one evening at the festival. He told me that there was going to be a very good trio playing that week and he thought that it would be an ideal group to accompany me. It was the trio of the pianist Les McCann. Eventually I met Les and mentioned to him that Souplet told me that he and I would play a set together the last night of the festival. He seemed to be for the deal, and so I asked him when we could get together and arrange our programme He said he would let me know in a couple of days.

Those days passed and he didn't contact me the day after. Then I began to get the feeling that this monkey didn't want to accompany me but wouldn't say it. I even told Souplet about my suspicion but he told me not to worry, that McCann had a stipulation in his contract about accompany another guest artist and everything would be OK.

But every time I saw him and asked him about a rehearsal he would have an excuse and say we still have time to get together. I was only supposed to do three or four numbers. On the last day, I happened to see Les that afternoon and asked him if yes or no he wanted to accompany me. I had heard his trio and although I had never heard of him, I liked the way they played and figured that they were not too modern for my style.
Les gave me a rendezvous for that night at 10, saying that we could talk over some numbers before intermission time and everything would be

alright. Ten o'clock that night there was no Les McCann and he didn't show until intermission. He was supposed to play before Basie, and I was to do my bit after he and his trio. He offered no excuse for not being there at 10, but I tried to get with him regardless. I asked him if we played "Tea for two" would that be alright with him? He said he didn't know it. I asked him if he knew "Sweet Georgia Brown" or "Caravan" and he told me he didn't. After that answer, I knew he was a liar and had not wanted to accompany me from the moment Souplet had suggested it, but he didn't have the guts to say no. After he told me that he didn't know "Caravan", I told him to forget it and walked away. I had decided that my contribution to the festival had finished before it began.

I started talking with Budd Johnson who was one of the tenor men with Basie and told him the Les McCann story. He wasn't Les McCann for me anymore but Les My Can.. Bud suggested that I ask Basie if he would allow his rhythm section to play with me and said that Frank Wess, the other tenor man could accompany me on piano. Then Budd said that he personally would put the proposition to Basie which he did. Bill (Basie) was very understanding about the deal and thought that My Can had played a dirty trick on me, which he had. Basie agreed to let me use his rhythm section and two minutes later he had another idea. He said that the band would go on and play a few numbers and then he would present me doing a couple of numbers with the band.

And when Basie introduced me the reception I received was the greatest I ever had in my career and I was so thrilled that when I spoke in the mike I offered to pay a drink for everyone there. If the public had really taken me at my word, it would have taken me a year to work out the debt to pay for all those drinks because there were at least 3000 people there.

Basie asked me who I wanted to come out front with me to assist in the rounds of solos. I was so excited that I couldn't answer. I had been an admirer of Basie's style of band since the first time I heard it on radio in Egypt in 1939. I had also heard his recording of "Blue and Sentimental" in a movie house in Egypt and didn't know until years later that it was Basie and the big tone of Herchel Evans on tenor and Prez on clarinet. I never saw Herchel because he died before I returned to the States. Basie had a band that I would have loved to have been a member of, but it never happened.

And now, here I was on the verge of being accompanied by my favorite big band and that's all that I could think of. I should have asked for Budd Johnson and Quentin "Butter" Jackson to come out front with me because we were buddies and they had recorded with me the year before when both of them were in France with the Quincy Jones orchestra. I didn't speak up quick enough, so Basie motioned for Frank Wess and Frank Foster to come forward. Wess played flute and Foster tenor on the two numbers I did with the band which were "Perdido" and "Sweet Georgia Brown". I have never been so well accompanied and pushed as I was this night. Thad Jones, Snooky Young, Sonny Cohn and Lenny Johnson were in the trumpet section and they were making up riffs behind me that had me blowing my buns off.

The two numbers I did with Basie had more effect on the public and meant more to my prestige than any amount of numbers that I probably could have done with My Can. There was no broadcast of the festival that night but the radio who had recorded it for further broadcast made a copy of it and I happened to be able to get one which I shall always cherish.
For the next years to come my life was set in a routine; Gigs, Jazz Festivals and concerts in Europe, Balls mostly in France with young French bands such as Jean-Marie Masse and Pierre Guyot's band

or Francis Guillon, and band leader from Poitiers or the Freres Julien, two twins from Sète. Pierre was a talented young alto sax and his brother René was playing bass. I had also formed a quartet with four young Franch musicians, Bernard Estardy, piano, Nino Ferrer, bass, Peter Giger, drums and Charles Barrié, sax-tenor. Whenever I had the chance I would play with my own group but often I would receive propositions from the band leaders mentioned above or from other countries to play soloist with their band.
The 1st of October 1962, I lost my father who had been ill for quite a while. It was as painful for Lily as it was for me. He was a great man. He was 83 years old.

For five years straight I was engaged once a year to play in the Jamboree and went twice to Madrid, once in the Whiskey club and once at the Bourbon Street. Both clubs were owned by a Frenchman named Jean-Pierre Bourbon. Except for the first time at the Jamboree, the pianist was a blind Spanish fellow named Tete Montoliu. Tete played a sort of Tatum and Bill Evans style. He had a lot of technique and like all those blind pianists had a very sensitive ear. His bass player was a German named Peter Trunk, real great and a good German drummer . One time there was also a fine alto player from Florida named Dick Sanders, and a wild tenor man from Denmark named Ben Jaedig. That band really wailed. I also gave concerts in Bilbao and San Sebastian.

In 1963 we decided that our flat was too small and we had sold it and taken a larger appartment in the 12th arrondissement in Paris. We had been living in the Latin Quarter for twelve years but the traffic was becoming so bad in that district and it was becoming so difficult to find parking space that we decided to leave for a less crowded part of Paris. Of course we missed the atmosphere of the Latin Quarter, the side walk cafes, the lively markets, the tourists.
It was a big change for us but time didn't stand still.

I went back different times to the Chikito in Switzerland, the caberet where I had met Lily in 1950. I went there with different French group that I had formed. Once with Guy Lafitte who had become the best French tenor sax, a real disciple of Hawkins. Another time I went with Dany Doris, a talented young vibraphonist. As I had been nominated Honourary president of the Jazz Club of Zurich, I would often have visits at the Chikito from groups of members of the jazz club, which visits would delight me.

In May 1965, I played there for a month and the boss asked me if it would be alright if he engaged the violinist Stuff Smith for 15 days to play as an added attraction with me and my group. Of course I agreed. I knew Stuff from way back and liked his hard swinging and groovy style. That man could swing like nobody else. Unfortunately he was in a bad state of health, suffering with stomach ulcers. He was not supposed to drink at all but couldn't help from having whiskey that he would dilute with plenty of water. Sometimes he would feel good and the next day be very moody. The poor fellow died the same year in September in Munich but was buried in Denmark.

My next thrill came in 1966 when I went to England for the first time to do a tour in that country. I had met an English fellow at the Trois Mailletz named Ronald Sweetman who was working in Paris and was a great jazz fan and record collector. He was also writing articles for different jazz magazines. When Ron eventually returned to England he told me that he was going to try and get me over there.

There was a regulation between the American Federation of musicians and the British musician's syndicate, whereby an American musician could play in England in exchange for an English one playing in the States. But that exchange didn't work for an American musician living in France. At one time I wanted to hire an English musician to work two weeks with
my band in exchange for me going there at a later date to work two weeks with an English group. But I was told by the person I had contacted that it was not possible.

So Ron kept knocking on doors and speaking about me until he finally caught the ears of someone that could see his idea in bringing me there. I was so close to the country and many American musicians were going there and transportation from the U.S.A. costed more than it would from France. Eventually I was contacted by a booking agent named Jim Godbolt and we got together on the loot which was no hell after all I had heard about the good bread that was paid in England.
