But I was told by the person I had contacted that it was not possible.

So Ron kept knocking on doors and speaking about me until he finally caught the ears of someone that could see his idea in bringing me there. I was so close to the country and many American musicians were going there and transportation from the U.S.A. costed me more than it would from France. Eventually, I was contacted by a booking agent named Jim Godbolt, and we got together on the loot which was bread no hell after all I had heard about the good/man that was paid in England. But I wanted to get my foot in there at least one time, so we came to an agreement. When the contract arrived it was not from the Jim Godbolt Agency but the Harold Davison Agency which is the biggest booking agency in England, and was responsible for bringing most of the American musicians to that country after the second world war.

I arrived in London with Lily the 6th of April and learned that the tour would be made with the Bruce Turner orchestra. I knew of Bruce but had never met him. He had the reputation of being one of England's greatest alto sax players, and as the tour continued, I found this to be true. But first I must say that Lily and I liked the looks of everything from the moment we landed at Heathrow airport. And we became more and more excited as we approached the great city of London. A kitchenette apartment had been reserved for us in a big residential hotel known as the White House.

That afternoon we had a rehearsal at the Six Bells in Chealsea, which is a district of London. The Six Bells was a very well known place by musicians and jazz fans and there I met Bruce and the boys, Ray Crance, trumpet, Pete Strange, trombone, Tony Baylis, bass, Ron Ruben, piano, and Doug Higgins, drums, Jack Higgins, not related to Doug, was in charge of the jazz department at the Harold Davison Agency, but Jim Godbolt was going to take care of the band during the tour.

We had a second rehearsal the 7th and pkayed our first concert at Osterley which was the town where most of the American musicians that were booked by the Davison agency started their tour of England. Most of those musicians were accompanied by the Alex Welch orchestra which is one of England's best jazz groups. Why Bruce Turner was chosen for me, I never knew. But I can say, and very happily, that I enjoyed every moment that I spent with Bruce Turner and his boys.

Ron Ruben was a fine pianist. Lily, Bruce and myself travelled in Ron's car, and one day, I was amazed when he told me that his real instrument was bass. He played piano so well that I thought it was his instrument. I never had the opportunity to hear him play bass, but if he played more of that thing then he did piano or even as much, then he was hell on wheels.

The tour taken me to Birmingham and the name made me think of Birmingham in Alabama, but the difference in the two places was like night and day with the one in England representing day. That was the second concert and the following places we played were Bexley, Morden, Hitchen, Haywards Heath, Norwich, Nottingham, Redcar, Chester, South-ampton, Chealsea at the Six Bells, Newcastle, Manchester, the 100 club in London which was the closing date of the tour on April 24th.

Many of the places we played were small towns but we always had a swinging full house. Bruce and the boys really pushed me and I found out that Bruce was very popular everywhere he went. The Harold Davison office was satisfied with the results of the successful reports they received about the tour. So was I, and also to have seen the dream of my friend Ronald Sweetman come true in the form of me making a tour in that great jazz loving country.

We gave a party at Max and Betty Jones' home for the Bruce Turner gang, and a few intimate friends. Max had been a well known critic and reporter for the Melody Maker musical magazine for many years. Bruce and the boys had a surprise gift for me which was a silver beer mug ingraved: "To Bill - the Guv'nor" from Bruce, Pete, Tony, Ray, Ron and Doug. That was a real sender for me and a gift I shall always cherish. Being called 'Guv'nor' in England is an honour in most cases, and these fellows were honouring me.

Then we went to visit for a few days our friends Ronald Sweetman and his wife Jennifer in a beautiful little town called Steyning in the Sussex country. Jennifer, by the way, is a very well known artist who paints under her maiden name of Jennifer Dickson. Their house was called 'Ellington house'. I hope you know why! We had a swell time, and Jennifer and Ronald gave a party in our honour with 60 guests.

During my stay in England, I met many English musicians that I had heard about, listened to on records but had never seen in person. To name a few: Danny Moss, who lived in Steyning, Sussex, where my friend Ronald Sweetman and his wife Jennifer lived, Ronnie Scott, owner of the famous club known under his name in London, Kenny Ball, a fine trumpet man and singer and many whose names I don't remember. But one I could never forget was Aker Bilk. The reason is that Aker had a private membership club in Soho on Greek Street, which was directed by his brother Dave and I spent quite a few after hours there with Lily, members of Aker's orchestra and jazz fans. I renewed my acquaintance with a pianist named Lennie Felix, whom I had met in the 50's at the Trois Mailletz. Lennie had become real popular in his country a few years after we met. Also met the famous singer Geroge Melly in Manchester.

Back in France, I was engaged in July for a tour with a fashion show for four weeks with a group of four dishy girls who were models. The show played in casinos all over France. We even went to Tunisia for four days and gave a show in front of the son of President Bourguiba. The fasion show was going on for an hour, than I played a half hour. I had my pianist, Gabriel Garvanoff, a fine young musician with me, but we had to play with the bass and drummer from the casinos. There was also another attraction with us, a comedian named Jean Raymond.

We did 10,000 miles with our car in four weeks, not counting the trip to Tunisia. The atmosphere was gay and if it was quite tiresome to do all this travelling, we had a lot of fun anyway. And the food in France is superb.

But it was less fun when we came back to Paris where bad news was waiting for us. We had met two years previously a woman who was in the real estate business. She seemed to be a smart business woman and was quite a nice person. We had confidence in her ability, and had invested our savings in her housing construction company. But the company went bankrupt and we lost every penny that we had saved for years without any hope of getting our money back. It was no use to cry over spilled milk, but it was a bitter lesson and we would be more careful in the future with our savings.

I had been approached by a French musician named Jeff Gilson. Jeff was a pianist and arranger. He was quite talented as an arranger, and we were going to work quite a bit together. First he had formed a big orchestra, and we gave a concert at the Theatre de l'est Parisien. Then we gave two concerts of sacred music in two churches in Paris. One in the church"St.Etienne du Mont" and the other one in "St.Jean de Belleville", both times with the participation of the Abbey de Fatto, who was an ex-jazz musician. I had been working with him in Claude Bolling's band. The concert in St. Etienne du Mont was televised. I played and sang Negro-Spirituals.

We gave other concerts with a small formation with Jeff's rhythm section, and the alto sax Hubert Fol, at the O.R.T.F. theatre, and for some cultural centres in France. Jeff asked me to record an album called 'Jazz Dor God'. I played two numbers: "Jericho" and "Sometimes I feel like a motherless child".

After three rehearsals at a club called Tally-Ho, the first concert took place the 21st of April at the Rugby Football club in Osterley where the first one with Bruce Turner had been played. The sextet was known as a semi-professional orchestra because Tony and Alan had another profession and did not depend on music as a living. But they played better than some professionals that I had come across in my travels and the group as a whole were real tight and could swing like mad.

The next stop was Birmingham again, then Manchester and Morden. Buck Clayton was in London during this time and Ben Webster was playing at Ronnie Scott's club. We were engaged to do a recording for a producer named Alan Bates which was for the 27th of April.

I arrived at the studio that morning and learned that Buck had been taken to a hospital the night before, suffering from a nose haemorrhage. The rhythm section was from the Alex Welsch orchestra and Jack Higgins was in charge of the date.

As I was the first soloist to arrive and we three were supposed to record a few tunes alone and play some that had been arranged by Buck, I got started with the Rhythm section and had gotten three in the bag before Ben arrived. He was supposed to have come to the studio with Buck and didn't know that Buck had been taken to a hospital. Jack had to call Ben and tell him to take a taxi to the studio.

Ben eventually arrived and we did some original numbers and one that I composed in the studio and called it "Pound Horn", because I had learned that studio trumpettists that doubled on flugel horn were paid an extra pound when the horn was used at a session and English musicians called it a pound horn.

Ben did some numbers alone with the rhythm section. There was one number that I would loved to have re-recorded, which was 'Satin Doll', but Jack Higgins insisted that some unknown girl singer he wanted to push perhaps, record a number and that did not leave time enough to do anything more. We had recorded the album between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. The rhythm section had a T.V. date with Alex Welsch and could not stay any longer. I was not very satisfied with the "Satin Doll" version I did record.

The next day I played the 100 club and Nottingham the 29th. Replaced Buck with the John Chilton Swing Kings at a place called 'Dog and Fox' in Wimbledon, the 30th. Here was another surprise for me when I learned that John Chilton was a musician and a trumpet player to boot. When I did my first tour in England, John was collaborating with Jim Godbolt in the booking agency business. We had quite a few get togethers, but he never spoke about being a trumpet man or even a musician. And no one else ever mentioned it to me. So naturally, it was a surprise when I learned this about John, and it was a bigger surprise when I heard him play, because he has a real funky style which is seldom heard these days.

The only trouble I experienced during the tour and which was embarrassing for the orchestra and myself was the night we played in Blackpool, the 25th of May at the Casino Ballroom, which was located in an amusement park. Lily, Alan Littlejohn and myself arrived with Lew Hooper in his car. The rest of the gang had left London in a rented van as the English call a small bus, with the drums, bass and Alan's horn. After a couple of hours of waiting for the others to arrive, and when they were not there at a certain time, we started to worry about them.

Eventually a 'phone call came from somewhere, and it was one of the musicians in the van calling to say that they were having trouble with the motor and did not know when they would arrive. Everybody that was connected with the ballroom started to do what they could to try to find some local musicians to fill in until the boys in the band arrived. And we were fortunate enough to find a pianist, bass and drummer. I had my flugel horn and trumpet. Lew had his tenor, so I let Alan use the flugel horn and we started the concert. Kenny Ball was playing a date not far from Blackpool and stopped to say 'hello' to us. Some of his musicians were with him, and the trombonist, clarinetist, joined us for a couple of numbers. Of course, we could not play our regular programme but we gave the public a good jam session and no one asked for a return of their money. We had finished the concert when the other fellows arrived. Naturally they regretted what had happened and so did we. But it was one of those things that could happen to anyone.

The first of May, the Milliner-Littlejohn sextet and myself became the first jazz group to do a concert in the Purcell Room which adjoins the Royal Festival Hall. This was a swell place, and I could sing without a mike which is something, because I don't have a very strong voice as far as singing is concerned. It was one of the most successful concerts and another first in my career.

Next we played Hitchen, Haywards Heath, Blackpool and finished the tour in Manchester at the Sports Guild. Buck's condition had improved and he was booked at play this last concert with me, but he had another haemorrhage and could not make the date. The sextet surprised me with a different of silver beer mug from the one the Bruce Turner boys gave me. This one was inscribed: 'To Bill, with admiration and affection from the Boys - Tony, Alan, Matt, Lew, Mal & Dave'. They also gave Lily a small one inscribed: 'To Lily, with love'and the name of the fellows as they were inscribed on my mug, - beer mug, that is.
Lily and I visited friends in Scotland, We had a lot of fun with those whiskey lovers, went back to Steyning again, and returned to France the 16th of May.

The 29th of May, I played a big festival in Birmingham with the Milliner-Littlejohn sextet and Ben Webster. I returned to London in October for a festival at the Hammersmith Theatre and blew this one with Alex Welsch, which was a greater deal. Ben Webster was there also and it was my first time to become acquainted with a fine trumpet player whom I had heard on records but never met. His name is Ruby Braff and when we met, the feeling between us was like we had known each other for years.

Ruby was with the George Wein Newport All Stars. I had met George a few years before. The first thing that we did, Ruby and me after meeting was to have a drink, and then we were ole' buddies. Ruby played more horn in person that I had heard him do on records, and he has a beautiful style.

The 1st of July, 1967, we moved from Paris to Fontenay Sous Bois where we still live, because we had decided that the rent of our other flat was too high for our deflated purse! We found a very nice four roomed apartment on the sixth floor of a modern building, and we had a gorgeous view over the woods of Vincennes and even Paris.

I had met a fmous French singer named Michel Polnareff during a tour in France. He liked my way of playing and he asked me if I would be willing to do a duet with him at the Olympia Music Hall for three weeks in October. We would play 'Summertime' together, me having a few chorus on trumpet, then him, imitating the sound of a trumpet with a wa-wa. I accepted as it was good publicity to work at the Olympia and Polnareff had a big name. The number had a big success. Polnareff had a big voice for such a little fellow, and he had a powerful mike while I had an old mike, but I made my success.

But I had a bad souvenir of Polnareff because after the Olympia, his manager asked me if I w uld play the number again for a televised show. Lily asked what the conditions would be but we could never get a straight answer. Finally, he agreed on our terms.

There was another problem. I was going to be in Switzerland at the time for a concert tour, but I had a day free and I could come back for the programme but I wanted the manager Polnareff to pay the travel expenses as I had to go back to Switzerland to continue the tour. He accepted, but as all these agreements were taken at the last minute, we did not have time to make a contract.

We did the show but I have never been paid for my travel expenses, and I did not get the promised fee either. The television people said that that was a private agreement with Polnareff and they could pay me only the average scale of a musician. We tried to contact Polnareff's manager a hundred times, but could never get him anymore on the phone. So in my opinion, the two of them stink, because I had to travel two days having very little sleep and to do a T.V.show for nothing, in fact, pay the trip with my own money!

In December, I played in Geneva, Switzerland , and gave a few concerts with some nice Swiss musicians, Henri Chaix, a pianist of the style of James P. Johnson, and Willie 'the Lion' Smith; Pierre Bourru, a good drummer,and Michel Pilet, a sax tenor, with a nice sound in the style of Hawkins.

In February 1968, I was elected a member of the French Academy du Jazz. The function of the Academy du Jazz is to pick the best jazz records issued during the year and give it an award. There were distinctions for different categories, Blues, New Orleans, Modern Jazz, Singers, etc. We would also elect the best French musician of the year. A well known foreign musician who has been the European scene for years, the trumpetist Arthur Briggs, and an American named Sim Coppans, who had a jazz programme on radio for many years, were members of the Academy. We three were the only members who were not French.

In May, Jeff Gilson asked me if I would accept to record an album of Negro Spirituals for a guy named Pou-Dubois who owned a studio. We recorded some well known spirituals and some which were completely unknown. Jeff made the arrangements. We made a contract stipulating that I would get royalties when Pou-Dubois would sell the tape and the record would be issued. We recorded the 8/9/11th of May, 1968. I had some nice French musicians with me such as Eddie Louis, Guy Peterson, etc.

But Pou-Dubois didn't sell the tape to a record company. He made a transaction with the International Guild du Disque in Switzerland, without stipulating that I was supposed to receive royalties. In fact, he signed a statement declaring that all the musicians and artists had been paid and had no right to claim payment or royalties. So I couldn't get any money from the Guild and it was not worthwhile to sue Pou-Dubois at the moment as he was not solvent, according to some people.

May and June 1968 were bad concerning work. Paris was having a revolution and there was a general strike. Every gig, concert and job were cancelled. The Latin quarter was on fire. Police attacked by students were using lacrymator gas. All the clubs were closed. There was no gas for cars, metro and buses were not running. When peace was restored, we still suffered the consequences and hardly worked all summer.
In September, I was engaged for a concert in Antwerp with Ben Webster, Buddy Tate, Jimmy Woody, Wallace Bishop, Milt Buckner and Joe Turner. It was nice to blow with those guys who were all friends.

Then I went to Copenhagen and made a tour with a nice Danish trombone player, John Darville and his group. They were nice musicians and pals and we played Arhus, Holback and did a radio show. Then I went to Oslo, my first time in Norway, and played with a dixieland band, the Big Chief Jazz Band. All were very nice fellows and we had a ball and drank quite a bit. We played at the Dow Tow Key Club and did a T.V. I went back to Denmark. I saw my old friend Timmie Rosenkrantz and his wife Inez Cavanaugh. He had a club and Mary Lou Williams was playing there. I also saw May Mezzrow, the wife of Mezz Mezzrow. She was a cook in a restaurant in town. I was happy to see all these people, especially Timmie, who was such a nice fellow.

Buddy Tate had been in Paris and in Europe for a concert tour. I asked him if he would be interested to make a record with me for Pathe-Marconi. He liked very much the idea but had difficulties with the manager who had brought him in Europe. Jean-Marie Monnestier who was against the idea. He told Buddy that if he made the record, Monnestier would not pay his fare back to the U.S.A. So until the last minute, we still did not know if he would be there for the recording. The studio had been hired, so were the musicians. The last concert of his tour was in Barcelonne, Spain, and Buddy had called me there, saying that he was trying to arrange things with Monnestier. In the morning, at 8 o'clock, we went to the airport to see if he was there. Was I glad to see him!...He had a bad cold and had not slept a wink. He told me that at 3 a.m. he was still argueing with Monnestier. We went to have breakfast, than to the studio, and we made a nice album titled: "Together at last". The other musicians were Georges Arbanitas on piano and organ, Pierre Sims on bass, and Charles Bellonzi on drums.

I did another recording for a British fellow who was trying to push a young British pianist named Mike Garret. I was told that Mike had been doing a lot of classical piano, was very talented and wanted to play jazz. We decided to record in Paris with Art Taylor on drums, Jean Francois Castoire on bass and Francois Guin, named "Frick" on trombone. We found out that Mike had never before played with an ensemble and didn't know the art of accompanying soloists. We did our best and called the album "Three Generations Jam". It was released in England by my great friend Doug Dobell,

The same routine went on during most of 1969. Concert tour in Switzerland with the New Ragtime Band directed by a very sensitive clarinet player, Jacky Millet. Concerts in France, with my group with Marc Hemmler, piano, Pierre Sim, bass, and Francho Manzzechi on drums. I was giving now and then, Negro Spirituals concerts. I was part of a show with a big choral from Lyon, "the Bardanes".

It has been two years since I had not been in London again, but the occasion came for the Expo which was a week long festival, sponsored by the Harold Davison Agency and George Wain, that featured many American musicians as well as English groups, and once again, I was to meet and work with a famous musician I had heard and read plenty about but never seen.

This was the pianist Jay McShann, and his personality sent me as soon as we were introduced. He, Charles Shavers, Buddy Tate, Albert Nicholas and I, did a public aduience T.V.show for the B.B.C. at Ronnie Scott's club. Jay played and sang some real gone blues which knocked everybody out and when it came to accompanying me on my numbers, it was the first time I had been sent the way he sent me, in many moons. I have a tape of that session, thanks to an English jazz lover and friend of mine, named Leslie Parr, and I at least can say that if Charlier Parker and Miles Davis were one time members of Jay McShann's orchestra, I had the honour of having him accompany me. He is a great piano man, and blues singer, that knows how to send a soloist.
There was a fine English bass man backing us up but the drummer was a little too modern and ligjt for our style.

It was October 27th when we did the T.V.show and the 28th was the concert at Odean - Hammersmith Theatre, which I later heard was the best night of the festival. The 29th I went to Bristol where I played at the Old Granary, which was a club owned by Acker Bilk. The band was from somewhere near Bristol, and we didn't rehears anything but we had a nice jam session the whole evening. Lily and I came back home the 2nd of November, happy as usual, with our visit to England.

For the second time, I went just after New Year to a ski resort in Auvergne, a province of France, called Spur-Besse. A young friend of mine, the clarinetist Marc Lafferie, was organizing a jazz festival and the conception of that festival was unusual and very sympathetic. He invited about 100 musicians, professional and amateurs and we were all living in the same building which usually was used as a hotel for holidays for people of modest background.

The festival runs for a week, I would give a concert, but Lily and I would stay for the whole week. Many great artists would play there, also: Albert Nicholas, Benny Waters, Memphis Slim, The Golden Gate Quartet, Guy Lafitte, etc. The atmosphere was very exciting. Not only were there musicians and their families, but also people who came from everywhere as paying guests and would stay for the week. So there would always be somebody to talk with, drink with, make music with. In the day time, we would go out for a walk, the majority would go skiing, then we would take a nap, go downstairs, play cards or dices, games. Bands would rehears, then aperitif time would come. After supper, we all would go to the concert hall. Two or three bands were playing each night. After the concert, about one o'clock, a lot of people would go four floors below in a club called "The Terrier", which means "The Burrow", and jam there for hours, often until three or four in the morning.

After Super-Besse, we went to Nice where we got a taste of spring, then in April, we went to Morocco to Meknes, Rabat and Casablanca. It had been very long time since my last trip there. This time, I was playing with a band directed by Jacques Largeaud, who played organ and piano. He was also a school teacher, and was very nice and interesting fellow and we had a swell time. A few weeks laterm I went back to Copenhagen to do a T.V.show with Teddy Wilson. The funny thing is that we flew in the same plane and did not see each other. He must have been in first class and I in tourist class. Ben Webster was living in Copenhagen, and also did the T.V.show,

I went back to play at the Trois Mailletz. I had been angry for some time with Madame Calvé, but decided to forget the difference. Past was past, and it's nice sometimes to play in a club. Another club where I started to play was the Caveau de la Huchette, also situated in the Latin Quarter, which had been bought by Danny Doris, the vibraphonist with whom I had worked quite a few times. The atmosphere of the Huchette was more easier going than at the Trois Mailletz, where people came more to listen to music. In the Hutchette, people were coming to dance and musicians were coming and going all the time, but it was a hot and smoky place.

A famous well known French composer and singer, Guy Béart, contacted me. He had a T.V. programme called "Bienvenue" which means "Welcome" to Guy Béart. He wss having that programme about twice a month, andhe was inviting all kinds of personalities for his show. He told me that he wanted to make a show called "Bienvenue to American artists", and asked me if I was willing to contact the American musicians available in Paris. I rang Mickey Baker, guitarist, Kenny Clark, drummer, Art Simmons, piano, Benny Water, sax-tenor, Cecily Forde, singer and some others. We did the show and one month later, Guy Béart called me again and said that he wanted to make another show with Duke Ellington who was in town. Again I was in charge of forming a band. This time I rang the pianist Aaron Bridges, Michel Gaudry, a fine French bass player, Daniel Humair, one of the besst drummer in town, my friend, the sax tenor Guy Lafitte, Mickey Baker on Guitar. Guy Béart wanted Cecily Forde again. Cecily is not American, she is a very nice singer from Trinidad in the style of Sarah Vaughan, and Guy Béart had been impressed with her performance for the first show.

We were all very excited to be with Duke. He came on the T.V. set at 5 p.m., dressed in a light blue costume(it was in July). Guy Béart introduced him to the audience, because Guy Béart always had his emission semi-public with personalities, artists, guests, press, and a lot of beautiful girls, who were engaged especially to add more class to the show.

We played twonnumbers for Duke, than Béart asked him a lot of questions about his career, about jazz.."what is jazz? what is the future of jazz?....what do you think of free jazz?...do you sing?... please sing a song...." Duke has a superb sense of humour, and he knows how to wrangle his way out of the most tricky situation...it was a pleasure to hear him talk.

Then he sat at the piano and played some of his compositions. Later,he played two numbers with us, and at the end, we had a jam session. Nothing had been prepared or rehearsed in advance. The atmosphere was terrific. I was amazed at the patience of Duke. It was 1 a.m. when shw show was finished. For unknown reasons, it was two years before the programme was shown on T.V.

1971 was going to be quite interesting, at least concerning traveling. I went back to Superbase,than to Switzerland, where I recorded two sides with the New Ragtime Band. Back in Paris, I recorded an album with the band of Raymond Fonseque,a very good trombonist who had a group of seven

musicians with piano, bass saxophone, banjo, washboard, clarinet and trumpet. Marcel Bornstein, who plays a very good trumpet, had played with Reveliott's band, and Sidney Bechet. We recorded 10 original compositions of Fonsèque and myself, and we were very pleased with the album which was different from other things that I have recorded. We nammed the album "Bill and the Boys" B.C. with Raymond Fonsèque and his Original Jazz Band.

In June, I participated in another French Festival located in Normandy, in a village called Luneray. This festival was taking place in a potato storage barn, and there was an attendance of 10,000 people in those days. Plenty of amateur bands were there, and 4 or 5 professional ones. Also, 2 or 3 wellknown artists as attraction. The music was non-stop from 10 in the morning until 9 in the evening. People could eat and drink there at a very moderate price. The organisation was super and all the people of the village lead by Mr. Jean Suplice, were participating at the festival. I never saw a public more enthusiastic and disciplined. Nobody drunk, everybody from children to old age people were listening. The entrance fee was small but all the benefit of the festival would go to social welfares and charities.

The 21st of June, I did a concert in Joinville, a suburb of Paris with Benny Carter, Ben Webster, Kenny Drew, Art Taylor, Michel Sarbadi, Johnny Griffin, The Golden Gate Quartet. I could only make one concert because I had to leave the next day for Morocco, but there were going to be three concerts in the same theatre, the 21st, 22nd, and 23rd. On the programme would also be Claude Bolling, Memphis Slim, Slide Hampton, The Delta Rhytmn Boys. The festival was organized and sponsored by a woman named Lallie Patrick, but unfortunately, the organization was terrible. She didn't make any publicity, in fact, she had been promised publicity by guys like Jacques André and Michel Perrin, who were jazz journalists, but they really let her down, and the festival was a flop, about 150 people at each concert. What a pity with such named musicians. Quite a few artists didn't get their money. Ben Webster didn't show up for the last concert. Lallie Patrick had a restaurant in front of the Marne river in Joinville. Ben who was drunk probably wanted to make pee-pee in the river and fell in the water. He was rescued by the cook of the restaurant, who heard his calls for help!

In Morocco, I went in Tanger to give a concert. The band leader was Jacques Largeaud and he had an amateur drummer who was a native from one of the oldest African tribes in Morocco, whose name was Slim. Slim had a very shabby set of drums.

During the intermission I was surprised to see Max Roach come into my dressing room. He was having a vacation in Tanger with his wife. It was nice to see him and during the second part of the show, I introduced him to the public and asked him to join me for a few numbers, and he accepted. It was a thrill. Slim couldn't believe his eyes, seeing Max Roach playing his old set of drums as if they were a new set just arrived from the factory.
After Tanger, I went to Corsica in July. It was my first time in Corsica which is a very picturesque island. From there I went to Palermo for another festival.

The next exciting thing in the travels of my horn and me happened the 21st of November, 1971, when I was engaged to go to West Africa. It came through the U.S. Cultural Center's African programming office. My wife and I left Paris (Orly airport) the night of November 21st at 10:35 on an African airline plane, and arrived at Abidjan airport in the Ivory Coast at 5 o'clock in the morning of the 22nd. I had been in North Africa quite a number of times, but never in other parts of Africa, so naturally, I was excited about being in a part of the world I had seen in movies and heard so much about. Lily and I were both cool, but our hearts were beating like the drums accompanying an African ballet.

The assistant director of the U.S. Cultural Center, a young man from Boston named Robert La Gamma, his wife and the director of the National Orchestra of the Ivory Coast, a Monsieur Jean-Joseph Pango, met us at the air-port and these personalities gave us the feeling that we were going to enjoy our stay in Abidjan. We had no idea of what to expect in a part of the world; we had never visited before, but when the time came for us to leave, we knew that we would never forget that country and the wonderful people we met. Africans and Europeans included.

I was engaged to play three concerts within eight days. It was a mysterious deal from the first time I learned that I was to play with a big band because the U.S. Cultural Center's director in Paris could never get any information about the composition of the orchestra. A tape of some things I had recorded was sent to them and some orchestrations. I had some big band arrangements but not knowing the instru-
mentations of the orchestra or what type of musicians they were, I didn't send those arrangements and decided to play it by ear.

The death of Louis Armstrong on the 6th of July, 1971, two days after his 71st birthday(which was on July the 4th) was quite a shock to me and my wife, because Pops seemed to have been well on the way of recovering good health. I suppose that his sudden death was quite a surprise to most of the jazz world. I did not cry when I heard the sad news, as some people may have done, but my heart was heavy as lead. I admired Pop's way of playing when I heard his first record. The one I heard was when he was with Fletcher Henderson.

And when I got to know him as well as I did, and listened to so much of his horn playing, my admiration of him grew more and more. I am proud to say that I got to know him so well that me and my wife met him and his wife Lucille quite often whenever they came to Paris.

Louis, who was also known as Gate-Mouth, then Satchel-Mouth, which was shortened to Gate, Satchmo and was also called Pops, was a genius. He gave much to the jazz world with his original style of trumpet playing and jazz singing. There has been quite a few geniuses in jazz music after Satchmo, but many of them died young. But the world was fortunate to have had it's Louis, Pops, Gatemouth, Satchmo Armstrong for so many happy trumpet and singing years! He did so very much for jazz and to bring joys to the world of jazz music lovers. God Bless his soul.

Charlie Shavers' death was a shocking surprise to me, and Lily, because we had not heard that he was sick. It was the passing of two great trumpet men within a few days of each other, because Charlie was a great trumpet player and musician who was also an arranger I knew Charlie quite well because I was living in New York when he made his real debut with the John Kirby orchestra. Rightfully, I would say that Charlie was the backbone of the "World's greatest Little Band" because the numbers they recorded and played on radio were arranged by him and many were his compositions which I had the honour of playing some of them during my short stay with the group after Charlie had left, and the band was beginning to lose it's popularity.
472 (465 (b)) Bis Bis

I wrote about the time I did the Mildred Bailey radio show and Charlie was in the studio orchestra. But we did actually play together once, and that was at a festival in London in 1967, which I also wrote about. The last time we saw him was in February the 14th, 1970, in a suburb of Paris called Drancy. Charlie was making a tour with Budd Johnson and Oliver Jackson. I was engaged to play the concert with my group and Charlie's group with a French pianist and bassist played the last part of the concert.

Charlie passed away two days after Louis and the music world lost two great jazz men. But thanks to recordings, like some others that left things for them to be remembered by, Louis and Charlie left their music for all to hear and appreciate; May God Bless Charlie Shavers' soul also.

So when my first contact with the orchestra was made, it happened in Treichville, a suburb of Abidjan, the second day after my arrival. There was a reception for Lily and I in the building where Monsieur Pango had his office and then we went to a one room place near-by for the rehearsal. The line up of the orchestra was three trumpets, one alto, one tenor, two clarinets, two electric accompaniment guitars, one electric bass guitar, a drummer, a tom-tom player, a male singing quartet, and a female choir of eight. The girls were dressed in their native costumes and some were beautiful. Monsieur Pango plays alto, accordion and organ, but he didn't take any part in the numbers I rehearsed for the concerts.

The musicians were mostly young students from different parts of the country and were not very much in the know about jazz, but they loved it & were very cooperative. They had rehearsed in advance standards such as 'Perdido', 'Basin Street Blues', 'St. Louis Blues'. We rehearsed also a couple of Negro Spirituals with the male singing quartet and this was going to be a big success. A couple of the musicians could speak a little English, but I speak French not too badly and as French is the national language spoken in the Ivory Coast, everything went fine. The only thing wrong was that they could not play fast and everything I did was in the same tempo.

The U.S. Cultural Center's director was on a trip, but he had put his villa at our disposal with his boy, a native from Biaffra named Benson. The villa was situated in Cocody and was beautiful. We also had a car and a chauffer at our disposal.

We rehearsed the morning and afternoon of the 23rd, also the morning of the 24th and played the first concert that night at the University of Abidjan. It was the rainy season in the Ivory Coast and that day, about 4 p.m., a storm started. Usually, it finished in an hour or two, but that day, we couldn't see the end of it. The concert was open air and we really thought that we wouldn't be able to play. But about 8 p.m., the rain almost stopped, and we left for the university.
Robert La Gamma invited us to Thanksgiving dinner along with Monsieur and Madame Pango the 25th.

The 26th, we were invited to the residence of Mr. and Mrs.Root, the American Ambassador, who was giving a luncheon in our honour. This was a different reception from the kick in the ass I got when I was in Egypt, and couldn't even get a look at the Ambassador when the fellows I was with and myself needed help. We gave a concert that night at the cultural center in Treichville and Mr Root came and had a ball.

We were invited for lunch with Mr. Pango at the house of an African Notable in Grand Bassam. We were delighted to be invited in an African family, have the chance to see their house, their way of living, and to be able to eat African food.

We went also to a restaurant in front of the Lagoon owned by a French woman, and we ate their fancy food: monkey, antilope, bats and agouti. They told us that it was a squirrel, but somebody told us afterward that it was like a rat.

Monsieur Pango has a brother who is a Catholic Priest and a very amazing man. He is also a fine musician. His name is Father Pierre-Michel Pango and he lived in Bingerville. He composed the National anthem of the country which is titled "l'Abidjanaise", when the Ivory Coast got it's independence from France. He directed choirs in Europe and has written many songs and religious compositions. He teaches children and directs a choir in Bingerville, which is a town a few miles from Abidjan.

My last concert was in Bingerville on Sunday the 28th. We had a nice lunch in the garden of the African cultural center with Mr. and Mrs. Pango, some of their eleven children, and Mr Pango's assistant-Mr. "Bill" Yappi. About five, we arrived in Bingerville. The concert had been arranged in the afternoon, so that the kids of the village could attend, and it was the largest crowd of the three concerts. It was open air and the weather was fair. There were hundred of kids, if not thousands, and thousands of adults -black and white. There are many Europeans and white people from all parts of the world in the Ivory Coast and they seemed to be like one big happy family. The other concerts were mixed crowds and very successful because there is seldom a jazz concert there, which made my appearance at three concerts very special occasion.
But the crowd at Bingerville topped many of the festivals, I've played in Europe as far as attendance is concerned.

I heard that there was a trumpet player named Fax Klare that had a club in Treichville and that he did a good imitation of Louis Armstrong. I did meet another trumpet player whose name I don't remember who said that he also had a club in Treichville and all 11 pieces orchestra. Sunday night we decided to visit these clubs and I was in the mood to do some real blowing if the musicians in anyone of the clubs inspired me. But when we arrived at Fax's club, it was closed and it was just about 10 p.m. It was the same when we arrived at the next club, closed on Sunday, and they were the only two clubs that featured live music and I wanted to hear what type of music was played in those places.

The most popular male singer is a young African named Francois Lougah, We met him at the U.S. Ambassador's Luncheon, and he came to my last two concerts. He's a pop singer, but a jazz fan. Another singer I heard about who is quite popular in the Ivory Coast is Ernesto Djedje, another pop singer.

The 29th we went to the U.S. Cultural Center to say 'goodbye' to the staff, Mr. Pango and the members of the band. We received numerous gifts and we were feeling sad. We were going to Dakar, Senegal and parting from the Ivory Coast gave Lily and I the feeling that we were losing a very dear friend.

We stayed in Dakar only three days. Concerning my only concert in the country, if could have made a good Mack Senett comedy film. A group of musicians of lead and bass guitars, a tenor sax man, drums and piano player were to accompany me. A rehearsal was called for late in the afternoon of my first day in Dakar at the club where this group worked. I asked the fellows if they knew certain compositions which were jazz classic, such as 'Peridido', 'Tea for Two', 'St.Louis Blues', etc.......They didn't. I asked them what numbers did they know? They couldn't name one tune. And what made matters worse was that the pianist or any of them could not read chords. I always carried two chord books with me. One in English, the other in French.

Finally they pretended to know "Moanin", the composition of B. Timmons, but when I started to play it with them, it sure was not the same 'Moanin' that I knew. So I was obliged to mark them off and tell the director of the American Cultural Center that it was impossible for me to work with these men. It was the A.C.C. that had engaged me for the concert, but the director had never heard anything about me before and did not know anything about jazz.

So he started to ask me if I could play "alone" for the concert. I explained to him that I needed at least a rhythm section and he said that he would see what he could do, but that the band was supposed to be the best in town.

A friend of my wife and I, Colette Lacroix, had given Lily the phone number of the director of the most important newspaper in Dakar, called "The Sun". When we were met at the airport by the Director of the Cultural Center, Lily asked him if any report had been printed in the papers about my arrival and the concert. He said that nothing had been printed concerning the matter. So Lily phoned the Director of the 'Sun' newspaper, who seemed to be a nice person to talk with. He said that he had heard me play several times in France when he was a student there, that he would not be able to attend the concert because he had to leave Dakar, but he would be able to come to the rehearsal and he came with a reporter and photographer. He was quite upset when he saw that it was not possible for me to do anything with those musicians that were to accompany me.

He said that if the American Cultural Center really wanted to do something cultural for his country and the people, they should send a couple of American music professors to teach the young students and musicians, the different arts of America, and the right approach to the form of jazz that was known in American, and other parts of the continent.

The director of 'The Sun' had come to the rehearsals also with a young musician in his early thirties who was a trumpet player from Ghana. His name was Mackenzie. He knew quite a lot about jazz and was a quiet/nice person. He told me that he had seen the director of the Cultural Center the previous week and told him that this band would be incapable to accompany me. He had offered to form a little group and make them rehears, but they had declined his offer.

We asked him if he could contact some better musicians. Unfortunately he said, two were out of town, but he knew a lead guitar and a guitarist and also a drummer. The assistant director,who by then was getting very worried said that he was going with him and we went back to our hotel and waited and waited.

About 11 that night, Mackenzie and the Director and his assistant came to our hotel and said that they had not been able to find the musicians who were not in. The director asked me if I could play the concert alone....which was proof that he really did not know anythinG about jazz. He was quite surprised that the press of Dakar was making an event of my concert, and I think he felt that he was in the circumstances in a bad position. The concert was for the next day. Mackenzie said that he was going to continue his search and we went to bed disgusted.

The next day we had an appointment at 9 a.m. at the A.C.C. Mackenzie arrived at 10:30 a.m. and said that he had found two musicians, that they were coming later. Meanwhile, the Cultural Center had heard about a group in a military band who were supposed to play jazz and they were trying to get in touch with the Commander of the camp and make an arrangement to have the rhythm section to come to rehears with me. The director also called a friend of his that had a piano, and she agreed to lend it for the concert. They also rang a fellow who was played classical music but knew a few jazz tunes, and he agreed to come to the rehearsal around 4 p.m.

Nothing got started until 11:30. The army trio arrived first, with first class new material, drums, bass, guitars. I started to audition them. Alas...they really couldn't play jazz, and the drummer was incapable of keeping tempo. Next, was the group of Mackenzie. The lead guitarist knew a little about reading chords and was able to help the bass guitarist with some of the chords. The drummer of the group that I had rehearsed with the day before and who was not too bad was there also. Mackenzie was also playing flute and was willing to help as much as possible. I decided to use those guys but their sound equipment was not good. The Director of the center decided to call the commander of the army camp, and try to arrange something in order that we could use the army groups' equipment. It was settled by offering the group a meal and lunch time, and passes for the concert.

I rehearsed until about 1 p.m. and then went to lunch,after which we came back to the hall and rehearsed some more. It went on until 7p.m. because these fellows did not catch on to things very quickly. Except Mackenzie, they were not even what one could call second class amateurs. The pianist didn't show up. But I managed to get enough numbers together to make a decent concert.

After the rehearsal, it was time to have supper and get dressed for the concert which was to start at 9 that night. I had asked the director's assistant to bring me some whisky because I knew I was really going to need something to stimulate me more than ever before, and I also knew that Americans in the Cultural's Center could have nice supplies of most anything they needed.

Just before the concert started,the director's assistant came to my dressing room with a thermos bottle that was able to hold two cups of coffee. I could have been knocked over with a feather when I poured a drink in a glass and found out that it was half water. I came out of the dressing room and asked a young fellow who had not entered the concert hall if he would go to the nearest bar and bring me a double whiskey,and he did.

The hall could not hold about 120 people and it was full to capacity with important guests, notables, students and a few europeans. The first half of the concert was not too bad with the two guitars and Mackenzie playing trumpet in the style of Art Farmer and flute. I went to a bar near the hall when intermission time came, and the two guitar players must have done the same thing, because they did not remember much of any of the numbers that we had rehearsed. Mackenzie was trying to keep them straight without showing to the audience that things were not going right. Lily was also in the audience, and I kept looking at her and smiling whenever it was possible for me to do so. That was the only way I could keep from crying. I can't remember having such a miserable night as that one, and I have had some...I think that if someone had said anything disagreeable to me that night after the concert, I would have broken my trumpet over their head. But nobody did, in fact,I had a great success...if I am ever asked to go to that country again to play again, it will be with musicians that I engage.

The organiser of the yearly "Jam Potatoes" festival in Luneray, Normandy, France, a Mr. Jean Suplice, found out that from the time I had bought my first horn and started to play and 1972, it happened to be 50 years.
He decided to make a big thing from that for the festival. He arranged for me to become a honorary citizen of Luneray and the ceremony took place the first day of the Festival - the 11th of June.

We arrived at the city hall which is in France is called Hotel de Ville, and were greeted with the music played by a group of hunting players in their traditional costumes. The Mayor of Luneray, who is also a senator and the deputy of the country, which is called Seine Maritime, did the honour of making me the honorary citizen, and presented me with a certificate stating it's cause. I was obliged to make a speech which I can do on an occasion like that, about as well as I can walk on my hands, but I said something in French and it came out not too bad.

After the ceremony, we went to the big potatoes storage plant where the festival always takes place. It was eleven in the morning, and we heard the choir of Luneray directed by Mrs Francoise Suplice, who also played organ. The choir was composed by about 40 people, and sang spirituals and many religious songs of the type one can only hear in a Negro baptist church. For that wonderful celebration of my 50 years of trumpet, I also played a number with the choral, which was inspired as much by having me to play with them as I was hearing them sing.

That day, I played with five different groups including a family group from England which had the mother player accordian, the father playing clarinet, the eldest son who was 15 at the time, played piano, a daughter, 11, was the singer, and it was really enjoyable to hear her singing 'I ain't gonna give nobody none of my jelly roll'. The youngest son plays trumpet and he was 9 years old. He did a good interpretation of Louis Armstrong, doing 'Sleepy time down South'. The name of the family is Tomasso. The father is Ernie and he's a fine and I would say, underrated clarinetist in his own country.

This 50 years of trumpet did not mean that I had been a professional musician that long, because it had taken me almost 3 years of learning the instrument and two more years before I joined an orchestra of any importance. But the word 50 years of trumpet playing spread and there were quite a number of celebrations, articles in jazz magazines, T.V. shows, etc., and my birthday which came at a time when I was relaxing at a friend's country home in Switzerland, was celebrated more so as a salute to the trumpet years than my real age.

This happened at the country home of Felix Debrit, in Lugnorre. Felix was the fellow that assisted me in getting to play in Switzerland in 1949-1950. Many of my Swiss musician friends were invited as well as my very good friend Johnny Simmen and his wife, daughter and many more people that I knew and quite a few that I had never met before.

A young man named Alesch was also a guest of Felix and he did such things as making trumpets out of cardboard, putting them on long sticks and placing them where the road turn off and on to the lane which went tothe house of Felix, $o that people coming to the party could find the house easily. He also had balloons blown up that came to the number of 68 - years that corresponded my age, and which I sent up to the sky at a certain time. Each balloon had a ticket on it with my address and a statement that I would send anyone who found my balloon my auto- graphed photo. That was an idea of Alesch and it was beautiful to see all those different coloured balloons going up to the blue sky and over the lake, until they were out of sight. I only heard from two people, one in some small town in Switzerland, and another from Coma, Italy.

There were quite a number of Swiss jazz musicians that came to the party which got off to an early start that afternoon and finished in the wee hours the next morning. An American bass player named Bob Carter came all the way from where he lived, somewhere in Germany, near Munich. I had worked with Bob a few days in Mulhouse, France. There were at least 8 trumpet players. A few were only amateurs and I had worked with some of them. There was even a violinist and many other instruments. Lily had prepared a lot of food and chilli con carne. The weather was beautiful and we all stayed outdoors.

Felix had a piano in one of his rooms on the first floor. Some musicians started a jam session, but so many musicians came until eventually the piano was moved outside and there was continuous music until the piano was taken back inside around 3 o'clock in the morning. Fortunately, the nearest house to the one of Felix is about 25 yards away, and it's a weekend place for the people that own it. If they were there that night, they must have enjoyed the music, because Felix did not receive any complaints from them, and a good time was had by all.

I started the year of 1973 by playing the old one out and the new one in at the casino of Chamonix. That was where Lily started working to organize my first tour of France in 1952. Two days later, I was in Super-Besse, another resort for the annual jazz festival. In April, I went to Algeria for 3 concerts, but was there for one week. The last time I was in that country, was in 1956, and it still was a French Colony. The custom of dressing for most of the natives had not changed much except that most of the women did not cover their faces as they did before.

I went there for the American Cultural Center which was collaborating with the Algerian cultural center in Algiers. From the Algerian side of the deal, I was supposed to play with a group of their musicians who played jazz. About 5 days before I was to leave Paris, I received a phone call from the center in Paris asking me if I could form a group to take with me because the Algerian musicians wanted more money than they had accepted before. The director of the Algerian center would not agree to their demand.

It was short notice for me but there are certain musicians that I engage to do galas and concerts quite regular, and it was lucky for me that they were free and willing to make the trip with me. And it was also a blessing for me, because I did not have to spend hours rehearsing with a strange group, although I've done that many times, and shall probablu have to do it many more times. I play the game as it should be played. It was naturally more agreeable to have musicians with me that knew what I would do and what I expected of them.

Pierre Sim, bassist, Alain Fougeret, pianist, worked with me often. Michael Silva, an ex-drummer of Sammy Davis Jr., had also been an a few jobs with me. Erwin (Vany) Hinder, the tenor and clarinet man and I had been together in a club called "Cave de la Huchatte" often. Sim and Alain were French, Vany-Swiss, Michael and myself were American, so the group was international.

We arrived in Algiers the 8th of April and left for Oran, a city in Algeria, the next morning at 7:30. We were obliged to take a plane to Oran at that hour because there were only two flights there every day, one every morning, and one in the evening. When we arrived in Oran, we had to wait for hours to get rooms, because no reservations had been made as it should have been. We found out also that no publicity had been made for our concert. So only about one hundred people came to the concert, having heard a last minute announcement on the radio in the evening.

After the concert, we were all invited to the home of the American Consul. He and his wife were a young couple with two or three children. As we were to take our early plane back to Algiers, we managed to stay drinking and talking at the Consul's home until the time to pick up our luggage at our Hotel, and take a couple of taxis to the airport.

There was another concert the 11th of April in Blida, which is about 35 miles from Algiers. The 12th and 13th we did concerts in Algiers. They were the most successful, because Algiers is so much larger than the other places we played, the publicity was done better because the Hot Club of Algiers, the Cultural Center of the city, and the American one all worked together to present these concerts. The director of the American Center, a Mr. John Melton and his wife did everything possible to make our visit enjoyable. He gave us the use of a car whose chauffeur was a young Algerian named Omar, for whom I became his adopted Papa. We visited places that we had not seen during the two previous times we were in the country and we visited the Casba which really had not changed and was as picturesque as the last time we saw it.
The two concerts were very successful with a large attendance, mostly Algerian and a few Europeans. The public was very enthusiastic, and the last concert was broadcasted directly from the theatre.

The fellows in my group left Algiers the 14th for France. Lily and I left for Morocco the following day. Omar drove us to the airport and the Meltons met us there. Our flight was for 4:10 that afternoon. We had drinks with the Meltons and Omar while waiting for our flights to be announced. This, we never heard, and the Meltons were obliged to leave as their children had gone to see a movie and were to be met by their parents about 4'30. We asked at the entrance of the waiting room if our flight had been called and were told to hurry as everyone for that flight had gone through the customs and were getting ready to board the pkane. The five of us had not heard the call, and that was very strange to all of us.

An hour after we boarded the plane, it had not moved an inch, and everybody was beginning to get nervous. Then there was an announcement that the plane was waiting for an Ethiopian Minister or something. It was six o'clock when this big shot arrived. We did not see him as we were in tourist class and he was in first class.

Soft music was playing during the time we were waiting. When it was announced that this minister has arrived, and the plane would take off, people started whistling, which has the same meaning as booing. The music immediately became very loud in order to try to keep this fellow from hearing the whistling of dissatisfied people, bit I am certain that he heard it. Later, there was an announcement that the minister wished to excuse himself, because he had no idea that there were other people on the plane. How he could have had an idea of that sort is unbelievable to me, because he must have known that he did not have a private plane waitinf for him. So we arrived two hours late at the Casablanca airport, which also caused the leader of the orchestra I would be doing some concerts with, to wait two hours with wife and children. We arrived very late in Meknès that night.

We left Morocco for France the 21st of April and the 30th, we were in Barcelona, Spain, where I played a new jazz club called Cova del Drac, which means 'Cave of the Dragon'. Left Barcelona on 7th of May, and the 11th, I was in Bilbao at a club called Casa del Loco. Translated in England, it means Crazy House. It was really crazily decorated, but the owners and employers were not crazy. They were two brothers and a pianist who were italians that had lived in Spain for a number of years. They also owned a restaurant near the club which was situated in the arcade of a very large building. The pianist's name was Filippo Carletti and he was a very good accompanist whose solo work was very lively. The bass player was Eric Peters and the drummer, a French boy, whose name I don't remember. He and Peter were established in Spain. I stayed the Casa Del Loco for two weeks.
The next interesting thing of 1973 was the jazz festivals of Montreux, Switzerland and Pescara in Italy, a concert in Modena, also in Italy, and the festival of wine in Lilly's home town, Neuchatel.

I played the Montreux festival the 4th of July with my friend Guy Lafitte the tenor sax, Daniel Humair, drums, and a native of Switzerland, a fine young bass man named Jack Sewing, born in Holland, and Marc Hemmerler; also of Swiss nationality. On the same bill were Stephane Grappelli, Teddy Wilson, Barney Kessel, Freddy Randall, to Danny Moss, tenor sax Dave Shepherd, clarinet, Dave Hewitt, trumpet, Brian Lemon, piano, Kenny Baldock, bass, and Johnny Richardson, drums.
The Pescara festival I played on the 14th of July. Lily and I had spent 3 days in the dream city of Bologna before going to Pescara.

I did this festival with the rhythm section of a very good French group called "The Swingers", whom I had worked with quite a number of times. Earl Hines, Memphis Slim, the blues singer and pianist, also Max Keminsky, the trumpet man, whom I knew way back when I was working in the U.S.A. and whom I had not seen for years, were also on the programme that night.

The next day I moved on to Modena for a concert with an amateur orchestra from Genoa. We had a very nice rehearsal, but everybody was worried because the clarinetist had forgotten his instrument in Genoa, and people were running all over Modena trying to find a clarinet for him. The concert was given in the most famous square in town, just behind the cathedral. Someone found an instrument for the clarinetist, and the concert was a great success. There seemed to be people there from the age of 7 years old to 90 and although the orchestra whose name was "the Genoa Dixieland all Stars", and they featured mostly dixieland naumbers, they were capable of playing other things with me. The trombone player was the best musician in the band and the only professional. But the band had made tour and recorded with great stars such as Albert Nicholas and the violin player Jo Venuti. They all enjoyed playing with me and promised to have me dome to Genoa to do some concerts with them.

The festival of wine in Neuchatel is to celebrate the harvest of grapes to make wine and it's a three days celebration. This year, it takes place from the 5th to the 7th of October. Several other orchestras played at the same place as I, but the band who was engaged to play at-the-same-place-as-I with me was the New Ragtime Band from Porrentruy. I never saw so much wine passing around me before.(Neuchatel wine is a very dry white wine). It is difficult to imagine how many gallons or barrels of it was consumed during those three nights. The nights were really jumping and although I drank some wine, I stuck mostly to whiskey. I prefer wine with my meals more so than a drink to get happy on.

On the same bill,was a big Swiss orchestra with whom I had worked two years before, "The friends of Jazz", from Cortaillod,under the leadership of Henri Du Paquier, sax-tenor, with Etienne Perret,trumpet, I was surprised and delighted to hear how much they had improved, and they had a big success.(Cortaillod is a small town near Neuchatel).

The "Genoa dixieland All Stars" did not loose any time in arranging some concerts in their part of Italy. Lily and I flew to Genoa the 17th of October and the first concert was that night in a town called Novi Ligure, a few miles from Genoa. The second concert was at the club the orchestra owns in Genoa. It was quite a large place and I was told after the concert that there had never been so many people in that club as there were that night. The third and last concert was at least 200 miles from Genoa in an industrial town called Piobino. The 20th of October, we left Piobino in the car of the trumpet player whose name is Fausto Rossi. We arrived in Genoa that afternoon around 5 and had a flight to Paris a few minutes later.

December the third and fourth, I recorded with my long time friend, Stephane Grappelli, the great jazz violinist. Stephane and I have played together on many occasions since my return to Europe but this was the first time we have recorded an album together since the 1935 to 1938 era. We've played attractions in clubs, for galas, done television shows, but making records for the first time since before the last world war, was something I had been looking forward to for a long time. Stephane always was a great jazz man and today, I think he is the best jazz violinist in the world.

I have been called an"ambassador of jazz,"because I've played it all over the world and in places in Europe where people told me that they did not believe that I would appear in such places when they saw the posters advertising the date, because some of those places were very small towns, and those people did not believe that a musician with a big reputation could come and play in their humble surroundings.
Actually, as most musicians know, a place is never too small or too large to sell his wares, as long as the loot is good and he collects it and I've had no trouble collecting mine in Europe.

Whenever I did a gala or concert with Jean-Marie Masse of Limoges, he always introduced me as "the gentleman of the trumpet" and said that I was the most Parisian of all the American musicians that have ever been to or live in Paris, because I was born in Paris, Kentucky and now live in Paris, France. So I'm giving this book the title of "From Paris to Paris with a Horn"......and as the French say, "Vive le Jazz" !!
